Since animal blood is a viable alternative (Louis's rats, Angel and Spike's butcher's blood), the justifications for drinking human blood - taste, reaching full potential, spiritual peace - all fail against the principle that a world with less unnecessary suffering is better. Then the consistency argument turns on us: factory-farmed meat inflicts unnecessary suffering for the sake of taste while vegetarianism is fully viable, so condemning vampires while eating chicken is inconsistent - we as human beings are vampiric.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 26 "But Isn’t It Only Natural" — Adams answers Plato's ring-of-Gyges challenge with Heroes: even when invisible, wrongdoing corrupts the wrongdoer, because justice is to the soul what health is to the body. Claire's refusal to claim credit for the fire rescue shows thumos (spirit) responsive to logistikos (reason), Sylar's uncontrollable hunger for powers is epithumetikon (appetite) ruling the soul, and Hiro's Vegas cheating shows how injustice makes life spin out of control; Claire's apology to Brody illustrates the Pagan Golden Rule — help your friends, harm your enemies — tempered by Plato's caution that enemies may become friends.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 16 "The Finder of Lost Children" — Timothy Dean Roth reads Kill Bill as a modern Divine Comedy: Tarantino punishes by contrapasso like Dante—O-Ren dies by Japanese steel, Budd by snake, Elle by blindness, Bill by a broken heart—and both treat vengeance as a form of truth-telling and an act of love. Hattori Hanzo's warning that revenge 'is a forest' echoes Aristotle on how hard it is to set the limits of anger, while the stories-within-stories of orphaned Nikki and O-Ren enact the cycle of violence vengeance perpetuates. Against this, Aquinas's doctrine of double effect shows every one of the Bride's killings is defensive self-preservation, and the film ends where Jules's arc ends: in mercy, mutual forgiveness and a whispered 'thank you' of grace.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 12 "If I Were a Carpenter" — Butler asks what makes an activity work, testing the market definition against Socrates' refusal of fees, Aristotle's Politics, Arendt's labor/work/action distinction, Eva Kittay's care work, and the split between extrinsic and intrinsic value. He reads Cash's catalog through it: "One Piece at a Time" (the Detroit line worker stealing a Cadillac he builds but cannot afford), "Get Rhythm" (the shoeshine boy singing through menial labor), "I Never Picked Cotton" (escaping work into an empty identity), "Let Him Roll" and "Southern Accents," and the San Quentin monologue after "Wreck of the Ol' 97" where Cash refuses to be told what to play before inmates. The chapter closes by lining up Kant's categorical imperative, Jesus' Golden Rule, and Rawls's veil of ignorance: nobody would choose a society of company-store wage slavery without knowing they were not the worker, and Cash, knowing he stood on the stage rather than in the cellblock, used his freedom to side with prisoners and carpenters anyway.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 20 "From Cash to Kant—and Back Again" — Yolanda Estes pairs Cash with Kant as two duty-based moralists: Cash's Golden Rule in 'The Preacher Said, Jesus Said' parallels Kant's formula of humanity (never treating persons merely as means), and Cash's 'good heart' matches Kant's good will, since songs like 'Sam Hall,' 'Folsom Prison Blues' (the man shot in Reno 'just to watch him die'), and 'I Hung My Head' weigh inner motives over outcomes. Because earthly law never balances the moral scale, she reads Kant's kingdom of ends and Cash's apocalyptic kingdom of God in 'When the Man Comes Around' and 'God's Gonna Cut You Down' as parallel objects of faith: we must live as if perfect justice already prevails, working to improve this world rather than waiting for the next.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 22 "Wonder Why We Ever Go Home" — Duke Richey maps Buffett's West — 'Ringling, Ringling,' the Rancho Deluxe soundtrack, Tully Mars — onto Josiah Royce's philosophy of community: only people who root in a place, face its history ('wise provincialism'), and sacrifice selfish desires for the whole can build Beloved Communities, a lesson enacted when cattle rustlers Jack and Cecil accept community sanction and find belonging working the Rancho Deluxe. Wallace Stegner's coral-reef metaphor from Angle of Repose supplies the image of communities built up millimeter by millimeter yet still vulnerable to pollution and over-fishing, with Royce's environmental regret (covering 'the wounds' of the landscape with gardens) anticipating the chapter's sustainability ethic. 'Wonder Why We Ever Go Home' thus asks what we really seek when we seek grace through community: not the nomadic Pickup Truck Death of every-man-for-himself, but cooperation that makes a society to match the scenery.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 19 "Cold Clammy Consistency" — Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents because they meet Aristotle's test of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgment that 'evildoers... taste better') and retain free will, since their blood-lust is a craving not a compulsion and Louis's rat diet in Interview with the Vampire, like Angel's in Buffy, proves an alternative exists. TASTE, full potential, and spiritual peace all fail to justify human blood, because killing a person brings more unnecessary suffering than killing a rat, the same suffering-based principle that condemns factory farming. The 'cold clammy consistency' punchline: since humans need not eat meat, condemning vampire blood-drinkers while dining on chicken, pork, and beef is hypocrisy, because we are vampiric too and only our choice of which life to ingest separates the monstrous from the virtuous.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 134 "Fifty Ways to Love Your Other" — The section reads Levinas's demand to experience the Other's suffering in the Other's place as Dick's empathy made literal: the shifting points of view that blur heroes and villains, Felix Buckman's tears, Molinari developing his people's symptoms, and the empathy boxes bonding users to Mercer's endless stoning, a fraud whose falsity is beside the point because the concern is the real thing. Villains are precisely those who refuse the transfer, and the ordinary one-way gift, buying a stranger a drink with no return, enacts the Golden Rule: even if the universe isn't real, Melina is right, kiss each other anyway.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 30 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Allaire argues walkers have no moral value and can be killed without remorse: a Bentham-style act-utilitarian tally favors killing any walker, and, following Kant, genetic humanity is neither necessary nor sufficient for membership in the moral community. Applying Mary Anne Warren's five personhood criteria, he shows walkers lack pain response (Hannah's severed half still dragging itself at Rick), language, planning (Glenn's gun-bag mission versus aimless shuffling), and self-reflection, so as beings incapable of duty they can have no rights. Morgan's inability to shoot his walker-wife and Rick's 'I'm sorry this happened to you' illustrate Kant's 'duality of the human situation' — we irrationally project personhood onto former people — and our hesitation is precisely the walkers' greatest advantage.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 15 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Svolba and Flanders read Curb as an extended investigation of civility—the rules of what people 'just don't do,' from using the doctor's phone to touring Susie's new house to singing 'Happy Birthday' at Ben Stiller's party. Larry plays Socratic gadfly: refusing the tour harms no one and treats no one unfairly, and Susie's only justification ('it's just not done') is circular, so his incivility can seem admirable, even like minor civil disobedience. Against this, the chapter argues (crediting Cheshire Calhoun) that rules of civility are conventional vehicles for communicating respect for others' feelings and interests—what matters to Susie ought to matter to Larry—and, more consequentially, that a social world full of Larry Davids would be unbearable. Larry's own Golden-Rule litmus test, by which he never talks in movie theaters because he would hate it himself, misses this point, since civility is precisely about what others happen to want and like.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 23 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Argues against the obvious reading that Larry is a rule-breaker: properly analyzed, he is a dedicated rule-follower, since a good rule-follower need only accept the legitimacy of some rules and consistently follow the ones he accepts. Bekka Williams works through cases like Rachel's ski-lift jump versus Jewish law in 'The Ski Lift,' the moving 10:30 pm phone cutoff in 'The Wire,' and Larry's rejection of his mother's tattoo-driven reburial in 'The Special Section' to distinguish breaking a rule you accept from rejecting a rule's legitimacy altogether. Kant supplies the point that duty is only visible when it frustrates self-interest (Larry absorbing the cost of his own waiting-room rule in 'The Interior Decorator,' refusing to fire the Tourette's chef), while J.J.C. Smart's attack on 'rule-worship' explains why Larry rejects purposeless rules like the drive-thru walking ban and the one-year wedding-gift cutoff. The underlying justification is the Golden Rule: the water bottle in 'The Doll,' the caviar allotment, and even the stolen memorial flowers in 'The Ida Funkhouser Roadside Memorial' are defended as fairness and reciprocity, leaving the jacket money in 'The Korean Bookie' as the single admitted counterexample.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 19 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter presents Barney as a Humean moral philosopher: reason is the slave of the passions, and norms like the Bro Code are invented conventions that evolve, Adam Smith's invisible-hand style, rather than being designed, revealed, or deduced. The Platinum Rule ('never, ever love thy neighbor') is grounded in Humean reciprocity: the eight-stage arc of attraction to fallout in Barney's Wendy the Waitress disaster, the Gerards' brunch tyranny, and Robin's romance with co-worker Curt shows the retaliation costs that make the norm a rational solution to coordination failures. Against the Golden Rule's painterly elegance, the anatomist's cautious observation of behavior explains why a norm banning neighborly love emerges even in a society of non-saints.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 19 "Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful" — Muntersbjorn argues that freedom comes in kinds and degrees and that selves are social fictions sustained by others, building on Annette Baier's claims that we are 'second persons' whose self-consciousness and freedom grow out of childhood interaction and mutual cross-examination. She reads the hosts' selective ignoring ('that doesn't look like anything to me') as Baier's dangerous art of self-deception, and contrasts Descartes' solitary introspection (hats and coats that may cover automata) and Russell's analogy-based answer to the problem of other minds with the hosts' deliberately scripted interpersonal checks that keep them from questioning their reality. Plato's Meno statues of Daedalus (opinion 'fastened up' into knowledge) frame hosts as property whose freedom is a matter of degree, and the chapter closes that if artificial beings are ever to become persons they must be treated as second persons first - the Golden Rule applied to the park.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 26 "Notes" — When Lucy shouts the Golden Rule at the Ghoul after he dunks her in a poison river to bait a gulper, the chapter takes her appeal seriously and grades the rival 'rules' of the wasteland (the Iron, Arsenic, Neon, and Bronze Rules) before arguing the Golden Rule needs St. Francis's 'in a similar situation' clause. Kant's criminal-versus-judge objection disqualifies the unqualified Platinum Rule of treating others as they want, Nietzsche's charge that mutual restraint denies life is parried, and Rawlsian imagining of ourselves in divergent positions explains why family partiality like Lucy's search for Hank is consistent with the rule. The chapter closes with Lucy's saving of the Ghoul retold as the Good Samaritan parable, extending the rule even to enemies.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 33 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — The chapter models court intrigue as game theory: games of incomplete information over Joffrey's legitimacy, the predictability of honorable opponents like Barristan Selmy, and Catelyn's reverse induction from the seemingly 'irrational' attack on Bran to deduce that Jaime threw him. Tyrion is the star player, converting one-shot death sentences into repeated games - recruiting Bronn as his champion at the Eyrie, buying off the mountain clans with Lannister arms - and showing how 'A Lannister always pays his debts' works as strategic reputation. Against Plato's view of love as the madness that ruins rational play (Maester Aemon's 'love is the bane of honor'), the chapter uses Nietzsche's 'drop of reason in madness' to argue that lovers' merged interests expand rationality itself, culminating in a Golden Rule upgraded to 'understand others as they understand themselves.'
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Adams pairs Anakin with Achilles to show how Palpatine's lesson that 'good is a point of view' - Nietzsche's claim that there are no moral facts, only interpretations - nearly destroys both heroes before a father's love pulls them back: Priam's tears before Achilles, Luke unmasking Vader. Against nihilism the chapter defends moral realism through Apollo's lion simile (compassion and respect are objective facts about what persons require) and Kant's self-critical inquiry, with the Jedi Council's twelve-way deliberation illustrating that some interpretations are better than others, beyond Hume's problem of induction. Both epics settle on a 'Pagan Golden Rule' - help your friends and harm your enemies, but never lose compassion for either.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 30 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Allaire defends the thesis that the only good walker is a dead one: walkers fall outside Kant's moral community because, as purely sensuous beings driven by instinct, they cannot plan ahead (Glenn's 'Vatos' heist, the walker-guts camouflage in 'Guts'), communicate, or reflect, and so can have no duties and no rights. Act-utilitarian weighing shows killing any walker is beneficial, and even Regan's respect principle does not apply; the chapter runs Mary Anne Warren's personhood criteria to show walkers lack consciousness, reasoning, and self-awareness. Our hesitation before walkers like Morgan's wife or Leon Basset is irrational projection onto beings no longer the persons we loved, so Rick's 'I'm sorry this happened to you' is mercy for a fate, not respect for a right-holder.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 19 "Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful" — Muntersbjorn reads Westworld through Annette Baier's claim that persons are 'second persons first,' arguing the hosts' captivity models how selfhood and freedom depend on others who challenge our self-deceptions. She uses Dolores's scripted 'that doesn't look like anything to me' and Walter's milk-pouring glitch to distinguish Baier's harmless 'ignoring' from dangerous self-deception, and invokes Descartes's window automata and Russell's thinking gramophone as versions of the problem of other minds. She concludes via the Golden Rule that if hosts ever become persons, they too will be second persons shaped by how we treat them.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 16 "“You Cannot Be Serious!” The Ethics of Rage in Tennis" — David Detmer asks whether John McEnroe's on-court tantrums are merely rude or genuinely immoral, judging them by two ethical theories. Under Bentham's utilitarianism he weighs the pleasure of entertained crowds against the harm to abused officials, then uses Mill's higher/lower pleasures distinction to discount the 'lower' amusement of gawking at boorishness beneath the 'higher' aesthetic pleasure of appreciating great tennis. Under Kantian deontology he argues McEnroe's public false accusations are wrong in principle: officials are better positioned to make calls, so the abuse is unjust, and by the categorical imperative read as a Golden Rule, McEnroe—who resents being wrongly criticized himself—is a hypocrite whose 'gamesmanship' unfairly exploits his star power against opponents.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 13 "7. Independence Day & Aliens" — Rowlands frames morality around consistency and impartiality (the golden rule), articulated by Kant's categorical/practical imperatives (treat persons as ends, not merely means) and utilitarianism's greatest happiness. Imagining philosophers arguing Independence Day's aliens out of eradicating humans, he deploys the principle of 'no moral difference without a relevant other difference' and the argument from marginal cases to defeat intelligence, telepathy, and bare species membership as morally relevant. He turns the alien-invasion parable on our factory farming of chickens and pigs (Singer-style speciesism), arguing we are crueller than the aliens and fall short of our own impartiality ideal.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 26 "But Isn’t It Only Natural" — Don Adams uses Heroes' superpowered characters (who could commit perfect crimes like Gyges with his invisibility ring) to argue Plato's case that virtue is its own reward. He maps Plato's tripartite soul onto the characters: Claire's thumos (spirit/honor) tempered by logistikos (reason) yields courage and wisdom, while Sylar's ruling appetite (his hunger for powers) is intemperance and injustice that makes his life spin out of control. Reading justice as psychic health, and glossing the 'Pagan Golden Rule' (help friends, harm enemies, but enemies may become friends), Adams argues it is 'only natural' for even the powerful to be virtuous rather than exploit others.

### The Capabilities Approach

The capabilities approach, developed by Martha Nussbaum in dialogue with the economist Amartya Sen, evaluates human well-being and justice in terms of what people are actually able to do and to be—their real freedoms or capabilities—rather than by resources, wealth, or subjective satisfaction. Nussbaum proposes a list of central human capabilities, such as life, bodily health, the use of the senses and imagination, practical reason, and affiliation, that a just society owes to each person up to a threshold level. The approach insists on treating each person as an end and attends to how circumstances and social arrangements enable or block genuine functioning. It has been influential in development economics, human rights, and theories of social justice.

- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 15 "A Fork in the Road" — Anderson contrasts two American freedoms through Springsteen and Tracy Chapman: the negative freedom of 'Racing in the Street,' 'Thunder Road,' and 'Born to Run' — Thoreauvian wildness, the outlaw who blows off duty, wins the dude from L.A.'s money and 'little girl' as a prize, then finds her crying on her daddy's porch — against the positive freedom of Chapman's 'Fast Car' heroine, who initially sees the fast car as a way to 'be someone' but finally sends the aimless drinker off and seeks empowerment of her own abilities. Drawing on Margaret Fuller (men squander freedom on appetite and domination), Charlotte Perkins Gilman (male-built structures channel women's freedom through men), and Nussbaum (flourishing, failure built into the structure), he argues that male negative freedom is dialectically coupled to women's oppression, that justice must trump the call of the wild, yet that men's own collateral damage — desolation, alienation — must also be addressed.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 17 "“There’s More to Life than Profit”" — Held argues business ethics stalls because it begins from capitalism's presuppositions instead of asking what we fundamentally value, staging the impasse as Quark versus Rom and as Friedman's stockholder theory against Freeman's stakeholder theory ('The Dogs of War', Zek's reforms, 'Profit and Lace'). He recovers Aristotle's Politics distinction between economics serving the household's good and chrematistics — money-making as sheer accumulation, embodied in Quark's 'pure profit' embezzlement — and corrects the libertarian caricature of Adam Smith: the invisible hand works only within commutative justice and virtue, markets serving welfare rather than profit. Through Sen's capability approach and Quark's own defense of greed as promoting human development in 'Prophet Motive', the chapter concludes profit is only a means to freedom and well-being — 'there's more to life than profit' — and the Rules of Acquisition themselves must stand before the ethical judge.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 14 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Shaun Young tests Jeopardy! against equality as an 'essentially contested concept': Aristotle's proportional equality (treat like cases as like) seems to justify the winner-take-all payout as deserved, Locke's reward for the industrious explains why equal outcomes would kill incentive, and Rawls's two principles - fair equality of opportunity plus the difference principle - capture the show's identical rules and level playing field. He then raises harder challenges: Dworkin's equality of resources, Kymlicka's charge that the Americo-centric clue bank shortchanges minority cultures (with Quebec's Bill 101 as legitimate differentiated rights), and the capabilities approach of Sen and Nussbaum applied to would-be contestants who cannot operate the signaling device. Citing Isaiah Berlin's pluralism, he concludes that no final verdict on Jeopardy!'s equality is possible - and that spectators would not want one, since Jennings's seventy-four-game streak thrills precisely because of inequality between players.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 27 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Nicolas Michaud argues the creature is a person on every serious criterion: it satisfies Kant's rationality test and Mary Anne Warren's five criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-concept) in both Shelley's novel and I, Frankenstein, and it possesses all ten of Nussbaum's capabilities for flourishing. The twist is that judging the monster a blameworthy murderer already concedes the personhood we deny him, while our exclusion of him is bare Othering and speciesism of the kind Tom Regan attacks in animal ethics. Michaud ends by reversing the question: after humanity's record of crushing minorities, which the creature learns from Volney's Ruins of Empires and weeps over with Safie, what argument could Victor give Adam for sparing us?
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 33 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Roger Hunt argues the films show that whoever assumes human superiority or ownership of created life gets eaten: Dieter Stark zaps a compy and is devoured by a swarm of them, Ludlow claims InGen's patent and becomes a hunting lesson for the baby T. rex. He stages the real debate over dinosaur moral status between the 'value of life' view (Harding and Sattler: experiment on them if enough sentient beings benefit) and Tom Regan's rights view - anything sentient has basic rights from unconditional individual value, and grading lives by usefulness is speciesism like racism or sexism. He then prefers Martha Nussbaum's capabilities approach: a T. rex penned in San Diego cannot roam, hunt, or play, so it cannot flourish, and the point is not granting rights but recognizing we have no right to block other beings' flourishing for fun.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 37 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — The chapter argues Finn is not yet a true hero but is on a quest to become one: against rule systems like Mill's greatest-happiness utilitarianism and Kantian respect for persons, virtue ethics asks not 'what should I do' but 'who should I be', and Aristotle's point that children lack fully developed practical reason explains why Finn's good intentions misfire - removing Donny exposes the house people to Why-wolves, and Penny's trick humiliates him in the City of Thieves. Martha Nussbaum's ideal of every person as free and of equal dignity grounds heroism in the common good, and her work on literature and popular culture explains how watching Finn's exaggerated choices trains our own moral judgment. Citing Franco and Zimbardo's psychology of real heroes - empathy, risk tolerance, persistence - and closing with Seneca's 'how nobly you live', it concludes that since Aristotelian virtue is a habit, anyone can start by admitting they suck at heroism and practicing, as Jake's advice puts it.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Matthew Watts sorts Fallout's artificial beings into cyborgs, synths, and pure robots and tests each against a theory of the self: Locke's memory theory explains the Robobrain socialites of Vault 118 and Nick Valentine's implanted prewar past, Parfit's psychological continuity (identity as a matter of degree) makes the Old World Blues Think Tank a caricature of a self stretched too thin, and Putnam's machine-table functionalism with multiple realizability (the Red Menace holotape running on any hardware) undermines Covenant's SAFE test by making function, not substrate, the mark of a mind. DiMA's excision of his own guilty memory in Far Harbor shows identity as Evan Thompson's enactive process rather than stored recall, since pruning memories can maintain or improve the self-in-progress. For moral standing below full personhood, Nussbaum's capabilities approach fits Curie's flourishing (research, companionship, watching a sunset in a synth body) and Singer's sentience criterion fits Victor the Securitron's avoidance of harm, exposing 'substrate prejudice' as a robot analog of speciesism - down to ED-E's triumphant arrival on the West Coast.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 31 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Schick asks whether humans need to alter consciousness (Weil, Maslow's hierarchy, Siegel's animal examples of reindeer, elephants, and rats seeking intoxicants) and concludes we have no such need, though we can flourish from it. He applies Sen and Nussbaum's capabilities approach, arguing cannabis enhances Nussbaum's second (bodily health, via endocannabinoids and medical uses) and fourth (senses, imagination, thought, via enriched music perception and possible creativity) capabilities. Citing Aristotle's and the Buddha's golden mean against abuse, and evidence of no lasting brain harm, he judges paternalistic prohibition an unjustified deprivation of the capabilities needed for a good life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 29 "27. Squid Game as Philosophy The Myths of Democracy" — The chapter argues that Squid Game exposes five 'myths' of democracy by showing how its trappings mask control by the wealthy few. Using Aristotle's Politics and Nicomachean Ethics it attacks the myth of free choice (the players' consent is coerced by debt) and the failure to cultivate virtue and transparency (Gi-hun deceives Il-nam in the marble game); it uses Sen and Nussbaum's capability approach to deny genuine empowerment; and it applies Plato's Phaedo two-worlds doctrine to argue the game instantiates no true form of truth, beauty, goodness, or justice. Il-nam's tie-breaking vote and Player 111's advantages illustrate that equality is only superficial, leaving a Hobbesian war of all against all inside a democratic shell.

### Respect for Persons

Respect for persons is the Kantian idea that every rational being possesses an unconditional worth, or dignity, that must never be treated merely as a means to someone else's ends. It follows from Kant's formulation of the categorical imperative requiring that we act so as to treat humanity, in ourselves and others, always also as an end in itself. Because persons are capable of setting their own ends and legislating moral law through reason, they command a form of regard categorically different from the price we attach to mere things. This principle grounds much of modern rights discourse and the moral prohibition on using, deceiving, or coercing people in ways that bypass their rational agency.

- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 95 "But It’s Just a White Lie!" — Asks whether superheroes may deceive the people they love, testing Kant's absolute duty not to lie against resolvable conflicts of negative duties: Peter may deceive Aunt May only because telling her would seriously harm her. But the chapter rejects the paternalistic silence Clark keeps from Lois and Peter from MJ, arguing that assuming the women cannot keep secrets or would crumble under worry fails to treat them with the respect owed to persons, so superheroes owe their loved ones the truth about who they are.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 22 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Held argues that our pleasure in Bond's kill-then-quip routine - 'Shocking' after electrocuting a henchman in Goldfinger, tossing Killifer to the sharks that ate Felix with 'You earned it, you keep it' - reveals tacit retributive and deterrent theories of punishment that place villains outside the moral community. Using the distinction between mere humiliation (deflating Dr. No's pretense: 'Minnows pretending they're whales') and Humiliation that denies common humanity, he shows Bond dehumanizes disfigured, 'othered' villains, even as the novels present them as disenfranchised figures - Dr. No rejecting his father's name, Mr. Big demanding recognition as the first great black criminal - whose rage is a warped demand for Hegelian mutual recognition. He proposes instead Jean Hampton's moral education theory, which treats criminals as moral agents capable of reform, concluding with Jaws's redemption in Moonraker as proof that no one is beyond it.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 21 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Watson and Arp ask whether Ironhide and Chromia's embrace means Autobots can love, rejecting programmed loving behavior, implanted souls, and wired-in human brains as insufficient for genuine personhood, then sort Transformer relationships into Western conceptions of love. Empedoclean cosmic Love and Strife map onto Primus versus Unicron; Platonic philia ascends to the Form of Beauty, with Transformer souls originating in and returning to the All Spark; Aristotle's three friendships separate Optimus and Sparkplug's virtue-friendship from Megatron and Starscream's mere utility; and Stoic-Kantian equal love explains Autobots saving Decepticons who immediately try to kill them, alongside Christian agape in Autobot family bonds.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 42 "The Valuable Self" — The chapter turns from metaphysics to morals: for Kant the self is the most valuable thing in the world, a subject that must never be used as a mere means, since turning a subject into an object is the ultimate immorality. The authorities' plan to hollow Arctor into an unwitting infiltrator, and Donna's lament that he 'didn't volunteer', make the point concrete: what is valuable in us is the self's fuzziness, including its mystery of free will, and to remake a person into a scanner, 'a mere thing that just watches and never chooses', is the ultimate crime.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 15 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Delfino and Taylor ask whether Morgan's zombified wife is still a person, which decides whether shooting her is murder. On the dominant Western view - Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellect, Kantian dignity against Singer's speciesism challenge - walkers lack intelligence and so are not persons, so Morgan should shoot. They then argue walkers are metaphysically impossible beings, square-circles: dead tissue that somehow sees, smells, and runs down prey without functioning organs, energy intake, or the reanimated neocortex that movement and sensation require. Zombies fascinate because they are projections of our fears - dead yet moving, an afterlife of horror - a Hamlet-like caught-between-being-and-nonbeing.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 27 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Nicolas Michaud argues the creature is a person on every serious criterion: it satisfies Kant's rationality test and Mary Anne Warren's five criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-concept) in both Shelley's novel and I, Frankenstein, and it possesses all ten of Nussbaum's capabilities for flourishing. The twist is that judging the monster a blameworthy murderer already concedes the personhood we deny him, while our exclusion of him is bare Othering and speciesism of the kind Tom Regan attacks in animal ethics. Michaud ends by reversing the question: after humanity's record of crushing minorities, which the creature learns from Volney's Ruins of Empires and weeps over with Safie, what argument could Victor give Adam for sparing us?
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 17 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter evaluates Marshall and Lily's promise to tell each other everything through Kant: lying violates the universalizable duty of truthfulness and treats the deceived as a mere means, as with Lily's hidden credit card debt in 'Dowisetrepla', the realtor's sewage-plant omission, and Barney's fully staged seduction of Meg that blocks her informed choice. Even Marshall's kindly lie about the doppelganger fails Kant's test, alongside his infamous refusal to lie to the murderer at the door. Yet Kant's letters on reticence in friendship and his grim view of marriage as shared ends where spouses may use each other 'as if' they were things suggest that telling each other everything may itself corrode respect - the tension Lily's never-opened bathroom door dramatizes.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 24 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Karavitis maps the three films onto the history of animal ethics: Jurassic Park treats dinosaurs as property on Aristotle's ground that only rational humans matter; The Lost World adds Kant's indirect duties, where the sporting rules of Tembo's hunt express duties owed to other humans rather than to the T. rex; and Jurassic Park III moves to Tom Regan, whose 'subjects-of-a-life' with inherent value fits raptors that remember, plan, and finally choose to spare the humans. The cow and goat fed live to the raptors test how far each view protects animals we treat as mere means.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 31 "The Devil and Philosophy" — George Dunn asks whether the Joker's 'some men just want to watch the world burn' motivelessness even makes sense. Against Baumeister's 'Myth of Pure Evil' and the Socratic-Aristotelian thesis that all wrongdoing aims at some apparent good, he tests Kant's claim that no human can be a diabolical being, Claudia Card's definition of diabolical evil as engineering others' moral corruption, and the Satan of Job as prosecuting accuser - which fits the Joker's ferry 'social experiment' and his breaking of Harvey Dent. The upshot is that the Joker's evil, fed by pride and the wish for credit for the conflagration, is instrumental, pathological, and banal after all, its best answer being the convict who throws the detonator out the window.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 26 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Christian Cotton asks whether Carrie's clandestine surveillance of the Brody home, though illegal, is morally wrong, distinguishing legality from morality. Locke's state of nature grounds natural rights to life, liberty, property - and by extension privacy - that government exists to protect and that no national-security goal automatically overrides; Mill's utilitarianism would justify violating one family's privacy to prevent an attack, but Mill's own harm principle and 'tyranny of the majority' caution blocks it when Carrie has only a hunch. Kant's respect for persons as ends in themselves condemns Saul's blackmail of Judge Turner as using a man merely as means, so the Right constrains pursuit of the Good.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 28 "15. The Way of the Doctor Is Deception" — Dodge takes Rule #1 - the Doctor lies - through the major theories of lying: Bernard Williams's definition (asserting what you believe false with intent to deceive), Aristotle's claim that all lies are base, Kant's categorical imperative and respect for persons (even the Vinvocci's shimmer disguises in 'The End of Time' abuse trust), and Bentham's pleasure-pain calculus, which condemns the faked death at Lake Silencio ('The Impossible Astronaut') for the grief it caused Amy and Rory yet rewards the greater happiness it made possible. Against the absolutists he sets Plato's Noble Lie from the Republic - the elite falsehood that keeps society functioning - as what the Doctor emulates by deceiving the universe into thinking him dead ('The Wedding of River Song'), and Nietzsche's point in Human, All Too Human that lying is ethically neutral when the pretense is sustainable, as when the Doctor hides the ganger-Amy switch from Rory ('The Almost People'). The upshot: the Doctor's lies are wrong in themselves but routinely justified by the good they do, which is why sometimes the hero lies.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 30 "18. The Virtues of Choosing Your Faction" — Pascoe contrasts Aristotle's and Kant's theories of virtue through the Choosing Ceremony. On Aristotle's account virtues are taught (intellectual) and then habituated into character (moral), tied to one's function, so Susan flourishes because aptitude, upbringing, and choice align while the transfer Al withers - but Tris, Divergent with multiple aptitudes, needs Kant instead: natural virtues are mere 'gifts of nature' that become good only through good will, and her perfect duties to herself and imperfect duties regarding family and faction can justify choosing Dauntless over staying in Abnegation. Kant wins the day: because a corrupted community like Eric's Dauntless redefines bravery into obedience, Tris must think for herself - 'maybe I am wired like the Divergent' - choosing her virtues out of duty and self-respect rather than inheriting them.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 14 "3. When to Hate and When to Be Irate" — Daniel Alloy opens with Aristotle's demand that one be angry 'as and when and for as long as one ought' and builds a theory distinguishing anger (a response to a specific offense, seeking proportional payback) from hatred (a response to a thing's very existence, seeking its destruction). He tests the theory on Louis's bits - hating deer as a class and fantasizing about giving them AIDS, the six-year-old 'Jizzanthapuss,' the Pig Newtons fight with a three-year-old, the Cinnabon clerk, the 'Awesome Possum' hipster, and the justified driver who yells 'suck a sack of dicks.' He argues justified hatred is impossible, since it would require a pure-malevolence being that could not be an autonomous person, so hatred is always wrong while properly proportioned anger remains a necessary part of the moral life. Kant supplies the self-respect dimension ('one who makes himself a worm cannot complain if people step on him'): failing to get angry at real wrongs done to you or your children signals a character deficiency, not virtue.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 20 "10. Trust Systems or People" — Malloy locates the heroes' core disagreement in trust: Cap trusts people, recruiting reformed villains (Hawkeye, Scarlet Witch, Quicksilver, Deadpool) and inspiring the 'kooky quartet', while Tony trusts systems, running the Initiative with pay and the threat of Prison 42. Using Adorno and Horkheimer's critique of instrumental reason, he shows Tony losing sight of what and why he acts - the Armor Wars killing Titanium Man, Civil War destroying the safety it sought - and treating people as means rather than ends in themselves. Via Darwall's two respects (grounded in Kant), Cap's recognition respect for autonomous persons beats Tony's appraisal respect for qualities (he respects even Doom's intellect), so only Cap's trust preserves freedom - and wins.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 25 "14. Of Course It Sucks—It’s Work" — Wible stages three theories of work against Dilbert strips: the Greek view of Plato and Aristotle that labor is freedom-sapping and leisure is the civilized ideal, Marx's capitalist critique in which workers become objects and machines (Wally gives off no human vibe, and robots are coming for the engineers), and Desjardins's human-fulfillment model built on Schumacher's creativity, challenge, development, honesty, and beauty, with Wells Fargo's fake accounts showing how jobs that force lying corrupt character. He endorses instead a Kantian middle ground anchored in Norman Bowie's moral minimum: never treating workers as mere means, so the CEO making intern Asok drink industrial sludge on stage is a violation of respect for persons, not just bad management. Sisyphus supplies the image of pointless labor, though even he might be redeemed if he loved the rock.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 26 "13. Gilead vs. the Self" — Holberg argues that on Kantian grounds Gilead is morally incoherent—Handmaids are treated as mere means, vessels without agency—and that it sustains itself by attacking self-respect through two temporal modes: the quick onset of fear (Aristotle's account in the Rhetoric applied to the machine-gun arrests of women at their jobs) and the slow grind of shame (empty time that turns women into 'objects not in use' and manufactures a veneer of consent: 'nothing is going on here that I haven't signed up for'). Agency needs recognition from others—love as the most basic acknowledgment, or invoking Moira ('Moira would never stand for this shit')—so June's 'I tell, therefore you are' and the reader's duty to affirm her judgment carry the feminist-Kantian point: dependency on others does not negate the self, it is what constitutes it.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 26 "14. Jerryboree!" — Arguing that even the interchangeable Jerrys of Jerryboree deserve better, the chapter uses Stephen Darwall's distinction between recognition and appraisal respect: Jerry lacks both, while Rick has appraisal self-respect (he loves his genius) but squanders recognition self-respect by portal-hopping away from every consequence. Jerry's spinelessness is then Sartrean bad faith, from celebrating being 'assigned a function' in 'The Wedding Squanchers' to needing the parasite Sleepy Gary to vouch for his very existence in 'Total Rickall' and lying to Keara in 'The ABCs of Beth'. The chapter closes with Thomas Hill's Kantian case that servility disrespects the moral law in oneself, quoting Kant's worm maxim against Jerry's failed him-or-me ultimatum in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption'.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 24 "Power Behind the Cloak" — The chapter asks whether Wong's hereditary service to the Sorcerer Supreme is culpable servility, framing the charge with Kant's line that 'one who makes himself a worm cannot complain' and Thomas E. Hill's Kantian account of servility as failing to claim one's dignity as a person. It answers with Hegel's master-slave dialectic: Strange, free to haunt the astral plane, becomes dependent on Wong for everything worldly, while Wong, by working on the world rather than merely commanding it, develops the self-consciousness Hegel says work produces—he serves the shared mission rather than the master—so the relationship is a partnership in which servitude grounds rather than forfeits Wong's self-respect.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 15 "5. The Morality of Manners" — Dougherty argues that in Downton manners are not incidental etiquette but a central means of demonstrating and cultivating moral character, above all respect for persons, though they can also mask its absence. Matthew's growth from calling valeting 'a very silly occupation' to honoring Molesley's dignity, and Branson's journey from tweed defiance ('uniforms of oppression') to worrying that a tuxedo is insufficient for the Dowager's dinner, show manners tracking their growing respect for the Crawleys as particular individuals. The chapter anchors this in Aristotle's person of visible virtue, Nancy Sherman's 'aesthetic of character,' and Sarah Buss's claim that manners constantly remind us that others are worthy of respect, while Sir Richard's boorishness and the Dowager Countess's weaponized courtesy show manners failing or serving self-interest. Mrs. Crawley's etiquette-breaking kindness, praised even by Violet, complicates the picture by showing care can be morally outrun by propriety.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 27 "a12.xhtml" — O'Hara argues that play is what makes hobbits - and us - fully human: Bilbo's childhood games of throwing stones, riddles and smoke-rings turn out to be training for the quest (his stone-throwing fells the spiders, his riddle-practice buys time with Gollum), and even Gollum's riddle-game makes him momentarily 'less a monster and more a person'. Following Schiller's and Huizinga's Homo ludens thesis that play completes humanity, he distinguishes play from idleness (Aquinas held recreation continues in heaven; Peirce called play 'vigorous exercise'), places leisure among the goods of Aristotle's 'we play in order to be serious', and contrasts Gandalf's beauty-directed fireworks with the orcs' merely useful explosions and work-chants. But play has limits: Kant warns against treating persons as toys, and Bilbo's lesson is 'Never laugh at live dragons!'
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 34 "Notes" — Koepsell argues the franchise stages the bioconservatism-versus-transhumanism debate: the villains are machine-altered (Immortan Joe's breathing gear, the People Eater's prosthetic nose, Master Blaster's contraption) while the saved live green and unmodified, so George Miller's films side with Leon Kass's bioconservatism against Nick Bostrom's transhumanist embrace of enhancement. Dignity — derived from Kant and contested between Kass and Bostrom — is the hinge, and the recurring green places (the family farm, the Sunshine Coast, the Crack in the Earth, the Green Place) mark the dignity of nature the Wasteland destroyed. The bioconservative lesson holds even though Max and Furiosa, patched with prosthetics, must partially embrace their posthuman condition to survive.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 18 "The Question of Ethical Advertising" — Novakovic and Whitney use the Heineken incident, where Betty discovers she was the target demographic for her husband's campaign ('Must be so funny, being in on it'), to test advertising against Kantian honesty and respect. Kant's humanity formula and the lying-promise example show that manipulation wrongs the consumer as a rational agent, and Don's defense that advertising sells 'happiness' fails because Kant allows making others' happiness an end but never at the cost of truth, whether the consumer is a stranger or a wife. The chapter sets this against the era's brainwashing anxieties (Hunter's Brainwashing in Red China, Packard's The Hidden Persuaders, Precon subliminal projection) and concludes that honest advertising must survive disclosure of its methods, noting that real sponsors like Canada Dry and BMW responded to the show with stripped-down 'transparent' ads that let viewers be 'in on it.'
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Robichaud asks whether Bill may turn Sookie into a vampire and answers with Kant's Formula of Humanity: consent matters because turning someone without letting them take up your end as their own treats them as a mere means. He argues the consent must be explicit (marriage is not tacit permission, as flirting is not consent to sex), informed (Fangtasia wannabes consent in the dark about unlife), and noncoerced (glamouring is like hypnotism, and Lafayette's begging under duress from Eric has no moral force). Even though Bill's forced turning improved Jessica's life, respecting her autonomy outweighed benefit, though Godric's turning of mortally wounded Eric may be excused by hypothetical consent.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 15 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Delfino and Taylor ask whether Morgan's zombified wife Jenny is a person, weighing Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellectual soul, and Kantian dignity against Peter Singer's speciesism challenge to the person/animal moral line. They then argue walkers are 'impossible beings' like square-circles: Jenner's brain-stem-only reanimation cannot explain Hannah the bicycle girl crawling without organs, walkers smelling Rick in the rain, or cafeteria walkers moving for weeks without energy. On either the soul view or materialism walkers are not persons, so Morgan should shoot, and zombies fascinate because they are metaphysical projections of our fears, caught between being and nonbeing.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 16 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case from Rick's eulogy for Wayne the organ donor: walkers deserve respect both as corpses governed by the deceased's presumptive choices and as 'residual subjects' still executing past choices, like Jenny returning to her family's house. From zombie dignity they derive a duty to kill walkers respectfully—Rick's quick merciful headshots versus Merle's sport killing—and defend the group's respect for Jim's autonomous choice to be left by the road to turn. They even argue Rick and Glenn do not use Wayne as a mere means because his organ-donor choice set the end his body now serves.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 10 "Second Hole On the Beauty and Sublimity of Golf" — Fudge and Ulatowski argue that golf's aesthetic appeal has two sources: the course as a designed landscape best appreciated (via Walton's 'Categories of Art') under the category of gardens, and the sublimity of players' character. They apply Kant's 'Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime' to distinguish beautiful courses (Augusta) from sublime ones (Pebble Beach, St. Andrews) and to explain Bobby Jones's self-imposed penalty at the 1925 U.S. Open as the noble sublime, since 'subduing one's passions through principles is sublime.' They link the consistent rule-following golf demands to Kant's categorical imperative and read human dignity as 'beyond price' against Hobbes's price-based account, while Schopenhauer's critique of the French garden frames the environmental objection to courses.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 13 "Fourth Hole “Quiet…Please!” Reflections on Golf and Civility" — McNaron argues that golf promotes civility both empirically and normatively through its rules (self-scoring, self-called penalties) and its etiquette (silence during a swing, care for the course). Using an Aristotelian virtue-ethics frame plus Kekes's 'conduct according to custom' and Calhoun's expressivist account of civility as communicating respect, he treats civility as a mean acquired by habituation and opposes it to skloka, the petty hostility of win-at-all-costs sport. He defends golf's quiet against charges of classism, reads Tiger Woods's outburst at a shutter-clicking photographer as justified anger at an etiquette breach, and names the Ryder Cup's jingoism, boorish spectators, and intrusive media as threats to golf's civil, contemplative character.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 20 "General Patton and Private Ryan The Conflicting Reality of War and Films about War" — Fiala uses Patton's opening speech ("an army is a team… this individuality stuff is a bunch of crap") against Saving Private Ryan's mission to rescue one soldier to frame war's basic conflict between the collective and the individual, and to expose the problem of "realism" in representing war. He aligns the collectivist realist ethics of war against the just-war tradition's deontological respect for individuals as Kantian ends-in-themselves, and contrasts Patton's aerial, above-the-battle viewpoint with Private Ryan's first-person D-Day realism. Drawing on Tim O'Brien's claim that a true war story is never moral, and on Nussbaum's and Glover's moral imagination, he concludes that no film can synthesize war's public and private perspectives—mirroring the failure of moral imagination that produces war itself.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 19 "Horton Hears You, Too! Seuss and Kant on Respecting Persons" — Kowalski reads Horton Hatches the Egg and Horton Hears a Who! through Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative. Mayzie's lying promise to Horton fails the universal-law test just like Kant's lying-loan and tax-shirking (Jo-Jo) cases, while Horton's insistence that 'a person's a person, no matter how small' embodies the ends-in-themselves formula treating the Whos as ends with dignity, not things. The essay argues Horton's fidelity is heroic rather than strictly required, revising Kant's moral absolutism (the inquiring-murderer case) so that when duties conflict one should act to disrespect persons least.

### Humanity as an End in Itself

The humanity formula is one of Immanuel Kant's expressions of the categorical imperative, requiring that we treat humanity, whether in ourselves or in others, always as an end and never merely as a means. Because rational beings possess an intrinsic worth, or dignity, that is not exchangeable for any price, they must never be used simply as instruments for someone else's purposes. The principle grounds duties such as honesty and respect and has become a touchstone for arguments about human dignity and the wrongness of manipulation and coercion.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 17 "Conquering the Inner Demon" — James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 24 "Following the Moral Law" — Applies Kant's Formula of Universal Law and Formula of Humanity on two levels. Individually, Buffy's sacrifice in Dawn's place in 'The Gift' and her post-resurrection return to duty in 'Once More, with Feeling' show her will determined by duty rather than the inclination to a normal life, while Oz's werewolf episodes show inclination swamping reason. Systemically, the Slayer's coercion of demons is justified only because their actions destroy a Kantian state of right in Sunnydale, and Kant's account of radical evil — subordinating the moral law to the maxim of self-love — explains why demons and human villains like Warren's Trio are evil; the chapter closes worrying that the Slayer, like the Initiative's Adam, answers to no one.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 32 "The Moral Sophistication of Buffy the Vampire Slayer" — Greene and Yuen reconstruct seven moral principles from Buffy's conduct — slay those who typically harm humans, never harm humans (Faith's accidental killing of the Mayor's henchman), spare the defenseless and the controllable (chip'd Spike, caged Oz) — and note that blackmailing Spike and roughing up demons would violate Kant's Formula of Humanity if the patients were rational persons, exposing the show's human/non-human moral hierarchy and its animal-rights parallel. 'The Gift' dramatizes deontology (Buffy refuses to kill Ben) against consequentialism (Giles strangles him), and the chapter ranks BtVS above after-school-special, culpable-clown, and faux-realist TV morality because it supports its stands by appeal to general moral principles while keeping Aristotelian habituation and real-life moral complexity in view.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 60 "The Sorting Hat Speaks Division and Divisiveness" — This section argues that patriotism violates the principle of equal moral worth shared by utilitarians and Kantians alike: Bentham's 'each to count for one, and none for more than one' means the Minister of Magic's pain counts no more than a house-elf's, while Kant's formula forbids treating anyone (Muggle or wizard) merely as a means. It reads Death Eater pureblood ideology as ordinary racism and sexism, cites Potterwatch's 'every human life is worth the same, and worth saving' and Hermione's S.P.E.W. campaign against 'slave labor,' and asks how preferring countrymen over foreigners differs from preferring people of one's race or gender, since neither is something a person controls.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 74 "Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power" — This section contrasts Voldemort and Dumbledore as two figures tempted by power. Tom Riddle's egocentrism - frightening and controlling other children at the orphanage, treating his 'friends' as mere followers, killing Lily, and splintering his soul for Horcruxes - violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means and fits Plato's category of the least trustworthy rulers. Dumbledore, though tempted in youth by Grindelwald's 'for the greater good' schemes and later by Marvolo Gaunt's ring, is venerable for Socratic self-knowledge: knowing 'I was not to be trusted with power,' he repeatedly refused the Ministry and so promoted justice by teaching.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 13 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Taliaferro, writing as a personalist, worries that Gibson's relentless focus on torture eclipses the whole person of Christ: like torture victims losing peripheral vision, viewers lose sight of his teaching, healings, nonviolence, and resurrection, and the satisfaction-theology framing risks relishing redemptive suffering itself. His reconciliation thought-experiment (Patricia's betrayal of Kris and the God-man who resurrects the murdered child) argues that the resurrection, not the passion alone, completes at-one-ment, since no amount of suffering can undo past wrong. He contrasts Gandalf's laughing return in The Return of the King with a Gibson Jesus who could not plausibly laugh after rising, and invokes Scheler's St. Francis, who loves the wholeness behind sickness rather than the sickness, to urge that the film's intensity edges out a life-affirming view of persons as irreducibly valuable in themselves.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 12 "“You Know . . . What They’re Up Against”" — Dees finds moral ambiguity lurking in Star Wars' black-and-white universe: Han Solo's Hobbesian ethical egoism ('I take orders from just one person - me') is shown to be coherent and gradually transformed by friendship with Luke and Leia into commitment to a cause. Lando's betrayal of Han on Bespin is defended as a straightforward Mill-Bentham utilitarian choice by a responsible official, weighed against Bernard Williams's Jim-and-the-commandant integrity objection, which the author rejects as moral vanity. Count Dooku's apparent idealism is exposed as evil's tool, and Anakin's massacre of the Sand People is condemned as non-ambiguous barbarity via Kant's formula of humanity (and Hume on reason's role with the passions), leaving only late Vader as genuinely morally ambiguous.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 17 "Send in the Clones!" — Hanley defends a provocative 'yes' to cloning, genetic engineering, and clone armies. He dismisses the 'yuck factor' as showing nothing inherently bad, argues via non-identity-style cases (a genetically corrected or maimed Luke is a different child who is not thereby harmed) that early genetic manipulation harms no one, and distinguishes brainwashing, coercion, and inducement (Obi-Wan's death-stick mind trick, Vader's threats to Lando, Jar Jar's exploitation) to ask when bending another's will is permissible. Turning to warfare, he applies Just War theory's conditions - judging Anakin's slaughter of the Sand People guilty on nearly every count - and concludes that troops with deliberately diminished autonomy may be the least objectionable solution to the ethics of recruitment, training, and deployment: send in the clones.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 43 "Power and Glory Tests of Virtue" — The chapter's thesis is that superhero ethics is not utilitarianism (whose perverse 'evil twin' governs Marvel villains) but personalism - the tradition from Borden Parker Bowne to Martin Buber, rooted in Kant's insistence that every person be treated as an end and never merely as a means, and aiming at his 'kingdom of ends'. Heroes who refuse to weigh one innocent against the many enact personalism, and it redeems even Galactus: lying defeated, he is saved by Captain America's and Reed Richards' insistence that 'We had no choice, Galactus', which wins the devourer into a moral community. The authors read the whole arc as the ancient warning against hubris retold in contemporary storytelling.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 93 "I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!" — Turns to Kantian nonconsequentialism: persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means, from duty rather than consequences, with negative duties (not harming) stronger than positive duties (aiding) — so Reed Richards may not kill a pedestrian for organs to heal Doctor Doom's victims, though a utilitarian would require it. Since neither becoming Spider-Man nor refusing to violates any negative duty, being a superhero is supererogatory: 'with great power comes great responsibility' is at most a duty not to misuse power, and precisely because heroes don't have to do what they do — as Clark Kent's Superman II choice shows — their choosing it is what makes them praiseworthy.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 13 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Dennis uses Kant to sort eaters into the fundamentally unfree (Herbert, raised on Atkins and thieving, who merely ploughs on), the fundamentally random (Rita, whose synapses and muscles would fire in chaos), and the autonomous, arguing that only an autonomous person can genuinely decide whether to follow Atkins — by weighing friends' testimonials against the medical establishment rather than habit, whim, or advertising. The categorical imperative grounds the autonomous life: 'lie when you can gain' fails universalization, and treating humanity as an end means offering a vegetarian guest food she is comfortable with instead of pressing Atkins meat on her. His own 'Dan Dennis Diet,' built by experiment and reasoning, illustrates autonomy in practice, and the case of Kitty shows that observing someone's diet never reveals whether its holder is unfree or autonomous.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 26 "James Bond and Philosophy" — McKinney argues that '007' is a technological construction distinct from the human James Bond: drawing on Dewey's broad view of technology as technique (the shaken martini as technological artifact), Heidegger's account of naming as revealing and enframing, and Don Ihde's technological embodiment (the party-game hand axe that is art, paperweight, or tool depending on perception). Film dialogue shows the naming at work: Moneypenny calls him 'James' but announces '007 is here' to M; Goldfinger greets '007' and is corrected with 'My name is James Bond'; M threatens '008 can replace you' and, in Die Another Day, declares 'You are no use to anyone now' while rescinding his status. The chapter closes with the Kantian point that persons must be treated as ends in themselves, yet the designation '007' constitutes Bond as precisely a replaceable means to MI6's ends.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 28 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Arp and Decker examine Bond's objectification of women - using a dancing girl as a human shield in the Goldfinger pre-credits sequence, M ordering Bond to 'pump her for information' - through three moral theories. Kant's humanity formula condemns treating women as sexual tools, but Kantian autonomy generates a stalemate since consensual, reciprocal liaisons like Bond and Anya Amasova's might qualify as permissible; Millian utilitarianism condemns the male gaze by its long-term social costs yet stalls against pro-sex feminist counterarguments. They settle on Aristotelian virtue ethics - the mean between extremes, with respect as the key virtue against the power-centered virtue of Machiavelli, Hobbes, and Nietzsche - to argue objectification is vicious, and they trace Bond's moral progress from skipping the young Bibi in For Your Eyes Only to the reciprocal relationships with Kara Milovy, Pam Bouvier, Wai Lin, and Jinx.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — Loftis argues Watchmen's real target is authoritarianism, with Ozymandias and Rorschach as corrupted rationalizers. Ozymandias calls himself a consequentialist, but his Bentham-Mill utilitarianism cannot survive Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' — an infinite future makes utility sums impossible — and it ignores the rights of the New Yorkers he slaughters as mere means. Rorschach's deontology is hypocrisy (he admires Truman's Hiroshima trade-off and says 'can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'), mistaking Kant's categorical imperative — universalize your maxim, treat humanity never merely as a means — for black-and-white thinking in service of fascist thuggery, while the nonideological Nite Owls embody the lesson that no one should be trusted with such power.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 15 "The Virtues of Superhumans" — Rachel Robison tests the Deadly Viper Assassination Squad against three ethical theories. Act and rule utilitarianism condemn killing Vernita in front of Nikki and revenge in general; Kant's categorical imperative condemns Elle's black-mamba betrayal of Budd (contradiction in conception), O-Ren's beheading of a dissenter (contradiction in will), and Buck's selling of comatose women (treating persons as mere means). She concludes the Squad instead follows a bastardized Aristotelian virtue ethics—Bill's Superman speech, contempt for Budd's shotgun bushwhack and Elle's poisoning of Pai Mei define courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness—so Beatrix would be cowardly not to seek revenge.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 17 "Conclusion June Love Beyond the Jordan" — Sennett builds "June Love" out of June Carter Cash's documented love, from the "Hurt" video's staircase glance to Rosanne Cash's eulogy that June saw your potential and "lifted them up" for you to see, and the love that steadied John through addictions and infidelity for thirty-five years. He stages the philosophy-of-love dilemma between appraisal theories (Velleman, grounding love in Kantian dignity that demands respect but cannot justify loving John rather than anyone) and bestowal theories (Irving Singer, on which love projects value and so cannot be justified at all), with Frankfurt's volitional account as a side note, and proposes June Love, loving the beloved's potentiality, as the hybrid that is both objective and active and can justify loving this person. He also distinguishes June Love from codependence: enabling entrenches the addict's destruction, whereas June's confronting-and-encouraging love, echoed in "Ring of Fire" and "Far Side Banks of Jordan," called Cash to transformation while leaving him himself.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 20 "From Cash to Kant—and Back Again" — Yolanda Estes pairs Cash with Kant as two duty-based moralists: Cash's Golden Rule in 'The Preacher Said, Jesus Said' parallels Kant's formula of humanity (never treating persons merely as means), and Cash's 'good heart' matches Kant's good will, since songs like 'Sam Hall,' 'Folsom Prison Blues' (the man shot in Reno 'just to watch him die'), and 'I Hung My Head' weigh inner motives over outcomes. Because earthly law never balances the moral scale, she reads Kant's kingdom of ends and Cash's apocalyptic kingdom of God in 'When the Man Comes Around' and 'God's Gonna Cut You Down' as parallel objects of faith: we must live as if perfect justice already prevails, working to improve this world rather than waiting for the next.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 25 "Seeing Ourselves Reflected Back" — Gray asks whether Cylons deserve moral consideration, starting from Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means: the New Caprica suicide bombings and Adama's plan to weaponize a Cylon virus treat captives merely as means, while Helo's sabotage of 'A Measure of Salvation' acknowledges their intrinsic value. D'Anna's dissent before being boxed and Athena's defection for Helo show the rational autonomy Kant's personhood requires; if that is dismissed as programming, Singer's sentience criterion (Leoben tortured, Gina catatonic) and Warren's multi-criterial personhood — including Boomer's 'I have a conscience' in 'Downloaded' — still open personhood to Cylons. The chapter ends on the humans' double standard (Athena accepted, guns drawn on Caprica Six) as a mirror for our own treatment of uncertain others.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 16 "“I’ve Never Been Good at Good-byes”" — Lee treats DS9's Cardassian Occupation as a case of transitional justice like post-Holocaust and post-apartheid reckonings, asking whether Odo, security chief on Terok Nor, was a collaborator. Applying Kant's deontology — the good will, both formulations of the categorical imperative, illustrated by Kai Opaka's Kendra Valley betrayal, Quark's smuggling in 'Little Green Men', and Sisko's fraud in 'In the Pale Moonlight' — he judges Odo's letting three innocent Bajorans die in 'Things Past' as negligence, but his years-long cover-up as using the victims merely as means to protect his reputation, and hence genuine collaboration, as was his neglect of duty under the Link's pull in 'Behind the Lines.' Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence then redeems Odo's final departure from Kira: returning to cure and educate the Founders in 'What You Leave Behind' is a moral duty owed to rational beings.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 8 "There’s No Place Like Home" — Luke Dick stages Immanuel Kant as the 'Supreme Critical Chancellor of Munchkinland' and runs the film through Kantian ethics: against hedonism, utilitarianism, and command-based religion, the formula of universalizability condemns the Wizard's lies and his use of the companions as mere means, while the ends-in-themselves principle raises the awkward case of Glinda and Dorothy keeping the dead Witch of the East's ruby slippers. Judging the characters, the Lion's rescue of Dorothy is morally praiseworthy (duty against strong inclination), the brainless Scarecrow falls outside Kant's jurisdiction, and the sentimental Tin Man is pre-emptively condemned. The chapter finally rebels against its Chancellor: cases like returning the slippers, or Toto versus Almira Gulch, show that a world of absolute morality lies only 'somewhere over the rainbow,' and real moral life in Kansas needs Baum's Tin Man heart reconciled with Kantian duty.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 23 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Michaud reads the Autobot-Decepticon war as a contest of ethical systems: Optimus's fair fighting, his refusal to ignore human casualties, and Bumblebee's friendship with the inferior Spike instantiate Kant's categorical imperative and the treatment of rational beings as ends in themselves. The Decepticons run through the egoist tradition - Hobbes's psychological egoism from Leviathan, Starscream's self-defeating normative egoism, and Megatron as Ayn Rand's rational egoist taunting 'You still fight for the weak; that is why you lose' - leaving the reader to choose between Kant's world of peaceful obligation and Rand's world of power where, like Starscream, you die alone.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 8 "8" — Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 17 "Close the Door, Put Out the Lights" — Scott Calef tests three ethical theories against Led Zeppelin's off-stage destruction: TV-tossing, samurai-slashed hotel rooms, food fights, sharks hung in closets at the Edgewater Inn, the red snapper incident, and Jimmy Page's relationship with fourteen-year-old Lori Maddox. Classical utilitarianism weighs Bonzo's glee against the traumatized chambermaid, displaced guests, and unpaid-for sleep loss, generally condemning the pranks while leaving the supposedly consensual snapper episode uncomfortably open. Kant condemns across the board: Plant's fake tour itineraries and the stolen 'Black Beauty' Les Paul fail the universalizability test, trashing hotel rooms is self-defeating when universalized, and treating the Portland woman as a mere means violates her dignity as a rational agent; Aristotle's golden mean finds the band's excess nowhere near virtue, whatever Caligula would say. The chapter closes by separating moral judgment of the men from appreciation of the music.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 18 "The Legend Has Come True. The Wind Has Come Back" — Haas opposes two princesses of Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind: Kushana of Tolmekia, whose 'whatever it takes' survivalism (invading Pejite, resurrecting a God-Warrior) is consequentialism pursued to its limit, and Nausicaa, whose attention to each act — befriending the biting fox-squirrel, staying her sword over her father's killer because vengeance would doom the Valley — restricts means, not just ends. The reductio comes from Pejite, whose torture of a baby Ohmu to bait a stampede on the Valley is exactly what strict outcome-maximization requires; against this, Kant's demand to treat beings as ends in themselves explains Nausicaa's 'mysterious power' of empathy.
