- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 24 "NOTES" — Daniel Malloy asks whether the T-101's self-destruction in the steel mill was suicide, and whether it was justified, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is philosophy's only serious problem and the ambiguous case of Socrates' hemlock. Using Heidegger, he argues the learning-mode Terminator qualifies as Da-sein whose death is being-toward-death — the end of possibility — so the T2 machine dies authentically while the T3 machine's 'We'll meet again' is inauthentic self-deception. Kant condemns the act because the Terminator uses itself merely as a means, and Kant cannot even conceive of its genuine conflict of duties (preserve its life vs. prevent Skynet), while Bentham-style utilitarianism initially endorses the sacrifice but is refuted by hindsight: Skynet rises anyway, and consequentialism gives no credit for noble motives. The chapter ends by concluding that dying for a cause is illogical, since the dead surrender all control over the meaning of their actions.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 25 "NOTES" — Jason Eberl answers John's 'you just can't go around killing people' by asking what exactly is bad about death, weighing Aquinas's claim that life is a fundamental good against Epicurus and Lucretius's arguments that death is nothing to us — applied to Sarah's 'you're already dead' and to the victim shot on August 28, 1997, who loses only one more day of a doomed life. Feldman's ante-mortem harm and McMahan's deprivation account explain how Judgment Day harms people before it arrives, while Nagel replies that experience itself is positive however bad its contents, which is why the survivors keep fighting Skynet. Utilitarian ripple-effects, Kantian dignity (the H-K crushing skulls), and Marquis's loss-of-future argument all condemn the Terminators' indiscriminate killing, and the chapter ends with the T-101's 'I know now why you cry' as recognition that death is an evil because it strips us of our emotional attachments.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Robichaud asks whether Bill may turn Sookie into a vampire and answers with Kant's Formula of Humanity: consent matters because turning someone without letting them take up your end as their own treats them as a mere means. He argues the consent must be explicit (marriage is not tacit permission, as flirting is not consent to sex), informed (Fangtasia wannabes consent in the dark about unlife), and noncoerced (glamouring is like hypnotism, and Lafayette's begging under duress from Eric has no moral force). Even though Bill's forced turning improved Jessica's life, respecting her autonomy outweighed benefit, though Godric's turning of mortally wounded Eric may be excused by hypothetical consent.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Uses Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy and Lacan's ethics of psychoanalysis to argue season two failed as tragedy because feminist morality became the inflated 'Good' that blocks the transgression of limits through which Dionysian wisdom is won. Season one works because Rust's philosophy filters the Carcosa horrors without moralizing, whereas season two — failing Aristotle's catharsis model and repeating Euripides' mistake — represses the sexual knowledge troubling Velcoro, Bezzerides, and Woodrugh, so Dionysus returns only as money and violence, as in The Bacchae. Ani's arc is read through Nietzschean ressentiment toward her father and Freud's return of the repressed, with Kantian sexual dignity ('maybe you were put on earth for more than fucking') and the male gaze as the contemporary Good the show never crosses.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 15 "6. In a Mirror Is Our Image" — Karavitis places thirteen robot and android episodes on a spectrum from the X109B14 computer of 'The Brain Center at Whipple's' to indistinguishable androids like Alicia, arguing that the moral duties we owe artificial creations depend on personhood. By Locke's memory-continuity account of identity, the mind-transferred couple of 'The Trade-Ins' remain persons, and so would androids created from scratch, which makes the routine destruction of Alicia, Grandma, and Jana murder. The animal-ethics tradition from Aristotle's property view through Kant's indirect duties to Singer and Regan's moral patients supplies the analogy, and the show's unstated definition of evil is treating persons as disposable objects.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 21 "“It Was a Mistake”" — James and Mona Rocha reconstruct the night of Shelly Pomeroy's party — Logan supplying the GHB, Dick drugging Madison's drink that reached Veronica, Dick and Sean goading Cassidy — and apply a three-part test of moral responsibility (causal contribution, foreseeability, intention) to conclude Dick and Sean deserve the most blame, Logan substantial negligence, and Madison very little since she did not know the drink was drugged. Veronica's own choices, crashing an unwelcoming party and taking an unknown drink, were prudential mistakes that put only herself at risk, not the moral wrongs that generate blame, so Cassidy remains fully culpable without Veronica sharing any of it. Even Kant's duty to safeguard one's own rational agency, they concede, at most makes taking the drink wrong in itself and never grounds blaming the victim, who deserves sympathy.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 23 "Getting Tough and Getting Even" — Jordan Pascoe uses the 'Like a Virgin' purity test — Meg's fake 48 making her a 'slut' while a low score would make a guy a stud — to argue slut shaming strips girls of Kantian personhood, treating as things those autonomous beings who must be respected as ends in themselves. Kant's bleak view of sex as a desire for a body rather than a person explains why Tad's drugging and popsicle-video blackmail of Carmen reduce her to an object, and why objectification goes viral: once an object of one person's appetite, Kant warns, a person 'can be treated and used as such by everyone.' Catherine MacKinnon's power-based account then explains the double standard — men's pleasure in forcing the world to conform turns promiscuous men into studs and promiscuous women into sluts — so the fault lies with the slut sneezers, never Meg, Carmen, or Veronica, who must 'get tough, get even' to demand respect.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 16 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case from Rick's eulogy for Wayne the organ donor: walkers deserve respect both as corpses governed by the deceased's presumptive choices and as 'residual subjects' still executing past choices, like Jenny returning to her family's house. From zombie dignity they derive a duty to kill walkers respectfully—Rick's quick merciful headshots versus Merle's sport killing—and defend the group's respect for Jim's autonomous choice to be left by the road to turn. They even argue Rick and Glenn do not use Wayne as a mere means because his organ-donor choice set the end his body now serves.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 5 "P A R T O N E" — Christopher Robichaud's essay asks what morality can demand of Dr. Manhattan after the accident strips him of the moral emotions (in Jesse Prinz's Humean vein) needed to value persons, which is why he can tell Laurie 'I read atoms' and rank human life beside rubble. It then asks what grounds morality's authority over a being no one can punish, rejecting divine command theory (Manhattan's 'clock without a craftsman') and doubting Kant's rational grounding applies to someone lacking moral concepts, so 'no one is above the moral law' may rest on a brute fact. It closes on political morality: a United States made a hyperpower by Manhattan's service (as in his Vietnam intervention) may not claim a double standard, since sovereignty blocks preventive war even when the US would win at little cost.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 7 "P A R T T W O" — Three Part Two essays. Robert Loftis argues Moore and Gibbons use Ozymandias's squid attack to indict consequentialism — Veidt uses New York's dead as mere means to world peace, and Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' shows the utilitarian ledger dissolves into an infinite future — while Rorschach's 'never compromise' mantra is a counterfeit deontology rationalizing fascist thuggery, the comic's real target being anyone who sets himself up as guardian of society ('Who watches the watchmen?'). Mark White argues the potbellied second Nite Owl is the truest hero on Aristotelian terms: his courage in the tenement fire and the prison break hits the mean between Laurie's caution and Rorschach's recklessness, making him a flourishing moral exemplar whom John Doris's situationism fails to unseat. Alex Nuttall asks whether Rorschach was wrong to walk out and expose Veidt, using Kant's murderer-at-the-door case to show there is a duty not to lie but no duty to tell the truth (blame falls on Veidt), while act and rule utilitarianism both counsel silence.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 24 "Hoop Dreams, Blacktop Realities" — Bernard Jackson Jr. argues that basketball is an institution where black manhood is socially constructed (leaning on Naomi Zack's feminist point that gender identity is imposed by social designation), and that love among black players is essential to that construction while toughness is equivocal - the 'soft' label stuck to the gentlemanly David Robinson even as the Pistons walked off without congratulating the Bulls. Reading the documentary Hoop Dreams, he shows Arthur Agee and William Gates being used as commodities by recruiters, Coach Pingatore, and family expectations, invoking Marx on exploitation and 'use value' (Spike Lee's Nike-camp speech) and Kant's demand that persons be treated as ends, never merely as means. He likens William Gates's return to Chicago's Cabrini-Green as a minister to Plato's enlightened prisoner going back down into the cave.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 15 "Virtue and Violence Can a Good Football Player Be a Good Person" — Davison defends a 'Violence Principle'—intentionally causing violent harm known to be unnecessary for a greater good is wrong—and applies it to in-the-rules football hits like Jack Tatum on Darryl Stingley and Warren Sapp on Chad Clifton. Against a consequentialist defense of intimidation, he invokes Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, not mere means, arguing players consent to accidental injury but not intentional harm. Citing the Socratic examination of the soul, he warns of moral danger to players who use excessive force and to fans who relish violence for its own sake.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 15 "5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds" — The Phillipses argue that abrasive forensic agent Albert Rosenfield is a model Kantian: his refusal to lie to spare Truman's feelings follows the formula of universal law, and his insistence that Truman be punished for the assault treats Truman as an autonomous end. They run Gordon Cole's manipulative lying through the universalizability test (it fails, unlike wanting pie), distinguish hypothetical from categorical imperatives via Cooper's rebuff of Audrey, and read Albert's 'I love you, Sheriff Truman' and Gandhi/King nonviolence as respect for persons as ends in themselves—duty done for the right reason.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 11 "Was it Morally Wrong to Kill Off Sherlock Holmes" — Terjesen asks whether Conan Doyle acted immorally in killing Holmes in 'The Final Problem,' framing it through property theory. He runs Locke's labor theory (illustrated via 'The Blue Carbuncle' gem), Proudhon and Marx's critiques, and both consequentialist and Kantian (respect-for-persons) justifications of intellectual property. He argues Conan Doyle's ownership of the iconic Holmes weakened as Paget, Gillette, Rathbone, and Dr. Joseph Bell co-authored the figure, so property rights alone can't justify the killing—but Conan Doyle's authorial dignity plus the narrative fitness of 'The Final Problem' and 'His Last Bow' make the send-off defensible.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, about whether marital fidelity can be chosen rather than accidental. Bill's confidence in his own and Alice's fidelity is a Kantian appeal - duty and rational principle over inclination - which Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, and Bill's night among the masked orgy, expose as vulnerable to uncontrollable desire and moral luck. Hoffman argues that by unmasking and honestly acknowledging these desires (and drawing on Kierkegaard on marriage existing 'in time') the Harfords consciously rechoose their marriage, so their fidelity is no longer merely accidental.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 20 "General Patton and Private Ryan The Conflicting Reality of War and Films about War" — Fiala uses Patton's opening speech ("an army is a team… this individuality stuff is a bunch of crap") against Saving Private Ryan's mission to rescue one soldier to frame war's basic conflict between the collective and the individual, and to expose the problem of "realism" in representing war. He aligns the collectivist realist ethics of war against the just-war tradition's deontological respect for individuals as Kantian ends-in-themselves, and contrasts Patton's aerial, above-the-battle viewpoint with Private Ryan's first-person D-Day realism. Drawing on Tim O'Brien's claim that a true war story is never moral, and on Nussbaum's and Glover's moral imagination, he concludes that no film can synthesize war's public and private perspectives—mirroring the failure of moral imagination that produces war itself.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 16 "The Duty of Reason Kantian Ethics in High Noon" — Evans argues that Marshal Will Kane in High Noon is Kant's ideal moral agent, acting from duty and a good will rather than from consequences. He shows the townsfolk, Kane's friends, Harvey Pell, Helen Ramirez, and Amy all reasoning consequentially or heteronomously (the mayor privileging the town's finances, Mildred lying about Sam per Kant's essay on the supposed right to lie), while Frank Miller's revenge is a maxim that cannot be universalized. Kane's maxim of standing against lawlessness regardless of cost satisfies all three formulations of the categorical imperative—universal law, humanity as an end, and autonomy—making him a member of the kingdom of ends and contrasting Kant with Mill's utilitarianism.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 16 "Is Oskar Schindler a Good Man" — Ebertz treats Schindler's List as a thought experiment on what makes a person good, judging Oskar Schindler against Kantian and virtue-ethical standards. On Kant he fails: many acts (lying, bribery, infidelity) violate the categorical imperative, and even his rescues spring from growing partial attachment to 'his Jews' rather than rational duty or a good will. On Aristotelian virtue ethics he only selectively exercises virtues, so is not fully 'good' either; Ebertz resolves the tension with a Principle of Moral Exemplarity, holding Schindler up as a flawed but genuine moral example whose care promotes human flourishing.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 4 "Love, Value, and the Human Destiny in Interstellar" — Belluomini and Dunn use Interstellar's clash between Cooper's partial parental love and Professor Brand's species-level 'Plan B' to ask why the survival of humanity matters and what 'saving humanity' means. Drawing on Aristotle, they treat Cooper's daughter Murph as 'another self' loved as an end in itself and tie the good to individual happiness (eudaimonia), so 5,000 faceless embryos could never be the intrinsic good a real family is. They then turn to Kant to argue humans have unconditional value (dignity) as rational beings, which both grounds a reason to preserve the species AND condemns Brand's 'monstrous lie' as treating people merely as means to an end they do not share.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 16 "7. More Mothers, Lovers, and Other Monsters" — Brace surveys the later-season mother figures—Mary, Kelly, Jody, Rowena, Mrs. Butters, Charlie—arguing they are repeatedly used as emotional tools against the Winchesters, which she reads through Kant's warning against treating persons merely as means. She stresses loss of free will and agency: Mary's British Men of Letters 'realignment' and Mrs. Butters's coercive programming strip their autonomy and reduce them to objects/killers, while their reclaimed agency and self-sacrifice restore their Kantian standing as ends in themselves.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 8 "1. Scamming for Fun" — Clipsham distinguishes Jimmy and Kim's 'scamming for fun' (deceiving Ken over rare tequila in 'Switch', or a montage of pointless cons in 'Marco') from the 'scheming for benefits' of Mike, Gus, and Chuck, who lie only to secure a specific end. Using Kant's prohibition on treating people merely as means, he argues that scheming for a benefit is more disrespectful than scamming for its own sake, because the latter treats a mark as an unwitting player in a game rather than a tool. He also rejects the worry that fun-scamming corrupts character, noting Jimmy was already dishonest and that Gus and Lalo's worst vices have no root in playful deception.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 25 "Real World Island" — Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue that Lost characters move from blameworthy to praiseworthy by ceasing to objectify others and instead objectifying themselves for a greater good. Using Kant's formula to treat persons as ends and never mere means, they condemn Ben Linus's lifelong manipulation while crediting his tearful mea culpa over Alex and his flash-sideways sacrifice for his student. Mill's utilitarianism justifies Sayid's assassinations and Kate's shooting of Un-Locke as trades for the greater number, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of cultivated respect and courage explains Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission and Jack's Christlike self-sacrifice at the Heart of the Island, framing self-objectification as redemption.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 19 "Horton Hears You, Too! Seuss and Kant on Respecting Persons" — Kowalski reads Horton Hatches the Egg and Horton Hears a Who! through Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative. Mayzie's lying promise to Horton fails the universal-law test just like Kant's lying-loan and tax-shirking (Jo-Jo) cases, while Horton's insistence that 'a person's a person, no matter how small' embodies the ends-in-themselves formula treating the Whos as ends with dignity, not things. The essay argues Horton's fidelity is heroic rather than strictly required, revising Kant's moral absolutism (the inquiring-murderer case) so that when duties conflict one should act to disrespect persons least.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 25 "It’s Not Personal . . . It’s Just Bizzyneuss Business Ethics, the Company, and Its Stakeholders" — Pierlott frames the shareholder-versus-stakeholder debate (Friedman versus Freeman) using Aristotle's function argument to ask what makes a 'good' company, then judges business relationships by Kant's humanity formula. McBean's manipulation of the Sneetches and the digital-TV cases show consumers used merely as means; McGurk's cavalier overworking of Sneelock in If I Ran the Circus and Maitland's sweatshop defense are answered with Marx's account of labor exploitation and Aristotle's voluntary-versus-mixed actions; the Once-ler's Lorax devastation shows firms externalizing environmental costs when profit is maximized at any value unprotected by law.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 13 "MOTHERHOOD" — Amy Kind examines the pervasiveness of parents lying to children (her own 'Bad Dream Spray') against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibition of lying, Mill's utilitarian permissiveness, and Sissela Bok's principle of veracity. She applies Kant's categorical imperative and formula of humanity – treating persons never merely as means – to argue that because young children have not fully developed their rational natures, the Kantian wrong of lying is mitigated, while illustrating the debate with South Park's Kyle reading Descartes, A Few Good Men's 'you can't handle the truth,' and Seinfeld's George Costanza ('it's not a lie if you believe it').
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 14 "MOTHERHOOD" — Bertha Alvarez Manninen reconciles her deepened respect for fetal life (after seeing her daughter on ultrasound) with a pro-choice stance by deploying Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist thought experiment and the real McFall v. Shimp bodily-integrity ruling. She argues that even granting the fetus full personhood, no one's right to life entitles them to another's body, buttressing this with Kant's formula of humanity that a woman must not be reduced to a mere incubating means, and calls for American mizuko-kuyo-style grieving rituals so 'pro-choice' is not conflated with 'pro-abortion.'
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 22 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Ashwell and Langton ask whether fashion is a 'badge of slavery' (Wollstonecraft), opening with Socrates in the *Phaedo* disdaining adornment and Rousseau's girl who becomes 'her own doll,' and using Kant's humanity formula and Nussbaum's seven-feature account of objectification. Focusing on denial of autonomy in ordinary followers, they distinguish the 'Servile Fashionista' (obeys experts) from the 'Sensible Fashionista' (follows what looks good), then argue that via Johnston's 'authority of affect' even the sensible one is under an *epistemic* bondage: fashion's extrinsic social pull is misperceived as the garment's intrinsic goodness, a projective illusion (like the Müller-Lyer) that on a Kantian view undermines agency and masks misogynist or racist norms such as straightened hair or the 'lotus feet' of stilettos.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 23 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Brophy prosecutes Santa for 'elfploitation,' treating the North Pole workshop like an overseas sweatshop (with Willy Wonka's Oompa-Loompahs and Rowling's house-elfs as parallels) and dismantling a Nozickian entitlement-theory defense: the elfs' 'consent' is coerced by their bleak alternatives, so absolute property rights fail just as Locke's desert water-hole owner must grant access. He diagnoses the elfs' apparent contentment as Marxian false consciousness, invokes Kant's humanity formula to condemn using rational elfs as mere means, and rejects the utilitarian 'greatest happiness' justification via Le Guin's Omelas and Rawls's veil of ignorance. He concludes with a call to boycott Christmas until Santa's labor practices become transparent.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 21 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span turns to the ethics and epistemology of college sex. Kania argues there is no clear line between close friendship and a sexual relationship, so condemning student-professor sex logically forces condemning student-professor friendship—rejecting Golash's split and defending carefully-conducted consensual relationships. Layne narrates Socrates/Alcibiades, Abelard/Heloise, and Heidegger/Arendt to contrast Socratic eros (Plato's Symposium, love as a friend of wisdom directed at the soul) and Heideggerian authentic love ('I want you to be what you are') against Abelard's exploitative lust. McDowell mines epistemology (justification, taking beliefs 'to heart,' reflective equilibrium) to argue better thinking yields better, more autonomous sex. Pinku weighs 'plain sex' against Nagel's interpersonal-arousal account of embodiment to ask whether sex needs love, and Brophy uses Kantian dignity (treating the body as a mere means, not an end) to argue that prostitution and webcam porn undertaken to pay tuition violate the student's autonomy.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 22 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — The essay argues that soaring tuition drives college students into sexual self-commodification—egg-selling ('Pay your tuition with eggs'), craigslist/backpage escorting, and dorm-porn webcam sites like VoyeurDorm and CocoDorm—and reads these cases through Kant's second formulation, condemning them as treating oneself and others as mere means rather than ends of intrinsic dignity. It applies Marx's notion of false consciousness to Natalie Dylan's virginity auction and Ashley Dupré's 'empowerment' claims, comparing them to women choosing high heels as internalized oppression. It uses Rousseau's Social Contract and Mill's On Liberty to argue that prostitution is a form of illegitimate 'voluntary slavery' because one cannot rightly alienate one's own inalienable freedom, and contrasts coerced cases (Helena in Singapore, Rosie Reid's traumatic auctioned deflowering, John Gechter's porn suspension from a Christian college) with less-coerced ones to argue moral concern should track the degree of circumstantial coercion.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 33 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Heather Salazar interleaves philosophical arguments with yoga exercises to awaken a 'hidden ethical self.' Using Korsgaard's notion of practical identity, she has readers meditate on their roles and conflicts, then argues in Kantian fashion that recognizing the shared reasons behind everyone's pursuits obliges us to value others as we value ourselves; extending Korsgaard, that we must value the life and happiness we prize wherever they appear, in animals and plants; and via Buddhist interdependence (the world in a cup of tea) that caring for others and the environment just is a way of caring for ourselves.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 18 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Anne Barnhill uses John Cusack's boom-box serenade in Say Anything, his poolside pleading in The Sure Thing, and Andy Bernard's 'Take a Chance on Me' serenade in The Office to defend 'prospective boundary violation'—violating a boundary that would not exist in a closer relationship in order to create that relationship. She rejects the Kantian reading of Korsgaard and Hill that treating people as ends forbids all non-rational manipulation, arguing instead that such charming pushiness is 'faking it till you make it,' which works via Aristotle's habituation whereby feelings catch up with actions. She then sets four rules (no harm, not too much closer too fast, genuinely wanting the relationship, and that the other would plausibly want it) to separate appropriate from wrong boundary violations.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 13 "7. Independence Day & Aliens" — Rowlands frames morality around consistency and impartiality (the golden rule), articulated by Kant's categorical/practical imperatives (treat persons as ends, not merely means) and utilitarianism's greatest happiness. Imagining philosophers arguing Independence Day's aliens out of eradicating humans, he deploys the principle of 'no moral difference without a relevant other difference' and the argument from marginal cases to defeat intelligence, telepathy, and bare species membership as morally relevant. He turns the alien-invasion parable on our factory farming of chickens and pigs (Singer-style speciesism), arguing we are crueller than the aliens and fall short of our own impartiality ideal.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 46 "43. Ex Machina as Philosophy Mendacia Ex Machina (Lies from a Machine)" — Grinnell argues Ex Machina is fundamentally about lying, read through Kant's deontology. He frames Nathan's rigged Turing test on Ava against Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge and Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative, deriving three 'wrinkles': lying is heteronomous programming rather than the autonomy Nathan seeks; the experiment is defensible only if Ava fails, since a genuine person may not be manipulated (Formula of Humanity); and the cascade of lies among Nathan, Caleb, and Ava vindicates Kant's absolute prohibition on lying. He uses Caleb's telling of Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Searle's weak/strong AI distinction to question whether Ava's 'pleasure response' amounts to genuine consciousness or personhood.

### Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI)

Applied ethics brings moral theory to bear on concrete practical problems, working out what we ought to do in specific domains such as medicine, business, the environment, and emerging technology. In bioethics it addresses issues like consent, euthanasia, and the allocation of scarce care; in the ethics of technology and artificial intelligence it examines privacy, algorithmic bias, autonomy, and responsibility for machine decisions. Rather than defending a single grand theory, it tests principles against hard cases and aims at reasoned guidance that practitioners and policymakers can use.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 13 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Theodore Schick takes Tolkien's remark that the Ring represents 'potency' externalized beyond its maker's control and applies it to emerging nanotechnology, genetics, and robotics. He sets Bill Joy's call for relinquishment against Eric Drexler's promise of universal assemblers, cell-repair machines, and soldier nanosuits, weighing the 'grey goo' risk against the Rings' own power to heal and preserve (Lothlórien, Bilbo 'well-preserved'). Against the Council of Elrond's solution of destroying the Ring, he argues our situation is disanalogous - Ring-making knowledge is now spread worldwide and there is no single device to destroy - so grass-roots social response, not bans, must tame the new technologies.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 40 "22b" — A paired legal-philosophy debate on whether steroids should be banned. Michael McGrath argues yes from Kant: PED use cannot be universalized and 'the ends do not justify the means,' so the Ken Caminiti, Mark McGwire, and José Canseco confessions stain America's pastime, whose stars are role models and whose users risk devastating health effects — down to wrestler Davey Boy Smith's fatal steroid-related heart attack. Simon Eassom replies no by reframing drugs as Performance Enhancing Technologies: rules merely define the game, enhancers (unlike bat-cannons or netted catcher's gloves) do not de-skill baseball, and banning them because we dislike them is a matter of taste — of aesthetics, not ethics.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 19 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Corlett applies the ethics of racism, due process, responsibility, and punishment to the film: he argues The Passion is not racist because it depicts dissenting Sanhedrin members, the supportive Simon of Cyrene, and the Jewish Mary and Jesus, so blame falls on individual wrongdoers like Caiaphas rather than on Jews as a group, and audiences' misreadings are not the artist's fault. He catalogs the violations of due process (guilty-until-proven-innocent before the Sanhedrin, beatings en route to the hearing, the swap for the convicted killer Barabbas) and the failure to separate religious from civil authority. On punishment he defends a principle of proportionality and desert: Jesus's innocence made his torture and execution unjust, but abuse does not negate proper use, so the film gives no argument against capital punishment per se while giving evildoers who escape earthly justice their deserts only if God is just.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 17 "Send in the Clones!" — Hanley defends a provocative 'yes' to cloning, genetic engineering, and clone armies. He dismisses the 'yuck factor' as showing nothing inherently bad, argues via non-identity-style cases (a genetically corrected or maimed Luke is a different child who is not thereby harmed) that early genetic manipulation harms no one, and distinguishes brainwashing, coercion, and inducement (Obi-Wan's death-stick mind trick, Vader's threats to Lando, Jar Jar's exploitation) to ask when bending another's will is permissible. Turning to warfare, he applies Just War theory's conditions - judging Anakin's slaughter of the Sand People guilty on nearly every count - and concludes that troops with deliberately diminished autonomy may be the least objectionable solution to the ethics of recruitment, training, and deployment: send in the clones.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 20 "It’s Not Our Lot in Life!" — Arp argues that C-3PO and R2-D2 satisfy the standard functional criteria of personhood - rationality, mental states, language, social relationships, and moral agency - opening with a blind listener who took Threepio's frightened chatter for a man, a Turing-test-style judgment from behavior alone. He catalogues evidence: Threepio's odds-calculating and Wookiee-winning deduction, Artoo's deceptive manipulation of Luke, the droid torture victim's screams at Jabba's palace, and the Chewbacca-Threepio quasi-familial bond on Cloud City. Since droids meet the conditions, their restraining bolts, cantina bans, and forced servitude are slavery, and the Galactic Senate should grant them limited rights - perhaps cheering a droid rebellion against the organic empire - a question the chapter urges on us as robotics approaches Moravec's predictions.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 24 "Poker and Philosophy" — Barnhill and Solomon use Robert Varkonyi's staged five-minute 'agony' over pocket aces — pure theater that lured Ralph Perry into an all-in at the 2002 WSOP (and later busted Phil Hellmuth's A-K with Q-10 suited) — to ask when poker deception is morally acceptable and when it crosses the line: the towed-car lie, the fake-Marine claim, racist goading, and collusion are wrong. Their answer is an implicit-permission theory: by sitting down, players waive the right not to be deceived, but only where deception tests poker skills, so bluffs, disguised strength, and silently reading exposed cards are fine. The underlying order of the implicit rules — the game must test only poker skills — also explains everyday white lies and what you may tell a mugger.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 21 "Deserving to Be a Vampire" — Ted Preston asks whether becoming a vampire would be morally good or desirable, working through Forever Knight's Nick draining his lover, Blade feeding on stored blood, and The Lost Boys' promise that Michael will 'never grow old'. He argues vampires are not evil by nature: if they cannot control their hunger they are pitied rather than blamed (though we remain Aristotle-responsible for choosing to become addicted), and consensual, non-lethal feeding is no worse than mortals eating animals, since the bite only becomes murder by choice. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, he uses Furley and Nussbaum's deprivation view - death vindictively empties our long-term projects like marriage or a career - so vampiric immortality genuinely preserves value, while the standard boredom objection fails because there are repeatable pleasures in a changing world. The thought experiment ends as moral psychology for mortals: since neither of us will become a vampire, live a life that would be worthy of eternity.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 20 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Tedesco dissects what the double-0 'license to kill' could actually mean, ruling out self-defense and mere on-the-job killing and concluding that Bond is a state-sanctioned assassin who earned his status through two assassinations in Casino Royale. He tests that status against Kant's categorical imperative - persons as ends in themselves, though Kant also defended capital punishment as respecting the murderer's choice - and against consequentialism, which vindicates Bond's elimination of Kananga but stumbles on the surgeon's organ-harvesting dilemma. Because ordinary morality mixes duty-based and consequence-based intuitions, the chapter leaves Bond's moral status genuinely open and links it to live policy debates on assassination and torture after 9/11, including Britain's Intelligence Services Act that leaves room for a real-life double-0 agent.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 23 "13 - Don’t Talk to Me" — Pitt argues the iPod is 'pernicious' not because technology is intrinsically bad — a device is judged by the uses it is put to and their consequences — but because its consequences are antisocial: silent subways, 'brainsnatched' beach-walkers, and the silenced graduate corridor where loud philosophical argument used to live. Comparing the gadget to Huxley's soma (each user programs his own blissful isolation, going so far as to avoid domestic conflict by plugging back in), he contends social skills — argument, eye contact, advocacy for ideas — are what drive both technological innovation (even Steve Jobs had a co-inventor) and functioning democracy. Hence the earbud habituation summarized as 'Don't talk to me, I'm listening to MY music!' is, he claims, one of the final nails in the coffin of the social skills a civil, democratic society needs.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 14 "“Sometimes You Just Have to Bow to the Absurd”" — Eberl weighs genetic enhancement and cloning through Trek's test cases: Julian Bashir's parents' enhancement leaves him feeling 'a fraud' ('You used to be my father. Now, you're my architect'), the Moab IV 'Masterpiece Society' breeds out 'the unknown, self-discovery, things that make life worth living', and the Jem'Hadar show desire itself engineered for control. He argues the right to an open future constrains designing children (B'Elanna's wish to de-Klingonize her baby, Worf pressuring Alexander), defends genetic treatment while rejecting genetic determinism, and uses Kass and Rovane with Picard and Shinzon, the Mariposa clones, and Trip's clone Sim to show clones are numerically distinct persons. Against Malik's Augments quoting Nietzsche — 'mankind is something to be surpassed' — the chapter argues the Übermensch demands self-mastery through philosophy, not eugenic engineering, tracing eugenics from Plato's Guardian breeding scheme through Buck v. Bell to modern prenatal selection.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 7 "Transformers and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction frames the volume around First Contact with a robotic civilization: citing SETI's Seth Shostak, they argue aliens are more likely to be AI machines than little green men, with the Autobot-Decepticon civil war catching humans in between on a moral as well as physical plane. They pose the book's questions about Optimus Prime and Megatron: whether Transformers have moral status and minds despite passing the Turing Test, whether they have souls and are capable of Platonic or erotic love, and what makes Optimus the same being whether robot or vehicle. Probing Transformer nature, they conclude, is really probing human nature, since Transformers are our own creations.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 9 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Hall predicts what real alien Transformers would be like: any starfaring civilization is at least Kardashev Type 1 and would send nanotechnological, shape-shifting robots rather than biological explorers, since minds upload into machine bodies and colonies go all-robot. He proposes a logarithmic 'Hall scale' of ethics, arguing that interstellar cooperation requires Level 10 morality whose expanding inclusiveness would give visitors enough concern for indigenous species to leave Earth as a nature preserve, since robots need only the matter and energy of Mercury and the outer planets, not our biosphere.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 20 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Arp defines personhood through five capacities (rationality, robust mental states, genuine language rather than information transmission, social relationships, and free autonomous action) and argues Transformers meet them all: Bumblebee's homing-signal syllogism, Frenzy's Air Force One hack, Megatron's curses when foiled, and Optimus's fatherly bond with Sam. A thought experiment of gradually replacing a man's brain, then body, with silicon shows that cognitive capacities, not carbon, make a person, so deceiving Decepticons are morally responsible persons who deserve blame and 'robot jail' rather than the scrapping reserved for mindless machines.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 28 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Koepsell accepts that Autobots are virtuous and Decepticons vicious, then asks whether ethical war-bots are even possible, using the military's autonomous-weapons program, Asimov's Three Laws, and a kitten-sensing washing machine to argue that designed-in 'ethics' is only the designer's morality, like A Clockwork Orange's conditioned Alex, because it involves no real choice. Searle's Chinese Room and Turing's test then cast doubt on whether any mind, even our own, makes genuinely free choices, so he concludes that the appearance of virtue - behavior that reliably works - is all we ever have for humans or Autobots alike, and we should build machines as well as Optimus Prime and Bumblebee.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 14 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Yuen reads the silver guillotine of intercision against infant circumcision: both cut unconsenting children as acts of faith, Mrs. Coulter's belief that severing dæmons prevents original sin mirroring the Abrahamic covenant of Genesis 17. Deploying W.K. Clifford's shipowner ('It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence') and Hume's claim that belief is an involuntary feeling no will can command, he argues that the real moral fault lies in acting on uninvestigated beliefs in ways that harm others, while Mrs. Coulter's non-consensual experiments on kidnapped children are wrong independently of what she believes. He concludes that if cutting Pantalaimon from Lyra is wrong, circumcision is wrong for the same reasons though less severely, at worst as irresponsible as exposing a child to chicken pox.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 14 "Questioning the Question" — Hartung takes Ross's snapping reply to Armitage's repeated 'Why are you helping me?' in Armitage the Third: Poly-Matrix as a misreading: she wants a practical reason for his choice, not theoretical evidence, and since no evidence can prove an android is a person, William James's 'Will to Believe' applies — Ross's belief in her moral standing is a live, forced, and momentous genuine option (suspending judgment means she is scrapped, and losing her means losing a possible life together), so his passions may legitimately decide. He contrasts this with evidentialist cases where suspending judgment is right (the shuttle company skipping inspection; Dr. Asakura's silicon-based-life hypothesis) and with Pascal's Wager, reading Mars's church-empty, hedonistic culture of sex-tourism Seconds as one that denies genuine options and so kills Thirds. The attached original screenplay 'Eye Am,' a sequel to Magnetic Rose, extends the theme as salvage officer Nadine Beckner is lured by the AI Eva/Sam impersonating her dead husband Heintz, with Schrodinger-style observer-affected reality deciding which version becomes real.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 26 "Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign" — Lewis defends the Cybermen: using the 'Genesis of the Daleks' dilemma he shows the Doctor reasons like a Kantian duty ethicist — refusing to kill innocent proto-Daleks whatever the consequences — rather than a utilitarian, and that performing bad actions does not make an agent evil. After the Mondas, Lumic, and Morrison origins establish that Cybermen seek to cure pain and death, he argues the Doctor's 'good to strive for but bad to achieve' argument in 'Age of Steel' is invalid, and that upgrading would be morally acceptable — an applied-ethics fix — if the Cybermen obtained informed consent and respected human autonomy instead of forcing conversions.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 76 "Sure I Deceived You, but What about Me" — Classifies Bob Arctor's undercover drug enforcement, Quail's covert action in 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale,' and Quaid's HUMINT work as species of spying — one party manipulating or dominating another, as James McCargar's secret-war tradecraft describes. It asks how manipulation is actually done, answering that the manipulator finds weaknesses and links desired behaviors to them, and turns the moral question back on the deceivers themselves.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 77 "Finding a Lever for Manipulation" — Explains the spy tradecraft acronym MISE (Money, Ideology, Sex, Ego) and walks through 'Fred's' recruitment method in A Scanner Darkly — building trust through drug purchases under false pretenses until the mark must betray another confidant for Fred's benefit. The same template covers Lori, Harry, and Hauser in Total Recall, for whom Quaid 'becomes nothing more than a means': monitoring his return to Mars, or locating the rebel leadership.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 81 "Like People, Like Organizations" — Extends the moral-damage analysis one level up: organizations develop their own moral personas, and the LAPD's compartmentalization — where 'Fred' may be spying on fellow detectives and is required to lie to his supervisor 'Hank' — normalizes law-breaking in the name of law enforcement. It argues that society's oversight, the intelligence committees created after the Pike and Church hearings, is the 'bullet-proof vest' allowing risky utilitarian spying to continue without corroding everyone involved.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 82 "Chapter 12 - Grow, My Dears, the Eugenicist Said" — Opens the eugenics part with Flow My Tears' Jason Taverner — a beautiful, charismatic, fast-healing 'six' from an abandoned government breeding program, 'not a Nexus-Six, but not unlike one either.' Defining eugenics through the dog-and-wolf contrast in selective breeding, it notes that the 'eu' (good) in eugenics smuggles in an ethical judgment, and poses the part's driving question: who decides what counts as a 'good' or 'bad' trait, and by what right?
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 83 "The Bad" — Faces the Nazi elephant in the room — the sixes' program terminated in 1943 'politically,' mirroring real eugenics in California — and dismisses reductio ad Hitlerum as fallacious while conceding eugenics' genuinely darker side in Tidman's sterilization bill, which halves the novel's black population each generation. It tests Nicholas Agar's parent-choice 'liberal eugenics' against sex-selective abortions and the widening rich-poor gap, before asking whether bred children should be seen as competitors or as successors to whom we give every opportunity.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 84 "The Good" — Makes the case for eugenics' good side through Jason's uncontroversially desirable traits, invoking Nietzsche's call to 'give birth to a dancing star' and create superhuman successors as a moral philosophy of human improvement. It then probes the limits — beauty is relative (Japan's yaeba), and screening would have lost Van Gogh and Stephen Hawking — before weighing Dick's own compassion for small lives (the electric toad, the avenged cat of 'The Alien Mind,' the potter Mary Anne Dominic) against the blunt statistical claim that healthier, more capable lives go better.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 85 "The Ugly" — Argues eugenics forces us to discard the 'noble lie' of egalitarian democracy we teach children for their own good, and shows the cost in Jason and Heather's contempt for 'ordinaries,' Jason's aging-obsessed narcissism, and the 'aristocratic values' that let him condemn his lover Heather to a labor camp without qualm. Police general Felix Buckman, demoted for compassion toward labor-camp inmates and later assassinated for criticizing the regime, embodies the democratic values the sixes' elitism destroys, with Marvel's X-Men as the analogy for a fractured next-generation humanity.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 86 "And the Next Step" — Surveys science fiction's next-step humanity — Wells's genetically stratified future, Stapledon's successions of human forms, and the Campbell-era optimism Dick resisted — then turns to contemporary 'posthumanist' theorists like Donna Haraway who want 'human,' 'natural,' and 'gender' fluidly redefined. Dick emerges as the voice of caution in this cross-pollination: expand the definition of what human means, but not at the cost of the compassion and empathy that make us human.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 118 "Chapter 18 - Replicating Morality" — John Sullins's introduction frames evil in Dick as the absence of empathy, noting that in Blade Runner the Voigt-Kampf test exists only because the Tyrell Corporation's replicants mimic every human trait except empathetic response. It argues that Roy Batty and Rachel cross a threshold that puts them in moral parity with humans (Roy's love of life extending to his would-be killer, Rachel and Deckard in love) while many human characters devolve, and poses the chapter's question: what gives a human, robot, or alien moral personhood?
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 122 "How to Build a Moral Robot" — This section draws design morals from Dick's warnings: machines built as ersatz humans deny the value of being human, robotic sexual partners are doomed deceptions (the novel's Deckard-Rachael encounter is the case study), and a genuine artificial moral agent needs empathy 'logically equivalent to agape,' though a machine reasoning on sound moral principles could still count as a limited moral agent with proportionate rights and responsibilities. The Three Stigmata's Palmer Eldritch, returned from deep space as a machine treating humans as resources, shows that the netherward pull toward machinehood threatens humans themselves.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 11 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — A palliative-care bioethicist dissects the 'Gray Matter' family meeting, arguing Skyler's ambush coerces Walt's autonomy through an implied threat of emotional isolation, while Walt Jr.'s honest 'I'm pissed off!' and Marie's defense of his choice are non-coercive. The chapter frames the issue with Kant's ideal of choice free from emotion and circumstance and Mill's insistence that even self-destructive decisions are beyond legitimate coercion, and indicts doctors too for 'selling' futile treatment rather than admit mortality. The verdict: Walt accepted chemotherapy through 'autonomous beneficence' - a freely made sacrifice for his son - so Skyler's manipulation was unethical even though the decision it produced was genuinely his own.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 25 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Answers Walt's claim that drug laws are arbitrary by separating legality from morality and defending objective moral principles, chief among them do-no-harm and a 'clear-headedness principle' obligating us to shun mind-clouding substances - a principle it attributes to thinkers from the Buddha to Kant while borrowing Aristotle's ideal of becoming brave, temperate, just, and wise. It sorts drugs by whether they cloud the mind rather than medical-versus-recreational, weighing coffee, Hank's cigars and homebrew, Skyler's cigarettes, and meth's 1200-percent dopamine spike (Spooge's neglected kid in 'Peekaboo'). Verdict: meth use is straightforwardly immoral, and therefore so are selling and cooking it - meeting Douglas Husak's challenge to actually give reasons for condemnation.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 26 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Asks what exactly makes a meth cook a 'bad guy' and finds the line hard to draw: Walt forces no one to use, so like tobacco farmers and gun makers he merely enables self-harm - yet Saul's proposed prison shanking and Walt's order to murder Gale show culpable enabling without direct harm. Gale's libertarian purity argument ('they're getting exactly what they pay for') and Prohibition economics even suggest that on utilitarian grounds skilled cooks might do less harm than worse ones, though the industry as a whole remains indefensible. The chapter's moral center is Jane's death - Walt's monstrous 'standing by' - and the closeness effect that makes the personal Krazy-8 murder feel worse than the gas; it concludes the good-guy/bad-guy frame itself fuels the failed war on drugs.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 21 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Nicolas Michaud treats Watson's 2011 defeat of Jennings and Rutter as evidence for Turing's test: had Watson's answers come from behind a door we would have judged them intelligent, and its goofy misses ('What is Toronto?????') reflect missing context, not missing thought, no more damning than a child's honest error. Against Searle's Chinese Room he deploys the systems reply - you plus the Big Book of Rules might be the thing that understands - and argues that nobody, human or machine, can meet Searle's impossible burden of proving understanding, since Watson can define words, associate connotations, and pick Jeopardy! out from not-Jeopardy!. Quoting Locke's definition of a person as a thinking being that can consider itself as itself, he concludes Watson approaches personhood and that we had better teach our 'intelligent offspring' kindness and fairness before they learn anything else.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 16 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Massimo Pigliucci reads Rise as a Greek tragedy of hubris and asks whether Will Rodman dosing his father with ALZ-112 was wrong, first dissolving the 'it's unnatural' objection and probing the cure/enhancement border with Daniels's Peter-and-Johnny growth-hormone case, vaccination-as-enhancement, and Eubulides's bald-man paradox. He then runs the decision through three ethical theories: Millian consequentialism condemns it by its results (his father dies and humanity goes extinct, though chimp happiness might outweigh that), Kant's humanity formula condemns using his father as an unconsenting experimental subject, and Aristotelian virtue ethics vindicates Will's compassion and courage - Pigliucci's own view, since sometimes our best is just not enough. He closes by rejecting Baylis and Robert's technological-inevitability thesis (we abandoned the Concorde, CFCs, and nuclear weapons before) and lets Jacobs's plunge into San Francisco Bay stand as the penalty for market hubris.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 26 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Michael Ruse reads the 1968 film as a study in forbidden knowledge: Dr. Zaius has sealed the cave of human artifacts because he knows a prior human civilization destroyed itself and fears the knowledge could cause a repetition. Weighing nuclear weapons, recombinant DNA, bird-flu research, and data-driven political manipulation, Ruse argues Zaius's censorship is both impossible and undesirable, since the search for knowledge is intrinsically valuable and containment only increases the need for research. The film's deeper lesson is evolutionary: intelligence and sociality co-evolved only to the level 'good enough,' so any species that acquires weapons of mass destruction will likely destroy itself, meaning the Planet of the Apes scenario would recur across the universe.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 28 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Lori Gruen uses Taylor's cage and Caesar's confinement in Rise to examine real chimpanzee captivity in research labs and sanctuaries, asking whether captivity wrongs apes even when it causes no physical or psychological suffering. Against the view that autonomy requires language-grade self-endorsement, she argues chimpanzees are autonomous: they make choices, deceive (Tristan's false alarm call among the vervets), follow social norms, and set things right (Sheba returning Sarah's book), so denying them freedom is itself a wrong, as Caesar's 'Am I a pet?' moment shows. Since wild habitat is vanishing, she concludes the best we can do is captive care that respects apes' wild dignity and lets them come as close to feeling at home as captivity allows.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 15 "Psych and Philosophy" — Guidry-Grimes treats Chief Vick's hiring of Shawn as a genuine problem in applied ethics rather than a joke: the Psi hypothesis fails Ockham's Razor and no controlled study supports paranormal ability, yet Vick - unlike viewers who know Shawn is a fraud - must weigh her obligations to victims, the department, and taxpayers on the evidence she has. The chapter argues that hiring Shawn is ethically defensible given his record of solving over fifty unsolvable cases, but it catalogues the costs: false hope for distraught families (Marc Klaas's resentment of psychic tipsters), damage to Lassiter's morale, wasted resources, and the fragile public trust bound up with taxpayer money. The conclusion is a compromise: Vick is ethically required to use every tool in the arsenal, including a successful 'psychic,' only in desperate high-stakes cases where the victim's family does not object, and otherwise merely permitted.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 10 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Judith Andre uses the show's cases - Alicia's overnight prison visit to Peter for case information in 'Conjugal', snatching evidence before the police in 'Hi', Kalinda's inadmissible but coercive evidence in 'Heart', and Will's advice to use perjured testimony in 'Long Way Home' - to ask whether the profession's zealous advocacy actually serves justice. She explains the adversary system's two-level defense (each side's pursuit of victory supposedly forces truth out, mirroring sport) and its weaknesses: money decides outcomes, and no one in the courtroom is responsible for the truth, as the buried Childs tapes in 'Hybristophilia' show. Individual liberty against state power justifies criminal defense at most, and she endorses David Luban's sober conclusion that the system is justified yet 'cannot mandate lawyers to cut throats', with Alicia remaining the show's uneasy, unreconciled conscience.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 11 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Jai Galliott takes the Season Three episode 'Whiskey Tango Foxtrot', in which Nevada-based drone operator Sergeant Elkins kills twelve Afghan civilians and is convicted of murder despite Alicia's scapegoating defense, as a case study in the ethics of drone warfare. Tracing just war theory from the Mahabharata through Augustine to Aquinas's jus ad bellum and jus in bello framework, he applies proportionality and discrimination to the strike and argues that sensor limits and the physical and emotional distance of push-button killing (Grossman's spectrum from knife combat to drones) erode operators' capacity for discriminate targeting. He concludes that drones are a moral hazard but a legitimate asset, and that blame must be apportioned among operator, manufacturer, and commanders rather than dumped on Elkins alone.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 19 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Da Silva asks what Nucky deserves for bringing the thirteen-year-old Gillian to the Commodore and failing to stop the rape, and whether Jimmy - whose very existence depends on that wrong - is entitled to blame him and to ally with the worse man. Working through the doing, enabling, and allowing harm distinction with euthanasia and Good Samaritan cases, degrees of blame, and Parfit's point about collective action, he argues Nucky did wrong but likely less wrong than the Commodore, while Jimmy can blame on his mother's behalf and need not regret a birth that was still good for him - against Benatar's antinatalism. Jimmy's coup fails him, but the moral reason behind it, Nucky's contribution to the rape, was genuine.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 22 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Pless asks whether Bender is responsible for his misdeeds given that MomCorp designed him to be an alcoholic kleptomaniac (revealed through Bender Vision in 'Mother's Day') and Planet Express regularly orders him into morally dirty work. Against Asimov's utilitarian Three Laws - embodied by the servile, selfless Robot 1-X of 'Obsoletely Fabulous' - Futurama's 'robot subjectivism' makes every robot a self-interested agent, and Bender's autonomy is proven by his refusal of Mom's 'kill all humans' order and by his fear of punishment in Robot Hell ('Hell Is Other Robots'), which also shows the show's universe is not morally relativist. Because Bender can rewrite his own code - his unprogrammed friendship with Fry, the adoption scam that turns heartfelt in 'The Cyber House Rules' - he sits on the same sliding scale of moral agency as humans, so if Bender can break his programming, we have no excuse for not exercising our own free will.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 11 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Chaib reads Craig Venter's 2010 synthetic bacterium 'Synthia' as a real-world Victor Frankenstein and tests it against Habermas's The Future of Human Nature, which condemns liberal eugenics because turning reproduction into manufacture undermines moral equality, rights, and autonomy - the same irresponsible isolation that made Victor abandon his creature and doom Justine. Rousseau and Thomas More supply the counter-program: hunger persists through unequal property ('This is mine'), not scarcity, so improving the human heart and social structures beats Venter's engineered fixes. Frankenweenie - where pets reanimated without love turn evil while Victor's beloved Sparky saves the town - lands the chapter's Arendtian moral that 'to live' is always plural (inter homines esse), so creators must care about their creations' relations with others.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 13 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Jacquette treats Frankenstein as the modern myth of scientific overreach whose two-century grip on pop culture (over a thousand films, Frankenberry cereal) rests on three stitched-together ingredients: Enlightenment faith in applied science, the mortality-awareness of the logician's 'All men are mortal,' and Prometheus-style retribution for challenging nature - while insisting Shelley's tale is science fiction, not supernatural. Victor's real crime is not daring science but abandoning his nameless creation to raise itself, so that 'if he had taken appropriate care of the monster he made, he might not have made such a monster.' The chapter closes with Wittgenstein's remark (Philosophical Investigations §261) that philosophy ends in the wish to 'emit an inarticulate sound,' matched to the Creature's ultimate question 'What was I?' answered only with groans, as Igor's hunting horn fades over the credits of Young Frankenstein.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 16 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Kokotz casts Victor as a pioneer of human 'enhancement' whose eight-foot daemon - stronger, faster, smarter, kinder, and vegetarian - actually achieved his goal of perfecting the human body, yet whose hideous appearance locked him out of society and love, twisting success into catastrophe: the 'Midas problem' of getting exactly what you wished for. Victor's deeper error was trusting Mill's On Liberty test that what people actually desire is thereby desirable; desires come from the human mind rather than nature, so a desired enhancement can make things worse, as the daemon's revenge on William, Henry, and Elizabeth proves. The lesson is institutional as well as conceptual: science must not proceed behind closed doors but under shared ethical oversight, since a Frankensteinian breakthrough carries too much responsibility for any single scientist to bear.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 23 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Galliott treats Frankenstein as the template for blaming lethal autonomous robots: Victor alone created his creature, but today's 'frankennovation' - Ronald Arkin's 'ethical governor' algorithms, DARPA funding, degree programs in robot warfare, and the South African robotic cannon that killed nine spectators - distributes responsibility across engineers, educators (Victor's father and Professors Krempe and Waldman, who never properly warned him about Agrippa's 'sad trash'), universities, and the military-industrial complex. Yet Shelley's articulate, Paradise Lost-quoting monster is a rational, intentional killer who can be held morally responsible and even punished, as Rob Sparrow demands of machines. Because responsibility does not dilute with numbers - two murderers do not get half a life sentence each - the chapter concludes that everyone in the chain, and all of us who do nothing to stop it, shares the blame for monstrous creations.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 38 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — John Karavitis uses Dean Koontz's series, in which Victor Helios/Frankenstein engineers a 'New Race' lacking free will and empathy, to test the bioethics of human enhancement: Michael Sandel's bioconservative Case against Perfection condemns enhancements that bypass effort and agency - performance-enhancing drugs, off-label Ritalin and growth hormone, designer children - as a 'Promethean aspiration to remake nature' that destroys human nature. Allen Buchanan's bioprogressive reply that evolution's blind tinkering can be safely improved upon is challenged by the bonobo/chimpanzee contrast, dogs versus wolves, and Belyaev's tame silver foxes, all showing that small genetic changes cascade into large behavioral and physical ones. Since behavior defines morality, the chapter concludes that genetically remaking ourselves risks remaking morality itself, ending in Koontz's posthuman world where 'efficiency equaled morality' and inefficiency was the only sin.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 8 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction argues that Crichton was doing philosophy rather than science: he imagined a possibility and probed its range because it could not be tested. It frames the whole book around Malcolm's question of whether we should, not whether we can, and around the gap between what we can do and what we should do with technologies like de-extinction. It connects the film to our illusion of control, insisting there are no ghosts or magic here, only nature, and that forgetting how edible we are turns us into 'bloody smears on the teeth of a T. rex'.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 14 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — A pub dialogue applies Aristotle's De Anima, where the soul is the first principle of living things, to cloning: since a living clone must have an emergent, unrepeatable soul, successfully cloning dinosaurs brings new life into existence, which is good, so cloning itself is ethical. It then argues that neither unguided natural selection nor a divine dragon-slayer who nonetheless allowed cloning technology gives us reason not to revive dinosaurs, against Malcolm's 'they had their shot'. But drawing on Plato's forms, it condemns Hammond for controlling rather than merely containing: the lysine contingency and enforced sterility leave the dinosaurs shadows of what they could be, denied their natural flourishing.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 37 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Jannelle Poetzsch introduces Hans Jonas's imperative of responsibility - 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life' - through Malcolm's charge that scientists never ask whether they should, since nuclear and genetic power now reach people no old 'love thy neighbor' ethic could imagine. Hammond is Bacon's 'knowledge is power' grown too successful: his 'thintelligence' embodies the gap between the power to act and the ability to foretell, so Jonas demands humility, worst-case rather than optimistic planning, and social institutions strong enough to check people who act merely because they can. Jonas also indicts capitalism's profit motive - Hammond risked his grandchildren and Costa Rican infants to manufacture a need for a dinosaur zoo - closing that the answer is not halting technology but thoughtfully restraining it, because some things cannot be re-caged.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 14 "Girls and Philosophy" — Greene constructs the conditions of a 'legitimate spoiler' - the thing cannot be too old (with never-expiring exceptions like Darth Vader being Luke's father, Snape killing Dumbledore, and the Planet of the Apes reveal), cannot be common knowledge (Anne Boleyn's beheading, the Titanic hitting the iceberg), and must be significant rather than mundane. Applying them, he concludes Girls cannot be conventionally spoiled: nobody 'ships' Hannah and Adam the way audiences shipped Ross and Rachel, because the show's plot turns are mere backdrop for its conversations and meltdowns. The only true way to spoil Girls is to reveal its hilariously written lines in advance.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 24 "Girls and Philosophy" — Wible asks whether the workplace abuse in Girls - Hannah's two unpaid intern years, the harassment at the law firm, the 30-day e-book deadline that triggers her OCD, Marnie hostessing at a gentlemen's club - is defensible by young workers' inexperience and the 'experience paradox.' Against the boot-camp defense he argues from the meaning of work (Gini's 'I work, therefore I am,' Schumacher's good work) and from Marx on alienation from the products of labor, but his core standard is Kant's: persons must be treated as ends, never merely as means, which the editor who wants the book and not the person violates. He concludes that young workers' vulnerability (no savings, no leverage, reluctance to blow the whistle) warrants paid internships, transparency, and two-way respect.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 32 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Staging a modified Turing Test in which the author interrogates BMO about Football, Bubble, her broken egg, her glitch and the Mo Co factory, the chapter asks whether her answers display human-like intelligence or merely a machine's 'pretend' intelligence. Beemo's evasions about emotion ('I felt like crying') become the pivot for asking whether anyone can define feeling beyond the words they were taught for it, since we are told as children that crying means sadness. Turing's conversational test is then weighed against our bias that a boxy Gameboy cannot really think - you are, the author notes, proof that arranged matter can love and feel - and the chapter closes on the ethics of the question: Princess Bubblegum's hacksaw shows that convenience is exactly the criterion we must never use to deny personhood, as slaveholders once did.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 11 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Mahon reads Jobs's 'reality distortion field'—the phrase Apple engineer Bud Tribble borrowed from the illusion-casting Talosians of Star Trek's 'The Cage' and 'The Menagerie'—through the ethics of deception. He argues that unlike the Talosians' non-consensual illusions (trapping Captain Pike to breed slaves), Jobs mostly changed people's beliefs about what was possible rather than deceiving them, often believed his own claims (even about his cancer), and sometimes freed people from false beliefs as the 1984 'Big Brother' Macintosh ad dramatized, so the field that produced the 'insanely great' Stevenotes, the impossible Macintosh schedule, and Dilbert's Dogbert parody needed little moral justification—and made Jobs's revolutionized industries possible.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 14 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Munkittrick argues that because personhood cannot be defined (trait lists like 'long-term planning' are circular) and behavior cannot prove an inner mind—as Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment shows—people have always identified persons intuitively, and Pixar trained Millennials to do exactly that. He reads the Pixar canon in three stages: Toy Story's self-aware Buzz as nascent non-human personhood, the Human-as-Partner films (Ratatouille's Remy and Linguini, WALL-E and EVE, Monsters, Inc.'s Sully and Boo, Up's Carl and Dug) as mutual recognition of persons across species lines, and The Incredibles as showing that even enhanced 'super-humans' face otherization—so a generation primed by these films will accept AI, animals, and uplifted beings as bearers of rights.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 25 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Iuliano asks whether it even makes sense to blame Apple (not Tim Cook or the board) for the Foxconn suicides, child labor, pollution, or tax evasion, laying out the two conditions of moral agency—autonomy and the capacity to know right from wrong—via the blameless wasp. He then canvasses the corporate moral agency debate: Peter French's Corporate Internal Decision structures, which filter employees' personal reasons into corporate ones (the dividend example), and List and Pettit's functionalist group agency, whose judgment-aggregation paradox (three executives, an environmentally friendly but harmful factory) shows Apple's moral conclusions can diverge from every member's—against Quinton's 'sum of its parts' reduction—so holding the corporation itself responsible plugs the responsibility deficit left when no individual is blameworthy.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 21 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Tim Aylsworth uses Dennis's boat speech - women will not refuse him 'because of the implication' that things might go wrong for them out on the open ocean - to build the necessary and sufficient conditions of sexual consent. Working through Gang cases (Dee and the high-schooler, Lil' Kev the apparently intellectually disabled boyfriend, the Waitress's MDMA black-out asking 'Did you rape me last night?', Dennis's milky negotiation with Margaret McPoyle while held hostage), the chapter argues that a 'yes' counts as consent only when given by fully-informed, competent moral agents in a context where they can freely express their genuine preferences. The upshot vindicates Mac's 'sounds like these women don't want to have sex with you': a fear-induced yes is no consent, as with the prisoner and the boss's secretary, because the woman's genuine preference is not to face that choice at all.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 31 "18. Sex for Dummies, Humans, and Time Lords" — Lewis argues the New Series' sexual revolution (Captain Jack, Vastra and Jenny, the Doctor's multiple marriages) teaches that any relationship between rational, autonomous, consenting adults is morally permissible. Building on John Corvino's defense of homosexual sex, he dismantles the 'unnatural means immoral' argument definition by definition (unusual, not practiced by animals, contrary to innate desire, contrary to natural purpose or divine intent, disgusting), rejects the empirical slippery slope as a fallacy, and uses Whoniverse cases - young Amelia Pond's non-autonomous choice to leave with the Doctor, the Slitheen pig as mere causal agent, manipulation that would undermine informed consent - to show that only autonomy grounds sexual morality. Objections to same-sex or human-alien relationships turn out to confuse the aesthetic ('ugly') with the ethical ('wrong').
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 32 "19. Of Downton and Drones" — Jai Galliott contrasts the roughly level killing field of WWI, in which William dies and Matthew is paralyzed in the trenches alongside aristocrats who suffered proportionally the heaviest losses, with today's drone age, in which remote pilots drawn largely from the lower and middle classes bear the burden of fighting. Tracing unmanned weapons from WWI tele-operated motorboats and the Sperry and Kettering aerial torpedoes to Reaper drones flown by a 'PlayStation generation,' he argues that radical technological asymmetry breaks Just War Theory - undermining last resort and proportionality and the mutual imposition of risk that Kahn and Sparrow make the basis of combatants' rights. He proposes that highly asymmetric force be restrained into something like international policing, while conceding, like Mrs. Patmore with her electric mixer, that nothing will stop us being dragged into the drone age.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 36 "22. Lady Edith and the Trials of the Modern Woman" — Gordon Hawkes uses Lady Edith's last-minute walk-out from the abortion clinic to stage the abortion debate: the classic anti-abortion syllogism, embryology's claim that 'Marigold once was an embryo,' and Mary Anne Warren's functional personhood criteria - echoed in Thomas's 'no bigger than a hamster' jab - which Tooley and Singer extend to infanticide on newborn George. Against the function view the chapter marshals the comatose Matthew and the sleeping Alfred, arguing that value lies in the kind of being one is, while size, development, environment, and dependency make no moral difference.
