- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 25 "The Value of Finitude" — The chapter tests each motive for uploading to San Junipero and finds it wanting: Kantian cosmic justice fails because the resort neither rewards the good nor can punish the wicked; Tolstoy's cosmic-insignificance dread fails because a finite life can still be meaningful, and even Epicurus and Lucretius deflate the fear of death (while Nagel notes death's evil lies in foreclosed possibilities, and Williams's Makropulos case warns eternal life breeds boredom). Nozick's experience machine is the closest analogy, but the chapter argues San Junipero differs — residents know it is digital and share it with other conscious people — before Nussbaum's argument lands: without finitude there is no risk, so no courage, sacrifice, or deep love, which is why Kelly's forty-nine real years with Richard outweigh forever with Yorkie.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 28 "Leo Tolstoy, Sorcerer-Defender Supreme" — The chapter pairs Strange's midlife collapse with Tolstoy's crisis in A Confession—both famous egotists who found their glittering lives 'a stupid fraud'—using Tolstoy's fable of the traveler licking honey above the dragon of death to read Strange's desperate medical questing as vain honey-licking. It lays out Tolstoy's doctrine of nonresistance: violence is forcing others against their will, every act of violent resistance multiplies evil, and the state's division of cruelty makes killing mechanical, then asks whether Tolstoy could accept Strange's metaphysical war, concluding from Tolstoy's remark that he would axe a bear to save a peasant (but not kill the highwayman) that he could endorse magical violence against Dormammu while still forbidding violence against human beings.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 10 "1. Finding the Meaning of Life in Downton Abbey" — Blessing pits Steve Jobs's 'Do What You Love' creed (and Oprah's 'follow your bliss') against Downton's world of inherited roles, where nobody from Anna to Lady Mary chooses their work. She distinguishes happiness from meaningfulness, since Matthew's war wounds and Mary's grief over his death are painful yet deeply meaningful, and tests subjectivist theories such as Nietzsche's meaning-as-passionate-process against Nozick's demand that a meaningful life leave permanent traces and Susan Wolf's hybrid 'loving objects that are worthy of love.' Kant's duty to develop one's talents rather than idle for pleasure, and Lord Grantham's self-description as 'a custodian, not an owner,' anchor the show's counter-ethos of duty over desire, embodied in Carson, Mrs. Hughes, and Mrs. Patmore's pride in unloved, socially necessary work. The chapter concludes that Downton validates hard honest work as an end in itself, challenging the narcissism of the 'holy You' and expressive individualism.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 16 "The Spice of Meaning" — Builds, in Aristotle's manner of starting from the views of the wise, a three-way comparison: the Harkonnens seek power for its own sake and hollow Dr. Yueh into an instrument, the Fremen live meaningful but suffocating lives inside unquestioned ritual identity, and the Atreides model a virtue with no formula. Duke Leto's abolition of the beggars' water-towel ritual and his politically motivated spilling of water at the dinner party show good intentions failing when they break bonds of meaning without renewing them, while Paul and Jessica break Fremen rules in ways that repair social bonds and leave a more just society. The chapter ends with the worm-rider on shifting sand as the image of a never-finished, context-sensitive struggle for meaning.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 38 "Notes" — The chapter asks why audiences relish stories of civilization's end and answers with psychology: the wasteland is Hobbes's 'nasty, brutish, and short' (raiders abducting Hank, Vault-Tec's experiments on dwellers), yet Ernest Becker's death-denial and Maslow's hierarchy of needs explain the appeal — fiction lets us confront mortality safely while watching characters meet needs for security, control, and meaning. The show's scenes carry the argument: the Vault 33 Council suppressing Lucy's search party trades freedom for safety, Maximus letting Titus bleed out reclaims control of his destiny, and Lucy's gift of life-sustaining vials to the unconscious Ghoul models hope and retained humanity. Apocalypse originally means 'an uncovering', so these narratives reveal what viewers value and let them rehearse their own endings.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 24 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Kevin Fitzpatrick uses Vivi Orunitia and the self-aware Black Mages of Final Fantasy IX, who call death 'stopping,' to ask whether the fear of death is justified, answering that death harms only insofar as it frustrates a person's values, such as Vivi's morality, his thirst for knowledge, and his care for others' happiness. He brings in Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us because the dead feel no pain, casts Necron, who wants to return all life to a painless 'zero world' because fear of death has corrupted it, as a darker Epicurean, and weighs the deprivation objection, death cheats us of future goods like Chocobo Hot and Cold, against the puzzle of when death's harm could even occur.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 9 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Henry Jacoby's introduction frames the volume around mortality: winter is coming, all men must die (valar morghulis), yet through honor, duty, and philosophy 'first we'll live' meaningful lives. Playing on Arya's mantra 'fear cuts deeper than swords,' he claims logic cuts deeper still - swords defend bodies, but logic defends our ideas, beliefs, and values - leaning on Socrates' claim that no evil can befall a good person, since the virtuous soul stands in harmony against desire and influence. He previews the essays: Hobbes as a maester, the dark side of chivalry, Robb's questionable war, Arya and Zen, and Ned's need of Machiavelli.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 18 "7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife" — Builds a dilemma from 'Existential Crisis': Michael's prospective retirement (via Todd May's Death) makes finitude look meaning-destroying, while the humans' endless existence — 802 reboots, Mindy St. Claire's eternal Cannonball Run II in the Medium Place — threatens boredom and disconnection from past selves. Testing God-free answers, it runs through Camus's Sisyphus, Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view, Susan Wolf's requirement that we love what deserves to be loved (Eleanor's philosophy study, friendship with Tahani, romance with Chidi), and John Martin Fischer on free authorship and narrative order (Eleanor's note to herself in What We Owe to Each Other). Conclusion: Eleanor and friends can lead meaningful lives even if damned and repeatedly rebooted.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 33 "18. Heaven Is Other People" — Treats the show as a theological sitcom whose afterlife (Gen's algorithmic judgment, cubicles, the Jeremy Bearimy timeline) critiques a pop-Christian eschatology of disembodied Heaven and eternal conscious torment while missing the bodily resurrection of Nicene and N.T. Wright's account. Levinas supplies the positive frame: ethics precedes ontology, the face of the Other demands responsibility before any impersonal verdict — which is why Gen's points system 'wouldn't cut it' and why the show's two-shots, Eleanor's spontaneous good acts, and Chidi's 802 yeses to teaching her matter. Bonhoeffer's religionless Christianity completes the reading of Eleanor's repentance, Donna's and Tahani's confessions, and Michael's self-sacrificing Christ figure: salvation comes through intersubjective, grace-infused transformation, so 'Heaven is other people'.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 148 "The End of the Story" — Completes the parallel: Socrates died refusing to abandon the examined life, and his martyrdom, like Dumbledore's staged death that protected Snape's spying, served the common good, since there can be no common good without individual goodness. The chapter closes with two Muggle lessons, live devoted to something larger than yourself as Lily Potter, Dumbledore, Harry, King, Gandhi, Jesus, and Socrates did, and find mentors, as Harry found Dumbledore and as readers can find in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics or Confucius.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Shores reads Volume 1 through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a self-test of life-affirmation: Adam sealed in a coffin embodies recurrence in its 'most terrible form,' Future Hiro's string map dramatizes Nietzsche's claim that every action is indissolubly tied to all others, and Linderman's speech divorcing happiness from meaning is answered by Nietzsche's demand to crave nothing more fervently than the eternal return. The chapter stresses where the show diverges: Claire insists 'the future is not written in stone' and the heroes rewrite destiny, while Arthur Petrelli ironically holds a copy of Thus Spoke Zarathustra while contradicting it. Hiro's failed attempts to save Charlie and his father (Kaito's 'we cannot play God') frame the amor fati question of whether free will means changing events or willing them eternally.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 19 "9 Homeward Bound with Indiana Jones" — Charles Taliaferro and Annalissa Lane use Gabriel Marcel's creative fidelity — being 'at home' with oneself, others, and the sacred through availability ('avec') and presence rather than treating persons as furniture — to chart Indy's growth across all four films. Willie and Indy's vanity-driven near-tryst in Temple, the partnership of convenience with Marion in Raiders, the Zeppelin reckoning with Henry Sr. ('I was less important to you than people who had been dead for 500 years'), and the honest jeep argument about the broken engagement in Crystal Skull mark stages from self-deception toward being fully present to another. The church wedding closing Crystal Skull completes the journey into openness to the sacred, showing that home is a way of being rather than a place.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 14 "Game Over" — Anna Janssen reads Zelda as a meditation on death: Link embodies the worst version of immortality, an eternal purgatory of endless resurrection for the player's benefit, while the dungeon bosses — who stay dead once defeated — are the only truly mortal, and hence most human, beings in Hyrule. Hegel's demand that man reconcile himself with mortality, Nietzsche's erosion of dualist soul-belief, and Bernard Williams's worries about the tedium of immortality frame the discussion, with Wind Waker's reincarnating hero giving the immortal-soul view its due. Turning off the console becomes a metaphor for the unknowable nothingness of death, and the series' formula and save-games a structured coping alternative to a chaotic universe.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Berk maps Fury Road onto contemporary theories of meaning in life through three characters. Nux begins a Supernaturalist — Immortan Joe is his god and Valhalla his afterlife — collapses into nihilism after the humiliating 'Mediocre!', and ends a Naturalist who gives his life meaning by sacrificing himself to collapse the thruway and block Immortan Joe's armada. Max moves from pure survival to Susan Wolf's Hybrid Naturalism (subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) when he commits to retaking the Citadel, and Furiosa, already there, embodies the film's own Objective List theory: virtue, autonomy, and relationships.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 6 "Part Five D Is for Destiny" — The editor's introduction retells her childhood memory of being left behind at a Wisconsin carnival, narrated in Lost-style 'flashback' and 'flash-sideways' segments, to argue that the show grips everyone because it stages the universal fear of being cut off from all we know and love. She calls this a philosophical fear that forces the questions 'Why am I here? Does my life matter?' and then previews the volume's five parts: time travel metaphysics (Fortune), epistemology (Origin), social and political philosophy (Unity), ethics (Necessity), and religion (Destiny).
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 15 "NOTES" — Barris argues Lost fascinates because it dramatizes the basic structures of life itself: the castaways are Heideggerian thrown into an island none of them chose, brought there by Desmond's lapse at the Swan and by interlocking backstories such as Sawyer's bar conversation with Jack's father. Against the existentialist claim (Sartre, Camus) that life is simply absurd, he uses Wittgenstein's On Certainty - doubting everything presupposes certainties - to argue life is a riddle of partial sense, which is why the show's connections between Hurley and Libby or Jack and Desmond always hint at meaning without resolving it. The finale answers only the question of life after death, leaving life after birth as open as our own.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 9 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Mussett asks whether Peter Parker's painful life counts as a good life by testing five philosophers' answers against the comics and films. Kurtz's secular humanism finds Peter wanting in pleasure and acclaim (Uncle Ben dead by his inaction, J. Jonah Jameson's smear campaigns), while Rand's Objectivism condemns Spider-Man as the embodiment of the 'morality of sacrifice' she rejected, noting Steve Ditko's Objectivist devotion. Epictetus scores Peter highly on duty but fails him on self-mastery, since his happiness hinges on attachments to Aunt May and MJ he cannot control; Frankl would see Peter's meaning in his irreplaceable responsibility, evidenced by his refusal of Dr. Judas Traveller's offer of a peaceful life at the cost of innocents (Amazing Spider-Man #402); and Aquinas vindicates Peter's suffering as good pain in a virtuous, charitable life.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 20 "10. Gods Are Overrated" — Michaud runs Hume's problem of evil against a Superman who is nearly all-powerful, all-knowing, and good yet takes dates with Lois while animals and children suffer pointlessly — and unlike God he cannot hide behind mystery, only laziness. God-like protectors breed excuses ('Superman is our great excuse' for doing nothing about homelessness or starving children), and belief in afterlife and divine rescue cheapens this life; following Nietzsche's death of God, the chapter argues we should stop believing in saviors, face the infinite night, make our own meaning, and be more like Batman — self-reliant people who try to save others themselves.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 5 "Introduction Welcome to the Psychosphere" — The editors' introduction asks why viewers willingly linger in True Detective's bleak Louisiana bayou and season two's Vinci, suggesting we may recognize something of ourselves in those worlds. It argues detectives and philosophers share the pursuit of truth, framing Rust Cohle and Marty Hart (and Velcoro and Bezzerides) as morally compromised lawmen who open the door to philosophy, invoking Socrates' 'unexamined life is not worth living.' It previews the book's coverage of pessimism, good and evil, tragedy, personal identity, and time via Socrates, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Lacan, and Zizek.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 7 "Dare to Enter the Zone" — The editors' introduction argues that The Twilight Zone made 1950s television, dismissed as an 'idiot box' and 'vast wasteland,' into a venue for thinking: Serling, like Socrates the gadfly of Athens, built episodes as thought experiments in which experts' promises unravel. Taking Nietzsche's Twilight of the Idols epigraph ('I never found anything but the apes of their ideal'), they claim the show dramatizes the gap between our ideals (friendship, justice, truth, loyalty) and our treachery, from Henry Bemis's books to 'The Hunt,' where even the Devil cannot fool a dog. We laugh at the absurd endings because we are 'the species most deserving to be laughed at.'
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 11 "3. The Short-Sightedness of Henry Bemis" — Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a tragic dilemma about freedom and dependence: Henry Bemis's wish to escape the 'cages' of the bank, his marriage, and the clock is granted by nuclear annihilation, only for loneliness and monotony to become a worse prison. The shattered glasses are not just a cruel joke but the loss of the technology connecting him to books and other minds. The chapter argues Bemis's folly is the misanthropic fantasy of excepting himself from the technological system and from dependence on others, and that our remedy is philosophical rather than technical: glasses that reveal our limits and mutual dependence.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Held asks what a god is and which gods deserve worship, using Rachels's definition (all-powerful, perfectly good, perfectly wise) to show no DC deity - dying Zeus, cruel Darkseid, creation-unmaking Parallax - qualifies, and that mere power generates fear, not the moral authority that could ground worship-worthiness or a parent-like right to command. Against the Christian campaigner Darrel Keyes, who calls Wonder Woman's cults idolatrous, he notes her gods visibly exist while his God is both unprovable and, per the Anselmian concept problem, indescribable without ceasing to be supreme. The chapter ends by relocating worship on earth: since we need orienting values whether or not gods exist, 'we could do worse than submit to the loving authority' of the justice, care, and integrity Diana embodies - pray to 'yourself, your own strength and character.'
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 33 "Hoosiers and the Meaning of Life" — Michael Peterson argues that Hoosiers is a microcosm of life's meaning: Aristotle's eudaimonia frames the characters' searches (Norman Dale rebuilding his career, Shooter his self-esteem and his bond with son Everett), and Dale's 'in my book, we're going to be winners' speech shows that character, unselfish teamwork, and playing to potential - virtue learned by doing, as coaching models moral instruction - matter more than the scoreboard against South Bend Central. The film's second chances (Principal Summers's clean slate, Whit's return, Dale's hiring of the town drunk Shooter) reveal that character alone is insufficient: mercy and forgiveness, which Hannah Arendt traces to Jesus, reframe an unchangeable past and open a future. Peterson then surveys worldviews - naturalism (Bertrand Russell's 'accidental collocations of atoms'), postmodernism (Derrida's deconstruction), Hinduism's Atman-Brahman - and argues only Christian theism, in which God's nature is love (Aquinas), can ground the character and forgiveness the film dramatizes.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 26 "Is the Gridiron Holy Ground" — Hamilton analyzes the fusion of football, patriotism, and religion (Friday Night Lights' Odessa, Super Bowl rituals) as Rousseau's 'civil religion' from the Social Contract—socially unifying but content-empty and anti-intellectual, keeping faith bifurcated from real life. Drawing on Augustine's account of virtue as 'rightly ordered love' and vice as disordered love, he argues football has been wrongly elevated above higher goods. He rejects Higgs's incompatibility thesis for a Christian worldview approach—exemplified by Tony Dungy, Lovie Smith, and Joe Ehrman's 'men for others'—that makes the gridiron holy ground.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 6 "Introduction Warm-Up" — Andy Wible's introduction argues that if Plato and Aristotle were alive they would be avid golfers, because both golf and philosophy seduce great minds with problems that look easy yet prove endlessly difficult. It frames golf as 'a Sudoku that cannot be solved' and pairs it with the eternal questions (right and wrong, who am I, beauty, God, meaning) to preview the volume's chapters. Golf becomes a vehicle for the examined life, enlivening philosophy through the lived experience of the game.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 9 "First Hole Golf and the Importance of Play" — Al Gini defends play as intrinsically valuable and essential to being human, drawing on Huizinga's three criteria of 'true play' and William James's ideal of the amateur who plays 'for the love of it.' Using his golf-obsessed father as an extended case, he shows how golf functions as a self-contained, absorbing 'refuge from ordinary life' that delivers completion, coordination, and cooperation, echoing Plato's claim in the Republic and Laws that sport forms both person and community. The chapter treats golf as an end in itself whose joy sustains a flourishing life rather than as a means to external reward.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 32 "Sixteenth Hole Golf and the Meaning of Life" — Randy Lunsford uses Annika Sorenstam's early retirement to ask what makes golf—and life—meaningful, surveying religious versus scientific accounts of purpose and E. J. Bond's claim that meaning comes from pursuing objectively valuable ends, not just satisfying desire. He tests Epicurean hedonism and Nozick's experience machine (we want to really shoot the course record, not merely feel we did), Taylor's reworking of the Sisyphus myth (meaning via injected desire), and Schopenhauer's pessimism that satisfied desire only yields boredom. He argues golf's very finitude—eighteen holes, like a mortal life—gives it meaning, so excellence, relationships, playing by the rules, and taking responsibility for each shot are what make both golf and life worthwhile.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 10 "Introduction The Love of Wisdom" — Editor David Baggett frames the collection with his own lifelong love of tennis (watching the 1980 Borg-McEnroe Wimbledon final, idolizing Borg and Gerulaitis) and argues tennis is an ideal springboard for philosophy, glossing 'philosophy' as the etymological 'love of wisdom.' He invokes Plato's idea that instances of beauty in this world make the heart ache for beauty's truest source, applying it to the sublime excellence of great play. He positions the whole book as using tennis to reach questions that matter, including the meaning of life, citing David Foster Wallace's quip that the title Tennis and the Meaning of Life is 'redundant.'
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Douglas McFarland argues that Hereafter is philosophical in Nehamas's sense of an 'art of living': its three characters (Marie, George, the boy Marcus) must fashion meaning in the face of absence and abandonment rather than settle the existence of an afterlife. He aligns their struggles with Augustine's grief over his mother's death in the Confessions, Montaigne's 'I portray not being but becoming' and his revision of Socrates' Phaedo claim that philosophy is practice for death, and Sartre's view that God's absence grounds the freedom to make meaning through work. George's turn from listening to the dead to genuinely seeing the living Marcus, and his letter to Marie, mark authentic self-fashioning in the here and now.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 7 "Introduction" — Mark Conard's introduction opens with thumbnail plots of Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, and Out of the Past to ask what noir has to do with philosophy, then frames the definitional problem (genre, style, cycle, or mood) as itself a philosophical question about essence. It surveys the volume's thirteen essays, noting that French existentialism was contemporaneous with classic noir (1941-58, Maltese Falcon to Touch of Evil) and shares its themes of moral ambiguity, reason versus passion, and pessimism even without direct influence. It previews the arguments to come, including Nietzsche's death of God as a lens on noir, neo-noir realism, Aristotelian tragedy and catharsis, and Schopenhauer's parallels in Ride the Pink Horse.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 15 "Film Noir and the Meaning of Life" — Steven Sanders uses film noir to motivate philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, reading its pessimistic sensibility (Touch of Evil, Detour, Out of the Past, D.O.A., Vertigo) as the presupposition that life is meaningless per se. He runs through Schopenhauer's pessimistic arguments from the vanity and transience of existence, Nagel's rebuttal that our not mattering in a million years does not stop things mattering now, and the tension between Sartrean existentialist freedom and noir's Freudian fatalism of the inescapable past. He then lays out three models of meaninglessness (Baier's worthlessness and purposelessness, Camus/Nagel's absurdity met with irony), reading noir protagonists as ironists, before rejecting the noir view that life must be meaningless and arguing that meaning is a matter of degree, requiring realizable projects of positive value.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 18 "Rebel without a Cause Stanley Kubrick and the Banality of the Good Patrick Murray and Jeanne Schuler" — Murray and Schuler argue Kubrick's unifying sensibility is a dogmatic Hellenistic-style skepticism (via Hume's 'The Sceptic' and Seneca) that yields 'the banality of the good': in a world of cosmic futility and near-state-of-nature human nature, decent characters like Dax are helpless while the wicked (Barry Lyndon, Alex, Quilty) have vitality. They read Kubrick's Playboy remarks on human insignificance as Humean size/duration tropes, and diagnose his Sartrean 'create your own meaning' answer as a self-refuting false philosophy. Using Marx's critique of Hegel's accommodation to capitalism, they contend Kubrick's skepticism and irony merely reflect the 'bourgeois horizon' rather than comprehending it, ending in present-pleasure hedonism ('fuck' as the last word of Eyes Wide Shut).
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 19 "The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders" — Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 22 "The Shape of Man The Absurd and Barry Lyndon Chris P. Pliatska" — Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Camus's Sisyphus and, chiefly, Nagel's distinction between conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) and philosophical absurdity (the collision of participant and external viewpoints). He argues Kubrick's painterly tableaux, slow reverse zooms, and the detached narrator force viewers from identification into an external, sub specie historiae perspective, exposing Barry's ambitions as conventionally absurd. That recognition then turns back on the audience as the inescapable philosophical absurdity of the human condition, though Pliatska finds Kubrick's tone more lamenting than Nagel's ironic equanimity.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' on television, not merely illustrates it, by ranking degrees of filmic philosophizing (via Wartenberg, Shaw, Mulhall) and showing the Whedenverse meets them. It reads Angel/Angelus and Fred/Illyria as cinematic thought experiments that generate 'metaphysical complexity' about personal identity, playing memory- and continuity-of-consciousness theories (Locke, Parfit) against a soul theory, and reads Connor's origin as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will. It contends Whedon endorses a Noddings-style ethics of care and an existentialist yet God-independent morality, epitomized by Angel's 'Epiphany' speech ('the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing') and 'Deep Down,' plus the 'Man on the Street' Academic monologue, staging a negative project against the claim that ethics is incoherent without God through the self-sacrifices of Simon, Cordelia, and Buffy.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 12 "Sherlock Holmes Artist of Reason" — McInerny argues Holmes is not a bloodless reasoning machine but an 'artist of reason' who fuses intellect with imagination ('the scientific use of imagination'). He lays out Holmes's four-stage method—fact-gathering interview and investigation, deep-thought hypothesis framing, denouement, and post-factum briefing—and notes his use of reasoning backward, reductio ad absurdum, and hypotheses over guesses. Finally he casts Holmes as a metaphysician who assumes a purposive, intelligible cosmos ('What is the meaning of it, Watson?'), a teleological order akin to Aristotle's Final End that grounds the local intelligibility Holmes exploits.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 18 "The Grim Reaper on Baker Street" — Glass-Turner examines death across the Holmes canon, opening with Kierkegaard's claim that death's explanation discloses the explainer's own inner being and pairing Holmes with TV's Dr. House as materialist puzzle-solvers who rule out the supernatural ('no ghosts need apply'). She weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the wrongness of murder, then argues Holmes's pig- and cadaver-experiments coexist with reverence for the dead and hints of belief in an afterlife ('compensation hereafter' in 'The Veiled Lodger'), reading him via William James as open to more than the physical. She closes on Holmes's calm acceptance of his own Reichenbach death and Conan Doyle's later turn to spiritualism after his wife's death.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a member of the 'cult of the cool' whose reticence and final resigned 'What's the difference?' surrender embody apatheia and acceptance of fate/logos. He tests Spencer Selby's claim that Clay and the sharpshooter Nikki must fail because their motives are immoral, arguing instead via an Aristotelian principle (virtues are stable dispositions) that their sudden lapses—the flimsy suitcase, Nikki's racial slur that loses him the lucky horseshoe—are Kubrick stacking the deck rather than genuine character. He closes by weighing Clay's life against models of a meaningful life (exuberance/romanticism vs. rationalism/self-fulfillment), faulting Clay for never subjecting his chosen ends to self-critical reason.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 23 "Vernacular Metaphysics On Terrence Malick’s The Thin Red Line" — Pippin reads Malick's The Thin Red Line as deliberately invoking then refusing Hollywood war-movie conventions (group solidarity, trackable characters, heroic assault) so the viewer is left 'lost' and forced toward a metaphysical rather than political or sentimental reckoning with death. Through unattributed poetic voice-overs—Train's Manichean questions, Witt's search for the calm 'immortality' he saw in his dying mother, Welsh's cynicism, Bell's romantic idealism—and lingering non-plot shots of nature bathed in sunlight, the film pursues a 'vernacular metaphysics': ordinary soldiers straining ordinary speech to ask what it is to live under certain death. Pippin aligns this disclosive, prediscursive truth of the image with the Hegel-to-Heidegger-Merleau-Ponty tradition of art as truth-bearer, while Witt's Emersonian 'one big soul' and his self-sacrifice ('all things shining') stage the film's unresolved question of whether nature and death can be seen as good.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 25 "“Profoundly Unreconciled to Nature” Ecstatic Truth and the Humanistic Sublime in Werner Herzog’s War Films" — LaRocca argues against Thomas Weiskel that the 'humanistic sublime' is not an oxymoron, using Herzog's war films (Lessons of Darkness, Little Dieter Needs to Fly, Rescue Dawn) to show a sublime that returns us to the human at the limit of existence rather than transcending it. Building on Kant's link between the sublime and human dignity—and Kant's claim that sublimity lies in our ideas, not in nature—he reads Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' (fabrication that exceeds the 'accountant's truth') as the vehicle: staged monologues, borrowed music, and recontextualized documentary footage disclose an inner reality. Herzog's Heideggerian gloss on aletheia as un-concealment aligns cinema itself with truth, and Dengler's bear ('the only friend I had was death') exemplifies war as the space of radical mortality where the humanistic sublime dawns for the safe spectator, contrasted with Malick's more Darwinian, nature-indifferent vision.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 13 "A.I. Artificial Intelligence and the Tragic Sense of Life" — Dunn interprets A.I. as a meditation on the 'tragic sense of life': treating David as a person, he argues the film dramatizes three doomed human desires (love, uniqueness, immortality) and tests two failed escapes from mortality, science (Professor Hobby, the Flesh Fair, David's suicide leap) and religious faith (the fraudulent Blue Fairy at drowned Coney Island). Defending the maligned finale, he reads the simulated Blue Fairy and the one-day resurrection of Monica as raising whether a perfect simulation of love can be 'real enough,' with David achieving a sober humanistic acceptance of impermanence.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 14 "5. Could Hell Be Any Worse than Doc Benton’s Immortality" — Hellwig uses Dean's choice of Hell over Doc Benton's organ-replacement immortality in 'Time Is on My Side' to examine medical immortality. He pairs Dean's worry—that maiming and replacing your body makes you unrecognizably human—with Bernard Williams's Makropulos argument that immortality ends in categorical-desire-exhausting boredom, adding a third condition to Williams: a recognizably human life requires being able to self-identify with one's own body, illustrated by real disfigurement cases and Aubrey de Grey's biogerontology.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 21 "11. Why Sacrifice Yourself" — Browning interrogates the nobility of the Winchesters' repeated self-sacrifice, asking whether their deals (Dean's soul for Sam, John's soul for Dean) are selfless or selfish—driven by codependency, fear of being alone, and ego. He weighs utilitarian justification (sacrificing one who saves the world) against the trickster's 'Mystery Spot' lesson that 'nothing good comes' of it, and invokes Kant's notion of a true gift expecting nothing in return, alongside Milbank on life-as-gift, to question whether self-sacrifice is the 'ultimate ethical agent' when death isn't final.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 23 "12. Finally Free" — McCrossin argues Supernatural is a rare popular treatment of the theological (not merely secular) problem of evil, with Dean's rant echoing Job and the Book of John's Lazarus (why does God let good people suffer, and why withhold guidance?). Tracing the four showrunner 'eras' as a theodicy incubator, he reads Cas's consolation—life is an obstacle course whose obstacles Chuck may have designed but whose race 'we' ran—through Kant on freedom under determinism, concluding the show's novel theodicy is that meaning comes from being the storytellers of our own lives once Chuck stops writing them.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar, Six, Adama and Roslin to debate God's existence and meaning. Against Baltar's scientific naturalism they present Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, first cause, and the argument from design applied to the universe's ordered laws) and dismiss Pascal's Wager as insincere, like Baltar's. They then raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will defense and Hick's soul-making theodicy against Hume's faulty-architect analogy. Finally, contrasting Russell's meaning-amid-a-godless-cosmos with religious faith, they argue atheism need not entail nihilism and that survival and human solidarity give the Colonials common ground.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" — Jonathan and Jerry Walls read Harry Potter's Deathly Hallows through the question of death and afterlife. Harry's willing death-march models Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. At King's Cross the maimed Voldemort-soul embodies William James's 'sow a character, reap a destiny': having refused remorse, he has become evil beyond repair, whereas the repentant Dumbledore has grown. Against Heidegger's atheism, Rowling's Christian resurrection imagery, backed by Locke on memory-identity, Kant, and Pascal, makes our character-forming choices infinitely consequential.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Henry Jacoby argues that despite House's line that we are 'selfish, base animals crawling across the Earth,' House lives a meaningful life. Rejecting God-, soul-, and afterlife-based meaning (House's Euthyphro-style objections and his '97 Seconds' near-death experiment), Jacoby locates meaning in the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason as humanity's proper function. House's relentless curiosity and puzzle-solving, tied to action and to saving lives, exemplify reason governing desire and yield eudaimonia - so 'doing things changes things,' and House, however miserable he seems, leads the examined, meaningful life.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 6 "Part Five D Is for Destiny" — This editor's introduction (Sharon Kaye) frames the whole volume by recounting a childhood memory of being lost at a carnival and using it to argue that the show taps a philosophical fear of being cut off from everything we know, forcing the viewer to confront questions like 'Why am I here?' and 'Does my life matter?' It organizes the nineteen essays under the acronym F.O.U.N.D. (Fortune/metaphysics, Origin/epistemology, Unity/social-political, Necessity/ethics, Destiny/religion), presenting Lost's plane-crash premise as an occasion for asking the meaning-of-life and fate-versus-free-will questions the survivors face.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 15 "NOTES" — Jeremy Barris argues that Lost dramatizes the structure of life itself, using Heidegger's claim that the inquirer's own being is the clue to all questions and his notion of 'thrownness' to read the castaways' accidental arrival as a mirror of our own bewildering birth into circumstances we did not make. He reframes the show's central puzzle as 'the question of life after birth,' contends against Sartre and Camus that life is neither fully sensible nor fully absurd but a half-understood riddle, and invokes Wittgenstein's On Certainty to show that total doubt is impossible because understanding senselessness presupposes understanding something.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — Brett Chandler Patterson reads Lost alongside C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia as myth rather than allegory, arguing both use a fantasy world of second chances to stage redemption in community. He aligns the castaways' violent arrival on the island with the Pevensie children's magical passage into Narnia and Edmund's betrayal-and-forgiveness arc, using the island's life-and-death setting to force existential commitment. Emmanuel Levinas's ethics of responsibility to the face of the Other and H. Richard Niebuhr's relational theology are invoked to argue that healing and faith come not individually but in communion with others.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 28 "NOTES" — Daniel B. Gallagher uses Thomas Aquinas on the knowledge of God to read the characters' searches for meaning on Lost. Aquinas's 'approaching Peter' image—recognizing a human without yet knowing it is Peter—models how everyone confusedly knows God as the object of happiness while mistaking finite goods (Jack's curing, Kate's deception, Jin's job, Charlie's brother) for the ultimate good, paralleled with the castaways staring at the unidentifiable Smoke Monster. Gallagher then applies Aquinas's sin of acedia (spiritual sloth that deems the good unattainable) to Desmond's fear over Penny and Charlie's despair before Rose tells him faith is never impossible, tying the desire for happiness to Augustine's restless heart.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 27 "15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances" — Karavitis groups twist-ending episodes into nostalgia, time-travel, and second-chance types and reads them through Kierkegaard's Either/Or distinction between the aesthetic and ethical modes of life. Living aesthetically—chasing present gratification—leads to despair, as in 'A Nice Place to Visit' (Rocky's boring 'heaven' is Hell) and 'A Game of Pool' (Jesse wins only an eternity in Limbo). Living ethically—taking responsibility and moving forward—earns a real second chance, as when 'Printer's Devil' editor Winter reclaims his soul; life must be understood backward but lived forward.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 3 "Introduction" — Jacob Held defends the philosophy-and-popular-culture project against snobbery and argues that King's horror is genuine philosophy because it forces readers to confront finitude, meaning, and their deepest values. He reads King's own account of 'existential horror' through Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian pairing, casting the horror tale as a Dionysian crack in an Apollonian order that ends by restoring equilibrium, and frames doing this fun, relatable work as its own eudaimonia poised between nihilism and Aristotelian flourishing. Using Lovecraft's Cthulhu and King's Desperation/The Regulators (Tak), he claims horror shakes us into reaffirming the values that orient us and so bridges abstract academic philosophy and lived experience.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 6 "“Sometimes Dead Is Better”" — Katherine Allen reads Pet Sematary and The Tommyknockers as bioconservative fables staging the transhumanism debate: Louis's resurrected, 'fundamentally wrong' cat Church and cannibal son Gage, and Bobbi's tooth-shedding 'New Improved' becoming, dramatize Kass, McKibben and Fukuyama's warning that erasing our limits erases our humanity. Against them she sets Nick Bostrom's 'Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant,' in which death is an unquestioned evil we should slay, and Bernard Williams's worry about the tedium of immortality. King's insistence that 'sometimes dead is better,' and that forbidden knowledge (the Micmac ground, the buried ship) works like an addiction, sides with the deathist view that mortality and finitude give life its meaning.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 15 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Barnwell argues that fatherhood can constitute the ultimate meaning of a man's life, answering the paradox that a meaningful life 'all about the kids' seems not to be about the father by noting fatherly acts are still the father's own freely chosen activities. He confronts Camus's Myth of Sisyphus – the worry that childrearing is endless pointless rock-pushing across generations – by insisting children, unlike rocks, have intrinsic value, and invokes the Sartrean existentialist idea that choosing an activity confers value on it (illustrated by his buying oatmeal for 'Sally').
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 30 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Morgan asks when it is wrong for fathers to impose their ideals on children, arguing that forcing activities (like violin practice) risks alienation because meaningful pursuits must be embraced 'from the inside.' Using Robert Noggle's Rawls-derived hierarchy of goods (basic, pre-primary, primary, secondary, specialized), he grants fathers may guide toward universal goods but rejects Noggle's claim that parents may impose a full religious worldview, favoring David Archard's weaker right to 'guide family life' while respecting the child's growing capacity to choose – permitting compelled practice of talents only in light of the child's emerging identity.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 6 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — In this Foreword, John Rousmaniere argues that sailing's 'numinous' moments — like his own experience of stillness on a becalmed ketch mid-Atlantic, when the skipper cut the engine and the crew felt suspended between sky and sea — are paths to genuine philosophical truths, not embarrassing flights of fancy. He enlists William James's 'Varieties of Religious Experience' and James's nautical metaphor for free will (the passenger who volunteers to take the helm) to argue that such mystical feelings can 'team up' with reason rather than opposing it. He insists mystery and craft must work together: piety is no substitute for seamanship (Shelley drowned in an unseaworthy boat), yet competence and numinous experience nurture each other.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 10 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Jack Stillwaggon recounts his 1965 voyage as a seventeen-year-old crewing the replica HMS Bounty from New York to Florida — fires aboard, thirty-five-foot seas, seasickness, a crewman nearly left to die — and asks why modern people abandon comfort to court danger and discomfort. His answer is that we face the sea to prove something to ourselves about our worth and abilities: like the paratrooper who stays under fire or the soldier earning his 'red badge of courage,' the survived ordeal becomes a cherished high point that adds meaning to an otherwise 'silly' comfortable existence, leaving him more at peace and expecting more of himself thereafter.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 13 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Richard Hutch develops a phenomenology of 'moral presence' — an assertion of human integrity in the face of despair when nothing else can be done — from the autobiographies of solo ocean sailors. He identifies three pathways: technical finesse (Robin Knox-Johnston, whose 'God helps those who help themselves' pragmatism Hutch reads as the Taoist wu-wei, action through non-action), cosmic quest (Bernard Moitessier's mystical communion, slingshot instead of radio), and personal test (Kay Cottee's epiphany near Cape Horn, transforming terror into fascination via Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans). He frames sailing as tragic-comic drama with technology as a deus ex machina, arguing that doing nothing is often the zenith of value.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 19 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Nicholas Hayes describes the Chicago-to-Mackinac race, cataloguing its boats (passenger trains, Model Ts, booster rockets, retreads), its nights (darkest, stormy, breathless, velvet, brightest), and its sailor-types (tweener, superhero, teammate, yogi, minister, salt) to build toward a claim about an 'awareness shift.' He argues that far from land and its electric lights, sailors slip into a place where the emotional self meets 'the most real and primitive world' and confronts a new relationship with time, culminating on the 'day of hope' in the realization that one controls nothing but oneself and owns nothing but one's time — 'Everything is now' — a transcendence he loosely likens to skepticism and enlightenment themes.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 27 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Hilaire Belloc's essay 'The Channel,' serving as the volume's literary epilogue, argues that the 'glamour in the mind' and 'freshness of beginnings' our ancestors knew can be recovered by using the body simply and hardly — best of all by sailing a small boat under twenty-five feet across the Channel. Narrating his own first crossing from the Goodwins to Calais, drifting on the ebb and waiting for the flood, he presents sailing as the 'old drama by which the soul of a healthy man is kept alive,' teaching terror, salvation, exultation, and repose as lived realities rather than mere words. He closes by withholding the tale of the stormy return, imploring readers not to hear of it but to sail it themselves.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 30 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Tallman offers a naturalistic (atheist) justification for celebrating Christmas, arguing first that the holiday's date and rituals (December 25 solstice, Christmas trees, Odin-derived Santa) predate and are not exclusively Christian, so non-believers may find their own meaning in them. Drawing on George Santayana's and Steven Cahn's 'religious naturalism,' she argues rituals and moral communities give meaning without supernatural belief, so atheists engaging even overtly religious rites (like Westerners doing Hindu-rooted yoga) are not being disingenuous. She locates a secular 'spirit of Christmas' — giving, love, community — in It's a Wonderful Life, where humans, not God, save George Bailey, and closes on a Venn-diagram overlap of Christian and naturalist Christmases.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 36 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Arp frames a dialogue between two ex-seminarians who once got matching cross tattoos: Bill, who added more Christian ink, and Rick, who now regrets his cross as an atheist secular humanist. Bill defends God via Aquinas's combined proof from motion and causation—tracing the tattoo artist and even the Big Bang back to an unmoved mover / uncaused cause—and the 'three Ms' of mind, meaning, and morality, gesturing toward Paley-style design. Rick counters with a self-sustaining infinite series, the interaction problem between a supernatural God and nature, and the charge that God is a comforting fiction, so morality and meaning are humanly made rather than divinely guaranteed.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 6 "Introduction" — Rowlands introduces the 'sci-phi' project: science fiction confronts us with the alien 'other' as a mirror in which we understand ourselves, so lowbrow sci-fi films like The Matrix, Total Recall and Starship Troopers make abstract philosophy concrete. He argues philosophy is doing rather than knowing, invoking Fishburne's 'know the path vs walk the path' line and Nietzsche's dictum that one repays a teacher poorly by remaining a pupil. He mentions his own earlier 'fyborg' thesis that human cognition is embedded in the wider informational environment, prefiguring the extended mind.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 7 "1. Frankenstein" — Using the De Niro monster of Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Rowlands argues absurdity arises from a clash between the view of ourselves from the inside (a locus of meaning) and from the outside (sub specie aeternitatis, insignificant). The monster is assembled from second-hand parts and thrown into a hostile world he did not choose, just as we are stitched together by genes and environment we did not choose (Sartre/Heidegger thrownness). He develops Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, arguing the horror is futility not difficulty, to frame the problem of the meaning of life that underlies every deep philosophical problem.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 15 "9. Blade Runner" — Using Blade Runner's replicants ('I want more life, fucker!') and Roy's dying soliloquy, Rowlands asks how death can harm the one who dies. He states the Epicurean argument (while we live death is not yet; when dead there is no one to harm) and answers via harms of deprivation, illustrated by Tyrell's imagined brain damage. Drawing on Wittgenstein (death as the limit of life) and Heidegger's being-towards-death/being-towards-a-future, he distinguishes weak (non-conceptual) from strong (conceptual) possession of a future, arguing death harms more those with more invested. Linear time and the ultimate horizon of death are what let a life have meaning at all.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 31 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — John Davenport argues The Lord of the Rings is religious not as Christian allegory but as an epic fairy tale in Tolkien's sense from 'On Fairy-stories,' delivering 'eucatastrophe,' the sudden joyous turn that, like Kierkegaard's faith in a salvation beyond our own power, hints at eschatological hope. Using Sir Gawain and the Green Knight as Tolkien's model for Frodo (both accept an impossible burden, both fail and bear a scar of mortality), he identifies the destruction of the Ring via Gollum, Eowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth as eucatastrophic 'turns.' Davenport concludes the veiled religious message is that evil cannot stand forever, yet deliverance requires our sacrifice and faith beyond rational hope that 'day shall come again.'
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Jason Eberl and Jennifer Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar (skeptic) and Caprica Six/Roslin (believers) to debate God's existence, presenting Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, governance) against a self-explaining big bang, and noting Baltar's self-serving faith resembles Pascal's Wager. They raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will account of moral evil and Hick's soul-making theodicy (via Hume's faulty-architect analogy) for natural evil. Writing as a theist and an atheist, they argue meaning survives without God in human solidarity ('the gods shall lift those who lift each other'), and that faith and reason can share common ground.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" — The Walls brothers read Harry Potter's confrontation with death through Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death: Harry's calm march to the Forbidden Forest and Colin Creevey's sacrifice exemplify accepting mortality, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. The King's Cross scene lets Dumbledore be Harry's Heideggerian hero from the past; via William James's "sow a thought … reap a destiny," Aristotle, Locke on memory-identity, and Kant on the afterlife, they argue our choices forge a character — and Voldemort's refusal of remorse seals his ruin.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Jacoby argues that despite House calling us "selfish, base animals," House lives Socrates' examined life and Aristotle's life of reason. He dismisses God-given meaning using the Euthyphro dilemma and rejects the soul and afterlife (the "97 Seconds" self-experiment), insisting "our actions here are all that matters." Meaning must be both subjective and objective; House's puzzle-solving realizes humanity's rational function, tied to action and virtue, and — per Aristotle — yields eudaimonia, so his life is meaningful even when it doesn't feel that way to him.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 6 "4. Star Trek The Next Generation as Philosophy Gene Roddenberry’s Argument for Humanism" — Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 44 "41. Blade Runner as Philosophy What Does It Mean to Be Human" — Shanahan argues Blade Runner is philosophical despite Ridley Scott's denial, using the replicants (Roy Batty, Rachael, Leon) as defamiliarizing 'mirrors' for the human condition. He shows the Nexus-6 replicants satisfy Descartes' two criteria for a thinking soul (linguistic flexibility, novel problem-solving) while human characters like Deckard prove as cold and empathy-deficient as the machines, collapsing the human/replicant distinction the Voight-Kampff test presumes. He then reads Rachael's implanted memories through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, Roy's 'tears in rain' death through Epicurean worries about finitude, and frames the whole via Plato's Cave line 'they are like us' — the replicants model our own concerns with memory, death, and the meaning of a temporally bounded life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 54 "51. Magnolia As Philosophy Meaning and Coincidence" — Engelen interprets Paul Thomas Anderson's Magnolia as a meditation on sense-making and Camus's notion of the absurd: the film's raining frogs and the interlocking coincidences (Sydney Barringer's death, the narrator's insistence that 'this cannot be one of those things') stage our compulsion to find meaning colliding with a universe that yields none. He reads characters' struggles with trauma and regret through Epictetus's Stoic dichotomy of control and Jung's synchronicity, and the 'Wise Up' sing-along as a call to accept what cannot be changed. The chapter endorses Camus's third response to the absurd—neither denial nor suicide but defiant acceptance—linking it to Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Nagel's take on life's meaning.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 57 "54. The Man from Earth as Philosophy The Desirability of Immortality" — Berk brings The Man from Earth—about John Oldman, a 14,000-year-old non-aging man—into dialogue with Bernard Williams's 'The Makropulos Case,' which argues immortality must become boring and identity-destroying (the dilemma of exhausted versus radically changed categorical desires). Against these 'immortality curmudgeons,' the chapter argues John's mild boredom, enduring loves, friendships, and pursuit of knowledge show an immortal life can stay worth living, invoking Fischer's 'repeatable pleasures.' It also engages Nussbaum's 'Mortal Immortals' and Beauvoir's All Men Are Mortal (the miserable Fosca), which tie courage and love to finitude and sacrifice, noting John is only 'medically' rather than 'genuinely' immortal and so can still make sacrifices.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 63 "60. Little Women as Philosophy Death or Marriage and the Meaning of Life" — The chapter tests Susan Wolf's 'fitting fulfillment' theory (meaning as subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) against Greta Gerwig's Little Women, arguing the March sisters and most historical women are ill-fitted to it. Jo is forced to make her writing 'mercenary and commercial' and marries; Amy abandons painting and marries Laurie because 'marriage is an economic proposition'; Marmee, Hannah, and Mrs. Hummel live from duty and self-sacrifice without joy. Invoking Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but becomes a woman' and Imposter Syndrome, it concludes fulfillment is indicative but not necessary for meaning, urging a purely objective theory that can value women's lives 'appropriately appreciated at least in principle.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 70 "66. Marc Maron as Philosopher Comedy, Therapy, and Identification" — Kapica argues Maron's 'WTF' philosophy—both indignation and liberation—turns Kenneth Burke's rhetorical theory of identification and 'consubstantiality' into comedic catharsis, treating stand-up as therapy. He reads Maron's opening move from 'What is the meaning of life?' to 'How am I being used?' through Richard Taylor and Camus's Sisyphus: in 2009, a broke and failing Maron is Sisyphus, and WTF is his license to invent meaning. Via his cold-sore and sobriety bits and his WTF podcast interviews (Seinfeld, Gallagher), Maron makes his audience a surrogate therapist, using performed vulnerability to bind them into an 'acting-together' that Kapica claims genuinely saved Maron's life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 82 "77. Journey as Philosophy Meaning, Connection, and the Sublime" — Hamer argues Journey works through the interplay of connection, the sublime and meaning. The wordless multiplayer bond with an unnameable stranger before vast vistas dramatizes emotional connection where the ancestors' greed failed. The looming mountain and immense dunes evoke the sublime, read through Burke's pleasurable terror and Kant's mathematical and dynamical sublime (imagination overwhelmed while reason comprehends; feeling power over a nature that cannot harm the deathless player, then rebirth surpassing the sublime into joy). The cyclical return to the start recasts the game as Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: a meaningless repeated ascent that players nonetheless replay, so we must imagine the Traveler — and ourselves — happy to make the beautiful repetition our own.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 16 "6. Religion, Loss, and Afterlife" — The chapter asks whether Doctor Who is a religion, testing it against Hopfe's and Ninian Smart's criteria and concluding it is best understood as a Humanist-and-religious 'philosophy'—sacred and 'holy' (Otto) but lacking a genuine transcendent 'unseen.' On loss, it uses Kierkegaard's 'aesthetic life' and 'rotation method' to explain why we fear endings and regenerations, urging viewers to root life in lasting meaning rather than fleeting pleasure. On death, it deploys Socrates in the Apology and Phaedo and Aristotle on courage (Jabe, Harriet Jones, Donna sacrificing themselves) to argue death is nothing to fear, and reads the Matrix and Nethersphere as the show's two Socratic afterlife options.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 18 "Epilogue" — The closing essay exhorts readers to 'approach life as the Doctor'—engaged, compassionate, and critically thinking—insisting each person is important and that fandom passion, even when fractious, expresses the Doctor's engaged life (invoking Voltaire on free expression). Using 'Father's Day' and 'The Day of the Doctor,' it argues we cannot change the past but must seize the present, and ties 'truth' and 'trust' to a shared root to claim a meaningful life requires trusting oneself and others rather than merely proving oneself right. It affirms that wisdom is lived truth, that being wrong is how we mature, and that courage is doing what must be done while afraid.

### Virtue Ethics (arete)

Virtue ethics, in the tradition stemming from Aristotle, locates the moral life in the cultivation of good character rather than in obedience to rules or the calculation of consequences. Its central notion is arete, or excellence, a stable disposition to feel and act well that is developed through habit and practice over time. On this view the key ethical question is what kind of person one should become, and virtues such as courage, temperance, and justice are the traits that enable a human being to live and function well. Aristotle sets out this approach in the Nicomachean Ethics, tying virtue to the fulfillment of our nature as rational, social beings.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 10 "George and Virtue—Like Oil and Water" — Daniel Barwick runs George through Aristotle's function argument and finds him wanting: a paradigm of 'the many' who thinks happiness is fortune and momentary victories over others (free parking, perfect airport pickups) rather than activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. His 'do the opposite' epiphany in 'The Opposite' embraces the more extreme vice rather than steering toward the rationally chosen mean, and his self-hatred, laziness, and pleasure-seeking fail all three of Aristotle's tips for hitting the mean. Since George will never practice virtuous action until it becomes habit, Barwick concludes George is doomed to his miserable existence - which is, conveniently for us, why he is funny.
- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 24 "Elaine, Kramer, and Newman Not Wise" — Aeon Skoble argues Seinfeld explicates Aristotelian virtue ethics against utilitarian and Kantian rivals: Jerry's 'I don't want to be an orgy guy' and George's fear of becoming 'one of those guys' ask what sort of person to be, not which rule to follow. George's 'do the opposite' in 'The Opposite' is an update of the Delphic oracle - only he who recognizes his own idiocy (Socratic ignorance) can act well, with Jerry deducing the logic and serving as his phronemos, alongside Superman. Elaine's rule-worship and Jujyfruits utilitarianism backfire, Kramer lacks the social dialectic virtue needs, and the ironic appeals to Newman as arbiter expose the paradox that choosing a role model wisely already requires the wisdom one lacks.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 22 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Aeon Skoble uses Tolkien's characters to defend Aristotelian virtue ethics against Kantian and utilitarian rivals. Sam's loyalty is a virtue because critically directed at a worthy friend while Wormtongue's loyalty to Saruman is not; Sméagol's instant murder of Déagol reveals prior vice that let the Ring corrupt him quickly, whereas Bilbo resists it for sixty years; Aragorn's temperance and teachableness contrast Boromir's resentment and pride. Working through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean (courage between cowardice and rashness), practical wisdom, and the phronemos as role model, he argues that rule-following cannot capture moral perception (do we owe truth to Black Riders?) and that utilitarianism absurdly requires Galadriel's foresight.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 19 "Kant, Aristotle, and the Cheater" — Answering Cal Ripken's Socratic question 'What is cheating?' (raised by Sammy Sosa's corked bat and Gaylord Perry's spitball), Randolph Feezell stages a dialogue between Abbey's Kantian absolutism, Trev's traditionalism, and Ron's win-at-all-costs realism. Kant's categorical imperative grounds the absolutist: intending to break a rule to gain an edge is making yourself an arbitrary exception to rules that bind all players equally. Aristotle's virtue ethics then lets the traditionalist say that some strategic rule-breaking belongs to a sport's 'prescriptive atmosphere' (stealing signs, the balk pickoff, catching framing), since honesty and courage are means between excess and defect guided by judgment rather than exceptionless rules, while corking a bat stays cheating because it defies the tradition and hides from umpires.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 11 "Why Not to Buy the Porsche" — Skoble uses Manhattan's confrontation scene — Isaac telling Yale 'you're too easy on yourself... you'd rather buy the Porsche' over the hominid skeleton — to build an account of integrity as fidelity to correct moral principles, requiring an integrated character in which reason and desire agree. He distinguishes integrity from mere consistency (the 'consistent Nazi') and from stubbornness, and models it on Plato's just person who 'harmonizes the three parts of himself'. Aristotle's account of habituation defends Isaac's slippery slope: Yale's repeated lies for expediency are forming the kind of character who would inform on friends, so integrity is an objective yardstick of a well-lived life, as Isaac's amends to Tracy at the end confirms.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 18 "“Just What They Say It for I Never Knew”" — South argues Allen's signature old recordings from the American songbook are a philosophical device grounded in Aristotle: the Rhetoric's view that emotions carry cognitive orientations that reshape judgment, and the Politics' claim that music forms character, explain why songs comment on the plots they score. He reads Hannah and Her Sisters through 'You Made Me Love You', 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered', and 'I'm in Love Again' — scoring Elliot's inconstancy, Mickey's 'You don't deserve Cole Porter' judgment of Holly, and her growth into someone whose new musical taste signals ethical maturity — and Everyone Says I Love You as a darker cycle where fantasy and finitude ('It's Later Than You Think') drive the compulsion to love again. The happy ending is precisely why Allen called the film a 'cop out': its music says love fades and is out of our control, while the plot pretends otherwise.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 43 "NOTES" — Argues Snape's redemption is gradual virtue-building rather than instant transformation, since vice and virtue are habits built up over time and his resentments persist even as his actions serve the good. His doe Patronus, matching Lily's, manifests Aristotle's beloved as a second self, his remorse, an emotion he shares with Harry but Voldemort cannot feel, begins to knit his damaged soul whole, and Harry's forgiveness, naming his son Albus Severus for 'the bravest man I ever knew', completes the arc love began.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 31 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Jonathan Sanford distinguishes necessity of the end, of compulsion, and of nature to argue Christ's passion was both necessary and free: justice requires reparation for the harmony Adam and Eve broke, God cannot simply waive it without making a mockery of sin, yet no compulsion operates on Christ — unlike the blind inner drives Nietzsche's will to power or Schopenhauer's will would represent. Using Aristotle, he argues Christ's fully virtuous character (practical wisdom plus courage and temperance become a 'second nature') makes disobedience nearly unimaginable, and his divinity makes it impossible, so his choice 'could not have been different' precisely because it was perfectly free; the Gethsemane agony shows not division in the God-man but the difficulty of holding his human and divine wills in unity.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 81 "Superheroes and the Ring of Gyges" — The chapter's heart: Glaucon's Ring of Gyges and 'harsh view' of human nature — justice as the weak's compact against the strong, a lineage running from Hobbes to Nietzsche — are powerfully denied by superheroes and by Frodo, who resist the power of the ring. Socrates' tripartite soul and justice-as-psychic-harmony are read as preparation for the Republic's real answer, the ascent to the eternal Form of the Good, which the chapter extends through Aristotle's teleology and virtue ethics: super-powered people, denied any standard social role, must wrestle with what their potential is for — from Kingdom Come's retired Superman and Spider-Man 2's Peter Parker to Astro City's Samaritan, with Uncle Ben's 'With great power comes great responsibility' as the upshot.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 99 "Reasons to Be Moral" — Extracts two candidate answers from Spider-Man — Reason One, that immorality rebounds on you (Uncle Ben's death), tested and weakened by the Ms. Poore poverty-theft case, and Spider-Man's agonized "Because it is right" to the Green Goblin, the Kant-and-Bradley motive of duty — and finds both insufficient to show morality is rational. It then tests Plato's answer that only the moral have harmony of soul (reason governing appetite and spirit) against Flash Thompson and self-forgiving sinners, and Aristotle's "virtue is its own reward" against the thought experiment of virtuous Arachnid-Girl rotting in prison while the fraudulent Norm Osborne flourishes.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 131 "Switching Identities" — Maps Superman and Batman onto Plato and Aristotle — the otherworldly philosopher of the heavenly Good versus the this-worldly master of logic and applicable science — then argues that Bruce Wayne's years of intentional self-transformation may have swapped the mask, making Batman the core identity and Bruce the disguise. With Mark Waid, he sees Superman inwardly embracing his alien otherness as the path of authenticity, both cases yielding a fused "heterosis" of identities; Aristotle, Pascal and William James back the closing lesson that who we are is a matter of what we repeatedly do, so every mask may eventually become the face.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 21 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Bill Davis argues that Narnia works as a classical moral-education environment: against Experiment House's science-worship, Narnia supplies the three ingredients Aristotle and Aquinas require, namely instruction, virtuous exemplars to imitate (Reepicheep's courage, Puddleglum's temperance), and habituation through repeated right action, which together transform Peter's indecision, Edmund's treachery, Lucy's envy, and Jill's timidity. What finally lasts beyond Narnia, he contends, is a transforming encounter with Aslan: Eustace's dragon skin torn off by the Lion, Jill's drink at the stream where 'there is no other stream,' and Digory's tearful confession. He closes by arguing today's self-esteem-based character education cannot replicate this, since it pursues virtue from love of self rather than love of the good.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 13 "Poker and Philosophy" — Young reads David Sklansky's fundamental theorem of poker — play as if you could see all the cards — through Aristotle and Husserl. Aristotle's phronesis and virtue-as-habituation explain how excellent players come to perceive the particulars (pot odds, opponent tendencies, the best possible hand) and stay unharmed even when losing with the best play, while Husserl's Cartesian Meditations, translated hand-by-hand into poker terms, supply analogical appresentation for knowing the other minds seated across the table. Chris Moneymaker's 2003 'Bluff of the Century' all-in with nothing against Sammy Farha shows how bluffing randomizes play and lets you shape the truth you seek, until a slow-played quad aces ends the night in Socratic humility about the limits of knowledge.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 26 "U2 and Philosophy" — Werther answers Tollefsen with Aristotle's Politics: musical images of character effect real 'change[s] of soul', so a three-premise argument concludes that repeated exposure to U2's images of fine character and good action can habituate delight in virtue - King's courage in 'Pride (In the Name of Love)' (whatever the botched time of day, and as proved when Adam Clayton stepped between Bono and an FBI-confirmed death threat), the indignation and shame at global poverty in 'Crumbs from Your Table', and the compassion of 'Miracle Drug' for the locked-in writer Christopher Nolan. 'Exit' purges the band's demons and 'Until the End of the World' offers purification through holy fear, matching the medical and religious readings of Aristotelian catharsis. C.S. Lewis's Abolition of Man closes the case: without the aid of trained emotions the intellect is powerless, so a culture raised on U2's feelings may be better prepared to act well than one raised on syllogisms alone.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 14 "“Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place" — Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics: the survivors' mall orgy curdles into boredom ('What have we done to ourselves?'), illustrating pleonexia, the graspingness for more than one's share of the goods of fortune that Aristotle roots in an unlimited desire for mere living - which may even explain why Romero's dead return, grasping from beyond the grave for more un-death. Aristotle's dismissal of the life of enjoyment as fit for cattle, his account of eudaimonia as the life in which our rational capacities flourish, and his defense of acquisition bounded by the good life explain why unlimited consumption zombifies the living, and why Peter and Fran must finally leave the mall empty-handed.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 18 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Taliaferro and Le Gall rebut Paul Johnson's 1958 charge that Doctor No combines 'the sadism of a schoolboy bully', adolescent sex longings, and suburban snobbery.
