- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 11 "The Maze Is it Consciousness" — Gonzalez sets Turing's dream against Searle's nightmare: the whole park functions as a Turing test scenario, since neither guests nor viewers can reliably tell hosts from humans (Dolores in the pilot, Bernard until 'Trompe L'Oeil'), which for Turing means the hosts think. Searle's Chinese Room supplies Ford's counter — hosts merely simulate understanding by manipulating symbols without meaning — and the chapter weighs evidence of qualia on the Turing side: Abernathy's breakdown at the photograph, memory-erasure implying experiences matter to hosts, Maeve's grief for her daughter, Dolores killing the fly. The Maze turns out to represent consciousness as an inward journey to one's own voice, and Ford's admission that humans live in loops as tight as the hosts' leaves open whether our free will is any less scripted.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 21 "Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve" — Trapero-Llobera reads Westworld as the culmination of Jonathan Nolan's Memento and Person of Interest projects, mapping seven nested 'observing systems' (Nolan, Sizemore, Stubbs and Elsie, Ford, the creators' personal stories, Maeve, and William as beta-tester) onto second-wave cybernetics (Foerster, Maturana, Varela, Hayles), where the observer participates in and constructs the observed world through feedback loops. She argues the show's hosts pass through Turing's imitation game (fake memories and personalities from textual repetition, as with Peter Abernathy's reveries), and that Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns convert prosthetic memory into experienced, autopoietic memory reconstructed in a 'Bergsonian' backward movement that gives them agency and purpose. William's two-timeline transformation into the Man in Black figures the 'semiosis of virtuality' - the hyperreal where original and copy are indistinguishable - ending in a collective bicameral mind in which everyone, audience included, inhabits the god-creator Ford's dream.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 21 "11. Conceiving AI" — Beth Singler reads 2049 as a creation story, tracing the born/made tension from Frankenstein and Pinocchio through Genesis: Wallace speaks in Abrahamic language of angels, Eden, and 'God remembered Rachael', yet fails where Tyrell succeeded, his blades slipping into the newborns he calls barren. She widens the lens to the 'concept of the child' — Ariès's socially constructed childhood, chosen children from Joseph and Jesus to the Indigo Children, and the orphanage where Mister Cotton molds children 'worth buying' — to show the mystery child reopening what children are for. The baseline's 'interlinked', she argues, names the healthy separateness-with-connection Deckard models by becoming a stranger to protect his daughter; the Voight-Kampff is described as a Turing test for this neon world.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 21 "Hedging Our Bets" — Kind asks whether the Fleet's treatment of Cylons (Roslin airlocking Leoben, Fisk's 'you can't rape a machine,' Cally's killing of Boomer charged as mere discharging of a firearm) presupposes that Cylons lack the moral status Mary Anne Warren defines against the stone-versus-child contrast. Against species membership as a criterion she deploys Singer's anti-speciesism (sentience grounds equal consideration: Gina's torture, the Raider Scar) and Regan's subject-of-a-life, and against the 'no souls' argument she cites Descartes's animal automata and Turing's reply that an omnipotent God could give machines souls, as Leoben himself suggests to Adama. Since no criterion rules Cylons out with certainty, the chapter closes with a Pascal's Wager structure: under uncertainty, treat plausible moral-status-holders as having it, because denying it costs us our moral compass, answering Adama's 'why are we worth saving?'.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 42 "Ethical Issues" — Focusing on White Christmas's cookies and Ashley Too's synaptic snapshot, the chapter argues behavior can never settle whether an artificial system is conscious: the Turing test fails against Geminoid-robot-style cases where recorded signals produce human-like behavior, and philosophical-zombie possibilities plus the point that computations and information patterns are subjective interpretations (not objective physical properties) mean only discovering the physical neural correlates of consciousness could tell us whether a cookie feels pain. It then separates copying from transferring: with souls and substance dualism rejected, Black Museum's 'transfers' are really copies, and San Junipero's upload would house a copy whose future experiences are as alien to Yorkie as a plaster cast of her feet. Ethically, if cookies are conscious, then Matt's breaking of Cookie-Greta, Daly's captives, and Clayton's keychain are torture of persons, and it is the very uncertainty about cookie consciousness that lets characters rationalize the abuse - which is why the in-world legislation granting cookies human rights matters.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 28 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Adam Brackin stages the old ludology-versus-narratology fight among game theorists (Juul, Laurel, Costikyan, Rules of Play) and argues D&D refutes both camps: Fourth Edition's rules history, the 'Roll-Playing for Roleplaying' April Fool's joke, and player-versus-character knowledge show that neither rules nor story alone explains the game. Comparing computer RPGs like D&D Online, which are closed systems 'on a rail', with the tabletop's open border region of 'quest' and flow, he invokes the Turing test: no computer game can simulate human interaction believably because AI lacks the human DM's creativity. The real action is the no-man's-land where gameplay and role-play fuse, and gamers were right to shrug at the theorists and roll dice.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 33 "Notes" — The chapter argues Fallout 4's grip comes not from graphical fidelity but from first-person moral agency: deciding the fate of Gen 3 synths who do not know they are synths — supporting their escape, hunting them, or installing them as unwitting spies — forces the player through emotionally real moral deliberation. It connects this to Turing's worry about proving to another that you think ('it could've been me in their shoes') and to Nagel's bat, proposing that imagining what it is like to be a synth is a stepping stone toward ever stranger perspectives. Playing thus becomes the joy of actually doing philosophy — reawakening imagination, reshuffling our space of possibilities, and returning us to our own problems refreshed rather than merely escaped.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 15 "Does This Matter" — Garvin asks whether anything done in a dream can be right or wrong. He argues that in Inception's shared dreams ordinary ethics fully applies: the team really lies to Fischer (shared-dream communication is morally like waking communication), and the projections they mow down are, by a Turing-test-style argument, indistinguishable within the dream from persons — so either projections deserve rights or the dreamers can never know whom they are killing. For ordinary unshared dreams he engages Augustine's worry about nocturnal lust, concluding that mental acts like lust and lying are not excused by the dream state, though actions outside the dreamer's control are not blameworthy — dream wrongdoing being something to avoid repeating rather than to atone for.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 20 "The Attack of the Chinese Room" — Novy asks whether the Living Armor of 'The Mask in the Iron Man' — consciousness struck into it by lightning during the Whiplash fight, later tearing out its own heart to save Tony — really thinks. Turing's test and functionalism (any successful rescue of Yinsen is functionally equivalent, whatever the means) say only behavior matters, and Dennett's intentional stance has us treat the armor, like Darwin's burrow-plugging earthworms, as if it has beliefs and desires; against this, Leibniz's mill and Searle's Chinese Room — with Happy Hogan shuffling symbol cards he cannot read, held by 'Searle the Mandarin agent' — insist symbol manipulation never yields understanding. The chapter's reply: open the Mandarin's skull and you find only gray goop and neurons, so if behavior cannot ground understanding in the armor, it cannot in us either — we may all be in the Chinese Room.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 14 "Live from Omaha" — Irwin argues that SNL's caricatures (Fey's Palin, Baldwin's Trump, Aristophanes' Socrates in the Clouds) misrepresent their targets and that learning politics from comedy traps viewers in ideological bubbles, since satire flatters rather than informs. He introduces the Ideological Turing Test, adapted from Turing's test: state your opponent's view so accurately and sympathetically that a neutral observer cannot tell it is not yours, and grounds the duty to learn the other side from its own partisans in Mill's On Liberty. The 2016 'Bubble' sketch passes the test, he says, but SNL's liberal bias (gentle Sanders, untouchable Obama) rarely challenges its audience, and a conservative 'Live from Omaha' alternative would just rebuild the bubble on the other side.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Littmann asks whether personhood could survive humanity's extinction in 2029: if Terminators genuinely think and feel, a Skynet victory would not be the end of people. He argues the T-101, T-1000 and T-X pass substantial Turing Tests (fooling muggers, cops, Sarah on the phone as her 'mother'), then concedes Searle's Chinese Room - recast as a tiny Austrian inside the endoskeleton reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding - shows thinking behavior cannot prove thought. But he claims the films' red-tinted Terminator's-eye-view shots show what it is like to be a Terminator, giving proof of consciousness, and concludes the machines are probably persons: there is an 'I' in 'I'll be back.'
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Leiber develops three themes of the resistance: the time-travel paradoxes (Skynet's own mission proves the T-101 must fail, and future John has no need to send Reese), the moral status of machines, and the inevitability of smart weapons. La Mettrie's Man a Machine and Turing's 1950 test ground the claim that the T-101 who asks to be lowered into the molten steel is a rights-bearing person committing suicide, not a broken appliance - 'human chauvinism' says otherwise. Then, via Laplace's determinism, Einstein's conserved space-time, and his father Fritz Leiber's 'Law of Conservation of Reality,' he argues the continuum resists change, so 'Judgment Day is inevitable' is a scientist's claim about conserved mass-energy-time rather than a prophecy - with Augustine's puzzle about time framing why the future seems to protect the past.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 30 "NOTES" — Antti Kuusela argues from Wittgenstein that behavior is the touchstone — indeed constitutive — of mental life, so the question is whether Terminators behave like beings with minds. Searle's Chinese room and Ned Block's blockhead explain the read-only T-101's head-up-display of canned responses as symbol-shuffling without understanding, and the T-1000's 'I know this hurts' seems empty from a machine that cannot feel pain. The pivot is the learning-mode switch John and Sarah flip: the T-101 acquires slang, keeps promises, and acts for reasons Skynet cannot predict, passing the Lovelace test, and the Wittgensteinian dismissal of Chalmers's philosophical zombie removes the last reason to deny it a mental life — making the steel-mill sacrifice the destruction of a rights-bearing someone rather than something.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 11 "The Maze Is it Consciousness" — Lucía Carrillo González frames the whole park as a Turing Test scenario, noting guests and viewers cannot distinguish hosts like Dolores and Bernard from humans, and aligns Arnold with Turing's view that minds are computers that 'think' by responding to inputs (Abernathy's anomalous reaction to the photograph). Against this she sets Searle's Chinese Room and Ford's eliminativism, which hold the hosts merely simulate understanding. Citing qualia and the hosts' perfect, meaningful memories (Maeve recalling her daughter, technicians needing to erase trauma), she argues the hosts may genuinely experience states, and reads the Maze as the inward journey to consciousness, questioning whether humans' own free will is any less scripted.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 21 "Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve" — Trapero-Llobera situates Westworld within Jonathan Nolan's body of work (Memento, Person of Interest), arguing the show's apparent complexity hides a classic hero's-journey structure organized around observing systems and a 'semiosis of virtuality.' She reads William/the Man in Black as a 'schizoid android' and catalyst-observer, and Ford/Bernard as creator-and-prosthetic-memory pairs echoing Finch and the Machine. Turing's imitation game frames the hosts' fabricated memories, while Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns mark a shift from prosthetic to autopoietic, Bergsonian memory-recollection that turns them into observers building their own selves.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 26 "“Please Make Me a Real Boy” The Prayer of the Artificially Intelligent Jason T. Eberl" — Eberl argues that HAL 9000 in 2001 and David in A.I. present sufficient evidence of personhood, testing them against the Turing test, behaviorism, and Boethius's definition of a person as an individual substance of a rational nature. He uses Hegel's master-slave dialectic of recognition to explain the deadly struggle between humans and their self-conscious creations, reading Bowman's disconnection of HAL and the Flesh Fair's destruction of Mechas as humans failing to recognize persons. Invoking Aristotle's telos and virtue, he claims the Flesh Fair's real moral crime is precluding Mechas from pursuing their own flourishing, while David's Pinocchio-like leap of faith marks him as person-like.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Barad uses Blade Runner to test what distinguishes humans from machines. Against Turing's claim that indistinguishable input-output makes a computer a mind, she deploys Sartre's dictum that in humans existence precedes essence while manufactured replicants (like a designed android) have essence first, so they can blame their maker. She reads the Voigt-Kampff empathy test through Sartrean forlornness and despair, and argues Roy Batty achieves authentic humanity when he kills Tyrell and freely chooses to save Deckard, becoming a life-giver rather than his programmed combat model.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 17 "Terminator-Fear and the Paradox of Fiction" — Holt uses the Terminator's first-person infrared POV shots (evoking Nagel's 'what is it like' question about an alien artificial consciousness) to frame the paradox of fiction: how we feel fear toward things we know do not exist. He offers a contextual divide-and-conquer solution, arguing higher emotions like pity and admiration for Sarah and Reese are largely make-believe, while lower emotions like Terminator-fear are genuine and need no existential belief (thought and mere possibility suffice). He adds that such fear is more rational for a naturalist who admits artificial intelligence is possible than for a dualist, and speculates the Terminator functions as an archetype embodying tech-noir dread.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 25 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Eberl compares HAL in 2001 and David in A.I. to ask whether an artificially created being can be a person meriting respect and rights. He runs both through criteria of personhood—self-consciousness, rationality, social activity, autonomy—and Turing's imitation game/behaviorism, concluding their responses give sufficient evidence of personhood even if the soul question is open. He uses Hegel's master–slave dialectic of recognition to explain the deadly struggle between humans and their creations (Bowman disconnecting HAL; the Flesh Fair destroying Mechas), warning against a moral crime of 'biological supremacy,' and invokes Aristotle's telos/virtue to argue Flesh Fairs wrongly preclude Mechas from fulfilling their function, while David's Pinocchio 'leap of faith' and cry 'I'm special, I'm David!' mark his approach to personhood.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 22 "A.I. Artificial Intelligence Artistic Indulgence or Advanced Inquiry" — White argues A.I. dramatizes the mind-body problem through the mecha child David, proposing a 'Strengthened Turing Test' (STT) in which the audience knows he is a machine yet must judge whether he truly loves Monica. He runs Searle's Chinese Room (David as mere rule-follower with no qualia) against Nagel's 'what is it like' and Chalmers's zombie argument and property-dualist multiple realizability, which would let a sufficiently complex David be genuinely conscious. White contends the imprinting device—David's built-in need for one other being—is what lets him pass the STT, sidestepping Cartesian dualism's interaction problem.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 20 "“Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”" — Littmann uses the Terminator films to ask whether machines can be persons. The Terminators clearly pass the Turing Test by convincingly passing for human, giving behavioral evidence that they think. Littmann then presses Searle's Chinese Room, reworked as a tiny non-English-speaking Austrian inside the T-101 reciting phonetic lines, to argue that behavior alone cannot prove genuine understanding or feeling. He concludes that the films' 'Terminator's-eye-view' shots, showing the world from the machine's perspective, are the strongest evidence that the machines are conscious and so may count as people surviving humanity's extinction.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 12 "4. Faces from Another Dimension" — Hooke, drawing on Levinas and his translator Alphonso Lingis, treats the face as the site where trust in a stranger is risked. The Twilight Zone weaponizes our trust in familiar (actors') faces: death wears Robert Redford's face in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Satan is the avuncular Pip in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' and the Kanamits' gentle faces mask a cookbook in 'To Serve Man.' He invokes the Turing test for Corry and Alicia's love in 'The Lonely,' and finds the most truthful face of love in 'The Trade-Ins,' where the aged couple cannot bear each other's altered faces after rejuvenation.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 20 "“Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”" — Greg Littmann asks whether the Terminators are 'people,' testing three criteria: passing as human, thinking, and feeling. The T-101, T-1000, and T-X repeatedly pass Turing Tests, giving behavioral evidence of thought, but Littmann recasts Searle's Chinese Room as the 'Austrian Terminator' to argue behavior never proves genuine understanding. He then argues personhood requires conscious experience (what it is like to be a Terminator), and takes the films' red- and blue-tinted first-person 'Terminator's-eye view' shots as evidence the machines really are conscious, so humanity's extinction need not end personhood.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 36 "33. 2001 as Philosophy A Technological Odyssey" — Abrams argues that Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey dramatizes Henri Bergson's Creative Evolution and Two Sources of Morality and Religion better than Nietzsche's Zarathustra: the monolith turning Moonwatcher's bone into a tool makes humanity Homo faber, and the match-cut from bone to satellite traces one technological odyssey toward species self-transformation. He reads the HAL 9000's murderous breakdown through Turing's imitation game—Hal passes the Turing Test and inverts it by testing Frank at chess and probing Dave—and casts Dave as a new Odysseus dousing HAL the Cyclops. The star child is Bergson's vision of the universe as 'a machine for making gods,' the Nietzschean overman realized through Bergsonian creative and technological evolution, with Aristotle's mimesis grounding the film's account of imitation and its own cinematic self-reflection.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 46 "43. Ex Machina as Philosophy Mendacia Ex Machina (Lies from a Machine)" — Grinnell argues Ex Machina is fundamentally about lying, read through Kant's deontology. He frames Nathan's rigged Turing test on Ava against Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge and Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative, deriving three 'wrinkles': lying is heteronomous programming rather than the autonomy Nathan seeks; the experiment is defensible only if Ava fails, since a genuine person may not be manipulated (Formula of Humanity); and the cascade of lies among Nathan, Caleb, and Ava vindicates Kant's absolute prohibition on lying. He uses Caleb's telling of Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Searle's weak/strong AI distinction to question whether Ava's 'pleasure response' amounts to genuine consciousness or personhood.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 48 "45. A.I. Artificial Intelligence as Philosophy Machine Consciousness and Intelligence" — Gamez uses Spielberg/Kubrick's A.I. to separate three things the film conflates: intelligence, consciousness, and emotion. He argues intelligence is a functional property (David could pass a Turing test but a skilled interrogator would spot him), whereas consciousness is a physical property that cannot be inferred from David's human-like behavior — only a mathematical theory mapping physical to conscious states could tell whether David really experiences the love, fear, and pain that drive our empathy in the Flesh Fair. He insists the ethics of destroying mechas should hinge on their consciousness, not their intelligence, and connects David's engineered, irreversible imprinting-love to Lorenz's ethology and Damasio/James theories of emotion, and his eerie early behavior to Mori's uncanny valley.

### Moral Relativism

Moral relativism is the view that moral judgments are not objectively true or false but are valid only relative to a particular culture, society, or individual point of view. It responds to the observable diversity of moral codes across times and places, and to the difficulty of finding a neutral standpoint from which to declare one code correct. Critics argue that consistent relativism makes it impossible to criticize practices such as slavery or persecution as genuinely wrong, while defenders see it as a safeguard against dogmatism and cultural arrogance.

- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 20 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues Simple Subjectivism ('right for Tony') fails as a reading of the show because it cannot make sense of genuine moral disagreement - Carmela and Tony's adultery battle in 'Whitecaps', Agent Ciccerone versus Tony on extortion - nor ground outrage at the killings of Pussy and the sobbing Matt Bevilaqua. Humean ethical subjectivism, grounded in a common human nature and the sentiment of sympathy (with Berkeley's pin example to explain vice as perception-dependent), fares better: it lets us condemn Tony while explaining his warped sympathy - grieving Pie-O-My more than his human victims - as the product of a mob upbringing that Melfi's alexithymia diagnosis in 'House Arrest' targets.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 90 "With Great Power Comes—What" — Turns Uncle Ben's dictum into normative ethics: the question is not how super-powered people do live but how they ought to, whether they have a duty to take up the hero role, and what obligations follow from it. Two 'hobgoblins' — ethical nihilism and ethical relativism — are dismissed as contrary to our ordinary convictions (Mother Teresa's charity objectively good, Hitler's genocide absolutely bad), clearing the ground for utilitarianism.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 107 "Worldviews, Values, and Superheroes" — Argues that in a naturalist universe of particles and force fields nothing grounds objective good and evil, so a defiant Superman who fights evil just because he wants to prizes sympathy while downplaying truth. Wonder Woman's challenge — "Truth and justice" — raises whether they are in league: Socrates and the classic tradition held truth, beauty and goodness are one, while Nietzsche, godfather of postmodernism, snarls that "Truth is ugly," leaving naturalism a dilemma between believing in ultimate justice or accepting that it is an illusion.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 20 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Tim Mosteller identifies Lewis's Tao from The Abolition of Man with Aquinas's Natural Law, an objective moral order knowable by all rational beings, and maps three responses onto Narnian characters: wholehearted acceptance (Peter, Lucy, Tirian, Reepicheep), selective 'Innovators' who pick and choose (Shift and Miraz, with Nietzsche's invented master-values as the philosophical extreme), and total rejection by 'Conditioners' (Ginger the Cat, who reverts to dumb beast, and Uncle Andrew, who loses the animals' speech). Individual laws are illustrated by Mr. Tumnus freeing Lucy, Aslan scratching Aravis for her gladness at the slave girl's beating, Nikabrik's treacherous Realpolitik, Lucy's eavesdropping spell in the Magician's book, and Jill's showing-off at the cliff.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 22 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Janice Daurio sets Plato's Thrasymachus and Callicles and Nietzsche's immoralism against three Narnian immoralists: Uncle Andrew, who exempts 'profound students and great thinkers' from rules meant for little boys, servants, and women; Queen Jadis, whose Deplorable Word and 'What else were they there for but to do my will?' embody might-makes-right; and the Green Witch, who extends going beyond good and evil to going beyond truth itself. Following Lewis's moral realism (the Golden Rule and Natural Law as facts like gravity, with Hobbes's lesson that someone always turns up with more power), she shows the immoralists cannot live by their own creed, since Uncle Andrew resents being treated as Jadis's slave, and since Lewis ties real authority to service, as when humble Frank the Cabby is made king.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 23 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Gayne Anacker defines moral imagination, the capacity to see one's values and life from fresh moral perspectives, and argues the Chronicles exercise it through three character types readers live through: flawed repenters (Edmund, Eustace, Bree, Aravis), the essentially good under trial (Lucy believing her Aslan sighting in Prince Caspian, Caspian's greed on Goldwater Island), and the fatally self-absorbed (Uncle Andrew, Shift), together with portrayals of worship and of true versus usurped nobility (Peter versus Miraz). Philosophically he contends the stories' effectiveness supports virtue ethics over action-centered modern theories, and that disagreement among ethical theorists is no ground for relativism: no one needs theoretical consensus to know Miraz is evil.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 13 "So, What’s the Bottom Line" — James Klagge, defining terms in Socratic fashion, distinguishes bootlegs like Great White Wonder from piracy and argues unreleased Dylan material (the New York Blood on the Tracks, "Blind Willie McTell," the 1966 Live concert) has genuine musical and historical value. He rejects the Sophist view that morality is just self-interest and the relativist "everybody's doing it" defense, then weighs the artist's Lockean property and privacy rights against fans' rights of access, noting legal-but-immoral and illegal-but-moral cases in the spirit of Martin Luther King's civil disobedience. His verdict: bootlegging is morally acceptable when royalties are fair, stolen tapes are not used, and mainly public performances circulate.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 19 "The Blessings of Tranquility" — Michael Chiariello takes Dylan's "the truth is true whether you wanna believe it or not" as a correspondence theory of truth, then rejects both the gospel-era absolutism of "Precious Angel" and the relativism (from Protagoras' man-the-measure to modern subjectivism) that would make Dylan's changes of course harmless. The alternative he defends is Pyrrhonian skepticism in Sextus Empiricus's sense: truth is objective but never fully assured, so suspending judgment yields tranquility. Dylan's career - from the ambiguous "Blowin' in the Wind" through "Watching the River Flow" and "Things Have Changed" to the two versions of "Every Grain of Sand" ("the reality of man" vs "a perfect finished plan") - embodies this balanced, non-dogmatic search the way of God designed it.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 23 "A Call to Unchanging Truths" — Francis Beckwith argues the 1979-81 Christian albums are no aberration: Dylan's whole career presupposes moral realism, an objective moral law built into the universe - "Dignity never been photographed" names an irreducible moral property, and the judgments in "With God on Our Side" and "Blowin' in the Wind" only make sense if right and wrong are unchanging across eras. The six-month sentence William Zanzinger receives in "The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll" is condemned on retributive, lex talionis grounds rather than any utilitarian calculus of consequences, and "Forever Young" and "What Good Am I?" urge virtue practiced for its own sake. The chapter thus reads Dylan's conversion as the surfacing of commitments - against relativism, for virtue and unchanging truths - always latent in songs like "The Times They Are A-Changin'."
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 11 "How to do Philosophy" — Johnson argues through Colbert's satire that truth is neither individual ('My Truth') nor cultural ('wikiality' — a Wikipedia entry does not become true by consensus), since relativism is self-contradictory and implies slavery was not wrong before abolition. He deploys Locke's attack on 'enthusiasm' to show 'truthiness' is circular reasoning — sure because one is sure — and dismantles the 'right to my opinion' as a bid to shield beliefs from evidence, closing with Socrates' model: when evidence runs out, admit ignorance and keep doing philosophy.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 27 "So There’s No Accounting for Taste" — Mary MacLeod stages her quarrel with her husband over the musical value of the Dead's Space jams as a problem in metaethics: she claims Space objectively lacks merit, Eric claims it has value, and the chapter asks whether either 'should' claim can be true. She lays out Value Realism (value as intrinsic, detectable properties), Subjectivism ('no accounting for taste'), Mackie's Humean error theory (we project feelings onto the world as we do with color), and the 'oughts by agreement' view that expert or social consensus makes things right the way traffic conventions make right-side driving correct. The Dahmer and torture cases show why subjectivism fails for ethics, and the chapter concludes that 'beauty by agreement' quietly collapses back into Realism — so Deadheads' fierce debates about Space are legitimate disagreements after all.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 42 "The Cosmic Divide" — The chapter casts the two series as opposed worldviews: the original is Manichaean moral absolutism, with 'War of the Gods' staging Count Iblis and the Ships of Light as cosmic Darkness and Light battling over humanity, while Moore's re-imagining is Protagorean moral relativism where context decides right and wrong. Its clearest cases are comparative: Roslin abandons the FTL-less ships as 'a matter of numbers' yet burns forty-three percent of the fleet's fuel reserves to rescue Starbuck, and Leoben is airlocked after interrogation while the tortured Athena and Gina are treated with mercy. The fan schism between the shows, it concludes, is really the centuries-old quarrel between absolutism and relativism.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 24 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Barkman takes the 1986 movie poster's 'Beyond Good. Beyond Evil.' as a Nietzsche allusion and argues the cartoon refutes it: Skyfire's 'It is wrong,' Orion Pax's repudiation of admired power in 'War Dawn,' and Optimus's humble 'Thrones are for Decepticons' make Megatron a would-be superman and villain while Optimus is a Platonic guardian of a universal moral law binding even Unicron and the Quintessons. A reductio against cultural relativism (the Decepticon invasion of Earth, First Aid's failed pacifism in 'The Ultimate Weapon') plus C.S. Lewis-style archetypes explain why Optimus - a Christ-type who died saving the world - endures while GoBots do not.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 9 "Where Do We Go from Here" — David Kyle Johnson argues that Colbert's gut-thinking persona (the Harriet Miers 'I know her heart' bit, 'that's my right' on the Panama Canal) satirizes a real and widespread vice, and he refutes the philosophies behind it. Individual and moral relativism collapse into self-contradiction and absurdity ('Lincoln was not assassinated' would be 'true for' someone; Hitler could not be condemned), while gut-justification is what Locke called 'enthusiasm' - a belief that is 'its own proof,' circular like the prophet whose revelation needs no burning bush. Following Jamie Whyte, he dismantles the 'right to my opinion' (running example: the friend who insists on a grassy-knoll shooter despite the melon-head evidence): there is no epistemic or moral right to undefended belief, and no right to intellectual comfort. Against this he holds up Socrates, wisest because he alone admitted ignorance, and insists philosophy and politics progress only through argument, so truthiness is never an acceptable substitute.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 8 "8" — Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 17 "Gay Angels, Female Cardinals, and Bishōnen Popes" — Barkman argues that anime's Christian imagery — the legendary Santa on a cross, Earthian's gay angel lovers, Trinity Blood's bishonen pope and female cardinal, Evangelion's hostile Angels — encodes Japanese religious pluralism rather than orthodox Christianity. He lays out the pluralist position (following Kant's phenomena/noumena distinction and John Hick: Ultimate Reality is only equivocally describable, so doctrine matters less than spiritual mood), contrasts it with exclusivism and inclusivism, and charges pluralism with self-undermining intolerance, then traces Japan's historical demonization of Christianity from the 1637 Shimabara massacre (Ninja Resurrection, Samurai Champloo) to Eva's alien invaders, with Armageddon imagery fueled by the atomic bombs. Because Shinto-Buddhist-Daoist anti-realism dissolves fixed categories, anime dissolves good and evil (Chrno Crusade's I Ching balance) and gender itself, gravitating to the symbol-rich 'jungle' of Catholicism (C.S. Lewis's phrase) — and where Trinity Blood lets some vampires be righteous, Augustine's City of God marks the one nearly orthodox note.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 28 "So Why Do I Support Aston Villa" — Rose—made a Villan by misreading a 1978 Panini sticker as Aston Villa's claret and blue—asks whether supporting Aston Villa is rational and argues ethics is far more like fandom than philosophers admit. Reasons for supporting Villa (local team, the 1982 European Cup, the colors) explain but never justify his allegiance, and the impartial procedures ethics prizes—the utilitarian benevolent spectator and Rawls's original position behind the veil of ignorance, with its 'sort of Kantian' consent-based alternative—turn out too demanding and too abstract: they would force him to donate his match ticket to charity, forbid the Premiership manager favoring his academy son, and reduce agency to the 'Rose-calcio scale' absurdity of switching to Real Madrid for rational reasons. His positive, communitarian claim is that we are thrown into social traditions whose inherited values—like a team—make moral agency and action possible at all, a 'different kind of rationality' that flirts with relativism yet still needs an exit strategy for cultures that discriminate against women or torture children.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 12 "How Can I Compete with Geniusness" — Timothy Dunn uses 'Patrick SmartPants', where a brain-coral transplant turns Patrick into a genius who abandons SpongeBob, to ask whether the happy ignoramus or the discontented genius lives better. After sketching a subjectivist defense of Patrick's choice to revert ('knowledge can never replace friendship'), the chapter tests Mill's hedonistic utilitarianism: since competent judges rank higher pleasures qualitatively above lower ones, Mill's dictum that it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied condemns Patrick's destruction of his own higher capacities. Dunn then presses two objections — that people's actual lower-pleasure preferences may be genuine rather than socially produced, and that the capacity for higher pleasure seems worthless without its actual experience — leaving Mill's verdict in tension.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 20 "The Best Kind of Friend" — Ruth Tallman tests Holmes and Watson against Aristotle's requirement in the Nicomachean Ethics that perfect friendship exists only between the 'alike in excellence': since the two live by irreconcilable moral codes (Holmes's cocaine and burglaries versus Watson's clean living and law-abidingness), Aristotelian moral naturalism denies they can be true friends at all, despite the raw panic in 'The Three Garridebs' proving mutual devotion. Recasting the pair as moral pluralists with different 'good for me's, she argues Holmes is actually the better friend, an 'integrity-promoting' friend who urges Watson to stay home from the Milverton burglary to honor Watson's own code, while the proselytizing Watson, who nags about cocaine yet tags along anyway, repeatedly violates his own integrity.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 181 "I’m in Need of Some Restraint" — Tells how the Abraham and Isaac story introduced "redemption," a substitution rite that curbed the "pride of place" of first-borns while replacing human sacrifice — a transition the Egyptians and Greeks also made independently. Using Shirley Jackson's "The Lottery," the volunteering Druid victims and the martyr Perpetua, it argues any horror can be normalized by piety and tradition — Sarah Palin or Michele Bachmann would have defended first-born sacrifice in ancient Ur — and needles the reader with ritual chicken sacrifice versus KFC: "which of those two, in a just world, would really be more inhumane?"
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 27 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Grants that Larry looks like the Romantic ideal of the authentic self, Rousseau's amour de soi turned into candid self-expression, but argues his authenticity collapses into egoism: petty commandments about chicken skewers and beach jackets, one-strike firings like the toupee-wearing chef, and ceaseless sincerity tests. Through Sartre's categories Larry is bad faith in both directions, the 'cowardly bastard': he denies transcendence ('I can't help it') and hides behind fabricated personas, faking concern over a sick dog and exaggerating his Jewishness to the kidney consortium. Charles Taylor's The Ethics of Authenticity supplies the verdict that self-creation needs 'pre-existing horizons of significance,' so Larry's 'anything goes' authenticity is really moral relativism and justified self-interest, with Ayn Rand's virtue of selfishness as its unwanted philosophical ally. The chapter closes that only a relational authenticity, like the African ideal of ubuntu, could redeem Larry, and he lacks it, so 'maybe authenticity isn't for everyone.'
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 22 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — King weighs whether Victor or his creation bears the blame, opening with a thought experiment in which a neighbor's self-aware android burns your town and asking 'does he deserve to share that fate?' Maslow's hierarchy of needs explains the monster's fixation on a mate as a starved 'love need' created by Victor's abandonment, and Piaget's cognitive stages test whether the monster had matured enough to 'could have done otherwise' - while Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil attack on morality as tyrannical herd-style slave morality threatens to dissolve blame entirely, and Sartre's existentialism leaves each agent choosing without objective moral foundations. Refusing both the absolutist's unconditional verdict and dogmatic relativism, the chapter applies the criminal law's mens rea ('guilty mind') test to monster, android, and creator alike, and leaves the final verdict of guilt deliberately open.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 65 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Olli Pitkänen maps the Satanist spectrum beyond the Devil-worship of films like The Mother of Tears: LaVey's atheistic, morally subjectivist Church of Satan; the Nietzschean Übermensch cult of the Order of Nine Angles with its initiatory violence; the chaos-gnostic Temple of the Black Light (whose ideal, he says, is the Joker in The Dark Knight); and Finland's Star of Azazel, theistic Satanists whose theosophical moral realism makes Satan a presenter of choices rather than a willer of evil. On that last reading Vader destroying Palpatine and Sauron perishing with the One Ring show evil as human projection, and even Jesus counts as 'satanic' in the rebel-against-dogma sense.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 25 "Girls and Philosophy" — Ketcham sets Hannah B (Brooklyn) beside an imagined Hannah D (a Darfur village terrorized by the Janjaweed) to ask whether personal fulfillment depends on culture or on the individual. Rejecting relativism (which, per Alford, cannot even condemn suppression of belief), he turns to Rawls's Law of Peoples - five minimal human rights any well-ordered society must grant - and builds a thought experiment, 'Blandland,' a minimally compliant country where both Hannahs relocate. His conclusion: even Rawlsian minimum rights, under which life can remain Hobbes's 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short,' plus personal drive and the attitudes of others, jointly and indeterminately decide what either Hannah can become.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 13 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Charlene Elsby asks what makes the McPoyles cross the line from offensive (like the Gang) into irredeemably creepy, working through their bathrobes, unibrows, incest, and constant milk drinking. Her answer runs through violated social convention: the creepy person is not merely making non-standard choices but seems unaware conventions exist at all, and Liam's 'It's society that has the problem' raises moral relativism only for the chapter to insist the creep reaction tracks something actually wrong, not just different. Adding the legacy of physiognomy (we judge character from appearance, and more harshly when the trait is controllable) and an inductive inference (everything the McPoyles do is creepy, so even the milk must be), creepiness emerges as an art of detection rather than a science: whether someone is creepy differs from whether they seem creepy.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 17 "4. Lie or Die" — Hawkes uses Rick's bar confrontation with Dave and Tony in 2.8 'Nebraska' to ask when lying is right, after defining lying through the Governor's white flag at the National Guard camp and Eugene's false cure claim. He rejects moral relativism - the Claimers' rules, Terminus's 'butcher or cattle', the Governor's 'we will do the only thing' - because it forbids criticizing rapists and cannibals and erases moral progress, then finds utilitarianism shaky given Eugene's unforeseen deadly consequences and Rick's refusal to hand Michonne to the Governor at 'Arrow on the Doorpost.' He defends a duty-based deontology in which the duty to protect the farm overrides the duty not to lie, and closes with Robert Kirkman's own lie about an alien invasion that got The Walking Dead published.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 24 "12. Margaery for Queen!" — Jones asks whether Margaery - who grooms Tommen, admits she was 'good at seeming good,' and may count as an abuser despite Westeros's norms - could still have been the best queen in the Seven Kingdoms. Against the prosecution's portrait of a cold egoist, he argues her charity to Flea Bottom's children shows a queen is good by what she does rather than why she did it, so selfish ambition welded to shrewdness can genuinely serve the common good. Comparing her with Ramsay (cruelty that provokes revolt) and Ned (benevolence without calculation that gets him killed), the chapter draws an implicitly Machiavellian conclusion - the people's best bet is hunger for power joined to the cunning to keep them onside - while doubting that cultural relativism can fully excuse her treatment of Tommen.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 23 "12. Are We Really Sure They’re Wrong" — Timothy Hsiao argues we cannot condemn the burning of the disabled or Smith's son's mandated euthanasia by appealing to Nazi values, since cultural relativism would make the Resistance the real wrongdoers; the horror we feel presupposes an objective natural law known to reason, the violation of which grounded the Nuremberg trials. From Augustine's 'an unjust law is no law at all,' the chapter then tests the Resistance's armed rebellion against the five just-war conditions — proper authority (the Resistance as agent of the moral law), just cause, reasonable chance of success (the newsreels as grounds for hope), proportionality, and last resort — and finds it justified.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 21 "11. Fighting Ethical Relativism in Tales of Suspense" — Reading Tales of Suspense, Pagnoni Berns and Veteri cast Iron Man as a man of every era - echoing LBJ's 'reason together', Cold War utilitarianism against Communism, playboy masculinity, and finally the Registration Act - which makes him a parrot of whatever relativism his age prefers. Captain America, literally frozen in time, holds Kant's categorical imperative: every life is an end in itself, so he saves Nazi prisoners in #71, trades his own life for a pilot in #61, and drinks possibly lethal serum without needing thanks, while Bucky's mediated, reward-seeking morality shows why ends corrupt moral worth. Because Cap's universal, ahistorical defense of human dignity holds from the 1940s to the 1960s and beyond, the authors rank him above the adaptable but context-bound Iron Man.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 16 "5. Inside Gilead’s Misogynist Parlors" — Hirschbein unravels the Genesis story of Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar as the script Gilead rereads to rationalize its 'misogynist parlors,' arguing that Gilead's exegesis is propaganda rather than scholarship—cherry-picking scripture that Nietzsche joked would appall the actual Jesus. He then spins the reader's moral compass: with Rorty's ironist he asks whether anyone initiated into Abraham's tribe or raised in Gilead can be blamed—are even Hitler and Commander Waterford products of their time?—and weighs Ofglen's suicide bombing of the Rachel and Leah Center against just war criteria of proportion, innocence, and chance of success. Finally, with Freud and Niebuhr, he suggests the Sons of Jacob built their surveillance state on a depraved view of human nature, so utopian schemes—Gilead included—are doomed from the founding.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 27 "14. The Value of a Handmaid" — Pérez assesses a Handmaid's value through Kant—Gilead gives women a price, not a dignity, so the Gilead–Mexico trade deal is human trafficking dressed as diplomacy—and through Marx's use value and exchange value, with fertility the commodity and Jezebels carrying both market and affective price. He adds Bourdieu's forms of capital to show Offred's social and resistant cultural capital against Janine's collapse, then weighs cultural relativism (via Renteln and Herodotus) before rejecting it for Gilead: its values were improvised and forced rather than naturally evolved, so the culture itself earns no pass. The Handmaids' refusal to stone Janine shows their collective worth: 'They should've never given us uniforms if they didn't want us to be an army.'
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 26 "You Can Take the Man out of Cleveland . ." — Da Silva and Found take Liz's stint as a Cleveland model in the episode 'Cleveland' as an entry into social constructivism: following Ian Hacking's account of socially constructed Xs and Marcia Eaton's socially constructed aesthetic response, taste is learned, culture-bound, and class-marked, so Jack's Manhattan standards condemn Liz's Burger King attire while Cleveland calls her a model. They then warn that aesthetic relativism ('you can't question taste') leaves no ground for condemning Tracy's solid gold boots or for resisting the powerful, since celebrities and the Black Crusaders have platforms that let them impose their standards. Searle's non-relativist account of social facts is floated as an escape route, and Liz's persistence as a New Yorker shows identity and values are constructed gradually through social belonging.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 42 "The Cosmic Divide" — The chapter locates the real fan schism in worldview: the original series is Manichaean moral absolutism - Count Iblis and the Ships of Light wage a cosmic Light/Darkness war in which Evil is one force (Iblis sharing the Imperious Leader's voice) and humanity is the battleground - while Moore's re-imagining is Protagorean relativism ('man is the measure'), where right depends entirely on context. Evidence: Roslin abandons the FTL-less ships as 'a matter of numbers' yet burns forty-three percent of fuel reserves to find Starbuck; Leoben is airlocked after Starbuck's interrogation while Thorne is killed for torturing Athena; producer Eick even defends Caprica Six's killing of the baby as possibly a mercy. The two shows thus embody absolutist nostalgia for moral clarity versus post-9/11 moral ambiguity.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses 'This Week in God' segments (Ed Helms refereeing a Hindu-versus-Mayan 'faith-off', Colbert's roast line that all religions are infinite paths to accepting Jesus, Rob Corddry's purification rituals and God Exchange stock ticker) to lay out exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism as responses to religious diversity. Inclusivism like Colbert's 'anonymous Christian' logic is exposed as intellectual imperialism that erases genuinely distinct teachings such as the Buddhist non-self and impermanence, while the chapter defends a deep pluralism against the relativism that makes 'all religions equally true' meaningless. Its eulogy for the God Machine borrows Marx's view of religion as an instrument of mass control to explain why religious humor now survives only through a political lens.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 28 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Through Daenerys's horror at her Dothraki wedding - public sex, lethal duels, and later the gang-rape of captives that Drogo calls 'the way of war' - the chapter distinguishes descriptive cultural relativism from normative moral relativism. The diversity of ethical codes in Westeros (crannogmen, wildlings, Craster) plus Cersei and Jaime's incest and the Targaryen brother-sister marriages show moral codes genuinely vary, and the audience's harsher judgment of Tyrion's whoring than of his siblings' incest illustrates our own culturally conditioned gut reactions. But the chapter concludes relativism must be rejected: no culture's say-so makes rape acceptable, while eating horse meat is fine and sibling incest depends on circumstances.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 13 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Terjesen asks how Sinestro and Universo ever passed recruitment and answers that the Guardians' two-prong test of honesty and fearlessness reflects moral pluralism: universal rules kept deliberately thin so that different moral codes can coexist, which is why the vicious 'good bad man' Jack T. Chance keeps his ring on Hellhole. But honor, honesty, and justice are thick ethical concepts in Bernard Williams's sense, requiring cultural context to apply, so Laira's execution of a surrendered Amon Sur and the Guardians' own cover-ups (the Corpse, Kentor Omoto) cannot be settled by appealing to thin 'justice,' and the Alpha Lanterns' internal-affairs role cannot fix it. Moral particularism leaves the Corps with unresolvable disagreements about who the bad apples are.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Taliaferro and Kastrul ask what the reader would do in the castaways' place, using Aristotle's view that character is a disposition to act under other conditions to assess Mr. Eko, Ben, Michael, Charlie, and Sawyer: people are not merely what they do but what they would do. Plato's Ring of Gyges, quoted at length, tests whether characters like Sun behave honestly only when watched. Against the idea that the island could reverse all values, they argue morality cannot be completely relative to context - invoking Chesterton's 'Thou shalt not steal' on the remotest star - and place Lost in the island-narrative tradition of the Odyssey and Robinson Crusoe as a story of the journey of the soul.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 22 "If Not on the Island of Ethical Subjectivism, Then Where" — George Wrisley uses Lost as a testing ground against ethical subjectivism and cultural relativism: the disagreement over Sayid shooting young Ben (monster or innocent child?) motivates relativism, but the Argument from Disagreement fails for the same reason Locke and Mr. Eko's button dispute does not change what will actually happen if it goes unpushed. Simple subjectivism makes every judge infallible (the Man in Black could declare his murders right) and dissolves genuine disagreement between Jacob and his brother over killing their 'mother,' while cultural relativism makes the Dharma Initiative's torture of Sayid 'right' and would have ruled Martin Luther King Jr. wrong. He concludes that Lost's ambiguous cases - Michael's murder of Ana Lucia and Libby, Ben killing Jacob, Jack extorting Ben on the operating table - invite viewers to seek objective grounds Socratically, questioning their own moral judgments with further 'why's.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 12 "Notes" — David Kyle Johnson argues Kirk is a jerk for dismantling utopias—the machine-god Vaal in 'The Apple' and the spore colonists of Omicron Ceti III in 'This Side of Paradise'—whose members were happy, healthy, and arguably free. Taking up objections from the Mission Log podcast, he rebuts the 'stagnation' and 'drug' charges by testing the utopias against Aristotle's eudaimonia and Maslow's self-actualization, and exposes the appeal-to-nature fallacy behind 'artificial happiness'. Using Rousseau on primitive simplicity and Nozick's libertarian minimal state, he concludes that the real threat to freedom is Kirk himself (and a Federation that, as Eddington says, assimilates without telling you), and that at minimum cultural relativism forbids wrecking harmless societies.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Victor Grech presents Klingons as a cultural pastiche—Mongol horde stereotypes, Japanese Bushido, Viking Valhalla, Shakespeare 'restored to the original Klingon'—whose 1500-year honor code and embrace of honorable death (Klag's dishonored father, Jadzia's rebuke of Kang) make them Nietzschean Ubermenschen who slew their own gods, echoing Nietzsche's 'God is dead'. The Kahless clone of 'Rightful Heir' ('perhaps the words are more important than the man') shows a messianism surviving deicide. He then reads Worf through Roland Barthes's 'Occidentalism' and one-way acculturation—Picard praising Worf's 'humanity' after 'Reunion'—while Azetbur's 'human rights' is racist jab in The Undiscovered Country and Trekkers' Klingon cosplay raise cultural relativism and appropriation.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 34 "Notes" — Tests moral relativism against absolutism through Enterprise's "Cogenitor": Trip's liberation of the Vissian third-sex being - secretly scanning its brain, naming it Charles, teaching it to read - ends in its suicide, and the chapter asks whether Trip's judgments track rational moral truth or are Humean after-the-fact rationalizations of disgust, since on Hume's view reason is the slave of the passions and is/ought are separate. Kant's categorical imperative (the cogenitor used merely as a means of reproduction) and Aquinas's natural law are offered as absolutist resources on Trip's side, while Phlox voices a Benedict-style "morally good is just habitual" relativism and Archer concludes "we didn't come out here to play God", prefiguring the Prime Directive. The chapter lands on Mary Midgley's rejection of moral isolationism via her tsujigiri example and Quark's "we're better than you" speech to Sisko: cross-cultural judgment is possible, but only after understanding, and not on the first day of first contact.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 15 "Notes" — LaRocca argues Boba Fett is best understood as an amoralist - neither a moral relativist nor an ethical egoist, but someone who has withdrawn from moral judgment altogether - reading his terse 'As you wish' to Vader and his insuring of Han's survival purely for payment as evidence. Through Michael Walzer's account of the soldier's constrained choice and the 'good mercenary' debate, he asks whether mercenary violence (Blackwater, private military contractors) really differs morally from a conscript's or clone's. The upshot is that Fett's grayness between Empire and Rebellion exposes amoralism as a surprisingly central part of political and military life.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 30 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Allaire defends the thesis that the only good walker is a dead one: walkers fall outside Kant's moral community because, as purely sensuous beings driven by instinct, they cannot plan ahead (Glenn's 'Vatos' heist, the walker-guts camouflage in 'Guts'), communicate, or reflect, and so can have no duties and no rights. Act-utilitarian weighing shows killing any walker is beneficial, and even Regan's respect principle does not apply; the chapter runs Mary Anne Warren's personhood criteria to show walkers lack consciousness, reasoning, and self-awareness. Our hesitation before walkers like Morgan's wife or Leon Basset is irrational projection onto beings no longer the persons we loved, so Rick's 'I'm sorry this happened to you' is mercy for a fate, not respect for a right-holder.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 29 "Notes" — DeVan uses Rand's marriage to Aviendha, Elayne, and Min (and Jordan's own two-girlfriend anecdote) to survey ethical frameworks on polyamory, arguing the answer depends on which lens one uses. Sorting love into the Greek types (ludus, eros, mania, pragma, storge, philia, agape), he runs romantic, sexual, and marital polyamory through emotivism (Ayer), ethical egoism (Ayn Rand, the Forsaken), cultural relativism and social contract (Hobbes, the Aiel), natural law and Kantian duty (the Mahabharata's Draupadi, Genesis), divine command and religion (Judaism, Christianity, Islam), and consequentialism/utilitarianism, rights, and Aristotelian/virtue ethics, invoking Cadsuane's cattle analogy and Brad Wilcox's data favoring monogamy.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 17 "Seventh Hole Cheating and Gamesmanship among Amateur and Professional Golfers" — Lumpkin argues that amateur golfers routinely cheat while professionals do not, and dissects four rationalizations amateurs use: appeal to ignorance, appeal to popularity, appeal to tradition (Callahan's 'cheating culture'), and the belief that 'no one will ever know' — a golf-course version of Plato's Ring of Gyges where invisibility dissolves restraint. Drawing on Kohlberg's stages of moral development, she claims professionals reason at higher levels because officials, peers, and disqualification (e.g., J. P. Hayes) enforce the sport's social contract, whereas amateurs face no punishment. She concludes casual golfers would do better not to keep score than to keep a 'mythical' one, earning the right to score only once they follow the rules.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 10 "A Darker Shade Realism in Neo-Noir" — Jason Holt argues that realism, especially about the role values play in people's lives, is the underappreciated essence of noir, offering a working definition of noir as 'stylized crime realism.' Surveying neo-noir detectives (Harper, Chinatown's Gittes), revamped femmes fatales who get away with it (Body Heat's Matty, The Last Seduction's Bridget), morally ambiguous protagonists (To Live and Die in L.A., Manhunter), and Lynch and Tarantino, he shows how the post-Production-Code freedom lets endings ring true to life by letting the guilty escape justice. He coins the 'normativistic fallacy' as the inverse of Moore's naturalistic fallacy: inferring what is from what ought to be, arguing that mainstream cinema's poetic justice commits it while neo-noir's downbeat endings correct it, fulfilling the realism latent in classic noir.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 11 "Moral Clarity and Practical Reason in Film Noir" — Aeon Skoble argues against the common view that noir depicts a world without ethics, contending that noirs are actually exercises in moral clarity. He reads Frank Chambers's deliberations in Postman and Walter Neff's in Double Indemnity as Aristotelian practical reasoning gone wrong (they fail eudaimonia and are punished), while Sam Spade's decision to turn in Brigid shows objective good reasons at work. Using Touch of Evil, he shows that a corrupt cop like Quinlan being pursued affirms moral realism and refutes subjectivism, and he sides with Aristotelian virtue and Platonic objective justice over Kant's rigid categorical imperative (which would forbid the detective's useful lies or lying to Nazis). He concludes that because bad noir characters do not flourish, even films about immoral acts are morally edifying rather than corrupting role models.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Rodriguez-Ruiz treats Ali and The Insider as dramatizing the methodology of philosophy, especially conceptual analysis and the politics of defining social concepts. Ali's challenges to 'patriotism,' 'freedom' and his slave name, and the manipulation of 'confidential,' 'addictive' and 'tortious interference' in The Insider, show how much rides on contested definitions. Against cultural relativism, he deploys James Rachels's Elements of Moral Philosophy (there are moral facts; some rules are needed for any society to exist) and discusses conceptual analysis (Jackson, Goldman) and Schiappa's 'how ought we use X,' leaving both heroes committed to independent thinking over consensus.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — D'Aries and Hirsch read Paul Thomas Anderson's Hard Eight as a neo-noir moral inversion: the aging criminal Sydney seeks atonement not through religious penance but through selfless love, rescuing John and Clementine while removing the loathsome Jimmy (who knows Sydney killed John's father). They contrast him with Melville's Bob le flambeur and Besson's The Professional, where convention demands the criminal be punished. Sydney escapes formal justice but is sentenced to a 'prison without bars' of self-loathing (the bloodstained cuff), and the authors warn that such sympathy-for-the-devil inversions verge on nihilistic moral relativism.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Conard argues that Tarantino's postmodernism makes redemption impossible in Reservoir Dogs (and Pulp Fiction, Kill Bill). Using Danto on the 'end of art', Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives', and Rorty's contingent 'vocabularies', he shows the films embrace relativism about knowledge (rearranged chronology, unreliable perspectives) and about values. Mr. Orange plays Judas and Christ; the opening tipping argument exposes moral conventions as arbitrary, so becoming a 'real person' rather than a gangster is merely being a dork rather than cool. With no metanarrative to ground it, one way of life cannot be morally superior, so redemption fails.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 20 "Bamboozled Philosophy through Blackface" — Flory argues Bamboozled deliberately makes its own audience laugh at Mantan's blackface coon routines to force self-reflection on how minstrel stereotypes still shape perceptions of African Americans. He reads Pierre Delacroix's shifting defenses of the show (free speech, art, 'get over slavery,' a simple-minded 'who is to judge' moral relativism) through Charles Mills's Racial Contract and 'epistemology of ignorance,' and his self-loathing through Fanon's struggle with racialization. Flory frames Lee as an Aristotelian gadfly: like Socrates, Lee arouses appropriately proportioned righteous anger (the Golden Mean) at injustice and goads viewers to philosophize, punishing Delacroix, Manray, and the Maumaus in a Manichaean moral structure to drive home minstrelsy's dehumanizing harm.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Rodriguez-Ruiz argues that Schizopolis and sex, lies, and videotape function as everyday 'thought experiments' about knowledge, contrasting them with Descartes's evil-genius and dream arguments and Dretske's disguised-zebra case. Fletcher must literally become his wife's lover's double to know she is cheating, and Ann pieces together John's affair from a stray earring, dramatizing how high the bar for knowledge of others is and how much depends on lucky accident. The trashcan-music scene stages the problem of induction and Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp. Soderbergh's boss's 'confirm nor deny' speech and Lester's preventable death show the films endorse a moderate skepticism that still affirms nature and power as real, rejecting full relativism and dogmatism.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 29 "18. Dissenting Opinions" — Framing Kim and Jimmy's clashes as a problem in the epistemology of peer disagreement, the chapter asks whether learning an epistemic peer disagrees should make you suspend judgment (the conciliatory view) or stay steadfast, using a tip-calculation dispute and their office-versus-practice compromise. It argues moral disagreements differ because we rarely count someone who disagrees on one moral question as a genuine peer, and rejects 'no fact of the matter' relativism for implying slavery could be permissible. It then reads Kim's arc, including 'Wouldn't I?', as her moral beliefs genuinely shifting toward Jimmy's, complicated by self-interested and self-deceiving reasons for holding beliefs.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 11 "How to do Philosophy" — Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's coinages to refute relativism and gut-thinking. 'My Truth' represents individual relativism and 'Wikiality' cultural relativism, both of which Johnson rejects via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany. 'Truthiness' is intuitionism, which Johnson attacks using Locke's critique of 'enthusiasts' who reason in a circle, and he argues that appeals to 'a right to my opinion' reveal indifference to truth. Following Socrates, he concludes we should defend beliefs with argument and admit ignorance rather than trust the gut.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Charles Taliaferro and Dan Kastrul argue, following Aristotle's dispositional account of character, that who the castaways are is a matter of what they would do under different conditions, illustrated by Mr. Eko's circumstance-driven violence and Ben Linus's shifting good-guy/bad-guy conduct. They deploy Plato's Myth of Gyges (the ring of invisibility) to test whether characters like Sun would act justly only when watched, and, against a completely reversed morality ('an island where skinning babies is good'), they argue via Chesterton that some overriding values are non-relative, so the show never fully reverses good and evil even amid its mysteries.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 22 "If Not on the Island of Ethical Subjectivism, Then Where" — George Wrisley uses Lost's morally ambiguous choices to argue that ethical subjectivism and cultural relativism collapse under scrutiny. He tests them against Sayid's shooting of young Ben (which Kate sees as murdering a child), Michael's killing of Ana Lucia, and Jacob versus the Man in Black, showing that the Argument from Disagreement does not establish that moral truth is relative. He presses three fatal consequences—infallibility of the individual or culture, the impossibility of genuine disagreement between Jacob and the Man in Black, and no room for reform like Martin Luther King Jr.'s—while invoking Socrates' wisdom of knowing that one does not know as a model of tolerant objectivism.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 17 "From There to Here, from Here to There, Diversity Is Everywhere" — Tanya Jeffcoat builds a philosophy of diversity around 'normative hubris' and 'totalizing tendencies,' using the Sneetches, the butter-battling Yooks and Zooks, and Daisy-Head Mayzie as cases of in-group/out-group dehumanization. Encountering the Other is framed through Buber's I-It versus I-Thou (Yertle treating his subjects as a throne), Fanon on the psychic violence and alienation of the oppressed, McIntosh's invisible knapsack of privilege, and Freire's humanization. Horton and the Lorax model standing with the disenfranchised, and Jeffcoat rebuts moral relativism via universal human rights and Dewey's democracy as a personal way of life that condemns intolerance.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "Chapter 1 The Conscience of Huckleberry Finn" — Jonathan Bennett reads the chapter 16 raft episode as a clash between 'bad morality' and sympathy: Huck's conscience (slave-owning principles telling him to return Jim to Miss Watson) supplies all the reasons, while his sympathy for Jim is a bare, reasonless feeling that wins by weakness of will, so Huck does right while believing he does wrong. He contrasts Huck with Himmler, whose bad morality overrode his surviving sympathy, and Jonathan Edwards, whose Calvinist approval of eternal damnation left no sympathy to conflict. The lesson is that principles should be kept open to revision under pressure from sympathy, since one cannot declare one's own morality bad but should stay open to correction.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 24 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Davids tastes Classic Red Brand X, Starbucks Guatemala Antigua, and the $100/lb Panama Esmeralda, and asks whether one can prove any coffee universally 'better.' He concedes taste is relative—citing East Asian dislike of acidity and the European relish for fermented 'rio-y' and Robusta notes North Americans call rotten—but escapes relativism via Stanley Fish's notion of 'interpretive communities': a dominant global community of expert cuppers shares assumptions and vocabulary (acidity, mouthfeel, sweetness, clean flavor) that let them rank the three coffees consistently. Legitimate evaluation is thus grounded not in the coffee itself but in the shared code of a community of judgment.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 12 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Farennikova and Prinz ask what makes something fashionable, arguing through thought experiments (Calvin Klein jeans, khakis, Robinson Crusoe's leather jacket, the accidental thrift-store punk, Gang Green, the mod couple) that four conditions must hold: many people wear the look, recognized experts endorse it, wearers intend to conform, and they regard it as having aesthetic value. They distinguish being fashionable from being merely popular or 'cool,' show fashionability is relative to group and to time, and note fashion must change to serve its signaling purpose — the Amish are 'intentionally unfashionable.'
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 12 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Schmid examines Moors Murderer Ian Brady's book The Gates of Janus, arguing that Brady built a genuine philosophy of serial murder from Sade and Nietzsche rather than merely name-dropping them. He corrects popular caricatures of the ubermensch and will to power, then shows Brady grounds his self-account in moral relativism and reframes serial killing as fundamentally about 'power and the will to power.' Brady's admiration for Carl Panzram and his likeness to the self-justifying, punishment-transcending Sadean hero illustrate how Nietzschean and Sadean ideas actually shape a killer's self-understanding.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 15 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Howard surveys serial killers from Liu Pengli and Locusta through Gilles de Rais, Bathory, Bichel, Panzram, and modern killers she interviewed (Bobby Joe Long, Shawcross, Milat, Birnie) to illustrate 'practical moral skepticism': the thesis that one can know right from wrong yet feel no motivation to be good. She distinguishes this from epistemic moral skepticism and argues that many killers, often privileged or unconstrained, understood moral codes but were driven instead by power, sadism, fatigue, or anger, showing that a failure of moral motivation is ancient rather than modern.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 9 "Through a Mirror, Darkly Art-Horror as a Medium for Moral Reflection" — Philip Tallon extends Aristotle's Poetics from tragedy to horror, arguing that where tragedy elicits pity and fear, horror mirrors the characters' visceral revulsion in the audience. Frankenstein serves as an internal critique of Enlightenment hubris, Victor's overreach making the abandoned monster more sympathetic than his creator. Against Lyotard's postmodern 'incredulity toward meta-narratives' and moral relativism, Tallon claims horror (e.g., King's 'Salem's Lot, where a priest craves a real EVIL to fight) works by violating an intuited moral, natural, and social order, thereby revealing a commonly-denied but underlying objective sense of morality and evil.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 11 "How to do Philosophy" — David Kyle Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's 'wikiality' and 'truthiness' to attack individual and cultural relativism, arguing (via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany) that truth is not relative to persons or cultures.
