He deploys Locke's critique of 'enthusiasm' to show gut thinking is circular, and invokes Socratic admission of ignorance against the claim of a 'right to your opinion.' The upshot is a method: defend beliefs with argument, be agnostic when evidence is lacking.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 24 "22. Rick & Morty as Philosophy Nihilism in the Multiverse" — The chapter argues that Rick Sanchez's nihilism is built on cultural relativism plus the metaphysical fact of a multiverse. It reads Rick's mockery of racist alien snakes and the Gazorpazorp matriarchy through Montaigne's essay on cannibals to establish cultural relativism, and treats the microverse 'battery' society through Marx's base/superstructure and Foucault's docile bodies to argue all social values are constructed for the rulers. Rick's dimension-hopping (the Cronenberg episode, the Vat of Acid) literalizes David Lewis's modal realism and Leibniz's possible worlds, so that no action matters because a counterpart always does the opposite; his resulting hedonism and Birdperson's 'Wubba lubba dub dub' reveal Rick as a depressed near-Camusian who cannot live his own absurdist creed.

### What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

In his 1974 essay "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?", Thomas Nagel argues that consciousness has an irreducibly subjective character: for any conscious creature there is something it is like to be that creature, experienced from its own point of view. Because a bat perceives the world through echolocation, we cannot genuinely imagine its inner life from the inside, only picture what it would be like for us to behave as a bat does. Nagel uses this to press a limit on objective, physical accounts of the mind, which describe things from no particular perspective and so seem to leave out the very feature—subjective experience—that makes a state conscious.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 40 "Unknown" — Holt takes Mouse's Tasty Wheat question - how do the machines know what it tasted like? - as the problem of other minds raised for machines, and defends mind-brain identity against multiple realizability with the artificial-pain analogy: like artificial hearts and prostheses, silicon 'pain' is a synthetic twin, not pain itself, so a single neural type may still realize it. He then sketches a speculative solution to the hard problem: consciousness is a 'had perspective' the brain creates - meaning-laden awareness of oneself and the world - which makes mind-brain identity intelligible and keeps the Matrix premise coherent.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 20 "“Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”" — Littmann asks whether Skynet's machines are people, testing three criteria on the Terminator films. The T-101 and T-1000 pass demanding Turing Tests by passing as humans; Searle's Chinese room — recast as a little Austrian inside the T-101 reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding — shows behavior alone cannot prove thought; and feelings are equally unproven by behavior, since the T-101 can smile on command. But the films' first-person 'Terminator's-eye-view' sequences, Littmann argues, display what it is like to be a Terminator and thus prove machine consciousness, so humanity's extinction might not be the end of persons.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 5 "Pink Floyd From Pompeii to Philosophy" — George Reisch's introduction reads the 1971 Live at Pompeii film, with the band playing to no audience inside a circular stone amphitheatre, as an ironic anticipation of The Wall, tracing how Waters's fury at stadium crowds (culminating in the 1977 Montreal spitting incident that spawned the wall concept) had not yet arrived. It frames the band's post-Barrett move from psychedelic whimsy to minimal formalism as philosophical stripping-away: Barrett wrote like an Aristotle fascinated by odd particulars ('Lucifer Sam,' 'The Gnome'), whose puzzlement at his impenetrable cat prefigures Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and the problem of other minds, while Waters pursued Plato's monolithic 'forms' of time, money, and madness. On this reading Dark Side's closing 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon' indicts Being itself, making life essentially and permanently tragic, a circular trap signaled by The Wall's interlocking 'we came in?' and 'Isn't this where...'
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 27 "Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up" — Tests three theories of mind against Spock's katra transfer in The Wrath of Khan and The Search for Spock and his mind melds with Kirk, the Horta, and Rock people. Descartes's divisibility argument backs the dualism the katra assumes, but the argument from parsimony (Ockham's razor), the problem of mental causation, and the conservation of energy weigh against it; Churchland's eliminative materialism plays by science's rules but runs into Nagel's 'what it is like' objection, dramatized by Geordi failing to describe anger to Data without circularity. The author lands, cautiously, on Searle-style emergentism — mind as an emergent, irreducible feature of neural complexity, as when Nomad and V'Ger exceed their programming — while conceding Kim's charge that it may be dualism in disguise.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 29 "Chapter 04 - Ewe, Robot" — Seegert opens with the V-K tortoise scene: Leon knows what a turtle is but cannot feel what it would be like to be one, making empathy the litmus of humanity, even though empathy just is imaginative simulation, so the test ironically demands that humans simulate better than the simulations do. He notes the double irony that replicants show empathy for each other (Roy mourning Pris) while Deckard shoots Zhora in the back without wincing, and that the test's real function is keeping androids enslaveable in an arms race of verisimilitude; the deeper anxiety the chapter sets up is not whether androids can pass for human but whether I might not be human myself.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 182 "Chapter 34 - Beyond Lies the Wub" — Dick's first published story dramatizes the moral status of a rational nonhuman: Peterson's wub, a telepathic, philosophical Martian pig-creature, reads minds, discusses Odysseus and individuation, and pleads that it is 'a sensible being like yourselves', yet Captain Franco - obsessed with eating it - freezes it mid-sentence, shoots it looking him in the eye ('Back on the farm we had hogs'), and serves it for dinner, dismissing Peterson's grief with 'It is only organic matter, now.' The wub's personhood is established entirely through language and philosophy, but speech fails to protect it from being treated as meat, and the closing irony - Franco resuming the wub's own Odysseus meditation, as if the mind survived its meal - underscores how thin the line is between person and livestock. The story thus stages the problem of other minds and the ethics of killing sentient beings who demand to be addressed eye-to-eye rather than dined upon.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 18 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Andrew Terjesen asks what Death could learn from living one mortal day per century in Sandman's Death: The High Cost of Living, after a little girl's 'How would you like it?' shamed the once icy Death into the practice. Using Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Nagel's bat to probe whether knowing what mortality is like requires first-person experience, he raises the 'Soul Man Effect' objection that Didi, like the fake black student in the 1986 film, always knows she will revert to being Death, and argues that simulation, not verbal description, is the efficient way to convey life's texture (Didi's hot-dog aftertaste). The real lesson, he concludes, is the existentialist one that each of us stands alone at death and that life's meaning lies in the unnoticed 'little moments' the dying regret missing, which only immersion in the distractions of living can teach Death, which is why the one-day-a-century program must continue.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 12 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Gordon Hawkes uses the P-zombie debate to ask whether there is something in a person no walker can eat. Rick telling Morgan over zombified Duane that 'that's just his body' voices Cartesian dualism, while Dr. Jenner's TS-19 scan - the neocortex 'you part' that never comes back - voices materialism, as does Dr. Stevens's dying claim that he is 'just evolving into a different, worse life form'. The chapter stages Chalmers's zombie argument (a molecule-identical twin with no inner experience) against Dennett's zimbo objection, with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' marking the interaction problem for dualism, and closes on the intuition that no brain scan of Test Subject 19 reveals what the zombie fever feels like.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 18 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Dave Beisecker amplifies Noel Carroll's paradox of horror: why would anyone enjoy watching, let alone compete for, AMC's 'stagger-on role' as a repulsive walker? Curiosity fails as an answer, since by Nagel's bat argument no amount of staggering around a set tells us what it is like to be a zombie - and since zombification destroys memory, desire, and self-concern, we would not survive it as persons in any interesting sense anyway. His solution is that zombies are the endearing losers and clowns of the undead world: playing one is a way to celebrate our inner awkward nerd and laugh at universal human ineptitude, which is exactly why Kirkman's shambling walkers, unlike fast zombies or glamorous vampires, invite impersonation.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 19 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Silcox and Cox present D&D modules as thought experiments in James Robert Brown's 'laboratory of the mind': the Tomb of Horrors' plane-shifting doorway forces Parfit's teletransporter question of whether the character who emerges is you, a copy, or an annihilation, extended to Tieflings and Warforged; Eberron's sentient Warforged raise Nagel's bat problem of whether a human player can know what it is like to be a machine, answered with the conclusion that players really explore human pretense, like Greek actors in masks. Mary Anne Warren's Space Traveler criteria for alien personhood strain against orcs who meet them yet attack on sight, and against the players who killed the lawful-good Flumph without parley. The deep difference is perspective: philosophy imagines sub specie aeternitatis while D&D demands immersion sub specie temporis, which nonetheless cultivates the open-minded intellectual virtues philosophers prize.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 20 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Von Gunten asks whether Bender, Calculon, and the robot mafia have moral worth, arguing first that they are sentient: behavioral similarity plus functional equivalence (pain as electric signals in neurons or circuits) defeat both behavior-only objections (the Sphex wasp's preprogrammed loop, knife-avoiding toy robots) and composition-based prejudice - Fry's 'I'm all squishy and flabby' defense at the Hal Institute - which would be 'biologism' analogous to racism. He then distinguishes moral patiency (Nibbler can be harmed but only behaviorally reinforced) from moral agency (deliberation and accountability), concluding that Bender's flexible life - Iron Cook, wrestling, folk music with Beck's head, jacking-on addiction - shows robots transcend their programming as humans transcend evolutionary presets. Limiting moral status to biology or species would be speciesism, so the thirty-first century's robots deserve the full protections and responsibilities humans have.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 22 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Stoody asks whether Hammond's dinosaurs are more than bones, blood, and DNA, and answers with Nagel's bat: there is something it is like to be eaten by a velociraptor, and even a complete neuroscience of a T. rex's brain would not reveal the bloodhound-rivaling smells it experiences. He reruns Jackson's Mary as Dr. Sattler raised in a black-and-white world who learns something new upon seeing violet West Indian Lilac berries, and rebuts the physicalist two-descriptions reply using Crichton's Michael Douglas pen name. He concludes that physicalism leaves out the what-it's-like aspect of consciousness, leaving a choice between substance dualism (dinosaur souls) and property dualism.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 28 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Christopher Ketcham writes a mock chronicle in which velociraptors escape to inhabited Nava, deliberately avoid humans, and over decades learn to share a hunting language with a Congo tribe, asking whether we would ever grant such beings equal intelligence and rights. He reads raptor pack behavior and cooperation through Dawkins's selfish gene, and uses Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to argue we can never peer into raptor consciousness, just as we brand human races inferior without looking. Citing Plessy v. Ferguson's whiteness-as-property and Mill's point that mistreating animals belongs in the same category as racial discrimination, he ends with a senate-hearing parody and the Neanderthal precedent: a human 'superiority gene' means coexistence with smart raptors would likely end as it did for them.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 30 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Rachel Haliburton asks what metaphysics underwrites Suzanne's world, where a mind can touch a perfect body. The materialist world inherited from Descartes reduces thoughts, meanings, and purposes to purposeless physical processes in which minds never touch bodies; Aristotle's teleological world, refurbished by Thomas Nagel's Mind and Cosmos, builds purposes into nature and treats subjective experience - what the tea and oranges are like for you - as real in its own right. She argues Suzanne's world, and our own ordinary mall-food-court world, is teleological: consciousness is 'biased towards the marvelous,' and we touch one another's bodies with our minds all the time.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 21 "Dracula and Philosophy" — McKinney argues Van Helsing should have studied Dracula's brain instead of staking him, because the Count is a philosophy-of-mind thought experiment: a mind that persists unchanged across bat, wolf, mist, and human bodies refutes mind-brain identity theory and fits functionalism (the mind as one song playable in many formats), while his telepathic bond with Mina and shapeshifting probe Cartesian dualism's mind-body interaction problem. Nagel's bats show that only Dracula could tell us what it is like to echo-locate or wolf-sense; yet since nothing like his unconstrained mind exists in our world, the novel finally maps what minds are not - evidence against the immaterial mind.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 25 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Versteeg and Barkman use Dracula's shapeshifting to stage Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?': even if the Count becomes a bat, whatever he recalls afterward is filtered back through his human-ness, so no non-bat can access bat-ness from a human point of view. A scene of Van Helsing and bat-Dracula both finding a girl's corpse distinguishes objective from subjective experience. Because physicalism predicts all of reality should be objectively accessible, the impenetrability of subjective experience pressures physicalism and leaves room for the immaterial soul Van Helsing's religion wants.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 22 "11. Of Bats and Supermen" — Springett argues Superman, not Batman, is the proper goal of transhumanism - Batman's training and gadgets are only a stage toward transcending the human condition - and that the eugenics and Social Darwinism objection fails because Superman directs his superior fitness at saving the less fit. Through Merleau-Ponty's embodied cognition (Lois's churning stomach over a deadline, Alfred retracing his steps and posture to recall a thought, the "Subway Superman" Wesley Autrey's instinctive track rescue) he shows that radically different bodies mean radically different minds and moral perception. That turns Nagel's "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" into "what is it like to be Superman?" - a problem of other minds for our transhuman future, with Watchmen's Doctor Manhattan as the warning of a transcendent being who simply stops caring about humans.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 32 "19. The Alchemy of Flat Worlds" — Staged as Professor Moby Dickens Melville's 'Philosophy of Worlds' course uniting Discworld wizards with the geometric Flatlanders of Abbott's novella, the chapter contrasts a storytelling, narrative-causality philosophy of Discworld with Flatland's mathematical, hierarchy-obsessed rationalism, and extends the contrast to physics (wizards favor loop quantum gravity, Flatlanders string theory) and theology (Hex's self-designed universe and words of power versus Flatland's circle-priests who rule women declared 'deficient in Reason'). When a Flatlander woman, Ms. Transversal, protests that calling the new softer approach 'feminine' repeats Abbott's sexism, the class closes with the narrator's suggestion, from a chalk-nub's-eye view, that everything we know may reflect the direction from which we see rather than the truth itself.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 34 "21. Welcome to My World" — Built on Jakob von Uexküll's Umwelt—the 'island of the senses' that enfolds each creature, illustrated by a moth that smells only a mate's pheromone and hears only the bat's echolocation—the chapter argues that every Discworld being likewise inhabits a sliced-down life world rather than the world as a whole. The ambiguous puzuma running near light speed, dream-spinning dromes that starve victims inside stolen Umwelten, the two-dimensional Shadowing Lemma, Gaspode's pathogen-warring skin, the hermit elephant's hut, and the re-annual plant that flowers a year before its seeds each show a life world carved out by what an organism can sense and use, whether its world runs on science or magic—prompting the suggestion that the Umwelt is more fundamental than either.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 17 "8. The Babe with the Power" — Michaud uses Bowie's Jareth and Labyrinth to make Berkeley's case that only minds and ideas exist: the taste of Sarah's tainted fruit, colors no culture without a word for 'blue' can see, dreams and optical illusions, and hallucinations all show the perceived world is a brain-made prediction, so the Goblin King's magic realm is 'more possible than we realize.' Because each of us builds a private world - Sarah and Jareth can never compare experiences ('I wonder what your basis for comparison is') - Bowie's death is literally the collapse of the world as he created it, 'as the world falls down,' though music may still reach across the void.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 12 "Violent Ends" — Richards asks what it is like to be a host, combining three lenses: Searle's biological naturalism (thinking machines must be built from materials with the right causal powers, and the hosts' synthetic flesh may qualify), Nagel's bat (even if hosts are conscious, their perfectly relived memories, curated pain, and blind spots like 'it doesn't look like anything to me' may make their experience as inconceivable to us as echolocation), and Chalmers's philosophical zombies (hosts behave exactly like us, yet beings identical to them with no inner light are conceivable). He reads Ford's contradictory testimony — praising Bernard's guilt as 'a thing of beauty' while denying consciousness exists — as a shift to a deflationary view with no threshold for being alive, and argues the show's choice to film human and host experience in the same style keeps the question deliberately open while fostering empathy.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 25 "What It Is Like to Be Out of the Asylum" — Ron Novy argues nobody can know what it is like to be Batman: deploying Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and a Mary's-Room variant with a color-deprived Barbara Gordon, he shows subjective experience resists even complete physical knowledge. Simone de Beauvoir's situated freedom then explains how 'one bad day' (Bruce's parents' murder, the Joker's Red Hood plunge into chemicals) threw each man into the same terrifying glimpse of Kant's noumenal world behind appearances, yet into opposite narratives of order and chaos. Even while sharing the joke that ends The Killing Joke, Batman and the Joker remain mutually unknowable, each the only one who can 'keep up' with the other.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 19 "Is a Man Not Entitled to the Sweat of His Brow" — Schevelier uses the Andrew Ryan assassination to teach phenomenology: the moment the controller stops responding, the 'mineness' of the experience collapses and the story stops being yours, revealing that Jack's (and the player's) freedom depended on a thin self-narrative the mind 'desperately struggles to create', per Lutece's epigraph. Nagel's bat shows why no brain scan captures what it is like to play, while Husserl, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty supply the toolkit; Heidegger's hammer, which shows itself in use or in breakdown, explains both immersive scenes like the Kashmir restaurant and what breaks them (bugs, wrong display, a talking protagonist). Following Merleau-Ponty's claim that art records subjective experience, the chapter treats Levine's team as artistic phenomenologists whose design question 'What is this experience we are trying to make?' turned Columbia and Elizabeth into phenomenological analyses to be read.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 19 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Silcox and Cox read D&D modules as thought experiments in James Robert Brown's 'laboratory of the mind'. The Tomb of Horrors' four overlapping plane-shifted buildings restate Parfit's teletransporter puzzle — did the character who stepped through get annihilated, or is an exact copy walking around elsewhere, and does the answer differ for a Warforged or Tiefling? — while the Eberron setting's magically sentient Warforged run into Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?': players cannot access Warforged experience and are really exploring what it is like for a human to suspend disbelief, like Greek actors donning masks. Mary Anne Warren's Space Traveler criteria for alien personhood collapse on contact with orcs who pass them yet eat you, and with the Flumph — lawful good, rational, but killed on sight by the authors' own party — showing personhood cannot be the only criterion for how to treat strangers; the closing twist is that philosophy contemplates scenarios sub specie aeternitatis while D&D forces immersion sub specie temporis, a habit of entertaining the impossible that is itself a philosophical virtue.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 33 "Notes" — The chapter argues Fallout 4's grip comes not from graphical fidelity but from first-person moral agency: deciding the fate of Gen 3 synths who do not know they are synths — supporting their escape, hunting them, or installing them as unwitting spies — forces the player through emotionally real moral deliberation. It connects this to Turing's worry about proving to another that you think ('it could've been me in their shoes') and to Nagel's bat, proposing that imagining what it is like to be a synth is a stepping stone toward ever stranger perspectives. Playing thus becomes the joy of actually doing philosophy — reawakening imagination, reshuffling our space of possibilities, and returning us to our own problems refreshed rather than merely escaped.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 21 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Henry Jacoby wields Westeros's strange beings against the mind-body problem: Nagel's 'what it is like' question becomes 'What is it like to be a direwolf?', and wargs like Bran-in-Summer and Orell's eagle ask whether one point of view can literally inhabit another. Against Descartes's denial of animal consciousness (only language users have souls; Mormont's raven crying 'Corn!' is a machine), he argues Ghost's pain behavior and direwolf physiology ground animal consciousness exactly as our brothers' behavior grounds theirs. Wargs do not refute materialism - in Westeros magic violates physical law without invoking nonphysical stuff - and 'Zombie Sansa', the philosophers' phenomenal zombie, together with the reanimated wights, is impossible in our world (with Russell, experiences are brain events known directly) and conceivable beyond the Wall only because the supernatural breaks the laws of nature.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 22 "11. Of Bats and Supermen" — Springett argues Superman, not Batman, is the right goal for a transhumanist future: through Merleau-Ponty's embodied cognition (Lois's deadline nausea, Alfred recovering a thought by redoing his posture, real-life 'Subway Superman' Wesley Autrey's gut-level rescue) he shows bodies shape thought and morality, so a super-body means a super-mind. Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' becomes 'what is it like to be Superman' — a problem of superhero minds, with Doctor Manhattan's indifference as the cautionary case — while Superman's rescues of the less fit show transcendence need not slide into eugenics or Social Darwinism.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Littmann asks whether personhood could survive humanity's extinction in 2029: if Terminators genuinely think and feel, a Skynet victory would not be the end of people. He argues the T-101, T-1000 and T-X pass substantial Turing Tests (fooling muggers, cops, Sarah on the phone as her 'mother'), then concedes Searle's Chinese Room - recast as a tiny Austrian inside the endoskeleton reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding - shows thinking behavior cannot prove thought. But he claims the films' red-tinted Terminator's-eye-view shots show what it is like to be a Terminator, giving proof of consciousness, and concludes the machines are probably persons: there is an 'I' in 'I'll be back.'
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Curtis argues liberal society should be wary of integrating True Blood's vampires: their feudal system of kings, sheriffs, and the magister, enforced through maker bonds and punishment, violates even Kukathas's maximally tolerant liberalism because members cannot freely exit and humans are mistreated with impunity. Adapting Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to the question 'What is it like to be a vampire?', he contends that glamouring, blood bonds, and an eroticized hunger different in kind from ours leave humans unable to verify vampire trustworthiness — echoing Aristotle's claim that one who cannot live in the polis is a beast or a god — so mainstreaming demands the AVL first expose and reform vampire institutions.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 25 "NOTES" — Peppers-Bates and Rust stage Weber's disenchantment of the world in Sookie's relationship with Bill: her scientific-naturalist demand to know what animates him meets his 'magic', and although Searle and Nagel show consciousness resists scientific reduction (so 'miracle' is not absurd for the mind), Bill's vitalist, quasi-Cartesian dodge is a bait-and-switch about digestion. Sookie's real question is Sartrean — whether vampires, seemingly driven by blood bonds, hierarchy, and appetite, can freely choose their projects — and the chapter answers yes: Malcolm's cruelty presupposes he could do otherwise, Sookie's 'blood tie thing' excuse is bad faith in Eric's eyes, and Eric's wooing of her after regaining his memory is a freely chosen project that re-enchants her world.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 26 "NOTES" — Curry asks whether even Sookie's telepathy can breach the privacy of mind: a third-person account of shifter Sam hearing a dog-whistle leaves out the quale — the homage to Nagel's bat — and Locke's inverted spectrum (Jason and Tara both say 'green' while living different experiences) shows qualia are incommunicable. Reading the astrology-believing Maxine's mind traps Sookie in a dilemma: if she fully becomes Maxine she is no longer the Sookie who knows, and if she keeps her skeptical psychology she never experiences what it is like to believe — so, drawing on Dennett's coffee example for one's own past qualia, even the show's most powerful mind reader can never know what it is like to experience things as you.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 12 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Gordon Hawkes uses Rick's words to Morgan over zombified Duane ('that's just his body—there's nothing of your son left in there') to set up Cartesian dualism against the materialism of Drs. Jenner and Stevens ('just tasty meat all the way down'), with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' as the standard objection. He then explains Chalmers's zombie argument that a physically identical unconscious twin is conceivable, so consciousness is non-physical, and Dennett's 'zimbo' rebuttal that a creature endlessly reflecting on its own states would believe itself conscious. The chapter closes by asking whether there is 'something it is like' to be a walker shuffling through Atlanta, and sides with Rick's anti-materialism.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 13 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann asks whether you survive a walker bite, rejecting the body view via Dr. Jenner's 'Everything you ever were or ever will be—gone' because a mindless corpse is not you. He tests philosophical behaviorism and functionalism against walker behavior—Jenny turning her old doorknob, walkers distinguishing humans by smell—then adapts Dennett's thought experiment into a walker-and-rope computer functionally identical to a human brain. Since we can conceive that groaning machine lacking inner experience, behavior and function cannot settle which systems are conscious, leaving the bitten dying in ignorance of whether they face annihilation or reanimation.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 18 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Dave Beisecker takes AMC's 'stagger-on role' zombie contest as an amplified version of Noel Carroll's paradox of horror: why relish playing a repulsive walker when zombification is the fate no rational creature would wish even on its remains? He rejects the curiosity solution through Nagel's bat—no staggering around a set could reveal what it is like to be a zombie, and we wouldn't survive zombification anyway except as our remains—and notes we fantasize about being survivors, not monsters. His answer is affection and release: walkers are the geeks and clowns of the undead pantheon, and playing one lets us comically own our inner loser, which is why Kirkman's symbol-free zombies invite identification where Nazi zombies would not.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 12 "Violent Ends" — Bradley Richards asks what it is like to be a host, using Nagel's 'what is it like to be a bat?' to argue that whether we can conceive host experience depends on how similar it is to ours, and Searle's biological view to ask whether hosts are made of the right stuff. He catalogs how host perception, emotion, and especially memory differ from human (Maeve's perfect reliving of memories versus our hazy constructive recall, 'is this now?'), and weighs Chalmers's philosophical zombies against the hosts. He notes the show depicts host and human experience in the identical cinematic style to preserve ambiguity, and links memory, self-consciousness, and freedom via Dolores's maze, suggesting hosts may be phenomenally conscious before becoming self-aware.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 18 "The Instructive Impossibility of Being John Malkovich" — Hagberg treats Being John Malkovich as a refutation of the dualist fantasy that one could achieve transparent knowledge of another mind by occupying it. Through the film's four levels—Schwartz as spectator inside Malkovich, Lotte's transgender re-embodiment, Schwartz's puppeteering, and Malkovich falling into his own portal to the 'Malkovich, Malkovich' hell—he shows, via Jamesian relational sensation and Wittgenstein's private-language argument, that it is always still Schwartz who senses, so no one ever becomes Malkovich. The self-enclosed Malkovich world, where everyone can only say 'Malkovich,' dramatizes that selfhood is relationally emergent (Royce, Mead) and that experience is inviolably one's own (Margalit on remembered emotion).
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 13 "“Freaks of Nature” Extrasensory Perception and the Paranormal in the Films of David Cronenberg" — Keith Allen uses Stereo, Scanners, and The Dead Zone to explore the philosophy of ESP: telepathy and precognition challenge C. D. Broad's 'basic limiting principles' about causation (action at a distance, backward causation, changing the future). He asks whether ESP has the phenomenal 'tang' of genuine perception (Hume on force/vivacity; Nagel's 'what it is like'), and uses BonJour's reliable-clairvoyant Norman case plus Gettier to argue about internalist justification and knowledge, asking whether Johnny Smith needs reasons to trust his precognitive visions.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 17 "Terminator-Fear and the Paradox of Fiction" — Holt uses the Terminator's first-person infrared POV shots (evoking Nagel's 'what is it like' question about an alien artificial consciousness) to frame the paradox of fiction: how we feel fear toward things we know do not exist. He offers a contextual divide-and-conquer solution, arguing higher emotions like pity and admiration for Sarah and Reese are largely make-believe, while lower emotions like Terminator-fear are genuine and need no existential belief (thought and mere possibility suffice). He adds that such fear is more rational for a naturalist who admits artificial intelligence is possible than for a dualist, and speculates the Terminator functions as an archetype embodying tech-noir dread.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Baltzer-Jaray uses Kant's phenomena/noumena split, Plato's Forms, and Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to ask whether Jack Skellington can know the essence of Christmas and whether Vincent Malloy can know what it is to BE Vincent Price. She argues Jack's lab-experiments on presents and snowflakes ('Jack's Obsession') can only yield phenomena, never the noumenal essence, so Kant would permit belief but not knowledge; Vincent, watching only Price's horror roles, grasps a mere phenomenal fragment. Via Nagel she concludes neither can occupy another's subjective viewpoint, so the lesson of both films is to celebrate otherness through communication rather than trying to be someone else.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 22 "A.I. Artificial Intelligence Artistic Indulgence or Advanced Inquiry" — White argues A.I. dramatizes the mind-body problem through the mecha child David, proposing a 'Strengthened Turing Test' (STT) in which the audience knows he is a machine yet must judge whether he truly loves Monica. He runs Searle's Chinese Room (David as mere rule-follower with no qualia) against Nagel's 'what is it like' and Chalmers's zombie argument and property-dualist multiple realizability, which would let a sufficiently complex David be genuinely conscious. White contends the imprinting device—David's built-in need for one other being—is what lets him pass the STT, sidestepping Cartesian dualism's interaction problem.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 25 "23_LaRocca_Chapter_022.html" — Jennifer McMahon reads Gabriela Cowperthwaite's Blackfish through Thomas Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and the problem of other minds, arguing the film's interviews with orca neuroscientists (Marino et al.) function as Nagel's proposed 'objective phenomenology,' conveying orca consciousness through objective indicators rather than mere anthropomorphic projection. She dissects the film's rhetoric around Tilikum and Dawn Brancheau, showing how the title, delayed naming, SeaWorld ad juxtapositions and emotional testimony first vilify then humanize the whale to argue captivity is morally unacceptable. Invoking Peggy Zeglin Brand's 'lenses,' Iris Murdoch's 'unselfing' and Marc Bekoff's inclusive ethic, she concludes the film approximates truth about orca minds even as it, like SeaWorld, is 'structured to sell.'
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 14 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Phillips argues that there is something-it-is-like to be a knowledgeable coffee drinker, using Nagel's bat and Jackson's Mary thought experiments — but where the bat is 'fundamentally alien,' coffee expertise is learnable, and via David Lewis's ability hypothesis the reader can apply book-knowledge of acidity, body, finish, and flavor to abilities they already have. He then invokes Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (Homer's enduring appeal, the Don Quixote wine-tasters) to claim aesthetic and moral judgments spring from the same refinable sentiments, so that examining your cup free of prejudice is, echoing Socrates' 'unexamined life,' something we almost owe ourselves: the unexamined cup is not worth drinking.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 13 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Zangwill argues that 'fashionable' is a relational, sociological property (like 'famous'), yet things also directly *appear* fashionable or 'cool' to us in first-person perceptual experience as if coolness were a simple, non-relational quality (illustrated by seeing 1965 Mick Jagger as 'groovy'). He claims these two aspects — the third-person sociological concept and the first-person phenomenological one — cannot be united, so the concept of fashion is 'schizoid.' Invoking Nagel on consciousness and Bernard Williams's charge of alienation in Kantian and utilitarian ethics, he concludes fashion involves a projective illusion and is a genuine source of alienation.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 20 "“Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”" — Greg Littmann asks whether the Terminators are 'people,' testing three criteria: passing as human, thinking, and feeling. The T-101, T-1000, and T-X repeatedly pass Turing Tests, giving behavioral evidence of thought, but Littmann recasts Searle's Chinese Room as the 'Austrian Terminator' to argue behavior never proves genuine understanding. He then argues personhood requires conscious experience (what it is like to be a Terminator), and takes the films' red- and blue-tinted first-person 'Terminator's-eye view' shots as evidence the machines really are conscious, so humanity's extinction need not end personhood.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 90 "85. Persona 5 Royal as Philosophy Unmasking (Persona)l Identity and Reality" — Lopez and Marquez use Persona 5 Royal's Phantom Thieves to explore Schechtman's 'characterization' question of personal identity ('Who am I?') via three bases: qualia (the privately felt sense of self expressed when Ryuji names himself a 'troublemaker' and Morgana insists he is 'NOT a cat'), Wittgensteinian hinge propositions, and language-games in which identity and 'justice' get their meaning through use. Ryle and Wittgenstein's behaviorist worries about private language are set against Nagel's bat and Chalmers's qualia. The Maruki arc—offering a pain-free false utopia and Sumire living as her dead twin Kasumi—poses whether Bentham's utilitarianism, James's pragmatism, or Baudrillard's hyperreality could justify a blissful simulacrum, which the game's 'true ending' rejects for painful reality.

### Personal Identity

Personal identity concerns what makes someone the same person over time despite change, and what the self fundamentally is. Philosophers have offered competing criteria: the body or brain, continuity of memory and psychology, or the persistence of an immaterial soul. Locke's memory-based view, Hume's bundle theory that finds no enduring self behind experiences, and later refinements have all sought to say why the child and the adult, or the person before and after profound change, count as one and the same. The question matters for responsibility, anticipation, survival, and the concern we have for our own futures.

- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 23 "Inauthenticity and Fascism" — David Detmer treats Zelig, the mock-documentary 'chameleon man' who turns black, Chinese, fat, or a Nazi depending on his company, as a stark dramatization of personal identity and the existentialist critique of inauthenticity. After rejecting the memory, bodily-continuity, and immaterial-soul criteria of identity, the chapter takes the existentialist line, quoting Heidegger on Dasein's selfhood, that a self is its choices, projects, and commitments, so Zelig's chameleonism is self-estrangement motivated by fear and the craving to be liked. Politically, the chapter draws Allen's lesson that genocides happen not because millions go mad but because millions passively conform, made literal by Zelig appearing at a Hitler rally, and supports it with Asch's conformity experiments and Milgram's obedience studies.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 19 "Horcruxes" — Uses Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, whose victims like Barty Crouch Jr. go on existing as empty shells without memory or self, to eliminate the leading views of the soul: the soul cannot be the source of life, of sentience, or even of Cartesian higher thought, since the soulless victim may still sense and think dimly. The chapter compares the Kiss's aftermath to severe dementia or to Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of whether the person rather than just the body survives.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 23 "Mind-Body Distinctions" — Eric Saidel launches his chapter from a puzzle: why would Sirius, outside for the first time in months, celebrate by chasing his tail in Order of the Phoenix? He asks whether an Animagus is a man in a dog's body, a dog in a man's body, or a third thing, and extends the question to Pettigrew, Rita Skeeter, McGonagall, werewolf Lupin, boggarts, and Polyjuice transformations such as Barty Crouch Jr.'s eerily effective impersonation of Moody.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 24 "Whose Reasons" — Tests the Cartesian division of the transformed Padfoot into mind plus body across four possible combinations and rejects them all: Sirius's human body cannot plausibly slip 'into non-being' during transformation (against McGonagall's quip), yet a Sirius-mind cannot explain tail-chasing and a dog-mind cannot explain Padfoot standing on his hind legs to embrace Harry at King's Cross. Mind-body dualism thus fails as an account of what the transformed person is.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — Concludes that transformed persons are unified mind-body wholes rather than pilot-and-ship pairings, enlisting Descartes himself, who insisted he is 'not only lodged in my body, like a pilot in his ship' but compounded with it into a single whole. The evidence is textual: Polyjuiced Harry naturally 'thunders' with Runcorn's powerful frame while acting for Harry's reasons, Luna recognizes Harry through Barny Weasley's facial expression, and Crouch-as-Moody makes sense as an indivisible embodiment, so Padfoot is neither man nor dog but a third kind of being, a man-dog.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 111 "“A Swirling, Silvery Mass”" — Opens Amy Kind's Pensieve chapter: the basin lets you offload memories like data from a hard drive, gain distance from obsessions, and, as Dumbledore tells Harry, spot patterns and links when reviewing them from outside. Its real intrigue is philosophical: if thoughts can be extracted from the mind, tampered with, stored elsewhere, shared, and discarded, then the boundaries of mind, memory, and self are up for grabs - and memory-based accounts of personal identity, on which philosophers have modeled our continuing existence, come under pressure.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 132 "The Inversion of Voldemort" — Distinguishes remorse from mere regret through Voldemort's cold 'I regret it' after ordering Nagini to kill Snape: remorse requires owning one's act, and at the final duel Harry addresses him as 'Tom Riddle' and demands he 'try for some remorse' - the death-to-self Riddle cannot perform. Dumbledore's remorse over the cursed Resurrection Stone ring and his arranged death, and Harry's voluntary death that destroys the Horcrux within him and restores his whole soul, exemplify dying to the past self for renewal, while Harry's renunciation of his temper toward Ron and Hermione and his love for Ginny mark his continuous moral regeneration.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 134 "The Fantasy Objection" — Takes up the integrity objection from psychoanalyst Melanie Klein: renouncing one's past self ('Bad Charles' versus 'New Charlie') risks self-deception, since the reformed person remains the self-same wrongdoer, as the alcoholic who stays sober for decades still knows himself to be. Taliaferro concedes the regeneration model can be abused but insists renewal requires a death-like renunciation, illustrated negatively by Snape, who loves Lily, feels remorse for the 'Mudblood' insult and for giving Voldemort the prophecy, yet cannot confess or release his resentment, and so remains unintegrated.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 142 "NOTES" — Argues via William James's 'sow a thought... reap a destiny' and Aristotle's account of how repeated action incrementally shapes the soul that Voldemort's flayed remnant is a character fully forged by choices, stuck with itself forever - a postmortem fate Heidegger's atheism cannot frame but Rowling's afterlife can. The section weighs Locke's memory-and-character account of identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the immortality question must govern how we live, and ends asking whether Voldemort's evil is ignorance, as Plato held, or a cultivated appetite that only vice can satisfy.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 111 "Chapter 17 - Questions of Identity Is the Hulk the Same Person as Bruce Banner" — Frames the chapter with a San Francisco criminal trial in which Bruce Banner's lawyer argues the Hulk — a large green figure — literally was not the same individual who now stands small and pale before the judge. Ruling requires criteria for "continuity of personal identity over time": what makes you the same person today as ten years ago, applied here to whether Banner should answer for the Hulk's rampage.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 112 "The Hulk’s Bodily Identity" — Tests the everyday bodily criterion of identity: the Hulk's body contains far more atoms than Banner's, but since all our cells turnover anyway — the "Stan Lee Schooner" has every part replaced yet stays the same boat, the Ship of Theseus problem — and the organ-donor case of "Herb Trimpe" shows a body with greater physical continuity to Kinghorn than to its owner, bodily continuity cannot be what personal identity consists in.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 113 "The Mental Realm of the Hulk" — Applies Locke's memory theory: the shape-shifting Martian Manhunter and the irradiated Fantastic Four stay the same people through mental continuity, and the early comics' Banner-minded Hulk meets Locke's criterion — but the later "Hulk smash!" Hulk, who recognizes Betty Ross yet lacks Banner's memories, fails it. The chapter then breaks the criterion itself with Reid's brave-officer objection (the general both is and is not the flogged boy), Alzheimer's and Doc Ock's amnesia attack on Spider-Man, and the circularity of distinguishing genuine from false memory (the deluded fan who "remembers" starring in Adventures of Superman).
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 114 "A Causal Account of the Hulk’s Identity" — Proposes that the Hulk is Banner because Banner "Hulks out" — the monster state develops causally from Banner's body and mind through radiation, danger and anger, rather than one person being swapped for another. But a mad scientist's cloning accident that splits Banner into two simultaneous rampaging Hulks breaks the account, since both would be causally derived from Bruce yet could not both be the one person — the fission-style counterexample that afflicts every theory so far.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 115 "Is There No Way to Tell" — Presents Derek Parfit's challenge to the whole enterprise: just as there need be no answer to whether a repaired machine is "the same" machine, Parfit's divided-brain case — each half housed in a new body — suggests a person can "survive as two different people without implying that I am these people," so identity questions may lack answers. Kinghorn resists the leap: difficulty finding the truth does not show there is none.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 116 "The Hulk’s Relational Identity" — Defends a relational account: a person's identity persists through continuing relationships with others (like a marriage or a corporation), against our post-Enlightenment fixation on private attributes. Objections — severed relationships, the castaway, others' biased projections — are answered by positing a God who relates to every person without distortion and guarantees each identity, and who, since divine power cannot do the logically impossible, could not make Banner identical with two numerically distinct Hulks at once.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 117 "What Should We Conclude" — Renders the verdict in the Banner trial: Bruce is the Hulk, because their relationships continue — when David Banner phones to say Betty Ross will be eliminated, Bruce forms the protective intention the Hulk then executes by destroying the three mutant poodles, and Betty, David and General Ross all relate to the Hulk as Bruce. Physical, mental and causal indicators are mere cues to the deeper continuity of relationships that constitutes who someone is.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 125 "Identity in Crisis" — Poses the persistence problem through Superman-1 and Superman-2: are they strictly identical? Perdurantism — persons as four-dimensional space-time worms made of temporal parts — makes them distinct worms with no parts in common, so Superman meeting his counterpart is no stranger than you meeting a friend; endurantism, with wholly present strict identity, could identify them across timelines but balks at the impossibility of Superman meeting himself.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 126 "Endurantist Past-Changing" — Chases the endurantist bullet: if one thing can differ across timelines, one and the same timeline can exist differently in different hyperhistories, letting Joe's murder of Wolfman make 1984 "not the way he remembers it." Yet even this yields only switching, not the dynamic change Crisis dramatizes, so the six-dimensional cosmos stands; Hanley closes with Wolfman's own secret plot device for bringing back the killed Barry Allen Flash.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 128 "Dual Identities" — Lists the classic hero/normal identity pairs (Batman/Bruce Wayne, Spider-Man/Peter Parker, plus Woody Allen's joke alias) and separates costume as role-transition — the Fantastic Four's public uniforms, doctors' scrubs, Bob's garage shirt — from costume as tool, Batman's fear-theater aimed at "a superstitious and cowardly lot" and the female heroes' calculated "gawk factor." What most superheroes do is the distinct third thing, masking: personas from the Latin for mask, keeping Peter's Spider-Man and Matt Murdock's Daredevil secret in both directions.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 28 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Uses Narnia's magical transformations to probe personal identity, starting with the qualitative/numerical identity distinction illustrated by the look-alike twins Shasta and Corin in The Horse and His Boy. Aristotle's essential/accidental properties frame the question of what Eustace can lose and remain Eustace, including turning into a dragon, and Rabadash into a donkey, showing persons are not identical to their bodies. Descartes's soul argument and Locke's memory theory are tested and rejected, the latter because it cannot handle Rilian's enchanted amnesia, Shasta's forgotten infancy, or Susan's disowned memories without circularity. The chapter defends instead a first-person-perspective theory on which a person is constituted by, not identical to, a body, illustrated by the repeatedly repaired Dawn Treader and by the heroes surviving death in The Last Battle as restored points of view.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 21 "“Nobody’s Bob Dylan”" — Vernezze and Lulewicz take Dylan's 1964 Halloween quip "I got my Bob Dylan mask on" as an entry into personal identity, testing each theory against his life: the bodily view (Zimmerman to Dylan) survives cell turnover but stumbles on brain-transplant cases; Locke's memory theory handles them but faces Reid's brave-officer regress and Alzheimer's cases, and Dylan's reincarnation lyrics ("Shelter from the Storm," "I and I") ignore memory altogether. The Christian soul view of the gospel albums ("When He Returns," "Gotta Serve Somebody") follows Descartes and Plato but cannot justify the swirl-to-filling inference that souls exist. The chapter ends sympathetic to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist no-self: Dylan's "I is another," his name as fabrication, and the cover album Self Portrait all deny a fixed self-created essence.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 8 "Dead People" — William Larkin uses Romero's films - Karen Cooper devouring her father in Night of the Living Dead, Roger begging Peter to shoot him in Dawn, Riley's 'Those people are all dead' in Land - to argue that persons are res corporealis, bodily continuers, rather than Descartes's res cogitans. Our terror of becoming a zombie ourselves and our grief at recognized neighbors in the horde reveal that deep down we think persons survive as corpses, so bodily continuity suffices for identity while psychological continuity is unnecessary. The Locke-style body-switching intuition (prince and cobbler) that supports the psychological approach is dismissed as theoretically biased data compared to what good zombie fiction draws out of us.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 9 "Zombies and Us" — Hamish Thompson asks why we kill zombies with so few qualms and whether zombification releases us from obligations to the person who was, testing brain-death criteria, altered-identity and self-defense justifications against Shaun of the Dead (Shaun's mother and Ed), Day of the Dead's Bub, White Zombie, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He borrows Hume's bundle theory - the self as a fiction, a bundle of perceptions rather than an essence - and Parfit's degrees of psychological continuity to dissolve the sharp alive/dead and same-person/other-person dichotomies that make zombie-killing easy. The payoff is that we are already partly zombie (Shaun's checkout line, Ed on the sofa, the author's all-night gaming), differing only in our capacity for brief autonomous, goal-directed choices like Shaun's three-plan montage.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 30 "Oh Yes, There Will Be Blood" — Rachel Robison asks why blood, of all substances, carries metaphysical powers in vampire lore - Elizabeth Bathory's youth-giving baths, Dracula's control over Mina once she drinks his blood, Sookie's bond with Bill in True Blood. Her explanation is historical: the ancient cardiocentric view (Aristotle, Empedocles, Chrysippus placing the rational center in the heart and making blood its product) plus Galenic humorism and bloodletting made blood the carrier of the self, so drinking someone's blood plausibly transmits bits of their personal identity, knowledge, and even domination over one's free will. She then tests the show's synthetic 'True Blood': either some essential property of blood (or of the act of drinking it) carries the power, or the legend is parasitic on our lingering habit of locating emotion and character in the heart ('hot blooded') - either way the myth stays credible because our metaphors of blood never died.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 18 "Be Slow to Judge" — Southworth tests Locke's memory theory on Wolverine: the Cassandra Nova/Xavier mind-swap shows identity follows mind, not body, and Wolverine's serial memory wipes (Team X, Weapon X, Apocalypse's brainwashing) mean that on Locke's connected-memory view several different people have inhabited his body — with House of M's total recall suddenly loading him with responsibility for all their deeds. Jamie Madrox's duplicates then carry Parfit's objection that shared memories cannot suffice for sameness of person, pushing toward physical continuity and the chapter's deflationary moral: be slow to judge who deserves blame.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 19 "Identities, Selves, and Others" — Patterson uses Thornhill's being mistaken for the fictitious George Kaplan to test theories of personal identity: the body theory fails a CIA thought experiment in which a Kaplan double is slowly rebuilt from Thornhill's own replaced cells; Locke's memory theory fails on amnesia scenarios and circularity, since one cannot have memories of a self unless one already has a self; and Parfit's psychological continuity survives, with Thornhill drifting along a 'Psychological Spectrum' toward 'one hundred percent Kaplan' as he plays the spy. The chapter then turns existentialist: with Sartre, no essential nature fixes who Thornhill is, so he is totally responsible for the self his choices create, from 'Expedient Exaggerations' to risking death on Mount Rushmore. Charles Taylor's claim that a self exists only in dialogue with a community explains why Eve and others literally help make Thornhill into the person he becomes.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 17 "Was Jerry Garcia the Soul of the Grateful Dead" — John Uglietta asks what made the Grateful Dead the Grateful Dead when they swapped five keyboardists yet stopped being themselves the moment Jerry Garcia died, prompting the rename to The Dead. Testing Aristotle's essential versus accidental properties, Peter French's structural account of group identity (the Yankees, the Glenn Miller Orchestra), same-stuff theories via a VW bus rebuilt piece by piece from its old parts — a Ship of Theseus puzzle — and Locke's memory theory applied to Phil Lesh's liver (but feared brain) transplant, he proposes that the band's essence was a group spirit born of members 'surrendering their own little trip'. The soul of the Dead was bigger than Jerry but smaller than the whole band, and its loss at his death was something the survivors could recognize but not replace.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 20 "Absolutely Curtains" — Michael Patton retells the Ship of Theseus (his 'Trump Princess' rebuilt part-by-part from spares, then duplicated from the salvaged parts) to ask whether Pink Floyd survived its upheavals: Bob Klose's pre-Piper exit, Syd Barrett's 1968 dismissal ('No, fuck it, let's not bother' on the drive to Southampton), Rick Wright's firing during The Wall, and Roger Waters's 1985 lawsuit to stop Gilmour and Mason using the name. Roster, stylistic ('Lucifer Sam' versus 'Money'), legal, and nominal criteria each fail, so he proposes an 'Officeholder View' of identity in which constituencies decide sameness — as when UFO Club's Joe Boyd saw a different Syd at the June 1967 show, while the author's locked-in brother Josh (like Bauby in The Diving Bell and the Butterfly) remained the same son and brother to his family. Parfit's claim that survival tracks memory and personality rather than body underwrites the 'death of a thousand cuts' scenario: the band's criteria, not Syd's own, ended the life of the person 'Syd Barrett', and he didn't get a vote.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 6 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction opens with Socrates on trial for corrupting the youth of Athens and quips that on stage before the youth of Athens, Georgia, Cash could claim he was only asking "What is truth?" It frames Cash as Kris Kristofferson's "walking contradiction" whose paradoxes generate the book's questions: how evil fits a world rated by a benevolent God, where the enduring "I" hides while Cash insisted he was always changing, and what makes a law unjust. It also presents the Man in Black as social critic lobbying officials at San Quentin and Folsom for prison reform and raising money for reservation schools, before welcoming readers with the 1969 Arthur, Illinois concert where hippies and Amish rubbed shoulders.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 8 "Authentic Cash" — Butler rehearses how the Johnny Cash persona was socially manufactured: Sam Phillips coined the name "Johnny Cash" for its rebellious marketing value, "Folsom Prison Blues" narrates a prison term Cash never served (and borrowed from Jimmie Rodgers and Gordon Jenkins), and the Man in Black image began as an accident of black shirts at a Memphis church performance. Against Jung's persona-as-mask and Dr. Phil's "authentic core self," and armed with George Herbert Mead's social theory of the self, he argues authenticity is not fidelity to a hidden inner essence but active engagement with the social processes shaping one's identity, the way paper money gains "cash value" through use. Cash invested the imposed persona with value by sincerely living it (for example, writing "Man in Black" to give the black clothes his own meaning), so the construct became genuinely his identity.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 9 "A Modest Conclusion" — Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro stage the diachronic-versus-episodic debate about the self (Galen Strawson's episodic view included) against Leigh Edwards's "no single Johnny Cash": the hotel-room-wrecking addict and the Billy Graham touring Christian do not fit one biography. They argue the private J.R. was a third option: on stage he becomes wholly absorbed in story characters (the Folsom narrator, the man who shot a man in Reno) while a self not defined by time slips in and out of the persona, evidenced by his account of gradually shedding "Johnny Cash" after shows. Johnny Cash the public quilt is compared to the Ship of Theseus, every original piece of J.R. replaced yet still owned by him, and the modest conclusion is that J.R., like anyone making a free choice, stood above the timeline of instants and could inhabit both the episodes and the grand narrative.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 26 "Memories Are Made of This" — Randall Jensen asks whether Cash's hope of reunion with the dead ('Meet Me in Heaven,' 'If We Never Meet Again This Side of Heaven') is even coherent, using the 'One Piece at a Time' Cadillac and a hypothetical 1954 Plymouth to retell the Ship of Theseus puzzle about identity through part replacement. He canvasses Platonic dualism from the Phaedo (Cash is his soul, the body a rusty cage), the materialist hope that God can reassemble a resurrected body despite dispersed matter, and the psychological-continuity view that persons are 'made of memories,' ending on the duplication problem: if God made two heavenly bodies both carrying Cash's memories, which one would be Cash?
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 19 "Case the Promised Land" — Herstein reads 'Thunder Road' as an event, not an object: the screen door slam and Mary's waving dress form a single event that language can only serially narrate, and Whitehead's event ontology (with Ricoeur's Time and Narrative on how we discover and rewrite ourselves in stories, and Emerson's 'monstrous corpse' of memory from 'Self Reliance') explains why the Seanachie's tale creates a world rather than describing one. His own autobiographical turn — first hearing the song while stuck in a dead-end life, then at the 1980 Los Angeles 'Factory' performance watching Springsteen's voice resolve two warring rhythms by adding a third — shows narrative running backwards, retelling and redeeming the past, which is why the burnt-out Chevrolets are already behind the dirty hood. The solo-harmonica version strips away porch, vision, and redemption to desolation, yet the conclusion is freedom: because the events of the world await our creative retelling, you are the Seanachie of your own life, and 'maybe I am that young, after all.'
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 9 "Retelling Our Stories" — Milsky uses Ricoeur and MacIntyre's narrative theory of personal identity to read the two Sharons: Boomer's fabricated human backstory suffers a 'factual disruption' when she shoots Adama, while Athena's 'disruption of belief' comes from falling in love with Helo. He argues such disruptions — also suffered by humans like Starbuck (recovered memories of abuse in 'Maelstrom'), Roslin (coming to believe she is Pythia's dying leader), and Helo — need not destroy identity, since narratives can be retold, as the Final Four do in 'Crossroads, Part 2' with Tigh's 'My name is Saul Tigh' speech. Third-party narratives (Six disowning Athena, the crew refusing to see Boomer as Boomer) show identity is partly socially constructed and can become self-fulfilling prophecy, with Boomer's blackouts resembling dissociative identity disorder.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 10 "Frak-tured Finality" — Booth argues that the 'Resistance' webisodes fracture BSG's narrative across television and Internet, forcing viewers to actively construct the story — Jammer's execution in 'Collaborators' and Duck's suicide bombing only make full sense if you pieced the webisodes together — and that this viewer-side fragmentation mirrors the characters' fractured identities. Drawing on Foucault's constructed self, Deleuze and Guattari's 'schizophrenia,' Goffman's performed roles, and Haraway's cyborg, he reads Baltar's 'Am I a Cylon?', Boomer's amnesia in 'Water,' Hera's human-Cylon hybridity, and Tigh's choice in 'Crossroads' to actively construct who he will be. The payoff: there is no central location for the self, the narrative, or Cylonhood — each becomes whole only through active construction.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 14 "“Sometimes You Just Have to Bow to the Absurd”" — Eberl weighs genetic enhancement and cloning through Trek's test cases: Julian Bashir's parents' enhancement leaves him feeling 'a fraud' ('You used to be my father. Now, you're my architect'), the Moab IV 'Masterpiece Society' breeds out 'the unknown, self-discovery, things that make life worth living', and the Jem'Hadar show desire itself engineered for control. He argues the right to an open future constrains designing children (B'Elanna's wish to de-Klingonize her baby, Worf pressuring Alexander), defends genetic treatment while rejecting genetic determinism, and uses Kass and Rovane with Picard and Shinzon, the Mariposa clones, and Trip's clone Sim to show clones are numerically distinct persons. Against Malik's Augments quoting Nietzsche — 'mankind is something to be surpassed' — the chapter argues the Übermensch demands self-mastery through philosophy, not eugenic engineering, tracing eugenics from Plato's Guardian breeding scheme through Buck v. Bell to modern prenatal selection.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 26 "“I Feel Exactly What You Feel”" — Runs Star Trek's transporter and android stories as thought experiments on personal identity: the body theory (Kirk rejecting android Korby — 'Dr. Korby was never here' — and Picard telling the resurrected Rishon Uxbridge 'you do not exist'), the brain theory ('Spock's Brain,' Bashir refusing to replace half of Vedek Bareil's brain), and Locke's memory theory as vindicated by the Trill (Lela Dax's 'a person is but the sum of their memories,' the 'Dax' extradition hearing over Curzon's crimes). Riker's transporter double in 'Second Chances' and the Tuvix fusion then break the memory theory through fission and fusion, prompting Parfit's move that psychological continuity, not numerical identity, is what matters in survival. Memory erasure in 'Dagger of the Mind' and Kurn's rebranding after the failed Mauk-to'Vor in 'Sons of Mogh' count as death if we are our memories.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 17 "Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the" — Robison asks how Link stays the same person through Ocarina of Time's child/adult switches, Twilight Princess's wolf form, and Wind Waker's consciousness-projection into seagulls and mages. Physical-continuity views fail because Link's body changes or is left behind; Locke's memory-based psychological continuity fails because adult Link's past hasn't happened yet when he travels back. After a Ship of Theseus variant (Ganon reassembling Tetra's sunken planks) she proposes that in Zelda's stipulative metaphysics, destiny, the goddess-given roles of courage, wisdom, and power, is the necessary and sufficient condition of identity, fitting videogame universes whose metaphysics are fixed by designers.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 14 "Epilog-Rolling" — Patton turns the Tin Woodman's backstory—the enchanted axe that costs Nick Chopper his legs, arms, torso and heart, then his head, each replaced by the tinsmith—into a cyborg thought experiment about how much of a person can be swapped out before the person is gone. After a framing nod to Plato's Republic on censoring frightening tales (his father's ban on 'mental violence' fantasy), he brings in Derek Parfit: the R-relation, the 'My Division' brain-split, and the Branch-Line teletransportation case are mapped onto the Woodman (including a hypothetical straw-bodied second Nick) to argue that survival gets different answers from first-person and third-person perspectives. The closing wildcat episode, where the tinned Woodman neatly decapitates a wildcat to save a field mouse, is offered as textual evidence that the tin head failed to preserve moral consistency—so the original Nick Chopper is gone for good, and the Scarecrow's shared brain explains why the two friends later refuse to part.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 20 "Getting to Oz" — Auxier uses the Wizard's demand that Dorothy kill the Witch to split 'ought' from 'can'—ethics from the metaphysics and logic of possibility—and then asks whether Oz is a genuinely possible world. He explains David Lewis's modal realism (every genuine possibility actual in its own causally isolated world) through counterfactuals about which network aired the film, dissolves the silver-versus-ruby slippers conflict by assigning book-Oz and film-Oz to different possible worlds, and argues that since no flat contradiction can be eked out of the Oz stories, Lewis is committed to Oz's being real—though Maguire's inter-world travel and Elphaba's hybrid, soul-less trans-world identity (her counterpart in our world being, playfully, Dorothy) stretch Lewis's 'counterparts' doctrine to its limit. Peirce supplies the closing caution, with Boole, that logic is a set of norms for how we can and ought to think rather than a proven mirror of other worlds, so believing in Oz's full reality remains permissible fun rather than an obligation.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 28 "You Can Go Home Again" — Fortune stages the movie as a morality play between two conceptions of personhood: the Wizard is an atomist, a self-sufficient ball from the Chuck E. Cheese ball pit who is the same humbug in Omaha or Oz and who reduces heart, brains, and courage to a testimonial, a diploma, and a medal, while Dorothy is a relationalist, a pineapple chunk that belongs on one particular pizza, a person constituted by her web of relations to home. 'There's no place like home' is therefore the relationalist's slogan, an acceptance of home for everything it is, good and bad, with Toto's fate still unresolved under Miss Gulch's law. He closes by suggesting the film's delayed television-era triumph is existential nostalgia: modern, rootless, ear-budded Americans keep watching because the relationalist country it mourns is 'what's in our blood.'
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 7 "Transformers and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction frames the volume around First Contact with a robotic civilization: citing SETI's Seth Shostak, they argue aliens are more likely to be AI machines than little green men, with the Autobot-Decepticon civil war catching humans in between on a moral as well as physical plane. They pose the book's questions about Optimus Prime and Megatron: whether Transformers have moral status and minds despite passing the Turing Test, whether they have souls and are capable of Platonic or erotic love, and what makes Optimus the same being whether robot or vehicle. Probing Transformer nature, they conclude, is really probing human nature, since Transformers are our own creations.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 13 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Spicher argues that when Bumblebee trades his beat-up 1976 Camaro for a shiny 2007 model only his appearance changes (an accidental change), never his identity, because transforming is part of a Transformer's essence like a human wearing a mask. Locke's memory continuity and Thomson's bodily criterion each fail - the embryo, coma, and corpse problems, plus the thought experiment of Megatron's memories transplanted into another body - so he defends an Aristotelian composite of form and matter in which the Spark is the soul-like form organizing the machine body, preserving identity through transformation as form guides matter toward actuality.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 11 "19" — Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 9 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction argues that His Dark Materials is philosophy-rich rather than a mere children's fantasy: its metaphysics of parallel worlds, dæmons, angels, armored bears, and mulefa poses genuine epistemic questions and ethical dilemmas. It frames the volume around the controversy over whether exposing children to Pullman's anti-religious vision is spiritual violence or an education in thinking for oneself like Lyra. It also sets up the trilogy's alternative afterlife, where Lyra frees the dead from the drab land of the dead to dissolve into Dust, and flags dæmons as puzzles of personal identity and soul-body interaction.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 25 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Harris and Baer use the Boatman scene ('Pan is me... we'd die') to test criteria of personal identity against the trilogy: Lyra and Will's inference to a thinking third part, the ghost, reenacts Descartes's dualist reasoning about mind-body distinctness, Iorek's lack of a ghost exemplifies the same-body criterion, and Pantalaimon's instant shape-shifting favors the psychological criterion, spelled out through Locke's prince-and-cobbler memory thought experiment and Parfit's psychological connectedness and continuity. They ask whether Lee Scoresby's dissolution into conscious atoms that reunite with Hester's counts as genuine survival, best accommodated by Locke's consciousness criterion or a panpsychist matter criterion, with Chalmers cited as the contemporary defender of conscious matter. The chapter closes with individuation, whether Lyra and Pan are one person or two, applied to a Primal Fear-style multiple-personality murder trial, the hypothetical of Pan killing someone while Lyra is innocent, and living wills in persistent vegetative states.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 18 "Coda" — Gimbel asks what makes a band remain the same band over time: Led Zeppelin survived replacing drummer John Bonham with his son Jason, yet Page and Jones insist no singer could replace Robert Plant.
