Drawing on Aristotelian virtue ethics and Ortega y Gasset, he defends the 'Virtuous Hunter' who follows 'Diana's Code,' handicaps himself for a one-shot kill, and feels for the prey — citing De Niro's Michael in The Deer Hunter and Woody Allen's Love & Death — while condemning canned hunts and demeaning language ('varmint,' 'harvesting') as vicious extremes on a continuum.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 25 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Duerr surveys the worldwide 'Master/Mistress of Animals' figure (Artemis, the /Kaggen of the Bushmen, the Huaulu Lord of the Forest) as a mythic sanction against over-hunting, arguing that the near-universal guilt hunters feel over killing sentient, human-like game reflects a real moral dilemma. She invokes Singer's utilitarian claim that painlessly killing non-self-conscious animals whose deaths are compensated by replacement 'may not be wrong,' reading the mythic 'solutions' (denial, propitiation, taking only what you need, restoring bones so game is reborn) as a folk 'hunting code of ethics' that manages the wrong of ending a life without starting another.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 13 "7. Independence Day & Aliens" — Rowlands frames morality around consistency and impartiality (the golden rule), articulated by Kant's categorical/practical imperatives (treat persons as ends, not merely means) and utilitarianism's greatest happiness. Imagining philosophers arguing Independence Day's aliens out of eradicating humans, he deploys the principle of 'no moral difference without a relevant other difference' and the argument from marginal cases to defeat intelligence, telepathy, and bare species membership as morally relevant. He turns the alien-invasion parable on our factory farming of chickens and pigs (Singer-style speciesism), arguing we are crueller than the aliens and fall short of our own impartiality ideal.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 13 "11. Futurama as Philosophy Wisdom from the Ignorance of a Delivery Boy" — Lewis surveys how Futurama's satire raises philosophical questions without taking sides. 'Zoidberg's Freedom Lesson' pits Mill's harm principle and free speech against Feinberg's offense principle; the mutants' and robots' oppression is read through Foucault's disciplinary normalcy and Locke's and Rawls's social contracts (state of nature, veil of ignorance). 'The Problem with Popplers' stages Bentham's utilitarianism, a might-makes-right food-chain view, and an intelligence criterion that commits Singer's 'speciesism,' with sentimentality winning. 'The Late Philip J. Fry' and 'Free Will Hunting' dramatize determinism, Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, and Sartre's existentialist free will, while 'Godfellas' and 'A Clockwork Origin' probe the problem of evil, fine-tuning, and Occam's razor.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 35 "32. Okja as Philosophy Why Animals Matter" — Jensen frames Okja around three views of the super-pig Okja's moral status: Mirando treats her as mere property, the Animal Liberation Front as a symbol to be sacrificed for the cause, and the girl Mija as a friend and person. He dismantles Mirando's 'human exceptionalism'—amoralism, Aquinas's natural-law teleology, the Kantian persons-only view, and Descartes' claim that animals are unfeeling automata—then develops the ALF's liberation through Singer's equal consideration of interests, Bentham's 'can they suffer?', and speciesism as prejudice, weighing consequentialist (utilitarian) against deontological (rights, Regan) foundations. He closes with hierarchical moral status and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many,' arguing Mija's love for Okja shows that at some point relationship matters more than moral calculation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 85 "80. Detroit Become Human as Philosophy Moral Reasoning Through Gameplay" — Engels and Evans argue that Detroit: Become Human stages moral reasoning through the interactive stories of the androids Connor, Kara, and Markus, whose 'deviant' awakening they read through Frankfurt's distinction between wantons and persons with second-order desires and through Kant's requirement of the ability to do otherwise. Scenes like Markus scavenging a pump regulator from a dying android, the blood-on-hands visualization after his speech, and Kara protecting Alice force players to weigh Kantian, utilitarian, virtue, and Gilligan-style care frameworks. Through Alice's reveal as an android and the grieving-widower scene, the game makes an implicit anti-speciesist argument (via Singer) that beings who can suffer are morally considerable, and that agency and responsibility emerge through suffering and struggle.

### Democracy as a Way of Life

Democracy as a way of life is John Dewey's conviction that democracy is not merely a form of government but a mode of shared, cooperative living rooted in communication, inquiry, and mutual respect. For Dewey, self-rule means people continually participating in the associations that shape them—workplaces, schools, communities—and reconstructing those institutions through intelligent, experimental problem-solving. On this view voting and elections are only the outer machinery; the deeper substance is a culture in which individuals grow by contributing to and learning from a common life.

- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 25 "Palpatine’s Legacy" — Decker reconstructs Palpatine's career as a case study in how democracies die: using Aristotle's definition of tyranny and the precedent of Pisistratus and Julius Caesar, he shows Palpatine manufacturing the Separatist threat so the Senate grants him emergency powers - a twist on Machiavelli's loved-versus-feared dictum in which playing the reluctant democrat is itself the means to absolute rule. The Attack of the Clones debate between Anakin ('Someone wise' should make people agree) and Padme becomes a clash between Leo Strauss's philosopher-king ideal of rule by the virtuous few and John Dewey's conception of democracy as a way of life trusting the intelligence of common people, with Rousseau's social contract framing the stakes. The chapter concludes that democratic ends require democratic means and that unaccountable 'watchers' - Straussian statesmen or Anakins - are exactly the path to Empire.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 11 "Unity Born from Diversity" — Shook narrates the 1984 Born in the U.S.A. tour — George Will's 'Yankee Doodle Springsteen' column, Reagan's Hammonton speech, Springsteen's refusal to be either campaign's tool — and reads the song as the hopeless story of a Vietnam-generation man's living death (the refinery that won't hire him, the dead brother and the Saigon woman) mistaken by flag-waving crowds for a patriotic anthem. He then maps the song's possible meanings onto democracy's possible destinies: Carl Schmitt's friend–enemy politics of national homogeneity and permanent emergency, Schlesinger's assimilationist Disuniting of America, and liberal cosmopolitanism's citizens of the world. Dewey's The Public and Its Problems wins: democracy must intelligently manage rather than eliminate diversity, each citizen holding a double loyalty to subgroup and to the democratic 'great community,' so being born in the U.S.A. is a responsibility and pride is properly placed in democratic ideals.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 22 "Hometown Security" — Keith reads 'My Hometown' — whitewashed windows, the textile mill closing, Bruce telling his son 'take a good look around' — through Putnam's Bowling Alone, Dewey's socially constituted self, and Mead, to argue that Bruce and Kate should recommit to their dying town rather than flee in the moving van. Leopold's 'two spiritual dangers in not owning a farm' and Berry's healthy community as ecosystem ground an 'enlightened localism' that avoids both the town's racist parochialism and rootless cosmopolitanism. Volunteering, local food, and town-meeting democracy are the hometown security the song's sadness calls for.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 25 "iPublic" — Dewey takes the iPod's beauty seriously (Chris Breen's 'beautiful and intuitive' player, Donald Norman's user-centered design) and uses John Dewey's Art as Experience to ask whether iPod use can be a 'consummatory' experience that ends with us no longer the same person — hearing a bitter song as insight into the social conditions that produced it — rather than the contrived 'now' of fashion and hyper-accumulation, per Benjamin's remark that there is 'always a sense of the same in the new'. Mass production flattened the aristocratic high-culture/folk division and handed the power to define 'cool' to advertisers and the market. The pragmatist test is political: with iTunes DRM and single-user design quietly individualizing consumption (the ritual of buying the Public Enemy tape at the mall versus the frictionless one-click download), the iPod is beautiful exactly insofar as its experiences help form a public — an inclusive, participatory democratic community.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 24 "Beyond Picasso and Ronaldo Living Artfully" — Elcombe asks whether Cristiano Ronaldo, transferred to Real Madrid for $131 million—more than Picasso's Garçon à la Pipe fetched at its record 2004 auction—can be an artist like Picasso. Traditional metaphysics built on Plato's perfect Forms and Aristotle's necessary-and-sufficient conditions locks Art in a special museum realm that soccer, as a purposive sport whose beauty is only a byproduct, can never enter, leaving the game merely 'beautiful', not Art. Dewey's Art as Experience reorients the question from what art is to what art does: artworks are consummations of experience, moments of 'thatness'—that meal, that storm, that Ronaldo free kick—that lift us out of the mundane while remaining within the game's durable rules and history (Ronaldo's artistry grows from Zidane, Maradona, Cruyff, Pelé). On this pragmatist view Ronaldo is an artist in the act, the six-year-old testing a new turn on the pitch lives artfully too, and soccer's artistry becomes groundwork for communication, democracy, and the good life—doing more real work than a painting almost no one ever sees.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 12 "The Jihadist Way of Life" — Argues the Fremen are 'shockingly American': their Spannungsbogen self-discipline, spiritual self-sufficiency, and endurance of hardship exemplify Emerson's self-reliance, while the jihad's aim of razing the rule of the Great Houses into relations of equals echoes Dewey's democracy as a way of life—faith in the potentialities of every human nature. The parallel runs through the 'American Taliban' John Walker Lindh and Paul's blind walk into the desert, both acting on values Americans prize. Herbert's remark that people surrender judgment to leaders 'wrapped in the myth fabric of society' grounds the pragmatist point that Fremen myth-making, like America's exceptionalist self-image, works—and Alia's 'my brother is pragmatic' seals it.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 29 "Psych and Philosophy" — Amanda Lusky argues Shawn is a model pragmatist in the lineage of Peirce, James, and Dewey: he treats ideas as tools judged by consequences, is tough-minded about facts over theory (James's temperament distinction), and applies the pragmatic maxim from the squirrel-and-tree dispute to his loosely formed but working hunches. His co-operative inquiry with Gus and the SBPD - Gus's safe-cracking knowledge in 'Sixty Five Million Years Off,' passing Lassiter's polygraph in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' - enacts Dewey's democratic community solving problems together, and the chapter reads his tolerance of Gus's paranormal leads ('The Devil's in the Details') as pragmatic openness that enriches Santa Barbara's democratic life.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 20 "7. What Kind of Revolutionary Is Mr. Robot" — Ralston traces Mr. Robot's hacktivist philosophy to David Graeber's anarchism behind Occupy Wall Street and to Anonymous's 'moralfags' who hack for a higher cause (Project Chanology as the template for fsociety), then stages the Dewey-Trotsky debate on means and ends: Trotsky's 'Their Morals and Ours' lets the end justify any means, while Dewey's means-end continuum demands experimental, democratic means suited to the end. The verdict: Mr. Robot's ends are anarchist and his means pragmatist - he will frame Terry Colby and risk lives at Steel Mountain, but rejects means like actual slavery that would betray the movement's own ideal of liberation.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 9 "Hope for the Future" — Applies Dewey's The Public and Its Problems to Alien and Aliens: the real villain is not the Xenomorph but a United Americas too weak to govern Weyland-Yutani, whose crude cost-benefit erasure of the Nostromo crew's interests shows a state that has lost the public's voice. Ash's arrogant 'perfect organism' objectivity, the appeal to blameworthy 'human nature,' and faith that big business runs everything illustrate Dewey's targets - Plato's static Forms, economic determinism, and rugged individualism - and since beliefs are habits of action (Peirce), the Company's deeds expose its professed principles as negligible fictions.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 15 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — MacMullan argues Stewart is America's most effective public intellectual working in the pragmatist tradition Cornel West describes, philosophy as continuous cultural commentary 'explaining America to itself' rather than academia's ingrown self-talk (the failure Rorty diagnosed). He shows The Daily Show performing this role through irony and critical cultural memory: the Colbert exchange rewarding Karl Rove's Plame leak with 'Chief Justice', 'Victory Lapse' on Republican outrage at Obama's bin Laden ad versus Bush's Mission Accomplished carrier landing, 'Gitmo's World', and the 'Meet the Depressed' Magic Bullet blender takedown of Obama's unkept promises. Stewart's Deweyan faith in democracy as a way of life appears in the Rally to Restore Sanity, his genuine debates with guests like David Barton and Marco Rubio, his anger at CNBC's Cramer for burning the house down with our money, and the 9/11 Zadroga Bill segments that shamed Congress into passing the law.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 12 "The Jihadist Way of Life" — Argues that the Fremen, despite their supposed Zensunni faith (which it argues was never a liberation theology), are quintessentially American: Emersonian self-reliance appears as spiritual self-sufficiency and the Spannungsbogen self-imposed delay, while Dewey's democracy as a way of life surfaces in the jihad's aim of replacing master-slave relations with relative equals under Shai-Hulud. It cites Herbert's 'Dune Genesis' on myth-making as pragmatically valuable and reads Paul, who ends Dune Messiah walking blind into the desert 'where we walk without footprints', as kin to the 'American Taliban' John Walker Lindh, whose conversion and jihad were driven by the same self-reliant, spiritual, pragmatic values.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 27 "A New Holiday Album A Lesson Is in the Lyrics" — Sudnick and Garrett stage the Dewey-Lippmann debate through Weekend Update's citizen journalists: Drunk Uncle and Girl at Party exemplify Lippmann's propagandized pseudo-environments and echo chambers, while Stefon parodies the expert gatekeeper his technocratic 'machinery of knowledge' would install. Dewey's The Public and its Problems answers that democracy needs public education, a free and publicly funded press, and wide participation, with Point/Counterpoint and Cathy Ann's plea to log off and meet face-to-face as comic images of deliberative citizenship. The chapter ends with Dewey's hope that artists, from Opera Man to Sandler's Chanukah Song, are the real purveyors of news in a democracy consummated by artful communication.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 23 "Trust in the Force of Others" — MacMullan reads Rogue One through Dewey's 'Creative Democracy': democracy is not Senates or constitutions but a lived faith in one's neighbors, and the Empire's deepest violence is the distrust it breeds — Cassian executing Tivik, Saw torturing Bodhi with Bor Gullet, Draven ordering Galen's assassination. Cassian violates Kant's Formula of Humanity by reducing Tivik to a container of secrets, and the Rebels' dirty-war methods strain Augustine's just-war conditions, yet Chirrut and Baze's friendship ('I'm not alone. I have you!') becomes the seed of recovered trust that stays Cassian's finger on the trigger at Eadu. The Yavin council's free debate and the Tantive IV corridor relay — Rebels dying to pass the Death Star plans hand to hand past Vader — enact Dewey's claim that democracy lives in personal attitudes and neighborly trust: rebellions are built on hope in each other.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 15 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Terrance MacMullan argues Stewart is America's most effective public intellectual, reviving the engaged tradition of Emerson, William James, Dewey, and Du Bois against the isolation Rorty diagnosed in academics. Using Cornel West's account of pragmatism as 'explaining America to itself,' he reads segments like 'Victory Lapse,' the Karl Rove 'what honor' bit, and 'Gitmo's World' as pragmatist cultural criticism, and casts Stewart's 'Worst Responders' campaign for the 9/11 Zadroga Bill and his amicable debates with conservatives as embodying Dewey's democracy as a shared 'working faith' in people.

### Falsificationism

Falsificationism is Karl Popper's proposal that what distinguishes genuine science from pseudoscience is not verifiability but falsifiability: a theory is scientific only if it forbids something and can in principle be refuted by observation. Popper rejected the idea that we confirm theories by piling up supporting instances, arguing instead that we can never prove a universal law true but can decisively show it false. On this account science advances through bold conjectures exposed to severe testing, with theories provisionally accepted only so long as they survive sincere attempts to refute them.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 16 "Pals" — Madeline Muntersbjorn uses Season Four's Initiative-versus-Scoobies conflict to dissolve the Science Wars: Professor Walsh's secret, unfalsifiable Project 314 makes her Karl Popper's bad scientist, while Buffy's gang embodies Feyerabend's pluralism and Peirce-and-James pragmatism — Buffyverse rules are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and the gang welcomes anyone willing to ask questions and do research. Her three ideals — pluralism, pragmatism, pals — culminate in 'Primeval,' where the combo-Buffy enjoining spell (Willow's spirit, Xander's heart, Giles's mind, Buffy's hand) literally enacts James's meliorism: the world may be saved if each agent does their level best, together. Walsh dies alone because she has no pals; Buffy saves the world 'a lot' because she does.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 19 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Steele starts from Orwell's worry that laypeople accept scientific consensus as unreflectively as tribesmen accept witch-doctors — sharpened by Lysenko and Nazi 'racial science' — and answers it with Popper's critical rationalism: since Hume's problem of induction bars proof from instances, we can only provisionally prefer theories that survive severe attempts at falsification, so trusting experts is reasonable exactly when their community tests rather than defends its theories. Kuhn's paradigms explain why dissident alternatives like Atkins talk past the dominant school (Atkins and Agatston are cardiologists, not dieticians), and the 2002–2004 studies showing improved lipids on more fat figure as the kind of surprise that precedes paradigm change. His verdict: neither trusting nor resisting experts is foolish; 'human knowledge is too important to be left to experts.'
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 7 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — 'The Year in Bullshit' catalogues the fraud climate surrounding the book's success: James Frey's fabricated memoir A Million Little Pieces exposed on Oprah, the wholly invented author J.T. Leroy, product placement and paid word-of-mouth advertising blurring the line between ads and ordinary conversation, and scientific fraud in pharmaceutical and federal research. It invokes Karl Popper's claim that science deserves respect precisely because it falsifies its own claims, presenting headlines about fabricated results as that ideal fading. Frank Rich's verdict that 'such distinctions have long since washed away in much of our public life' supplies the chapter's explanation of the book's appeal as cultural despair.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 94 "Combatting the Two Kinds of Bullshit" — Douglas argues that 'universal standards bullshit' — the assumption that evidence must meet one threshold before it counts as scientific — comes from textbook schooling and has no warrant: there is no such standard, and we shouldn't want one. She shows how it distorts debate on all sides, from Bush administration uncertainty claims to Michael Gough's Popper-inspired insistence that climate models cannot be tested, and argues that whether evidence suffices always depends on the risks of error — the gas-gauge warning versus the bomb in your car. Genuine politicization (suppressing evidence, firing researchers) must be condemned, but deciding how much uncertainty is acceptable is an ineliminably political and ethical judgment.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 9 "Is Monk’s Certainty Justified" — Rauhut tests Monk's method against two models of discovery: Holmes-style eliminatism, modeled on Popper's falsification via reductio ad absurdum, and CSI-style confirmationism in the mold of Hempel and Carnap (Gil Grissom letting evidence speak). Monk fits neither — in 'Mr. Monk and the Astronaut' he refuses to eliminate the alibi-solid Steve Wagner, and in 'Mr. Monk Falls in Love' he ignores a hatpin, a motive, and a confession pointing at Leyla. Instead Monk is an 'epiphanist': he registers every anomaly (the secretary hired from a Lamaze-class ad in 'Mr. Monk Fights City Hall', Crawford's odd phrasing 'No, she wouldn't be drinking now'), suddenly sees the one theory explaining all of them, and only afterwards manufactures shareable evidence for others. His absolute certainty, the chapter argues, rests on a metaphysical faith that only the true theory can explain every anomaly — a Leibnizian 'best of all possible ordered worlds' — the same obsession with order that makes him notice anomalies at all, though it makes him epistemically irresponsible by ordinary standards that weigh alternative hypotheses and simplicity.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 8 "Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory" — Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 26 "The Future of Sandy Cheeks" — Wilson González-Espada assesses Sandy Cheeks as a portrait of the scientist: she explodes the 'Draw a Scientist' stereotype — female, socially popular, working in an open treedome that mirrors peer review — yet the show muddles the nature of science, calling inventions 'experiments' and a clipboard of math 'science'. The chapter applies Popper's falsifiability to SpongeBob's one-sided evidence that Squidward is a true friend and Newton's principle of parsimony to Sandy's ghost scare, then closes with Aldo Leopold's land ethic, reading 'Jellyfish Hunter' and 'SpongeBob's Last Stand' as environmental parables about habitat and overexploitation.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 32 "Our Best Bet" — Terjesen argues Mycroft surpasses Sherlock because he truly grasps Hume's Problem of Induction: Sherlock's celebrated eliminations (the three key possibilities for Cadogan West in 'The Bruce-Partington Plans') and his newspaper-ad tests are inductive, Popperian conjecture-testing that can never confirm anything, while Goodman's 'grue' shows the same evidence always supports rival explanations. Watson's failed attempt in 'How Watson Learned the Trick,' the amateur reasoner's wrong solution in 'The Lost Special,' and Holmes's own 'Norbury' failure in 'The Yellow Face' prove that a correct method guarantees nothing. Mycroft, who 'would rather be considered wrong than take the trouble to prove himself right,' implicitly embraces Reichenbach's pragmatic justification — induction is simply our best bet — and therefore hunts longer for the facts that do not fit, acting only when England's fate is at stake.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 103 "Circles within Circles" — Applies Imre Lakatos's 'degenerating research programs' — geocentric astronomy surviving by adding epicycles — to conspiracy theories like Pentagon 'truthers' who must keep patching their account to explain debris, eyewitnesses, and phone calls. But David Coady's rejoinder, voiced through Lies, Inc. where the 'cranks' who doubted Whale's Mouth were right, and the makeshift excuses for Saddam's WMD, show the official story can be the degenerating program, so rejecting conspiracy theories out of hand leaves you easily manipulated.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 127 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" — The section argues Precrime needs no evidence of an actual murder, attempt, or plot because pre-criminals are charged with future-murder, which, unlike plots that fizzle or attempts that bungle, always succeeds absent intervention. Using Anderton's demonstration of Witwer's caught ball, it distinguishes a person's NA-future (if not arrested) from the A-future (if arrested), concluding that what happens after an arrest cannot falsify an NA-prediction, since the prediction only ever described the uninterfered-with path.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 15 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Cooke defends his three-year lawful-evil wizard campaign against religious and secular critics by dismantling each style of argument. The propaganda charge fails because D&D rulebooks present no 'attitudes for export' about the real world; the puzzle of imaginative resistance dissolves once Can'tian and Won'tian readings are rejected for a 'Hardian' view that some things are merely hard to imagine, undercutting Dadlez's explanation of the Romulan spy's angry opponents; and the Werther-effect-style empirical case against D&D collapses on the data like parallel panics over jazz, video games, and pornography. The remaining character-warping objection—the Platonic and Aristotelian habituation worry that enjoying evil play mistrains the sentiments Hume warned about—turns unfalsifiable in the way repressed-desire claims do, leaving a firm moral gap between imagining evil and doing it.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 15 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Bernard Rollin reads Dr. Zaius's tribunal as 'scientific ideology' in action - 'human see, human do' refuses to believe its own eyes, just as bishops refused to look through Galileo's telescope. He traces the ideology from Newton's 'hypotheses non fingo' through logical positivism's verifiability criterion (which validates the Hasslein Curve prediction while rendering 'there are intelligent beings in Heaven' meaningless) and Wittgenstein's point that 'killing is wrong' is not a fact of the universe, to the 'science is value-free' dogma that left animal pain untested and untreated - as he documents from his own campaign: the empty analgesic literature search, the 1985 federal legislation, and the pain physiologist whose dog research refutes his own denial. Zira's neurosurgery on mute humans repeats what Descartes's beast-machine doctrine licensed, and IASP's language requirement for pain collapses into a Cratylus-grade confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions ('You can't step into the same river once').
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 21 "Psych and Philosophy" — Mahon and Ceballos read the pilot through the big-lie principle credited to Hitler and Goebbels: the truth - hyper-observation plus a photographic memory - is too mundane to be believed, so only the biggest possible lie, 'I am a psychic,' saves Shawn from jail, exploiting the reverse psychology by which hearers assume no liar would say something so implausible. The lie's durability is then explained with Karl Popper's falsifiability criterion: like horoscopes and psychoanalysis, Shawn's psychic claim is unfalsifiable, so the ex-con's finger-counting 'tests' in 'Woman Seeking Dead Husband' can confirm it but never refute it - a virtue for a liar, and precisely what makes a claim unscientific. Finally the chapter shifts blame to the victims: like Madoff investors who 'kind of saw it coming,' the SBPD is self-deceived, complicit in a lie it half knows is a lie because the gift horse keeps closing cases.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 33 "Psych and Philosophy" — Courtney Neal explains that Santa Barbara believes Shawn is psychic because pseudoscience offers easier, more appealing explanations than the truth: in the pilot, 'he's psychic' beats 'he's the killer' as a narrative that fits the facts, and psychic claims are worded so they cannot be disproved. She shows how Shawn's real observational deductions are packaged through cold reading (the comic-convention scene in 'Shawn vs. the Red Phantom'), Robert Cialdini's social-influence principles of liking, social proof, and commitment/consistency, and the self-fulfilling prophecy of his reputation - so even Lassiter's skepticism cannot dislodge a belief the city keeps confirming.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 40 "Psych and Philosophy" — This chapter is a skeptical debunking tour of real-life 'psycho psychics' - Babylonian astrologers, the Delphi oracle that set Socrates testing the claim he was wisest, Nostradamus's hindsight-friendly quatrains, Blavatsky, Cayce, spoon-bender Uri Geller, and Sylvia Browne's failed Shawn Hornbeck prediction - arguing that no repeatable, peer-reviewed evidence of ESP has ever existed and that figures like cold-reading psychic detective Peter Hurkos thrive on gullibility. It ties to Psych through Gus's credulity about UFOs and werewolves and the real police practice of consulting psychic detectives that Shawn's con parodies, while Houdini's congressional testimony and James Randi's Million Dollar Challenge model the evidence-demanding skepticism the show's fake psychic gets away from.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 35 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Peter Stone applies Dawkins's memetics and Dennett's Breaking the Spell to the rise of 'Hallelujah' from the troubled release of Various Positions to ubiquity via John Cale, Jeff Buckley, Shrek, and Rufus Wainwright. On Dennett's account religious memes thrive through hyperactive agency detection, doctrines rendered unfalsifiable and thus immune to evidence, and 'belief in belief' - and 'Hallelujah' is religiously ambiguous enough, from David and Bathsheba to Buckley's 'hallelujah of the orgasm,' to be as religious as any singer or congregation wants it to be, whether as Rabbi Kagan's hymn of the heretic or the Holy Trinity Church's 'Amazing Grace' lyric swap. Machiavelli's maxim that fortune governs half the outcome frames the song's lucky trajectory, and its carefully engineered ambiguity makes it a set of very 'happy memes' likely to keep replicating.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 9 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Karavitis argues Finn's 'Finn-losophy' is a metaphysics that prefers magic over Princess Bubblegum's science, and that this choice shapes his ethics: magic is the 'easy way out' requiring no understanding (Jake's stretching, the Glasses of Nerdicon), while science demands observation, experiment, and falsifiable ideas—'reality is the ultimate spell-checker.' Because magic promises instant gratification, Finn rushes into danger ('Wizard,' 'Donny,' the Goblin Kingdom) behind an inflexible hero code, and his altruism misfires, as the never-ending prize-winning battles of the 'Mystery Train' episode illustrate. The chapter concludes that your view of how the world works—magical or scientific—determines whether you can grow ethically at all.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 26 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Russ Hamer takes Mac's 'Science Is a Liar Sometimes' defense - Aristotle, Galileo, and Newton each proved his predecessor 'a bitch' - and his claim that believing in evolution takes as much faith as belief in God, and answers with philosophy of science. Popper's falsificationism explains why Mac's 'I won't change my mind... regardless of the facts' is the essence of the non-scientific: only theories risking precise, falsifiable predictions (Einstein's light deflection) count as science, unlike vague astrology or Charlie's cherry-picked evidence that the Waitress will love him. Kuhn's distinction of normal and revolutionary science explains why past failures never discredited science - falsifications within a paradigm are tuning, and the Gang's group-configuration trials in 'The Gang Solves the Gas Crisis' are normal science at its best - so revisability is science's strength, not a reason to fear looking like a science bitch.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 38 "18. Gruesome Walkers" — Yuen turns the walkers into a lesson on Hume's problem of induction: the pre-apocalyptic belief that the dead do not rise was justified by all past experience until Rick wakes to a world where they do, and Rick's distrust of Alexandria repeats the same inductive move from Woodbury, Terminus, and Grady - useful, Hume says, since custom compels us, but never knowledge. Russell's chicken illustrates the fatal surprise, and Goodman's grue (the pun of the title) shows the outbreak could be a future-swinging regularity like the seventeen-year cicadas, undermining even Jenner's experimental science. Popper's falsificationism is offered as the rescue - Shane's reanimation falsifies the "walkers make walkers" theory, leaving the "everyone is infected" theory corroborated but never known.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 18 "8. Is It a Fact that Facts Don’t Matter" — Steele distinguishes facts as mind-independent reality from facts as expert-certified statements to show that Kellyanne Conway's alternative facts and Adams's own slogans trade on this ambiguity, and that Adams performatively contradicts himself every time he insists his predictions are true and matter. Analyzing the cognitive-dissonance hallucinations of Trump-is-Hitler and then Trump-is-incompetent, he argues that on Adams's own account brute facts proved irresistible, and that such belief revision is rational Popperian conjecture and refutation, plus the conservative strategy of saving fundamental theories (Coulomb's law) and dropping minor ones when the fuse blows. Against the claim that humans are irrational he recalls Aristotle's Rhetoric as persuasion's legitimate complement to the Prior Analytics, and leans on Percival to show propaganda fits a rational-reader model, citing the slow, fact-driven shift on gay marriage.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 27 "15. Bias Is Rational!" — Percival, whose Myth of the Closed Mind Adams cites, rebuts the Moist Robot Hypothesis that visual, emotional, repetitive anchors make us ninety-percent irrational. Against Kahneman's fast-and-dumb System 1 he sets Gigerenzer's ecological rationality (the gaze-angle heuristic that catches fly balls, the recognition heuristic that lets ignorant German students beat Americans on Detroit versus Milwaukee), then goes further with Popper's critical rationalism: babies as little scientists conjecturing and refuting, experience always theory-laden (the duck-rabbit), and Newton's boy on the seashore facing an infinite but navigable ocean of error elimination. The Stoic insight that all emotion is thoughtful and all thought emotional (the falling-tiles misperception that flips anger to relief) shows feelings track beliefs, so a free battle of the biases, not fact-free affirmation in the lineage of Le Bon and Pavlovian conditioning, is how rationality actually works.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 28 "16. Why Scott Adams Is Stupid" — Miori audits Adams's science talk through epistemology: warrant for belief, empiricism versus rationalism, Wittgenstein's demand for unambiguous clarity, and Clifford's epistemic responsibility, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence, which condemns sampling television news while blogging on climate science. Popper's falsifiability, learned from Einstein's willingness to be refuted against Freud's confirmation-seeking, exposes Adams's double standard in waving confirmation bias at critics while crediting his own predictions, and Feyerabend's epistemological anarchism is the view Adams most resembles, except that Feyerabend took responsibility and retracted. Cipolla's Basic Laws of Human Stupidity (the stupid person causes losses to both self and others) frames the closing charge: Adams suggests and retreats, sells product, and shirks the epistemic duty that experts in climate science and medicine shoulder.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" — Morgan explains what a dimension is mathematically (hypercubes, with 'Little Girl Lost' as a portal into the fourth spatial dimension) and then time as the fourth dimension in Einstein's relativity, using time dilation and the Grandfather Paradox to contrast 'Back There,' which inconsistently lets Corrigan alter some outcomes of Lincoln's assassination, with 'No Time Like the Past,' where Driscoll fails exactly as an eternally fixed past requires. He then surveys infinite-universe speculation, quantum Many Worlds, and multiverse cosmology as readings of 'The Parallel,' where Major Gaines slips into a near-identical reality, before closing with Popper: since no experiment could in principle falsify the existence of other universes, the multiverse is unfalsifiable — a dimension of mind, not science.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 15 "The Lasting Legacy of Logic" — Treats Carroll the Oxford logician as a teacher hiding five lessons in Wonderland: watch your assumptions (the King infers the Knave's guilt from an unsigned letter), know what your words mean (Humpty Dumpty on 'glory'), don't confuse categories (the King's 'Nobody' and the Hatter's personified Time), don't switch subjects and predicates ('I mean what I say' versus 'I say what I mean'), and don't confuse necessary with sufficient conditions (Alice's Ada and Mabel arguments, with a hammer-and-egg illustration). David S. Brown grounds the lessons in Hume on causes discoverable only by experience, Aristotle's law of non-contradiction and categories, the Marx Brothers' 'Either he's dead or my watch has stopped', and Popper's point that a successful prediction cannot prove a hypothesis, only a failed one can refute it.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 18 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Jones explains the Leonard–Leslie breakup ('Tell me, Leonard, how would we raise the children?') as a genuine clash of research commitments: string theory with its demanded extra dimensions versus Leslie's loop quantum gravity. Along the way he uses Popper's falsifiability and Kuhn's paradigms — the 1998 dark-energy discovery as falsification at work, Sheldon's alien-parasite hypothesis as paradigm-protecting refusal to accept that Amy is aroused by Zack — and the Dirac-to-Anderson antimatter story alongside Sheldon's North Pole monopole expedition to weigh theoretical against experimental science. Leonard emerges as the Feynman-style skeptic ('At best you can say, hey, my idea has internal logical consistency'), which is exactly what Leslie cannot forgive.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 28 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Pigliucci reads the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series (Helms's Dayton, Tennessee reenactment-town piece, Stewart's panel with ID proponent Dembski and the scrotum question) as one of the best media treatments of the creation-evolution controversy. Popper's falsificationism marks intelligent design as non-science, since Dembski's designer works outside testable law and miracles are, as Larson says, unrepeatable and unfalsifiable, while Stewart's bad-design jokes about the scrotum and Mayr's 99.99% extinction figure replay the problem of evil. A compressed tour of rationalism (Plato to Descartes's radical doubt) versus Hume's empiricism explains why science yields tentative conclusions, and the chapter ends that resolving the controversy, like Aristotle's eudaimonia, is a lifelong personal project.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 18 "Of Science, Sorcery, and Philosophy" — The chapter reads Strange's conversion from neurosurgeon to sorcerer as a Kuhnian paradigm shift: his medical materialism is 'normal science' puzzle-solving that keeps resisting anomalies (Pangborn's impossible recovery, the astral projection, the multiverse tour) until Kamar-Taj offers a rival paradigm with its own exemplars, which he can only adopt by learning 'knowledge how' through tedious practice. It explains incommensurability through Strange's inability to rationally persuade his old medical colleagues, then contrasts Kuhn with Popper's falsificationism, Feyerabend's 'anything goes' anarchism (sorcery once looked as disreputable as early heliocentrism), and Lakatos's progressive versus degenerating research programs to ask whether sorcery could count as a science in Strange's world.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 15 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Cooke defends his three-year campaign of a lawful evil wizard (Oraximon, who magic-missiled an innkeeper and hid the bodies in a rope trick) against religious and secular critics. The epistemic charge fails because rulebooks are invitations to imagine, not assertions, and the Smurfs-as-Krishna example shows an 'attitude for export' needs authorial evidence D&D lacks; Hume's twin claims about the impropriety of imaginatively endorsing flawed sentiments are dismantled by splitting Can'tians from Won'tians over Gendler's stories and defending a 'Hardian' view on which resistance is just difficulty, making imaginative resistance a chimera. The causal charge fails on the evidence (the Werther effect and its video-game and jazz cousins are post hoc plus confirmation bias), the character-warping charge risks the unfalsifiability of the repressed-desire diagnosis, and Plato's ban on the arts — enforced via the noble lie — would be the price if imagining were as bad as doing.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 22 "NOTES" — Asks how to tell genuine science from pseudoscience using Chandra Suresh's rejected Activating Evolution theory, Sheldrake's morphic fields, alchemy, and Behe's intelligent design. Kuhn's picture of normal science, anomalies, and revolutions explains why Suresh would need a full-blown crisis in evolutionary theory — such as people actually flying — before the community accepts him, and why time rather than mockery settles a theory's fate. Ockham's razor condemns the unnecessary organizing principles in both Sheldrake's and Suresh's theories, and intelligent design is exposed as bad method because, like creationism, it was devised to protect a prior commitment from disconfirming fossil and cosmological evidence.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Addey analyzes the show's web of coincidences - Sawyer and Boone crossing paths in the Australian police station, Jack meeting Desmond in the hatch - and distinguishes genuine coincidence from divine providence, fatalism, and determinism. She applies Jung's theory of synchronicity to Locke's walkabout conviction that he was 'meant' to reach the island, then uses the birthday paradox, the law of truly large numbers, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability to show why viewers and conspiracy theorists overestimate the improbability of such connections. Finally she evaluates Jacob's candidacy experiment as flawed social science: the candidates' circumstantial ignorance, maintained by the Others' deceptions, undermines the free and morally responsible choices Jacob claims to be testing, which is why the curious Hurley deserved to become protector.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 13 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Dueck takes Stan's closing pluralism in 'Super Best Friends'—all religions have something valuable to teach, as the interfaith superheroes' combined powers defeat Blaine—and tests it against Hick's pluralism, exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivist 'anonymous Christians', using 'Go God Go's warring atheist factions to show exclusivity is unavoidable even without God. Hume's miracle argument explains why Jesus's look-away water-into-wine trick convinces no one in the episode: testimony can never outweigh the laws of nature, so supernatural evidence resists natural evaluation. Popper's falsificationism warns that watering doctrines down to make religions compatible (the rabbit-pope of 'Fantastic Easter Special') leaves nothing to test, while James's will to believe and Plantinga's defense of exclusivism ground the conclusion that faith can be rationally justifiable where evidence runs out—beware the Blainetologists, but do not surrender ways of life that define us.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" — Morgan unpacks the science behind the 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions as in the portal of 'Little Girl Lost,' Einstein's time as a fourth dimension with time-dilation travel ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), and the grandfather paradox, which 'Back There' handles inconsistently (some events change, others cannot) while 'No Time Like the Past' gets right: past events are eternally true. Quantum many-worlds fits 'The Parallel,' where Major Gaines slips into a nearly identical reality, and infinite universes would make every possibility actual. But the cosmological multiverse, he argues with Popper's falsifiability criterion, is untestable and hence not science, remaining a dimension of mind and imagination.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 8 "Sherlock's Reasoning Toolbox" — Pigliucci shows that Holmes's celebrated 'deduction' is really a mix of induction and abduction, contrasting Aristotelian syllogism and Cartesian rationalism (with its failed Cartesian circle) against the fallibility of real investigation. He walks through Hume's problem of induction (Russell's inductivist chicken), the Mill-Whewell 'great induction debate,' and Popper's falsificationism—qualified by the Neptune/Uranus episode where scientists shielded Newton. Using 'Thor Bridge' and 'The Three Students,' he concludes Holmes is a pragmatic scientist wielding a whole toolbox, since there is no single scientific method.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 22 "12. Raven Seldon Predicts Disaster" — Malloy argues psychohistory rests on induction and therefore inherits Hume's problem of induction: Seldon generalizes from Trantor's past to predict the Empire's fall, but nothing guarantees the future will resemble the past, and the Mule's unprecedented rise shows there is no deductive guarantee (the future-unlike-past idea is not self-contradictory). He tests Popper's falsificationism, under which psychohistory is science because it makes falsifiable predictions and can never be confirmed, then notes Popper leaves hypothesis-origin and post-failure revision inductive, and finally offers Reichenbach's pragmatic 'vindication' of induction, likening it to Hardin making do with the only tools at hand in a Seldon Crisis.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 24 "14. Beyond Loyalty and Disloyalty" — Bartolo Alegre uses Seldon's trial claim that 'scientific truth is beyond loyalty and disloyalty' to ask whether even formal sciences like logic can be biased. Against Bogdanov's and Lenin's Marxist idea of a 'proletarian logic,' he shows that logical principles (non-contradiction, explosion) have been revised by paraconsistent logicians on purely mathematical grounds, using Hardin's symbolic-logic decoding of the Anacreon message and Orwell's doublethink as illustrations. Drawing on Popper's rejection of uninformative contradictions, Kuhn's sociological account of scientific change, and Lakatos's rational reconstruction, he argues science transcends individual scientists' loyalties only through a diverse, competing community of experts, as when Hummin's loyalty to humanity pushed Seldon to make psychohistory practical.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Briony Addey defines coincidence and distinguishes three theories the castaways might invoke to say events are 'meant to be' — divine providence, fatalism, and determinism — using Locke's belief in his walkabout destiny and Eloise Hawking's 'the universe course corrects' as fatalist cases. She introduces Jung's synchronicity and collective unconscious as an acausal explanation of meaningful coincidence, then debunks our intuitions with the birthday paradox, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability, before criticizing Jacob's deception 'experiment' on the candidates for failing standards of informed consent and culpable versus non-culpable ignorance.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 28 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Pigliucci uses the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series and the Dover trial to argue that intelligent design is not science because it is unfalsifiable and invokes supernatural causation. He cites Popper's falsificationism (and Popper's recantation about Darwinism), contrasts Descartes's rationalism with Hume's empiricism to characterize science as a tentative blend of the two, flags Feyerabend's 'anything goes' as an irrational view of knowledge, invokes Aristotle's eudaimonia to argue meaning in life is a personal work in progress, and turns Dembski's theistic-evolution concession into a Pyrrhic victory via the problem of evil ('argument from bad design').
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" — Morgan surveys the physics and philosophy behind the show's 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions and parallel universes ('Little Girl Lost'), time as Einstein's fourth dimension and relativistic time dilation ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), the Grandfather Paradox and the self-consistency of time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past'), the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics ('The Parallel'), and the cosmological multiverse. He closes with Popper's falsification criterion, arguing that unobservable other universes may be, like the show itself, forever 'a dimension of mind.'

### Ockham's Razor

Ockham's Razor is the methodological principle that, among competing explanations, one should not multiply entities or assumptions beyond necessity, so that the simpler account is to be preferred when it explains the evidence equally well. Named for the fourteenth-century logician William of Ockham, who favored parsimony in his rejection of superfluous metaphysical posits, it functions as a rule of theoretical economy rather than a proof of truth. It responds to the temptation to explain phenomena by inventing unobserved causes, urging that explanatory machinery be justified by what it actually accounts for.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 23 "Erotic Love and Friendship" — Maps Aristotle's three levels of friendship onto Buffy's three boyfriends: Riley is a utility friendship chosen for the rational goal of a 'normal' boyfriend (echoed by Warren's robot April and the Buffybot, which prove programmed perfection cannot be loved), Spike is a pleasure friendship driven by passion and danger that Buffy ends in 'As You Were,' and Angel is a complete friendship where each values the other for his own sake despite the gypsy curse. This lets the authors solve Aristotle's love paradox (is erotic love chosen or does it choose us?) by adding Augustine's and William of Ockham's third power of the soul, the will: an arational faculty that values the other as an end in himself, neither rationally chosen nor irrationally caused.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 28 "The Meta-Fear of Fear" — Noel Carroll traces Halloween's Undead imagery to the Celtic Samhain and its Catholic absorption into All Hallows' Eve, then asks the paradox: why do we take pleasure in images of the death that, as Heidegger says, is the deep source of Angst we spend our lives denying? He examines Ernest Jones's Freudian analysis - the vampire as wish-fulfillment disguising an incestuous desire, horror as the price the super-ego exacts - and rejects it as theoretically expensive, invoking the demand for simpler, more economical explanation. His own hypothesis is the 'meta-fear of fear': adolescent viewers (and aging ones) use horror films and the holiday's zombie costumes to test and master fear itself, with parody and Bergson's laughter as companion devices of emotional control - a folk remedy that needs no unconscious to work.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 27 "Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up" — Tests three theories of mind against Spock's katra transfer in The Wrath of Khan and The Search for Spock and his mind melds with Kirk, the Horta, and Rock people. Descartes's divisibility argument backs the dualism the katra assumes, but the argument from parsimony (Ockham's razor), the problem of mental causation, and the conservation of energy weigh against it; Churchland's eliminative materialism plays by science's rules but runs into Nagel's 'what it is like' objection, dramatized by Geordi failing to describe anger to Data without circularity. The author lands, cautiously, on Searle-style emergentism — mind as an emergent, irreducible feature of neural complexity, as when Nomad and V'Ger exceed their programming — while conceding Kim's charge that it may be dualism in disguise.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 20 "Zelda Is a Communication Game!" — Johnson argues that because Zelda has no single authorial vision (teams, outside developers, cryptic Aonuma interviews), the timeline is a 'communication game' fans play together. Interpretation follows the hermeneutic circle of Heidegger and Gadamer (parts inform the whole, as when Wind Waker's references to Ganon's earlier attacks make sense of the series), faces Leibnizian underdetermination since infinitely many theories fit the games, and uses Ockham's razor, whose failures (the y=2x formula) show that simplicity is relative to a community's training, as in Wittgenstein's pupil who suddenly counts '1,004, 1,008'. Hence Miyamoto's own claim that Zelda is a communication game: designers supply puzzle pieces, and the fan community creates the meaning.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 9 "Is Monk’s Certainty Justified" — Rauhut tests Monk's method against two models of discovery: Holmes-style eliminatism, modeled on Popper's falsification via reductio ad absurdum, and CSI-style confirmationism in the mold of Hempel and Carnap (Gil Grissom letting evidence speak). Monk fits neither — in 'Mr. Monk and the Astronaut' he refuses to eliminate the alibi-solid Steve Wagner, and in 'Mr. Monk Falls in Love' he ignores a hatpin, a motive, and a confession pointing at Leyla. Instead Monk is an 'epiphanist': he registers every anomaly (the secretary hired from a Lamaze-class ad in 'Mr. Monk Fights City Hall', Crawford's odd phrasing 'No, she wouldn't be drinking now'), suddenly sees the one theory explaining all of them, and only afterwards manufactures shareable evidence for others. His absolute certainty, the chapter argues, rests on a metaphysical faith that only the true theory can explain every anomaly — a Leibnizian 'best of all possible ordered worlds' — the same obsession with order that makes him notice anomalies at all, though it makes him epistemically irresponsible by ordinary standards that weigh alternative hypotheses and simplicity.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 8 "Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory" — Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 28 "Get Serious" — David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 26 "The Future of Sandy Cheeks" — Wilson González-Espada assesses Sandy Cheeks as a portrait of the scientist: she explodes the 'Draw a Scientist' stereotype — female, socially popular, working in an open treedome that mirrors peer review — yet the show muddles the nature of science, calling inventions 'experiments' and a clipboard of math 'science'. The chapter applies Popper's falsifiability to SpongeBob's one-sided evidence that Squidward is a true friend and Newton's principle of parsimony to Sandy's ghost scare, then closes with Aldo Leopold's land ethic, reading 'Jellyfish Hunter' and 'SpongeBob's Last Stand' as environmental parables about habitat and overexploitation.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 13 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Don Fallis proposes deception rather than language as the personhood test: following Dennett, a deceiver must be a second-order intentional system who can want someone else to have a false belief, as when General Thade lies to Senator Sandar about Ari's kidnapping, Zira and Cornelius feign muteness before the Presidential Commission, and Caesar fakes his own electrocution in Conquest. The roles' reversal makes this a test for the films' mute humans too, while Descartes's beast machines, Wittgenstein on dogs that cannot simulate pain, and Lloyd Morgan's canon voice the skeptical reading of fake alarm calls and Koko's 'Cat did it.' Against them Fallis invokes Occam's Razor over Hare, Call and Tomasello's food-competition experiments: apes track who sees what, but they fail the misinformed false-belief version, so real apes may not be 'sneaky enough to be people.'
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 11 "Psych and Philosophy" — Jones argues that Shawn's 'psychic' act is really hypersensory perception (HSP) - noticing cat fur, fine print, blood spatter - feeding inference to the best explanation (IBE), the natural abductive method Sherlock Holmes mislabels deduction, with Clever Hans and Ilga Kirks as real-world parallels. Applying IBE with Ockham's Razor to the two hypotheses 'he's psychic' versus 'he's hyper-observant,' she concludes the natural explanation should win for everyone: Lassiter's skepticism tracks the evidence, Gus knows better despite believing in ghosts, and Chief Vick shouldn't buy the supernatural story either. Juliet's belief survives only through background supernatural beliefs, a psychic-friendly culture, and ignoring the clues Gus feeds Shawn, which the chapter diagnoses as the same public misunderstanding of the scope and limits of science that keeps most Americans believing in ESP.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 15 "Psych and Philosophy" — Guidry-Grimes treats Chief Vick's hiring of Shawn as a genuine problem in applied ethics rather than a joke: the Psi hypothesis fails Ockham's Razor and no controlled study supports paranormal ability, yet Vick - unlike viewers who know Shawn is a fraud - must weigh her obligations to victims, the department, and taxpayers on the evidence she has. The chapter argues that hiring Shawn is ethically defensible given his record of solving over fifty unsolvable cases, but it catalogues the costs: false hope for distraught families (Marc Klaas's resentment of psychic tipsters), damage to Lassiter's morale, wasted resources, and the fragile public trust bound up with taxpayer money. The conclusion is a compromise: Vick is ethically required to use every tool in the arsenal, including a successful 'psychic,' only in desperate high-stakes cases where the victim's family does not object, and otherwise merely permitted.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 14 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Sharon Kaye stages a fourteenth-century debate over a contradiction: Jesus truthfully prophesied that the Antichrist will come, yet the Antichrist remains free not to. Peter Aureoli denies bivalence for statements about the future, Thomas Bradwardine has God swap among infinite possible-world 'movies,' and Ockham's follower John of Mirecourt concludes that Jesus simply lied - each solution self-defeating or heretical. Using Ockham's Razor and her comic fantasy of seducing the Antichrist, Kaye argues the unsolvable prophecy problem helped discredit prophetic religion, ushered in theological determinism via Luther and Calvin, and opened a secular age.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 15 "6. The PowerPoint Conspiracy Theory" — In a sustained deadpan parody, Ketcham builds a conspiracy out of Ockham's Razor: William of Ockham's minimalist principle explains PowerPoint's big-type bullet points, but the slide deck (secretly engineered by DARPA with Microsoft, exported via Siberia to Putin) becomes a weapon that breeds stupidity, conditions Trump to tweet-length simplicities like fake news and crooked, and finally rigs him, not the voting machines. The chapter also wields the Razor correctly, insisting that a minimalist explanation must still be good and complete, as when little Jill's one bullet point tells us too little. Testing moral realism, Kant's absolute prohibition on lying, and utilitarianism's greatest happiness against the conspiracy's missing facts, it concludes we lack the information to render any moral verdict, which is exactly what the conspiracy-minded minimalists want.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 17 "7. Scott Adams’s Joy of Logic" — Bilsker turns Adams's Joy of Work catalogue of irrational co-workers into a critical-thinking syllabus: faulty analogy (from dogs fetching sticks to potatoes dancing, and Francis Bacon's body-politic passage praising war as exercise), huge-pants faulty causation, the Reinhart-Rogoff debt paper that drove austerity policy on mere correlation until Herndon, Ash, and Pollin exposed it, complex and objectionable cause, the overapplication of Occam's Razor to moon-landing hoaxes, misplaced authority, begging the question, and egocentric biases like I Am the World. He then contrasts the classroom view that confirmation bias is an unconscious background program with Win Bigly's claim that bias is the operating system itself, worrying about the implication that reasoning with anyone is futile, and concludes that Adams overstates how incapable we are of overcoming our biases.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 19 "We’ve Run Out of Time… or Have We" — The chapter argues that the film's multiverse, where sorcerers 'harness energy drawn from other dimensions,' is best modeled on the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, walking through Tegmark's Level I-III multiverses, Schrodinger's cat, the double-slit experiment, and the measurement problem (Copenhagen, von Neumann-Wigner's mind-caused collapse, and Everett's branching) to show that interpreting the formalism is philosophy rather than physics. It defends many-worlds against the objections of counterintuition and Ockham's razor, and suggests that Strange trapping Dormammu in a time loop works like a quantum experiment, with branching worlds dissolving the grandfather paradox.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 22 "NOTES" — Asks how to tell genuine science from pseudoscience using Chandra Suresh's rejected Activating Evolution theory, Sheldrake's morphic fields, alchemy, and Behe's intelligent design. Kuhn's picture of normal science, anomalies, and revolutions explains why Suresh would need a full-blown crisis in evolutionary theory — such as people actually flying — before the community accepts him, and why time rather than mockery settles a theory's fate. Ockham's razor condemns the unnecessary organizing principles in both Sheldrake's and Suresh's theories, and intelligent design is exposed as bad method because, like creationism, it was devised to protect a prior commitment from disconfirming fossil and cosmological evidence.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 21 "10 Fact, Truth, and Evidence A Lesson from Dr. Tyree" — Dean Kowalski stages an imagined dialogue between Indy and William E. Tyree — Harrison Ford's real Ripon College philosophy professor, whom Ford's own script rewrite placed 'right down the hall' — to show that 'archaeology is the search for fact, not truth' is self-defeating if truth is correspondence with reality. Tyree's epistemology primer (principles of evidence, inductive generalization, hypothesis testing like Indy's Sankara-stone glow prediction, and Ockham's Razor) explains Indy's resistance to the God hypothesis despite witnessing the Ark, the Grail's instant healing of Henry Sr., and the invisible bridge he crossed on guesswork rather than knowledge. The resolution: Indy practices methodological naturalism, keeping deeper truths out of archaeology, without being committed to metaphysical naturalism.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Leuenberger argues that a LEGO MOC is a surprisingly faithful model of David Lewis's Humean supervenience: the world is just a vast mosaic of local matters of particular fact — homogeneous, arbitrarily recombinable atomic bricks (fundamental properties at space-time points) with no necessary connections, Hume's 'greater denier', versus gunky Play-Doh or jigsaw pieces. Ockham's Razor motivates the view (while also able to cut against a divine master builder, whom Lewis's world lacks, though LEGO-world builders likewise stand outside their creations), and Lewis's concrete possible worlds make every build a replica rather than a creation, answered to the 'incredulous stare' by quantitative parsimony. Four-dimensionally stacked creations model change as variation along temporal parts, while the causation objection — nothing in one LEGO creation brings about the next — marks the fundamental Humean/non-Humean divide.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 20 "Zelda Is a Communication Game!" — Carl Matthew Johnson argues that the split-timeline versus linear-timeline fan war, settled by Eiji Aonuma's 2006 Nintendo Dream interview, is really a hermeneutic meta-game fans play on top of Zelda. He applies the Heidegger-Gadamer hermeneutic circle — the Ganon references in Wind Waker make sense only from knowledge of the whole series, while gossip-stone text about Kaepora Gaebora feeds back into the whole — then uses Leibniz's curve-fitting problem to show timeline evidence underdetermines any single interpretation. Ockham's razor and Wittgenstein's counting-by-twos rule-following example reveal that simplicity is community-relative, culminating in Miyamoto's 2007 claim that Zelda was designed from the start as a 'communication game' among players.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 20 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Curry argues that angels like Anna and Castiel can reasonably be atheists, because a higher perspective confers no epistemic advantage about God: Anna admits only four angels have seen him and the rest 'take it on faith.' Aquinas's cosmological argument, illustrated by the endless causal chain behind the Impala, yields at most an uncaused first cause rather than an omnipotent, omnibenevolent one, and Paley's design argument, an Impala in the desert implies a designer, is undermined by Darwinian natural selection, which Castiel himself witnessed ('Don't step on that fish'). The free-will theodicy fails against natural evils like famine and childhood cancer, and the principle of parsimony tells angels to expect a natural explanation for their own existence, so Uriel's 'There is no will. No wrath. No God.' turns out to be rational.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 29 "NOTES" — Richard Brown uses the title 'The Terminator' itself to run the debate over definite descriptions: Russell's theory of descriptions makes 'The Terminator can't be bargained with' false (there are many T-101s, and no real-life Terminator at all), while Strawson insists Kyle's utterance genuinely refers to the machine at the door. Donnellan's referential/attributive distinction is staged through Lieutenant Traxler's 'The phone book killer has no pity' — true of whoever fits the description, or of the very Terminator Sarah has in mind — and Kripke's arguments from 'Russell English,' anaphora, and indirect quotation are weighed against Devitt's pronoun-of-laziness and reference-borrowing replies. The chapter sides with Grice's modified Ockham's razor: descriptions are not semantically ambiguous, so the title is literally false but apt, since Cameron referentially means the T-101.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 26 "When Life Gives You Chlamydia" — Andrew Zimmerman Jones explains Veronica's casework as inductive reasoning: Occam's razor dispatches Meryl's 'space laser' speculation and identifies Gia's stalker via the simplest explanation (the stalker drove off in the pick-up), while Keith's refusal to accept Abel Koontz's confession shows the razor's limits — Sheriff Lamb's laziness being Sidney Brenner's 'Occam's broom,' whisking inconvenient facts like Lilly's body temperature under the rug. Distinguishing Aristotle's particulars-to-universal induction from deduction, the chapter teaches the probability fallacy through the Mercer evidence (clippers, cologne, and GHB make it likely the rapist owns them, not that their owner is the rapist — the same confusion fueling suspicion of PCH-ers) and catalogues the fallacies — false dilemma, false cause, ad hominem, appeal to emotion — that Veronica's jealousy-driven reasoning commits in the Sully case. The chlamydia diagnosis revealing Cassidy raped her is the final lesson: new evidence overturns even well-confirmed conclusions, so certainty is a sucker's bet.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 21 "19_LaRocca_Chapter_018.html" — Rick Altman dismantles four and a half 'fallacies' that let film theory ignore sound: the historical fallacy (sound as a late add-on), the ontological fallacy (image alone is cinema), the reproductive fallacy (recording reproduces rather than represents sound), the nominalist fallacy, and the half-fallacy of indexicality. In the nominalist section he explicitly frames the dispute over whether the 'same' sound heard from different seats shares a real identity as the medieval realism-versus-nominalism debate, casting Plato and Augustine as the realists and William of Ockham as the nominalist, and warning that ultra-nominalism about sound jeopardizes shared understanding. He uses Peirce's index/icon/symbol distinction to argue electronics has desacralized cinema's indexicality.

### Climate Ethics

Climate ethics is the branch of moral philosophy that studies the ethical questions raised by human-caused climate change, including who bears responsibility for emissions, how burdens and benefits should be fairly distributed, and what is owed to future generations and to the world's poorest people. It grapples with problems of collective action, historical responsibility, and the difficulty of assigning duties when harms are diffuse and long-delayed. The field asks how principles of justice apply when the consequences of present choices fall largely on those who did least to cause them.

- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 25 "Dizzy with the Possibilities" — Allen Thompson treats 'Throwing Stones' — 'the future's here, we are it, we are on our own' — as voicing the existential dread of anthropogenic global warming and the felt 'end of nature' Bill McKibben named, defending the song as the band's a-political polemic against heartless powers. He argues via Steven Vogel that humans cannot literally end nature unless we are supernatural, and recasts the crisis with Thoreau and Gary Snyder as civilization's assault on the wild, the self-willed order we too belong to. Deep ecology then supplies the response: re-identify the self as wild — as Deadheads do by dancing wildly to the music — and build a civilization wildness can endure, with the band's 1988 rainforest-benefit press conference as evidence of the Dead's own ecological consciousness.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 16 "This Is Really Happening (So Do Something)" — Milsky argues that Radiohead practice what environmental virtue ethics preaches, organizing the chapter around Aristotle's akrasia (Nicomachean Ethics VII): Sting, who champions rainforests while advertising Jaguar and topping the 'dirtiest band' carbon table, acts against his own better judgment, whereas Radiohead — confronted with an audit showing their 2003 and 2006 tours emitted roughly 11,368 tons of CO2, mostly from fans driving — changed their actual practice (venues near public transit, car-pool lots, sea freight instead of air, LED lighting and auxilary power units). He reads the King Canute imagery of The Eraser and lines from 'The Clock' and 'And It Rained All Night' as environmental narrative in the tradition of Thoreau's Walden and Leopold's Sand County Almanac, obligating listeners to act or risk akrasia themselves, and presents the band's Friends of the Earth 'Big Ask' commitment as linking environmental virtue to human flourishing. 'Idioteque'''s 'this is really happening' becomes the wake-up call to the akratic fan driving to Lollapalooza with a bottled water.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 27 "Who Watches the Watchers" — Patton and Webb unpack Colbert's coinage 'freem' — freedom without the do — from the first episode's dedication to 'the heroes' who act patriotically by watching TV, through Bush's post-9/11 call to go shopping, the Wikipedia elephant vandalism, and the WristStrong bracelet as activism indistinguishable from consuming Viacom product. Using Singer's argument that social capital (roads, satellites, infrastructure) makes the 'it's your money' cry hollow, E.O.
