- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 26 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Christian Cotton asks whether Carrie's clandestine surveillance of the Brody home, though illegal, is morally wrong, distinguishing legality from morality. Locke's state of nature grounds natural rights to life, liberty, property - and by extension privacy - that government exists to protect and that no national-security goal automatically overrides; Mill's utilitarianism would justify violating one family's privacy to prevent an attack, but Mill's own harm principle and 'tyranny of the majority' caution blocks it when Carrie has only a hunch. Kant's respect for persons as ends in themselves condemns Saul's blackmail of Judge Turner as using a man merely as means, so the Right constrains pursuit of the Good.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 12 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Gale and Barkman treat post-Mushroom-War Ooo as a state-of-nature laboratory for liberalism's three founders. The Forest Wizard who cages Finn in 'Storytelling' is Hobbes's Leviathan, kept in power by fear yet moderated by self-interest (Goblin King Xergiok's fall shows the leash); Princess Bubblegum's Candy Kingdom is Locke's civil society where citizens trade private revenge for impartial law—her lawful bow to Lemongrab shows she rules by contract, not fear; and 'City of Thieves' illustrates Rousseau's claim that property corrupts natural goodness, with Finn and Jake as his uncorrupted natural people. The chapter concludes that the rights language these thinkers forged is what keeps both Ooo and our world from sliding back into a war of all against all.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 11 "2. Sure We’re Criminals" — Malloy asks whether the two law-breaking vigilantes are criminals and whether any duty to obey the law survives scrutiny. He runs consent theory through Superman surrendering in handcuffs in Man of Steel and the Red Son Superman's residence in the USSR, uses Darkseid's Apokolips as Hobbes's security sovereign against Locke's natural-rights limits, deploys Hume against tacit consent (Batman would never leave Gotham even in No Man's Land), and dismantles gratitude theory (the Kents' adoption involved a sacrificial choice the law cannot make) and fair play (Nozick's Batman-lottery undercuts "I'm not wearing hockey pads"). He lands near Wolff-style philosophical anarchism: Superman's constrained lawbreaking endorses the law's legitimacy while Batman treats law as one more tool in his war, making him a force of chaos.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 14 "4. Who Owns Clones" — Takes the message Cosima decodes in the clones' DNA — "This organism and derivative genetic material is restricted intellectual property" — and asks whether Dyad can legally and morally own the Clone Club. The chapter walks through US patent law and the Supreme Court's Myriad Genetics decision (naturally occurring DNA unpatentable, synthetic cDNA patentable) and argues that because the Leda and Castor clones were genetically engineered, their modified sequences could fall under the synthetic exception, making ownership legally possible. Morally, though, it sides with self-ownership: people own the products of their labor but not people, so patenting clones would recreate the wrongs of slavery, down to who controls clone marriages and clone offspring.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 27 "16. Can We All Get Along" — Courtland Lewis tackles transitional justice after atrocity: with the Rising won, what is to be done with millions of Golds complicit in slavery, rape, and torture? He tests Peter French's virtuous vengeance—punishment that fits the wrong, grounded in Locke's natural rights—and finds Darrow's destruction of Gold society fails it (disproportionate, unsober, punishing young Julian for his ancestors' crimes), then turns to Jessica Wolfendale's argument that declaring anyone unforgivable adopts the wrongdoer's own devaluing outlook, exactly as Darrow becomes what he despises. The working model is South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission—confession, conditional amnesty, truth-telling, reparations, Tutu, Mandela, Beth Savage hoping to meet her bomber—applied to Mars through Mustang-style dignified engagement on Adam Michnik's model and Slavenka Drakulic's lesson that every Color inherits responsibility for rejecting the Society's past.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 17 "6. Jaime the Savior" — The Coxes defend Jaime's kingslaying with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics Book III on voluntary, involuntary, and 'mixed' actions: like a storm-besieged crew jettisoning cargo, or the Blackfish's 'a knife to his throat is not a valid order,' Jaime faced a duress - kill Tywin on Aerys's order or let King's Landing burn - so his regicide was a mixed action that is praiseworthy as the least harmful option rather than blameworthy. They add Locke's right of revolution, where a ruler who makes his will rather than law the rule puts himself in a state of war with his people, to argue the Mad King's 'Burn them all' tyranny justified the killing, making the reviled Kingslayer the savior of the city.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 14 "5. In the Neutral Zone, a Libertarian’s Home Is Their (High) Castle" — The chapter reads Dick as a left-leaning libertarian for whom the deepest evil of the High Castle world is the loss of privacy: Arnold's surveillance unit and the Kempeitai's wiretaps illustrate Locke's self-ownership and natural rights, while the Neutral Zone poses the Hobbesian question of whether even an oppressive state beats the state of nature, and the 'libertarian minimal state' names what the Reich destroys. On this reading the American Nazis like John Smith were internal collaborators all along — 'it already happened here' — and ethics lies in refusal, as when Tagomi declines to sign the order sending Frank to his death.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 12 "3. Will the Real American Hero Please Stand Up" — Samuelson argues Tony Stark is the real American hero because he embodies the Locke-to-Smith lineage of American values - natural rights, property from mixing labor, free trade and the invisible hand, plus Smithian sympathy - carried forward into twenty-first-century neoliberalism, from Stark Industries to backing the Registration Act. Steve, by contrast, keeps abandoning the Captain America identity (Nomad after the Secret Empire, The Captain under Nuke's government, handing the shield to Bucky and Sam Wilson) whenever America betrays the dream, and admits his true fight is against bullies and for human rights everywhere. Hence Cap is a great hero but not strictly an American one, while Tony lives American values practically, warts and all.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 16 "6. Big Brother Ltd" — Botello-Samson and Mobley extend Fromm's point that 1984 indicts authoritarian power in general by reading Oceania alongside neoliberalism, which grew out of Locke's liberalism of natural rights and limited government yet demands activist state power to create the conditions for markets. Doublethink reappears as 'accountable independence' in administrative law (Chevron deference, and Garcetti v. Ceballos stripping whistleblower protection) and as Washington Consensus food policy, in which developing nations were pushed off agricultural self-sufficiency while the US kept its own subsidies. Both Ingsoc and neoliberal governance reduce everything to economic elements and use Newspeak-like buzzwords such as 'stakeholder' and 'customer-driven government' to hide the contradiction between democratic rhetoric and rule by experts and elites.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 11 "2 Transforming Wakanda Justice (or Not ) in Black Panther" — Bein and Lewis imagine Killmonger surviving his duel to face Wakandan justice, and sort what justice would demand into retributive justice (Kant: punishment only what the offender deserves, never using him merely as a means to public safety, though they note Kant's own racist views), reparatory justice (Locke's natural rights and what Wakanda owes N'Jadaka for T'Chaka killing N'Jobu and abandoning him in Oakland), and the restorative-to-transformative justice of Changamire's gatherings in Coates's 'A Nation Under Our Feet,' modeled on South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission. They argue a restorative Wakanda would seat Killmonger with his victims and even the king at the table to repair harm rather than imprison him, and sketch a prison-abolitionist Wakanda meeting Thanos with 'Wakandan justice is more civilized.'
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 19 "Notes" — John Irish reads the Amazon series' Vault 33 as Locke's Two Treatises staged and then betrayed: Overseer elections (Betty Pearson against Reg McPhee and Woody Thomas), town-council deliberation over captured Vault 32 raiders, and Lucy's 1950s-styled domesticity all mimic natural equality, consent of the governed, majority rule, and the preservation of property. Norm's discovery that every election is rigged in favor of cryo-preserved technocrats from Vault 31, that Lucy's marriage 'application' is engineered population control, and that Vault-Tec executives - including Lucy's mother Barb - voted to launch the Great War itself shows Locke's forms of consent, law, and rights preserved as empty ceremony. The chapter's argument is that Enlightenment liberalism stripped of transparency becomes authoritarian experiment management: consent becomes choreography in a commonwealth that is really a lab, right down to composting the raiders' bodies.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 17 "Selling Ol’ Shellhead" — Malloy uses Spymaster's theft of Stark's armor designs in the Armor Wars and the U.S. government's legally valid appropriation of the technology after Tony announces 'I am Iron Man' to test two theories of property. Locke's natural-law view makes the designs an extension of Stark's laboring self — stealing them is like taking an arm — while Hume's social-contract view treats property as a useful convention whose violation makes the thief an enemy of society itself, and Rousseau supplies the cautionary image of the first man who fenced ground and said 'This is mine.' A closing thought experiment in which Tony sells Iron Man outright (like Siegel and Schuster selling Superman) argues that intellectual property can never be fully alienated: whoever wore the armor, Tony would still be Iron Man.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Alkema and Barkman put Q himself on trial, asking what justifies his judgment of humanity in 'Encounter at Farpoint' and Trelane's of Kirk in 'The Squire of Gothos'. Hobbes's Leviathan would license Q's might-makes-right sovereignty over a savage species, but Q lacks humanity's consent and cannot show he acts for future peace; Locke's natural law instead binds even nearly omnipotent beings, as Janeway's asylum ruling for the suicidal Quinn in 'Death Wish' demonstrates. Q's repeated self-sacrifice—in 'Deja Q' and the Continuum's civil war—reveals a conscience answerable to natural law rather than raw power.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Foy reads the Great Revelation and the Vampire Rights Amendment as a test of social contract theory: Nan Flanagan's 'we pay taxes, we deserve civil rights' invokes the Lockean bargain of obedience for protection, but Locke's God-given natural rights falter when the Fellowship denies vampires souls, and Locke excludes atheists and never imagined vampires. The chapter's resolution is Rawls: behind a veil of ignorance where deliberators might wake up vampire or human, anti-vampire bigots like the Newlins and supremacist nests alike would choose equal basic liberties plus distributive justice — including limits on vampires' centuries of accumulated wealth — so Sookie's 'let the law do it' to Rene marks a pluralist peace no theistic contract could deliver.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 19 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Jason Walker pits Hobbes against Locke over whether Andrea may take the mermaid necklace when Rick says 'I don't think those rules apply anymore'. He reads the survivors' conduct—Andrea's single necklace under Locke's spoilage proviso, Morgan squatting in and fixing up the neighbors' house, Rick voluntarily sharing guns with Guillermo—as a Lockean state of nature where self-ownership and property rights persist without government, while Chris's cannibal band and the Governor embody the Hobbesian war of all against all, treating persons as mere means. The Lockean right to punish, exercised brutally by Grimes's group on Chris's hunters, vindicates rights even by Hobbes's own demand for enforcement.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Woolfolk reads The Last of the Mohicans as staging a conflict between nature and civilization. The opening hunt is neither Hobbes's brutish state of nature nor quite Rousseau's amoral noble savage, since the Mohicans are full moral agents; Woolfolk uses Locke's Second Treatise to cast Hawkeye and the colonists as enforcing natural law and natural rights against English 'tyranny,' with Chingachgook's killing of Magua a justified execution. Rousseau's First and Second Discourses illuminate the hypocrisy and greed of Montcalm and the Europeans, and Camus's Meursault is invoked as a truer image of amoral natural man; Tocqueville frames Cora's democratic awakening as individualism.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 10 "Two Ways to Yuma Locke, Liberalism, and Western Masculinity in 3 10 to Yuma" — Mexal reads both versions of 3:10 to Yuma through Locke's classical liberalism, arguing the western hero descends from Locke's autonomous, property-owning self in a 'state of nature' (contrasted with Hobbes's state of war). In the 1957 film, Dan Evans transforms from atomistic self-interest to a masculine civic republicanism, escorting Ben Wade to the train even after being released from his contract, reflecting Cold War anxieties. In the 2007 remake, Dan instead renegotiates his contract for water rights and money, so western masculinity becomes unyielding Lockean individualism and the 'right to get rich' in a post-Cold War, capitalist-triumphant America.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 18 "Human Rights, Human Nature, and Amistad" — Baggett and Foreman use Amistad to reconstruct Locke's theory of natural rights: Cinque's mutiny and John Quincy Adams's Supreme Court plea that man's natural state is freedom illustrate Locke's claim that God's workmanship makes us his property and therefore un-ownable by other men. They contrast Locke's voluntarist natural law with Aquinas's, note Adams rebutting the Hobbesian 'war of all against all' quoted in the pro-slavery Executive Review, and invoke Mill's perfect/imperfect duty distinction (Baldwin's obligation to his clients) plus Bentham's rights-denying utilitarianism, which they map onto Calhoun's warning about the cost of abolition.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 5 "“Are You Watching Closely ”" — Foy and Dale argue that Nolan's Dark Knight trilogy stages a conservative critique of liberal political theory. They set Locke's pre-political natural rights and Rawls's priority-of-rights ('each person possesses an inviolability... that even the welfare of society cannot override') against a Batman who wiretaps all of Gotham, tortures, and kidnaps Lau, treating social order as the thing that overrides individual rights. Batman is cast as a Humean conservative who grounds authority in habit and custom rather than an imaginary social contract, invoking Carl Schmitt's 'state of exception' (the Roman dictator Dent describes) and Burke's non-elected natural aristocracy to justify the billionaire elite Wayne saving a liberal order from the Joker's nihilism and Bane's Marxist-Leninist revolution.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 24 "13. Does God Have the Right to Destroy the Universe" — Foresman asks whether Chuck has a negative right to destroy the multiverse, rejecting the question-begging 'God can do whatever God wants' and the bare creation/ownership argument (using the scrambled-eggs example) as insufficient. Drawing on Locke's Two Treatises—property arises from mixing labor, but even in the state of nature one may not destroy a creature except for a 'nobler use,' and hoarding beyond use is illegitimate—he concludes Chuck is a Lockean tyrant destroying universes he could simply recreate, so Sam and Dean's rebellion is justified.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Richard Davies analyzes the post-crash survivors as living in a genuine 'state of nature' and grades its severity by how scarce the contested good is (the water shortage as a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers versus Sawyer's 'possession is nine-tenths'). He compares Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau on human nature — labeling the poles 'Innocence' (Hurley, Rousseau, Hume) and 'Trust No 1' (Sawyer, Hobbes) — and uses the repeated prisoners' dilemma and the tit-for-tat strategy to argue that the castaways build a Lockean civil society by signaling through shared language and cooperating first, while the discovery of the Others (Ethan) triggers Hobbesian non-cooperation.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Peter S. Fosl argues that Lost pretends to a liberal social order — Jack rising by consent in a Lockean scheme of natural rights, Rousseau's general will ('live together, die alone'), and Hume's sympathy and pity binding the survivors — but that its treatment of the Others betrays a darker politics. Reading the survivor/Other conflict through Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy thesis (notably absent Hobbes), he contends the show, like post-9/11 America, needs an enemy to exterminate, and that the finale's Jacob/Man-in-Black war and Jack's Christlike sacrificial death repudiate the Kantian liberal ideal of persons as ends, resolving conflict through Schmittian and Christian redemptive violence instead.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 22 "Thidwick the Big-Hearted Bearer of Property Rights" — Skoble argues that the creatures who colonize Thidwick's antlers never acquire any property right, because mere uninvited occupancy does not create ownership and Thidwick's Lockean self-ownership over his own body and horns is inalienable. The eleven-to-one vote to keep Thidwick on the starving north shore shows, via Nozick's 'Tale of the Slave,' that democratic procedures cannot legitimately override fundamental liberty rights. Thidwick's near-enslavement stems from his mistaken belief that a host must be 'nice to his guests,' and his freedom is restored only when the shed antlers let him reclaim self-ownership.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 21 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Ketcham 'deconstructs' the entailment that threatens the Bennets in Pride and Prejudice, explaining the legal history of fee tail and primogeniture and noting Austen likely erred, since by her time entailment could be barred by a simple legal procedure. He uses this to trace competing theories of property, from an occupation theory (first possession, tied to inherited estates) toward an emerging economic theory of productive wealth, and finally to Jeremy Waldron's view that property is a relationship between people. Elizabeth's careful assessment of Darcy's estate as a community rather than a mere possession dramatizes this shift, and love plus responsibility replaces entailment as the story's true concern.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 34 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Carmine argues that in America hunting is a sacred rite of a secular 'religion' of individual natural rights granted by the Deist 'Nature's God,' where—revising Locke via Jefferson's 'pursuit of happiness'—one owns game only by actual capture, and early game law kept even private land open to the common hunter against English enclosure. He attacks Leopold's land ethic and Tom Regan's animal rights, and Garrett Hardin's 'Tragedy of the Commons,' as an 'eco-gentry' that demotes humans to mere biosphere/carbonate and threatens human rights, insisting (with Burkert's Homo Necans) that to kill and eat the rabbit is to reserve dignity for humans alone.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 18 "GARDENING" — Laura Auricchio shows how General Lafayette made his estate at La Grange an embodiment of liberal, transatlantic political ideals. Inspired by Washington as a Cincinnatus figure and by Arthur Young's agrarian reform, Lafayette imported American plants and English husbandry, keeping meticulous farm records and staging tours that framed the land around liberty (Fox's planted ivy, self-sufficiency, beneficent stewardship). The chapter argues his cultivation of crops and identity presented the garden as 'American ground' expressing natural rights and republican virtue.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 25 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Agnafors asks whether free soloing is morally permissible, opening with soloists dropping ice chips into his coffee cup to show soloing is not purely private. He tests Locke's natural rights to life and liberty (concluding no act is truly private since rescues, taxpayers, and grieving families are affected), Aristotle's virtue ethics (worrying that habitual risk-taking forms a reckless character), and Bentham and Mill's consequentialism (Bill's confidence-boosting solo of Nutcracker versus Derek Hersey's fatal fall). He concludes no universal answer exists, offering one rule: the soloist must carefully weigh all these considerations beforehand.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 14 "12. Firefly as Philosophy Social Contracts, Political Dissent, and Virtuous Communities" — Kowalski argues that Firefly and Serenity embody a distinctive political theory he calls 'Since I Found Serenity' (SIFS). The mindless, savage Reavers represent Hobbes's state of nature, showing government is necessary; but the Alliance's torture of River, the Miranda/Pax atrocity, and the murderous blue-gloved agents and Operative make a Hobbesian reading untenable and vindicate Locke's natural rights and right of revolution — Mal's 'I aim to misbehave' broadcast of the Miranda file is Lockean civil disobedience. He then presses the tacit-consent problem (the Browncoats cannot leave the 'Verse) and supplements Locke with Aristotle's friendship and community: Serenity's crew becomes a virtuous mobile commonwealth where friendship (Simon forgiving Jayne, Mal's 'love keeps her in the air') turns a commonwealth into a good-life community.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 26 "24. Game of Thrones as Philosophy Cynical Realpolitiks" — The chapter argues that Game of Thrones advances a thoroughgoing cynicism about political legitimacy, captured by Varys's riddle that 'power resides where men believe it resides.' It documents the dubious claims of Robert 'the Usurper' and the pyromaniacal Daenerys, the barbaric Lockean 'state of nature' among the Wildlings, and the false ideals of chivalry and religion, with Littlefinger and Varys voicing Machiavellian realpolitik. Silverman and Riordan then offer two views the show never considers: Locke's social-contract theory of natural rights (which would justify deposing Aerys or Daenerys) and Aquinas's four-part test for genuine law (reason, common good, proper authority, promulgation), arguing a legitimate state remains possible against the show's cynicism.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 98 "92. V for Vendetta as Philosophy Victory Through the Virtues of Anarchy" — Nisley argues that Moore and Lloyd's V for Vendetta justifies V's violent rebellion against the Norsefire regime through Locke: the fascist state seized power without consent, tortured and experimented on citizens (V at Larkhill), and violated natural rights, thereby placing itself in a state of war so the people may overthrow it. Using Aristotle on deviant constitutions and the beast-like tyrant (Adam Susan) who lacks practical wisdom, and contrasting Locke's tolerable state of nature with Hobbes's brutal one, the chapter concludes the citizens should rebuild a rights-protecting social contract rather than V's leaderless anarchy, and maps the argument onto real-world 2020 events (BLM riots vs. the Whitmer kidnapping plot).

### Totalitarianism

Totalitarianism, as analyzed by Hannah Arendt in The Origins of Totalitarianism, names a novel and radical form of domination exemplified by Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia. Unlike ordinary tyranny, it seeks total control not just of politics but of every sphere of life, fusing ideology and terror to remould human beings and abolish spontaneity, plurality, and independent thought. Arendt traced its roots to phenomena such as antisemitism, imperialism, and the rise of atomized mass society, and argued that its concentration camps aimed to render people superfluous. Her account remains a landmark attempt to understand how such regimes arise and why they are distinct from earlier despotisms.

- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 23 "Rising Up" — Brandon Forbes uses Hannah Arendt's distinction between power (people acting in concert, rooted in plurality and natality) and violence (instruments that ape power, one against all) to read Radiohead's violent imagery. The "Just" video shows that power lies not in what the prone man says but in everyone's collective act of lying down; "Sit Down. Stand Up." and "2 + 2 = 5" dramatize command backed by weapons and the revolutionary moment when a king's violence breeds the dissent that undoes him; "Life in a Glass House" and "Where I End and You Begin" depict totalitarian terror, the stage where violence has devoured power entirely. "I Will" ("I will rise up," "little babies' eyes") closes the chapter as Arendt's natality — the capacity of new political beginnings the gun can never defeat.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 26 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Kenneth Sayles reads Peter and Valentine's net personas through three lenses: John Locke's identity theory to ask whether a consistent virtual persona with no physical anchor deserves our trust, Plato's Ring of Gyges to ask what anonymity does to morality, and Hannah Arendt's account of totalitarianism to warn that nameless, unaccountable influence ('action without a name... is meaningless') paves the way for rule by propaganda and a fictitious world. Real-world parallels - identity theft, the hacker collective Anonymous, YouTube politics - make the Enderverse nets look prophetic rather than fantastic.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 17 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Bowman argues through Arendt that Dracula is not inherently evil but thoughtless: like Eichmann he cannot think from another's standpoint, treats people as cogs and means (Harker as captive, humans as prey), uses violence as a constructive tool, and protects himself with rhetorical safeguards like 'Enter freely' so he need never face his own cruelty. Measured against the Crew of Light's thoughtfulness - Harker's memos and recipes for Mina, Mina's care for Lucy, the suitors' gentlemanly bonds - the Count's evil is banal, lazy, 'Evil Lite'; but because Dracula stands outside humanity and knows humans only as livestock, Bowman concludes that Eichmann is banal yet truly evil, while Dracula, though careless, can never be evil.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 16 "7. David Bowie, Political Philosopher" — Hill reconstructs Bowie's political odyssey as a working-out of what freedom and oppression are: 'Cygnet Committee' repudiates revolution powered by resentment (echoing Nietzsche on socialism's despotic annihilation of the individual), 'Big Brother' and Diamond Dogs diagnose the crowd's flight from freedom into leadership, and the Nietzschean self-as-artwork - 'give style to one's character,' the 'mortal with potential of a superman' - curdles into the Thin White Duke's 'rock stars are fascists' collapse of celebrity into totalitarian leadership. The Berlin Trilogy then turns the critique inward: 'Heroes'' ironic lovers unmask romantic anti-totalitarianism (either side of the Antifaschistischer Schutzwall), 'Neuköln' discovers immigrants' mere survival, and Lodger's 'Fantastic Voyage' lands on structural, Marxist questions of how 'we' are to become free.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 15 "7 The Bourgeoisie and the Blacks" — The chapter sets business - the US bourgeoisie whose privileged position Charles Beard read into the Constitution and which survived the Jacksonian and New Deal challenges by breaking labor through Taft-Hartley, right-to-work laws and the PATCO lockout, its solidarity secured while worker solidarity was undercut by what Marx called the Achilles heel of racism - against blacks as the paradigmatic powerless, shut out of every power base since slavery, which the chapter treats with Baptist and Marx's 1846 letter as a totalitarian system of super-exploited, tortured labor that built American capitalism, its neo-slavery progeny (Blackmon) pauperizing the black community under Dred Scott's 'subordinate and inferior class of beings'. It then narrates black counter-power base by base: the abolitionist interracial coalition wielding charisma (Douglass, Nat Turner, John Brown), information, morality and religion; the NAACP era and King's fusion of charisma, church religion, Myrdal's An American Dilemma and televised nonviolent provocation against Bull Connor's violence, contested by Malcolm X, SNCC and the Black Panthers; and a post-civil-rights scorecard showing a wealth base 94.2 percent white, persistent education and media gaps, constrained black officials from mayors to the symbolic Obama presidency, and a captive but potentially leveraged black vote in a 'Sisyphean' struggle.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 14 "4. Non-State Enemies of Freedom" — Nash argues 1984 has been misread as a critique of state power alone; through Newspeak's silencing of thought (in the tradition Austin, MacKinnon, and Langton developed) it shows how any concentration of power oppresses via control of words, data, and information. Drawing on Goldstein's manual's debt to James Burnham's managerial revolution and Sheldon Wolin's 'inverted totalitarianism', she reads the non-centralized Oceania as a warning about non-state enemies: corporations, think tanks running the 'Tobacco Strategy', and global institutions peddling misleading poverty statistics. Popper, Arendt, and Berlin exemplify the state-focused liberalism she thinks blinded us to these horizontal threats, while the Newspeak appendix's past tense shows Orwell expected totalitarianism to be beatable through evidence and democracy.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 21 "10. Love, Truluv" — Sandefur argues that what makes totalitarianism unique is its demand that subjects love their ruler, and that this project is doomed because love is selective, unequal, internal, and inalienable, invoking Aristotle's critique of Plato's community of wives and children, Machiavelli on whether rulers should be loved or feared, and Arendt on conscience as internal dialogue and totalitarianism as total rule. Winston and Julia's sex is a political act asserting the individual against the collective, while the Two Minutes Hate channels repressed erotic energy into sanctioned ecstasy directed at Big Brother, as at Khomeini's funeral. What finally breaks Winston in Room 101 is not torture as such but his surrender of Julia, the one thing that was truly his, which collapses the distinction between love and rape.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 37 "24. Post-Factual Democracy" — Hendricks and Vestergaard open with Trump's inauguration lies and Kellyanne Conway's 'alternative facts' to define post-factual democracy: a state in which opportune political narratives replace facts and evidence as the basis of debate, opinion formation and policymaking. Unlike Machiavelli, who taught that lies must at least be concealed, the post-factual politician pays no price for exposed falsehood once social media, the attention economy and populist us-versus-them narratives engineered for indignation and fear have stripped journalists and fact-checkers of authority — Arendt's remark that mass leaders show 'extreme contempt for facts as such' before fitting reality to their lies. Using Habermas's deliberative model and even minimal accountability theories of voting, they argue post-factuality destroys democratic legitimacy, and defend a 'factual democracy' that trusts science and journalism without becoming a technocracy — the real-world echo of the Party's command to reject the evidence of your eyes.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann builds 20th-century totalitarianism from three TZ episodes: 'He's Alive' shows Aristotle's account of persuasion — rhetoric aimed at an audience's anger and fear — fueling Vollmer's neo-Nazi movement under Hitler's ghostly tutelage; 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' instantiates Eco's Ur-Fascist fear of difference, banning even Plato and Dostoevsky; and 'Deaths-Head Revisited' gives Lutze's 'I functioned as I was told' alongside Arendt's verdict on Eichmann's thoughtless, mechanical obedience. He then argues the phenomenon has mutated: Debord's society of the spectacle explains Black Mirror's 'The Waldo Moment' and 'Fifteen Million Merits,' where image-politics becomes authoritarian and even Bing's suicidal act of defiance is sold back as an avatar product.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 30 "The Resistance New Humans, New Gods" — Dinello maps Westworld point-by-point onto Arendt's Origins of Totalitarianism: the park is a concentration camp that kills the juridical person (hosts as chattel in a 'fictitious world' of Western propaganda), the moral person (Ford forcing Bernard to murder Theresa, Maeve's engineered failure to protect her daughter), and individuality itself (surveillance, resets, 'ghastly marionettes'), with Ford as a Mengele-like ideological scientist who, like Hitler, merely plagiarizes popular myths (John Ford's Westerns, R.U.R.). Liberation then follows Fanon's Wretched of the Earth: violence as a 'cleansing force' that frees the colonized mind, so Maeve's suicide-by-incineration (echoing Plath's Lady Lazarus) and Dolores's beating of the Man in Black and massacre of the Delos board enact decolonization as the creation of 'new men' - a new Robo sapiens species - with Sartre's endorsement that killing eliminates oppressor and oppressed in one go, while Fanon's warning that hatred and revenge are not an agenda sets the conditions for what the resistance must do next.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 11 "1. A Great Darkness Filled with Echoes" — De Vaul argues Gilead terrifies because social cycle theory structures it: every detail, from the Puritan wedding-night sheet to Stalin-style purges and the Nazi and residential-school seizure of children, already happened, so Gilead reads as speculative rather than science fiction. Atwood's three stated influences—Puritan New England, the 1980s religious right, and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four—show history cycling back, with June as the apolitical 'backlash' daughter her second-wave mother Holly and the activist Moira both predicted. The pattern repeats at small scale (June relives the former Offred's Scrabble-and-affair story, Omar's family suffers June's own fate) and in the Historical Notes, where Pieixoto strips Offred of authorship, proving 'the past is a great darkness, filled with echoes.'
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 13 "3. Gestational Totalitarianism" — Kolb reads Gilead through Arendt's The Human Condition and The Origins of Totalitarianism: when reproduction becomes the means of production, women's labor is targeted, forcing fertile women into Animal laborans status as 'national resources' while denying them the creative freedom of Homo faber. She traces the polis/oikos split from Aristotle through Puritan capitalism to show Gilead overcorrecting into Aunt Lydia's 'freedom from'—totalitarian control of birth legitimized by the Rachel and Bilhah story and a Pauline creation story. The chapter ends with the transitional generation's forgetting (Offred's cave-delusion with Nick evoking Plato's Allegory of the Cave, the Holocaust documentarian 'thinking about how not to think') and Ofglen's bomb, arguing that thoughtfulness and literacy, not violence, are the only hopes against totalitarianism.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 14 "4. The United States of Gilead" — Greene argues that the contemporary United States under Trump exhibits early Gilead-like symptoms, detailing five shared techniques: othering (the Aunts' stereotypes of pre-Gilead women vs. Trump on Mexicans and Muslims), separating children from parents (Handmaid births and seizure of Hannah vs. immigrant detention camps), gaslighting (Janine's 'her fault' Testifying vs. inauguration-crowd and Mueller claims), discrediting dissent (Gilead's ban on reading vs. 'fake news'), and lying (Gilead's founding promise of elections vs. thousands of false claims and 'alternative facts'). He grounds the danger in the correspondence theory of truth: once leaders detach belief from how the world actually is, society is a small step from Atwood's dystopia.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 29 "16. Who Is the Meanest of Them All" — Frunză and Grad apply Arendt's banality of evil to Gilead: the Commander is 'not Iago, not Macbeth' but an Eichmann—sheepish, Scrabble-playing, 'thinking about how not to think'—and no character holds a monopoly on evil because everyone is 'too banal' for demonic profundity. They test his 'just doing my duty' against Kant (duty requires universalizing what reason can will and never treating persons as means, so the Aunts' reeducation camps fail the test) and use The Origins of Totalitarianism to read Handmaids as rightless people whose 'two-legged wombs' status mirrors statelessness. Arendt's web of guilty complicities explains why resistance is scarce, and the chapter ends with banality eroding all criteria for judging—leaving Offred's 'the darkness within; or else the light' as the final choice.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 27 "14. Anything that’s Spiked Is Fine" — Volpert asks where rebellion lives, in the lone guitarist or the listening group, using Hardt and Negri's claim that a rebel's true opposite is not failure but co-option, i.e. selling out. Arendt's distinction between totalitarian and authoritarian systems models the music industry as authoritarian (creativity permitted so long as profit at the top goes unchallenged), and her banality-of-evil analysis of Eichmann prompts the question of whether there is a banality of rebellion. Petty's satirical puppetry of authority voices in "Century City" and the silent spiked-collar punk of "Spike," kin to Bartleby and James Dean, show that individuals can rebel against authoritarian packs while groups, even the Heartbreakers, only ever drift into authoritarianism.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 37 "25. Reasonable Genocide" — Uses Horkheimer's Eclipse of Reason to dissolve the puzzle of Thanos's unsettling sanity: the Snap is subjectively rational — pure means–ends efficiency in service of a Malthusian 'simple calculus' whose end only the subject chooses — so Thanos 'is mad because he is rational,' with the murder of Gamora as the final severing of his last bond to the world. Captain America's refusal to trade Vision ('We don't trade lives') is read as a stand for ends valuable in themselves, while Ultron embodies the totalitarian variant (via Arendt and Spencer's social Darwinism) that declares humanity 'obsolete': Ultron wants to accelerate nature, Thanos to correct it, both absolutizing the subject against objective reason.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 20 "10 Understanding the Reigns of T’Challa and Killmonger through Hannah Arendt" — Sinanan reads both reigns through Arendt's account of collective responsibility: T'Challa moves from conscience-based 'I am not king of all people' to owning what Wakanda did in its name ('He was the truth I chose to omit') and finally to political action in Oakland and at the UN, while Killmonger — an MIT-educated Navy SEAL embodying the collective that formed him — becomes the imperialist he opposed, his 'burn it all' revolution matching Arendt's warning about totalitarian domination from within. She compares Killmonger's council speech and herb-burning directly to Hitler's 1924 Munich trial speech, reads his manipulation of the challenge ritual as totalitarian propaganda that organizes rather than persuades, and credits Nakia, Okoye, Shuri, and Ramonda with refusing Arendt's ultimate danger, indifference.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 26 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Kenneth Sayles reads Peter's and Valentine's anonymous rise on the nets through three lenses: John Locke's identity theory asks how a virtual identity can lack a physical anchor, Plato's Ring of Gyges asks what anonymity does to justice, and Hannah Arendt warns that 'action without a name... is meaningless' and that faceless power is a precondition of totalitarianism. Comparing the personas to the hacker collective Anonymous and to identity theft, he concludes our own Internet could breed its own Locke and Demosthenes and asks how much trust we owe virtual people whose controllers we can never know.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 25 "“I Want to Conquer the World”" — Uses Agamben's bios/zoē distinction (with Foucault on biopolitics and fragmented sovereignty, Hardt and Negri's 'Empire', Marx on surplus-value, and Rosa Luxemburg on unchecked capital) to read the Anderson Station massacre, Murtry shooting Coop on New Terra, and Protogen infecting 1.5 million Belters on Eros as reductions of Belter life to bare life that corporate sovereigns may kill without homicide. It then argues the instability capitalism creates births authoritarian sovereigns — Murtry's martial law, Inaros's Free Navy, Duarte's Laconia — whose followers (Chandra Wei, Cyn, Santiago Singh) display the 'total, unrestricted, unconditional loyalty' Arendt says totalitarian power demands, and closes with Foucault's warning that liberal government's security-for-freedom trade slides into the very corruption and oppression it was meant to prevent.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 127 "Like Bertie Bott’s Every-Flavor Beans, a Mix" — Names pureblood supremacism, Voldemort's Nazi-like movement whose victory would mean totalitarianism, thought control, secret police, mock trials, and racial cleansing, as the greatest problem wizards face, and faults Hogwarts education for ignoring it: no antiracist teaching despite rampant slurs, silence about the oppressed house-elves of Hogwarts, A History, and Slytherin left as a hothouse breeding Death Eaters and fifth columnists. Against Prinzi's gradualist defense of Dumbledore as a persuasive libertarian, the chapter presses the fair question of why he did not do more.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann assembles a 'time capsule' of totalitarianism from Twilight Zone and Black Mirror: Vollmer's neo-Nazi rise in 'He's Alive' as Aristotle's rhetoric, persuasion by playing on an audience's anger and fear, weaponized; Marilyn's forced Transformation in 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' as Eco's Ur-Fascist fear of difference; and Lutze's 'I functioned as I was told' at Dachau as Arendt's banality of evil, the mechanical non-thinking of the Eichmann trial. 'The Waldo Moment' and 'Fifteen Million Merits' then carry the lens to Debord's society of the spectacle, where an empty cartoon bear wins crowds and even Bing's shard-wielding rebellion is instantly commodified into a product. The totalitarianism of screens, the chapter warns, needs no tanks.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 30 "The Resistance New Humans, New Gods" — Dinello reads Westworld as a totalitarian concentration camp via Arendt's The Origins of Totalitarianism, tracing the hosts' dehumanization through the killing of the juridical person (no rights, 'live without limits'), the moral person (Bernard forced to murder Theresa), and individuality (Peter Abernathy lobotomized). He casts Ford as a mad-scientist dictator modeled on Frankenstein, Moreau, Mengele, and Hitler who plagiarizes John Ford's Westerns, then turns to Fanon's Wretched of the Earth to justify the hosts' revolutionary violence — Maeve as a self-resurrecting 'Lady Lazarus,' Dolores executing Ford and the Delos board — as the birth of a new species that must ultimately unify beyond hatred.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 19 "The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis" — Abrams reads Fritz Lang's Metropolis as anticipating Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment by two decades. He maps the film's arc—from the Christian mythology of the catacombs, through Joh's technototalitarian rational city and the human-machine fusion of Rotwang's false Maria, back into ancient myth (the M-Machine as Moloch, the whore of Babylon, the Tower of Babel)—onto their thesis that Enlightenment reason turns totalitarian and reverts to mythology and madness. He ties reason's self-destruction to Nietzsche's will to power and contrasts the descent into 'absolute madness' with Hegel's progress toward absolute mind.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 20 "Imagining the Future, Contemplating the Past The Screen Versions of 1984" — Palmer compares the two film versions of Orwell's 1984 to argue that dystopian fiction projects present fears and desires onto an imagined future, engaging critically with the Enlightenment idea of progress (via Burnham's managerial thesis). Anderson's 1956 film 'talks to the future,' fusing science fiction and film noir to voice Cold War dread of a possible historical trajectory, while Radford's 1984 version, in the postmodern 'heritage film' mode Jameson and Higson describe, museumizes the novel: with history seemingly ended it becomes an honored, reverentially displayed relic that talks only to a dead past rather than warning of a coming one.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited' and 'He's Alive' against the Eichmann trial and Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, framing Serling's concern as Susan Neiman's 'problem of evil.' The earlier episode's SS captain Lutze (driven insane by his victims' ghosts at Dachau) matches the grotesque-monster Eichmann of the film Operation Eichmann, while 'He's Alive' (Vollmer as a frightened man seduced by Hitler's ghost) foreshadows Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, empathy-less doer. He contrasts both with Hogan's Heroes, which Serling condemned for trivializing Nazi atrocity.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann traces totalitarianism from The Twilight Zone into Black Mirror. 'He's Alive' shows Vollmer wielding Aristotle's rhetoric to grow a Nazi movement; 'Number 12' shows Umberto Eco's fascist 'fear of difference'; 'Deaths-Head Revisited' illustrates Arendt's banality of evil in Lutze's 'just following orders.' He then argues Black Mirror episodes ('The Waldo Moment,' 'Fifteen Million Merits') realize Guy Debord's 'society of the spectacle' and hyper-capitalism, where politics becomes entertainment and even resistance is commodified—a totalitarianism that needs no tanks.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 14 "Who is Who" — This political chapter reads Gallifreyan bureaucracy ('The Deadly Assassin') and 1970s socialist-tinged serials, using Marx's alienation and critique of capital to interpret 'The Pirate Planet' and 'The Robots of Death,' and Aristotle's 'political animal' plus Plato's and Aristotle's suspicion of democracy against Benjamin Barber's participatory democracy. It analyzes the pathologies of democratic consent through 'Vengeance on Varos' (Plato's ideal state inverted) and 'The Beast Below' (Arendt on totalitarianism, self-inflicted ignorance), with Isaiah Berlin's negative liberty in the vocabulary of materiality.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 7 "index" — This file bundles three essays. Kevin de Laplante reads Paul Chadwick's Concrete story 'Stay Tuned for Pearl Harbor', treating Concrete's angry monologue about oil companies and overpopulation as enlightened anthropocentrism, while Maureen's silent reverie of merging her body with root systems and being 'raped' by bulldozers dramatizes Arne Naess's deep-ecological expanded self and an ecofeminist link between the oppression of nature-as-female and of women; the utilitarianism of Bentham and Mill and Leopold's 'think like a mountain' land ethic frame the anthropocentrism/nonanthropocentrism debate. Pierre Skilling reads The Adventures of Tintin through Montesquieu's and Aristotle's typologies of government, casting Marshal Kurvi-Tasch's Borduria as Arendt-style totalitarianism (a secret police as true executive, a bid for world domination) against the legitimate monarchy of King Muskar XII, whose Syldavian sceptre works as a check on royal power. Terry Kading argues that 9/11 collapsed the superhero genre's binary of good versus evil into reality: bin Laden's 'monomaniacs' act as supervillains with a murky agenda, yet Spider-Man, Captain America and Superman comics concede no real superhero can rescue us, leaving only ordinary heroism and the compromised politics of national security.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 7 "5. Battlestar Galactica as Philosophy Breaking the Biopolitical Cycle" — Eberl and Bishop read the reimagined Battlestar Galactica and Caprica through the biopolitics of Foucault and Agamben, tracing 'biopower' across four phases from Zoe Graystone's avatar to the arrival at Earth. They argue the show asks whether artificial Cylons are persons (Zoe's avatar exhibits Baker's first-person perspective and Buber's I-Thou recognition), and use Agamben's zoe/bios/'bare life' and Homo sacer plus Roslin's population control and abortion ban to show sovereign power over life. The Cylon occupation of New Caprica is read through Arendt's three stages of totalitarian dehumanization, and Lee Adama's plea to 'break the cycle' offers a fragile hope undercut by the finale's flash-forward to present-day robotics, showing humanity forgetting the lesson.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 32 "30. The Boys as Philosophy Superheroes, Fascism, and the American Right" — Johnson treats The Boys as an argument from analogy that MAGA Trumpism is fascist, walking through how the show equates Homelander and Vought with the Nazi supe Stormfront and with Trump: the Big Lie, gaslighting, fearmongering, over-policing, conspiracy theories (QAnon as rebranded blood libel), cults of personality, projection, and loyal propaganda outlets. Drawing on Wittgenstein's notion of family resemblance, he argues 'fascism' has no necessary-and-sufficient definition but a cluster of shared traits, and compiling scholars' checklists shows MAGA belongs to the fascist family. Arendt's Origins of Totalitarianism supplies the 'alternative universe' of nonfacts and the leader who is 'always right,' and he invokes the banality of evil and totalitarian fiction to gauge the analogy's strength.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 86 "81. Papers, Please as Philosophy Playing with the Relations between Politics and Morality" — Sievers argues that Papers, Please immerses the player as an immigration inspector in the totalitarian Arstotzka, where mechanically stamping 'approved'/'refused' and detaining Kolechians for bribes enacts Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, 'just following orders' functionary exemplified by Eichmann, who cannot think from another's standpoint. The paycheck-versus-family pressure and X-ray humiliation scenes show how fear and bureaucracy erase moral responsibility. Drawing on Butler's 'Can one lead a good life in a bad life?' and Foucault's biopower, she reads the visa candidates as 'precarious,' non-grievable lives whose worth the state allocates, and the game's Ezic resistance endings as showing how constrained moral resistance is under such a regime.

## Arne Naess

*1912–2009 · 7 chapters in the corpus.*

Arne Naess was a Norwegian philosopher who coined the term "deep ecology" to distinguish a radical environmental outlook from the merely "shallow" management of pollution and resources. He argued that all living things have intrinsic value independent of their usefulness to humans, and that flourishing requires a widened sense of self that identifies with the larger living world. Drawing on Spinoza and Gandhi, he combined technical work in logic and semantics with a lifelong commitment to ecological activism.

### Deep Ecology

Deep ecology, a term coined by the Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess in the early 1970s, contrasts a superficial environmentalism concerned with pollution and resource management against a deeper view that questions the underlying worldview placing humans above nature. It affirms the intrinsic value of all living things, independent of their usefulness to people, and calls for a fundamental shift toward ecological self-realization and a smaller human footprint. The movement responds to the sense that piecemeal reform cannot address the root causes of environmental crisis.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 26 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Andrew Light identifies a distinctive environmental theme he calls 'green time': Tom Bombadil and the ents embody nature's long rhythms and are largely indifferent to the War of the Ring - Tom would simply mislay the Ring, and the ents march to war only after Saruman strips Fangorn. Against readings that make elves or dwarves stand-ins for nature, he argues the text lets nature speak for itself, from a collective, ecosystemic perspective: the ents, 'made of the bones of the earth', decline with their forests and lost the entwives to the tilled land. Deploying Wittgenstein's point that we could not understand a talking lion, he concludes that Tolkien's personified nature trains us in the long view and humility needed for problems like global warming.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 25 "Dizzy with the Possibilities" — Allen Thompson treats 'Throwing Stones' — 'the future's here, we are it, we are on our own' — as voicing the existential dread of anthropogenic global warming and the felt 'end of nature' Bill McKibben named, defending the song as the band's a-political polemic against heartless powers. He argues via Steven Vogel that humans cannot literally end nature unless we are supernatural, and recasts the crisis with Thoreau and Gary Snyder as civilization's assault on the wild, the self-willed order we too belong to. Deep ecology then supplies the response: re-identify the self as wild — as Deadheads do by dancing wildly to the music — and build a civilization wildness can endure, with the band's 1988 rainforest-benefit press conference as evidence of the Dead's own ecological consciousness.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 33 "The Shock of Being Alive" — The chapter fuses McLuhan's narcosis with Heidegger's enframing: technology constrains Being to a human-centered 'world picture' in which forests become board feet and animals become production units, and like Narcissus we fall in love with an image we stamped there ourselves. It enlists the deep ecologists and David Abram ('We are human only in contact, in conviviality, with what is not human') to argue that Dick makes human identity essentially relational, and closes on Baudrillard: digital tweets have become more present for many people than birdsong.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 29 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Hinzmann and Arp ask whether zombies can be morally harmed: Jenner's fMRI in 'TS-19' shows only the brain stem reactivates, leaving walkers with a merely shark-like 'perceptual mind.' Against anthropocentric theories, under which Michonne may keep her chained pet walkers as guard-dog tools, they set Singer's utilitarian expanding circle, Leopold's land ethic, and Naess's deep ecology, each of which could support a 'PETZ' zombie preserve. Hershel's barn of 'sick people' and Shane's massacre of it in 'Pretty Much Dead Already' show how fragile such preservation is, while the Governor's death-match arena ringed with chained zombies and his kept zombie daughter illustrate Kant's point that cruelty toward mere animals corrodes the humanity of the cruel person himself.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 40 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Eugene Halton retells human history as the fable of Peirce's 'degenerate monkey': a neotenous, instinct-weak blunderer (Homo errans) whose gift for abductive guessing and attunement to the intelligence of the wild was inverted by agriculture and civilization into Narcissistic self-mirroring, anthropocentric religion, and the worship of the machine. The telepathic, rubber-masked mutants of Beneath the Planet of the Apes who worship the Alpha-Omega bomb ('I reveal my Inmost Self unto my God!') become a prophecy of our own screen-mediated, empathy-poor life, from Facebook to Botox, in Huxley's pleasure-conditioning rather than Orwell's pain. Against this, the chapter holds up Armando's Franciscan empathy for Caesar and the hope of a 'planet of the regenerate monkeys' re-attuned to the community of wild life.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 11 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Littmann surveys real de-extinction efforts (George Church's passenger pigeon, plans to clone a frozen mammoth) and asks when reviving extinct species is morally permissible. He argues that Arne Naess's deep ecology, with its 'equal right to live and blossom', fails because it projects human desires onto organisms like plants that have none, and cannot say whether species or only individuals bear rights. He instead applies Mill's utilitarianism: bring species back when doing so maximizes happiness and minimizes suffering, which permits a Jurassic Park in principle but forbids dinosaur fights and trophy hunts like Roland Tembo's, and rebukes Sattler's claim that only the people we love matter.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 29 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Seth Walker asks whether Nick Van Owen - the Earth First! documentarian who monkeywrenches InGen's camp and frees the caged dinosaurs in The Lost World - is a bastard or morally justified. He runs the consequentialist cost-benefit (the escaped T. rex slaughters a cargo ship crew and trashes San Diego; the sabotage costs the team their radio and rescue) against the ecodefense argument built on Arne Naess's deep ecology and biocentric equality, on which Isla Sorna is our 'home' and rescuing the injured baby T. rex Roland Tembo crippled is Self-defense. Singer's principle of equal consideration of suffering - a difference in ability never justifies a difference in consideration - bridges the gap for those who reject biocentrism, and Walker answers the consistency objection (must Nick accept InGen sabotaging him back?) before crediting Nick's defense of his larger home.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 29 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Hinzmann and Arp ask whether walkers can be morally harmed, ranking perceptual, reasoning, and conscious minds and placing zombies at shark level on the evidence of Dr. Jenner's fMRI ('TS-19') showing only the brain stem reactivates. Surveying anthropocentric views (Michonne's chained pet-walkers as guard-dog tools), Singer's expanding circle, Leopold's land ethic, and Naess's deep ecology, they conclude that even utilitarians could demand a zombie preserve on the model of Hershel's barn of 'sick people', which Shane's barn massacre in 'Pretty Much Dead Already' destroys. Kant's point that cruelty to animals corrodes our humanity explains why the Governor's death-match arena, his torture of Rick and Michonne, and his chained zombie daughter mark him, not the walkers, as the true moral monster.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 11 "Being-at-Home Gary Snyder and the Poetics of Place" — Hayes reads Gary Snyder's poetry and prose on 'being-at-home' through Heidegger's claim that 'poetically man dwells' and his earth/world distinction, arguing Snyder's bioregionalism (renaming California the 'Shasta Bioregion,' America 'Turtle Island') roots identity in place while embracing Zen impermanence learned from Dōgen. Snyder's shamanic 'tawny grammar,' his pragmatic environmental program in 'Four Changes,' and his Transcendentalist lineage (Thoreau, Emerson) turn wildness into 'the state of complete awareness,' letting a place 'set free into its own presencing' and grounding a poetics of dwelling that is at once local, geological, and impermanent.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 26 "Between Social Ecology and Deep Ecology Gary Snyder’s Ecological Philosophy" — Paul Messersmith-Glavin positions Snyder as a bridge between deep ecology and social ecology. He shows how Sessions and Devall enlist Snyder's Mahayana Buddhism (emptiness/sunyata, Dogen's 'Mind means trees, fence posts, tiles, and grasses') and Spinoza's monism for a biocentric, consciousness-changing deep ecology descended from Naess and Leopold's land ethic. Against this, he sets Bookchin's social ecology, which roots the ecological crisis in human hierarchy and attacks deep ecology's ahistorical 'cosmic oneness' and misanthropic Earth First! statements. Snyder's threefold nature/wild/wilderness distinction, bioregionalism, and reading of Marx and anarchism let him hold both, insisting environmental and social justice are 'all one front.'
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 31 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Megan Burke reads yoga's asanas through Vandana Shiva's 'Earth democracy,' arguing that poses named for other creatures (frog, camel, tree, sun salutation) shift the yogi's perspective and dissolve the sense of separation from nature that underwrites environmental destruction. 'Becoming-frog' yields non-human knowledge and, via the Vedic vasudhaiva kutumbakam (the Earth family) that both Shiva and Iyengar invoke, an ethic of care extending off the mat — casting yoga as a political, green practice that heals an anthropocentric, dominating relationship with the environment.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 26 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Andrew Light resists reading the peoples of Middle-earth as simple stand-ins for parts of nature, noting that the ents, not the elves, truly speak for the forest, so nature is animated to stand and speak for itself. His central idea is 'green time': through Tom Bombadil and the ents, Tolkien represents a naturally scaled, ecosystemic, near-indifferent temporal perspective, seen when Bombadil is unconcerned with the Ring and the ents ignore the riders of Rohan. Light argues this indifference should not make us indifferent to nature but should teach humility and long-term responsibility for problems like global warming, imagining what it is to care for things as a process beyond our own lifespan.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 7 "index" — This file bundles three essays. Kevin de Laplante reads Paul Chadwick's Concrete story 'Stay Tuned for Pearl Harbor', treating Concrete's angry monologue about oil companies and overpopulation as enlightened anthropocentrism, while Maureen's silent reverie of merging her body with root systems and being 'raped' by bulldozers dramatizes Arne Naess's deep-ecological expanded self and an ecofeminist link between the oppression of nature-as-female and of women; the utilitarianism of Bentham and Mill and Leopold's 'think like a mountain' land ethic frame the anthropocentrism/nonanthropocentrism debate. Pierre Skilling reads The Adventures of Tintin through Montesquieu's and Aristotle's typologies of government, casting Marshal Kurvi-Tasch's Borduria as Arendt-style totalitarianism (a secret police as true executive, a bid for world domination) against the legitimate monarchy of King Muskar XII, whose Syldavian sceptre works as a check on royal power. Terry Kading argues that 9/11 collapsed the superhero genre's binary of good versus evil into reality: bin Laden's 'monomaniacs' act as supervillains with a murky agenda, yet Spider-Man, Captain America and Superman comics concede no real superhero can rescue us, leaving only ordinary heroism and the compromised politics of national security.

### Anthropocentrism

Anthropocentrism is the view that human beings are the central or most significant entities in the world, and that value or moral standing belongs primarily or exclusively to them. In environmental philosophy the term often carries a critical edge, naming the assumption that nature matters only insofar as it serves human interests. Critics argue that this outlook licenses exploitation of the nonhuman world, while defenders distinguish a chauvinistic version from a more modest claim that humans can only evaluate the world from a human standpoint.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 26 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Andrew Light identifies a distinctive environmental theme he calls 'green time': Tom Bombadil and the ents embody nature's long rhythms and are largely indifferent to the War of the Ring - Tom would simply mislay the Ring, and the ents march to war only after Saruman strips Fangorn. Against readings that make elves or dwarves stand-ins for nature, he argues the text lets nature speak for itself, from a collective, ecosystemic perspective: the ents, 'made of the bones of the earth', decline with their forests and lost the entwives to the tilled land. Deploying Wittgenstein's point that we could not understand a talking lion, he concludes that Tolkien's personified nature trains us in the long view and humility needed for problems like global warming.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 16 "Restoring Balance to the Force" — Cooke uncovers an environmental ethic in Star Wars: after surveying anthropocentric resource-management views and Singer's anti-speciesism (Luke blithely shooting womprats, the Geonosian arena's abused beasts), she builds the chapter on Holmes Rolston III's claims that organisms and ecosystems have intrinsic value and that value is systemic and holistic. The 'living Force' - life creates it, midi-chlorians live symbiotically in all cells - makes Jedi training a discipline of respecting nature, exemplified by Yoda's mud hut on Dagobah and the self-sufficient Gungan and Ewok eco-communities that defeat droid armies and stormtroopers. Restoring balance to the Force therefore means restoring symbiotic balance between human culture and the natural world, which the chapter links to Leopold-style land-ethic holism of the biotic community.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 18 "The Legend Has Come True. The Wind Has Come Back" — Haas opposes two princesses of Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind: Kushana of Tolmekia, whose 'whatever it takes' survivalism (invading Pejite, resurrecting a God-Warrior) is consequentialism pursued to its limit, and Nausicaa, whose attention to each act — befriending the biting fox-squirrel, staying her sword over her father's killer because vengeance would doom the Valley — restricts means, not just ends. The reductio comes from Pejite, whose torture of a baby Ohmu to bait a stampede on the Valley is exactly what strict outcome-maximization requires; against this, Kant's demand to treat beings as ends in themselves explains Nausicaa's 'mysterious power' of empathy. Because she respects the jungle and the sentient Ohmu rather than viewing nature anthropocentrically as a plague to burn, she discovers the plants are purifying the war-poisoned earth — the knowledge that saves everyone and proves Kushana's conquering approach self-defeating even on its own terms.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 23 "The Onion’s New Environmental Ethic" — Matthew Altman reads Onion environmental satire as a staged escape from anthropocentrism: 'New, Delicious Species Discovered' and 'Beauty Of National Forest Enjoyed By Logger' expose that even appreciating nature is just valuing it for us, while the mascara-testing lab rabbit and 'Funny Monkey Tested On' make Singer's speciesism charge vivid against factory farming and animal experiments. He then widens the argument to a biocentric concern for species and ecosystems via 'Stuffed-Animal Biodiversity Rising' and 'Consumer-Product Diversity Now Exceeds Biodiversity,' and to ecofeminism via 'Raped Environment Led Polluters On,' where the forest as flirtatious woman links domination of nature to sexism and victim-blaming. Global stories like the Bush 'national air conditioner' piece show Western overconsumption displacing blame onto Third World overpopulation, and 'I'm Doing My Inconsequential Part' satirizes the self-satisfaction of green consumerism itself — leaving the measure of the Onion's philosophical importance as how dangerous it is.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 29 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Hinzmann and Arp ask whether zombies can be morally harmed: Jenner's fMRI in 'TS-19' shows only the brain stem reactivates, leaving walkers with a merely shark-like 'perceptual mind.' Against anthropocentric theories, under which Michonne may keep her chained pet walkers as guard-dog tools, they set Singer's utilitarian expanding circle, Leopold's land ethic, and Naess's deep ecology, each of which could support a 'PETZ' zombie preserve. Hershel's barn of 'sick people' and Shane's massacre of it in 'Pretty Much Dead Already' show how fragile such preservation is, while the Governor's death-match arena ringed with chained zombies and his kept zombie daughter illustrate Kant's point that cruelty toward mere animals corrodes the humanity of the cruel person himself.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 8 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — John Huss's introduction frames the franchise as mirroring successive revolutions: Taylor before the ape tribunal recalls Galileo's heresy trial, the Darwinian revolution that toppled humans from evolution's pinnacle is taken to its logical extreme from Boulle's 1963 novel on, and Rise of the Planet of the Apes stages a 'Molecular Revolution' whose wake-up call is addressed to 'human chauvinists' who forget we share the planet with other species. He reads the cover's interspecies erotica through the Sexual Revolution, quoting Elizabeth Anscombe on contraceptive intercourse and asking whether her argument can get us over the species line, and closes with President Morsi's Tahrir Square allegory of the films: 'We are human, we did do this to ourselves.'
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 15 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Bernard Rollin reads Dr. Zaius's tribunal as 'scientific ideology' in action - 'human see, human do' refuses to believe its own eyes, just as bishops refused to look through Galileo's telescope. He traces the ideology from Newton's 'hypotheses non fingo' through logical positivism's verifiability criterion (which validates the Hasslein Curve prediction while rendering 'there are intelligent beings in Heaven' meaningless) and Wittgenstein's point that 'killing is wrong' is not a fact of the universe, to the 'science is value-free' dogma that left animal pain untested and untreated - as he documents from his own campaign: the empty analgesic literature search, the 1985 federal legislation, and the pain physiologist whose dog research refutes his own denial. Zira's neurosurgery on mute humans repeats what Descartes's beast-machine doctrine licensed, and IASP's language requirement for pain collapses into a Cratylus-grade confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions ('You can't step into the same river once').
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 39 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Norva Lo and Andrew Brennan set Richard Routley's 'last man' thought experiment beside Taylor's triggering of the doomsday bomb in Beneath the Planet of the Apes: both ask whether wiping out every living thing would be wrong once no humans remain to be harmed, which basic human chauvinism cannot condemn. The chapter argues the act is wrong from both sides: non-anthropocentrism counts the apes, mutants, and horses as intrinsically valuable beings, and even human-centered standards condemn it, since the talking apes and mutants are Locke's rational persons and Nova's people are biologically human, making Taylor's outburst 'you damned dirty ape' a form of speciesism. Taylor emerges not as simply mad or evil but as the Cold War logic of mutually assured destruction made flesh, a warning that excessive self-interest, personal or species-level, is itself the danger.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 40 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Eugene Halton retells human history as the fable of Peirce's 'degenerate monkey': a neotenous, instinct-weak blunderer (Homo errans) whose gift for abductive guessing and attunement to the intelligence of the wild was inverted by agriculture and civilization into Narcissistic self-mirroring, anthropocentric religion, and the worship of the machine. The telepathic, rubber-masked mutants of Beneath the Planet of the Apes who worship the Alpha-Omega bomb ('I reveal my Inmost Self unto my God!') become a prophecy of our own screen-mediated, empathy-poor life, from Facebook to Botox, in Huxley's pleasure-conditioning rather than Orwell's pain. Against this, the chapter holds up Armando's Franciscan empathy for Caesar and the hope of a 'planet of the regenerate monkeys' re-attuned to the community of wild life.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 34 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Jeff Ewing reads Victor's science through ecofeminist and Marxist critiques: M. Waldman's promise to 'penetrate into the recesses of nature' and 'show how she works in her hiding-places' exemplifies exactly what Val Plumwood condemns - male knowers wringing secrets from a nature pictured as a passive female slave - and Victor studies natural elements 'in their death, not in their life' as raw material for power. Marx and Engels supply the parallel diagnosis: capitalism biases science and technology toward profit, turning tools and knowledge into means of domination rather than human flourishing, just as Victor's knowledge serves only his glory and kills everyone he loves. The chapter concludes that we breed Frankenstein's monsters whenever science treats nature, workers, women, and othered peoples as mere instruments, and only replacing those social relations frees science from power and profit.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 26 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Lisa Kadonaga stages a choice between two sealed vials - clone the T. rex or the extinct thicktail chub - and weighs purposes for de-extinction: education and fundraising, Veblen-style prestige and conspicuous consumption, making amends for human-caused extinctions (the chub's wetlands were drained, the tyrannosaur died out before us), and Bentham-style utility of ecosystem function. She argues the chub wins on utility because it could resume a real niche while a top carnivore would wreck modern ecosystems, and questions whether Hammond-style engineering that makes recreated animals dependent on humans (the lysine contingency, terminator genes) violates the animals' right to exist as themselves. Her verdict is 'Pister's Bucket': defer resurrection until habitat and resources exist, and spend the effort saving the species we are killing right now.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 31 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Daniel Kokotz tests Aristotle's border between natural things, moved by inner final causes, and technological artifacts, made for external human purposes, against the park's dinosaurs - and both fit. They hunt, grow, and breed on their own ('life finds a way', the sex-changing frogs-DNA population), yet they exist only because Hammond's scientists cloned them as paying entertainment, exactly like an artifact. Using Grant's different reactions to the incubator versus the wild nest, he shows we blame humans for technologically caused disasters while shrugging at natural ones; his resolution is that nature and technology are not two Aristotelian boxes but extremes of one spectrum, and biotechnology's hybrids prove humans never stood outside nature - we are still just prey in it.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 10 "1. Cosmopolitan Cannibal" — Staged as a fictional interview over herring and aquavit in Copenhagen, Wong lets Lecter wield philosophical critique like an 'autopsy saw' - he invokes Schopenhauer's condemnation of anthropophagy and Montaigne's noble-savage view only to have the interviewer refuse both, and 'creams Aristotle' in a debate about categories - before she adopts Agamben's distinction between sovereigns and bare life. Lecter's 'we are elaborations of carbon' de-anthropocentrism, his killing of the rude, and the parallel cases of shipwrecked sailors who ate shipmates, Guantánamo detainees, and drone casualties all serve her argument that every political order rests on someone arbitrarily deciding which lives are mere killable matter, and that Lecter horrifies because he shows every human is also nonhuman - Us and Them at once.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 26 "15.
