- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 12 "Our First Gaze into the Black Mirror" — Collins and Boesch use Prime Minister Callow's coerced live sex act with a pig in The National Anthem to weigh conflicting moral obligations: the public's initial 72% Kantian refusal flips to an 86% utilitarian capitulation after the kidnapper's finger video, and the withheld revelation that Susannah was released half an hour early undermines any consequentialist justification of the act. A virtue-theory reading faults Callow's character for faking the rescue video and putting self-interest first, and the UKN media's Kantian compliance collapses once ratings are at stake. The closing section applies Martha Nussbaum's theory of disgust (contamination transferring disgust from blood and vomit to the spectacle-watchers themselves) to argue the episode's graphic imagery functions as a moral emotion condemning the audience's own obsession with spectacle.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 23 "The Bill Comes Due" — The chapter uses Michael Walzer's Problem of Dirty Hands to weigh the Ancient One's secret lifelong use of forbidden dark magic against Kaecilius's summoning of Dormammu, arguing that only she faces a genuine dirty-hands dilemma because her end (defending Earth) is good while his is not. It asks why dark magic is forbidden at all and answers with rule-utilitarian reasoning that has taken on a deontological life of its own, then invokes Kant's murderer-at-the-door essay to argue, with Mordo's 'the bill comes due,' that whoever does wrong for good ends bears responsibility for the downstream consequences—and that Strange's willingness to break Kamar-Taj's rules while accepting the cost is what makes him a hero.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 28 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann defends Graff and Ender as act utilitarians in Mill's own image, noting that Mill's father raised him in calculated isolation and brutal study as a tool to reform humanity just as Graff engineers Ender, so both acted rightly given the stakes even though Mill's harm principle and his regard for animal suffering also condemn the xenocide itself. Against Crime and Punishment and 'The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas,' he argues Ender's Game shows consequences can genuinely justify breaking any moral rule when human extinction is on the table.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 20 "What Promotes Moral Behavior" — Matthew D. Atkinson and Darin DeWitt use the Canterbury's ignored mayday in 'Dulcinea' — Captain McDowell's 'let the good God Darwin sort it out' versus Ade Nygaard's appeal to law, karma, and obligation — to ask what binds people when no central authority enforces rules. Through Michael Walzer's just war theory they read the Earth-Mars war: moral language is not 'cheap talk' (even Errinwright must dress aggression as peace and manipulates Reverend Volovodov's words), aggression and imminence govern when to fight, and five 'how to fight' principles — noncombatant immunity on Eros and Ganymede, POW rights for the Martian marines on the Kittur Chennamma, leaders' rather than soldiers' responsibility (Fred Johnson's defection after Anderson Station), proportionality in Errinwright's 'a base for a base' Deimos strike, and the rejection of ends-justify-means utilitarianism — discipline even Holden and Amos as they reflect on free will and culpability. The chapter concludes The Expanse is optimistic: human decency survives even in the anarchic Belt because characters keep reflecting on what their obligations to one another are.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 12 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Don Fallis starts from Joffrey's lie about Arya and the butcher boy Mycah - which costs Mycah's life and Sansa's direwolf Lady's - to dissect lying versus other deception in Westeros: Catelyn accusing Tyrion is not lying because she believes it, Ned's coerced confession at the Great Sept is a real lie (Austin's duress excuse fails, as Thomas More's counterexample shows), and Ned's silence about Joffrey's parentage before the dying Robert is deception by withholding that he himself mistakes for lying. He asks whether lying is morally worse than misleading - Kant and Chisholm say yes, Williams and Scanlon no - testing breach of invited trust (Mirri Maz Duur's 'only death may pay for life'), responsibility-shifting to the audience ('That was a lie you told yourself'), and preserved autonomy (Kant's Groundwork, Mill's On Liberty). Finally, is it worse to lie to a king? Consequentialism explains the danger of misleading the powerful, oaths of fealty and divine right suggest a special duty, but Locke's demolition of divine right (seconded by Monty Python) leaves only the punishment, not the wrongdoing, greater.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 18 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Albert Anglberger and Alexander Hieke contrast Ned, the virtue ethicist's genuinely good man, with Cersei, a 'minimally extended' egoistic consequentialist whose only morally relevant subjects are herself and her children. Aristotle's apparatus does the work: phronesis lets Ned rank his daughters' lives above honesty when he confesses falsely ('the lies we tell for love'), his 'you're too fat for your armor' quip shows the golden mean among competing virtues, and Cersei's unbalanced maternal love is excess, hence not a virtue. They then unsettle moral judgment itself: utilitarianism would license the Slaver's Bay slaveholders, virtue ethics lacks action rules and cross-cultural agreement (charity is no Dothraki virtue), and Martin's POV narration gives direct access to Ned's inner life but only Varys's and Littlefinger's unreliable reports about Cersei - so our verdicts on her, like real-life judgments of others, rest on shaky evidence.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 10 "1 Acting Without Thinking The Sagacity of Indiana Jones" — Justin Kitchen rebuts the consequentialist charge (voiced by Big Bang Theory's Amy Farrah Fowler) that Indy plays no role in Raiders' outcome — the Nazis would have opened the Ark and died anyway — by shifting to virtue ethics: Indy's goodness lies in his character, not his consequences. His spontaneous 'I'm making this up as I go' decisions are read as Stoic sage-like action flowing from the two-stage moral education depicted in The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, from Krishnamurti's lesson on death to Epictetus's 'winter training' in practice. The cardinal virtues as knowledge explain his instinctive courage (lifeboat, lead-lined refrigerator) and temperance (running past treasure), while his snake panic, his flash of greed at the Grail in Crusade, and his strained bonds with Marion and his father show he is a hero approaching but not yet attaining sagehood.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 11 "2 Does It Always Belong in a Museum" — Edwardo Pérez reconstructs the reasoning behind Indy's unargued mantra 'It belongs in a museum' via Bentham's principle of utility: museums maximize happiness because scholars and the public can study and enjoy artifacts for generations, unlike private collectors like Panama Hat. The same calculus explains his rule-breaking — he leaves the Mayapore Sankara Stone with the villagers ('It'd be another rock collecting dust' in a museum) because a flourishing village outweighs his fortune and glory, and he concedes the government's Area 51 warehouse may have been the utility-maximizing choice for the Ark after what it did to Belloq and Toht. Indy's apparent inconsistencies thus dissolve into case-by-case consequence weighing.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 32 "19 Meddling with (Almost) Incomprehensible Powers" — Argues that archaeology can never escape politics: Nazi relic plunder for the planned Führermuseum, French removals at Angkor Wat, the UNESCO 1970 convention, and Zahi Hawass's cultural nationalism versus James Cuno's 'encyclopedic museums' all determine what Indy — or any archaeologist — may legitimately do. Measured against Alison Wylie's stewardship principle, Indy emerges as a 'loot-and-scoot' adventurer whose 'it belongs in a museum' cosmopolitanism sits uneasily with national patrimony claims, and the chapter weighs backward-looking title-based versus forward-looking value-based approaches to the Golden Idol, the Sankara Stone he returns, and the Cross of Coronado. It closes by asking whether the living can wrong the dead and vanished cultures, and whether the government 'top men' warehousing the Ark were right after all.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 10 "So, That’s It No Solution" — Rieder argues Iron Man is the one 'realistic' superhero: nothing about him requires a different world, only incremental nanotech advances — precision engineering, miniaturized computing, and carbon nanotubes a hundred times stronger than steel — already pursued at MIT's Institute for Soldier Nanotechnologies. He then uses Iron Man as a nanoethics case study, pitting cost-benefit analysis (with David Schmidtz's proviso that it is necessary but not sufficient for right action) against the precautionary principle exemplified by Bill Joy's call for relinquishment, asking whether an Obadiah Stane selling 'Iron Armies' to the highest bidder is a risk we may not take even if it is improbable. He leans precautionary: we may be morally required to forgo the experiment because the world's population never consented to the risk.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 26 "The Office and Philosophy" — Johnson works through the standard objections to affirmative action using Scranton material: Ryan's paralysis before the all-Black management team in 'Traveling Salesmen' shows a single-race workforce is not intrinsically bad, while Michael's Chris Rock routine and his do-it-yourself slur exercise in 'Diversity Day' show that Dunder Mifflin meeting every quota does nothing about racism. A hypothetical about Dwight's grandfather refusing to hire Stanley's grandfather at the beet farm frames the compensation objection, answered by the 'cycle of poverty' account of the present effects of past discrimination. Finally, a fictitious hiring of guard Hank Tate over a better-qualified white candidate - justified, following Nagel, by the consequences of calming branch unrest - sets up the conclusion that education, not racially preferential hiring, would break minority poverty without discrimination, so affirmative action is ultimately unjustified.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 11 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 27 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Defends South Park's anti-paternalism on both consequentialist and deontological grounds. 'Major Boobage' shows the futility of Gerald's cat ban meant to stop kids 'cheesing' — Kenny still gets high and Gerald himself relapses — while 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' shows how the KFC prohibition births a violent black market, with Cartman's $85 snack pushing him into the Colonel's Scarface-style drug war. On the deontological side, Mill's 'over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign', Locke's self-ownership, and Kantian respect for rational agents (via Nozick's inviolability, and the authors' autarchy-versus-autonomy distinction) ground the claim that coercion is wrong even when benevolent: 'Butt Out' has Kyle and Stan tell Rob Reiner that forcing others to quit smoking is fascism, while Big Tobacco's Kevin Harris wins their approval simply by informing and letting people choose.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Applies Aristotle's three friendships to Trek: Ferengi Rules of Acquisition dealings and treaties as utility friendships, Bashir and O'Brien's darts and racquetball as friendship of pleasure, and virtuous friendship as requiring emotion, mutual goodwill, and irreplaceable intrinsic valuing - which emotionless Data fails at with Jenna D'Sora in "In Theory". The core argument, following Badhwar, is that consequentialism is logically and psychologically incompatible with virtuous friendship: Spock's "needs of the many" maxim and Data's "for the greater good" experimentation on Geordi in "Descent, Part II" show friends being treated as sacrificeable instruments, while the Kobayashi Maru cheat shows consequentialist reasoning blessing outcomes over means. Kirk's reversal - "the needs of the one outweigh the needs of the many" in The Search for Spock - and T'Pol's years caring for the amnesiac Archer in "Twilight" exemplify acting out of friendship rather than for any further goal.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 40 "The Last Jedi A New Hope" — Johnson defends The Last Jedi's Luke against the 'you ruined Luke' charge: his pacifism was set up when he threw away his lightsaber before Palpatine in Return of the Jedi, and his call to end the Jedi follows the lesson Hobbes and Locke drew from the English civil wars - since religious matters cannot be settled by reason, only by violence, Jedi and Sith factions fighting for political power yield only bloodshed like the Clone Wars and two Death Stars. Luke also seeks to destroy the Jedi texts out of guilt by association for the Order's failures, and to the end he remains a consequentialist pacifist, defeating Kylo on Crait through a nonviolent Force projection rather than a real duel. Far from betraying the character, this growth into proactive nonviolence - capped by Rey's yellow-bladed, mainly defensive style - makes Luke 'the ultimate Jedi' and the Resistance's new hope.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 24 "13. Time to Choose" — Goldberg and Gavaler read Superman's first-year Action Comics adventures (reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock) as consequentialism on Millian lines, and Batman's Detective Comics year (letting the Joker's victims die while 'the time isn't ripe', the batarang deflected by invisible glass) as a dark, vengeance-based cousin of Kant's duty ethics. Moral luck is the pivot — deontology ignores it, consequentialism is hostage to it — but Superman's powers cancel luck, and in the opening Luthor/Joker two-bomb scenario Superman defuses while Batman chases the villain, so the chapter rules Superman's 'super consequentialism' the superior code.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 25 "14. Who Watches the Justice League" — Judges the two heroes by negative consequentialism (attributed to Hume and Popper): the better hero is the one who best prevents future suffering, including suffering he might cause himself. Superman qualifies because he hands the League—Batman above all—the means to defeat him (as in Injustice) and kills himself with gold kryptonite after executing Mr. Mxyzptlk in 'What Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?', while Hume's reason-is-slave-of-the-passions reading explains the Zod neck-snap in Man of Steel as passion-driven necessity. Batman's countermeasures in 'Tower of Babel' and Justice League: Doom stop every Leaguer except Batman himself ('My failsafe is the Justice League'), an arrogance that loses him this round.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 21 "Notes" — White reconstructs the 'Sacrifice' storyline - Maxwell Lord mind-controlling Superman, telling lasso-bound Wonder Woman 'Kill me,' and her snapping his neck - and asks whether it was right. He argues Wonder Woman reasons as a threshold deontologist: her usual respect for life holds until the certain cost of letting Lord live (he would wield Superman to kill again) crosses the threshold where the consequentialist body-count argument takes over, and she was justified, so she would do it again. The contrast with Batman's refusal to kill the Joker shows his refusal is virtue-ethical self-definition ('I won't become them'), while Diana, regretting the necessity but feeling no remorse, is an Amazon warrior for whom lethal protection of lives is sometimes exactly the job.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 15 "Virtue and Violence Can a Good Football Player Be a Good Person" — Davison defends a 'Violence Principle'—intentionally causing violent harm known to be unnecessary for a greater good is wrong—and applies it to in-the-rules football hits like Jack Tatum on Darryl Stingley and Warren Sapp on Chad Clifton. Against a consequentialist defense of intimidation, he invokes Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, not mere means, arguing players consent to accidental injury but not intentional harm. Citing the Socratic examination of the soul, he warns of moral danger to players who use excessive force and to fans who relish violence for its own sake.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 22 "A True MVP" — Kershnar analyzes what makes a football player valuable, arguing a player's value is his net benefit to his own team measured against a baseline. He compares three models—no-substitute, average/reasonable-substitute, and actual-substitute—using cases like Joe Montana backed by Steve Young and Emmitt Smith behind an all-pro line, and defends the actual-substitute model as the correct measure of value even though it yields counterintuitive results. He connects the account to a broader question of measuring a person's contribution to any organization or to the world.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 15 "Sixth Hole Virtue Ethics From Caddyshack to Better Golf" — McElreath tests three ethical theories against golf intuitions and argues virtue ethics wins. Consequentialism rightly judges a postal carrier's choice to work over golf but wrongly permits Judge Smails in Caddyshack to kick his ball when no bad consequences follow; Kantian ethics correctly condemns Smails's deceptive maxim as non-universalizable but mishandles the play-versus-work case. Virtue ethics, judging acts by what an ideally virtuous person would characteristically do, gets both right via the relevant virtues of justice and honesty, and he then applies benevolence, justice, and tolerance to argue golf should better treat women, minorities, disabled players (Casey Martin's cart), and homosexuals.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 6 "Not the Crime, but the Man Sherlock Holmes and Charles Augustus Milverton" — Rozema examines 'The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton,' in which Holmes burgles a blackmailer's house, feigns an engagement to the maid, and watches Milverton's murder without intervening. He argues that Kantian deontology (too abstract to judge rectification) and consequentialism (paralyzed by unpredictable outcomes) both fail to assess Holmes's acts, whereas Plato and Aristotle's virtue ethics fits: judging the man's character over the isolated act. Citing Plato's 'true falsehood' vs. 'falsehood in words' and Aristotle on voluntary acts and the storm-tossed captain jettisoning cargo, he concludes a virtuous person may rightly do what is normally forbidden against a vicious foe like Milverton.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 11 "Was it Morally Wrong to Kill Off Sherlock Holmes" — Terjesen asks whether Conan Doyle acted immorally in killing Holmes in 'The Final Problem,' framing it through property theory. He runs Locke's labor theory (illustrated via 'The Blue Carbuncle' gem), Proudhon and Marx's critiques, and both consequentialist and Kantian (respect-for-persons) justifications of intellectual property. He argues Conan Doyle's ownership of the iconic Holmes weakened as Paget, Gillette, Rathbone, and Dr. Joseph Bell co-authored the figure, so property rights alone can't justify the killing—but Conan Doyle's authorial dignity plus the narrative fitness of 'The Final Problem' and 'His Last Bow' make the send-off defensible.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 13 "Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization" — Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 9 "The “Big-Little” Film and Philosophy Two Takes on Spielbergian Innocence" — Arms and Riley argue that Spielberg fuses spectacle with intimate 'broken family' drama, then use War of the Worlds, A.I., and Empire of the Sun to press the philosophical problem of special (agent-relative) obligations. They show that Ray's redemption (even murdering Ogilvy to protect Rachel), Gigolo Joe's protection of David, and John Graham's failure all turn on duties to the innocent that consequentialism's agent-neutral, greatest-good calculus cannot accommodate, formalizing the clash as a valid argument against consequentialism. They suggest Spielberg grounds these special obligations in the intrinsic worth of 'the Innocent.'
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 18 "8. Which Brother Is the Good One" — Browning contrasts the brothers' ethics: Dean is a consequentialist who judges hunts by outcomes ('the ends justify the means,' killing werewolf Madison or faith-healer Roy for the greater good), while Sam is a deontologist who treats lying, stealing, and killing as wrong in themselves. Tracking episodes like 'Bloodlust,' 'Croatoan,' and 'Fresh Blood,' he argues the murder-versus-kill distinction and the blurring line between human and monster show Dean's darker consequentialism is better suited to the Hunter's war, though both are driven to do good.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 10 "3. Can It Be Right to Defend the Guilty" — Cook tests whether lawyers may defend the legally and morally guilty against several ethical theories, anchored by Saul's contemplated lie at Lalo Salamanca's bail hearing (knowing Lalo murdered Fred Whalen). Kant's contradiction-in-conception makes lying to the court a perfect duty to refrain from, but Cook shows this looks too rigid via the invented 'Jemma' surgeon case; act and rule consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Hooker) permit honest defenses while diverging on lies and mitigation. He argues Hume's sentimentalist virtue ethics best fits intuition: Saul's bail lie is wrong because motivated by self-interest rather than the procedural justice a virtuous advocate should feel.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 31 "20. Why Is Breaking Skateboarders’ Legs Wrong" — The chapter uses three characters to test three single-value moral theories: Chuck as a Kantian deontologist whose rigid loyalty to the categorical imperative and the 'sacred' law destroys his bond with Jimmy; Jimmy as a Mill-style consequentialist whose ends-justify-means scams (Sandpiper, the squat-cobbler film) let him decide what counts as good outcomes and cost him integrity, invoking Bernard Williams; and Mike as a Scanlonian contractualist who honors even immoral agreements like the Tuco hit. Through cases like the 'murderer at the door,' it argues each theory alone leads people to do wrong, so a moral life must combine outcomes, rules, and contracts.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 26 "15. Morality and Manipulation" — Kahn frames the Foundation series around personal autonomy, using Mill's image of humans as a growing tree rather than a machine 'built after a model' to condemn both coercion and manipulation. He shows Hari Seldon as a paradoxical champion of autonomy who nonetheless deceives his own followers about the fraudulent Encyclopedia Galactica and secretly forecloses their freedom of action via the Seldon Plan and Second Foundation—echoing the Mule's mind-control of Han Pritcher. He reads Salvor Hardin's maxim ('never let your sense of morals prevent you from doing what is right') as consequentialism that maximizes galaxy-wide autonomy, contrasts it with the deontology exemplified by Gaia/Bliss (who refuse to manipulate Trevize) and critics like Toran Darell and Branno, and leaves the reader to judge as Bliss urges Pelorat to think for himself.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as a would-be consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) whose plan to kill millions to end the Cold War exposes utilitarianism's neglect of rights and, via Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ends,' its dependence on an unknowable infinite future. Rorschach poses as a Kantian deontologist ('I shall not compromise') but Loftis shows his hypocrisy, black-and-white dichotomous thinking, and failure to respect persons betray Kant's categorical imperative. Loftis argues neither theory is truly held by either character; both are rationalizations of power, and the comic's real target, captured by 'Who watches the watchmen?', is authoritarianism itself.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 9 "What’s Wrong with Roland" — Greg Littmann asks why the Dark Tower judges Roland morally lacking for his sacrifices (his hawk David, Susan Delgado, letting Jake fall) and defends him on utilitarian grounds, invoking Bentham's greatest-happiness principle. He uses King's world as a series of thought experiments to test whether utilitarianism is too demanding—Susannah quitting the quest, self-sacrifice becoming compulsory, and the required sacrifice of innocents like the newborn Mordred or Jake when all universes hang in the balance. Littmann finds Roland 'innocent' because maximizing good can compel sacrificing innocents, but draws the real-world moral that being convinced you are doing right does not mean no innocents are being harmed.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "Chapter 4 Huckleberry Finn’s Struggle between Sympathy and Moral Principle Reconsidered" — Michael Lyons defends the 'pedestal' of moral principles against Bennett's chapter 16 reading. He accepts that sympathy rightly saved Jim and that Edwards's principled cruelty and Himmler's suppressed sympathy show principles must be revisable, but rejects the stronger claim that sympathy should override conduct while leaving conflicting principles intact. Reconstructing Bennett's argument into 'stronger' and 'adjusted' versions, Lyons argues principles remain the best primary guide once corrected by sympathy, and that Twain shows Huck retaining a natural, humanity-grounded morality even after rejecting society's 'deformed conscience.' He prizes incorruptibility, sticking to correct principles, as the mark of the highest heroism Huck could aspire to.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 25 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Agnafors asks whether free soloing is morally permissible, opening with soloists dropping ice chips into his coffee cup to show soloing is not purely private. He tests Locke's natural rights to life and liberty (concluding no act is truly private since rescues, taxpayers, and grieving families are affected), Aristotle's virtue ethics (worrying that habitual risk-taking forms a reckless character), and Bentham and Mill's consequentialism (Bill's confidence-boosting solo of Nutcracker versus Derek Hersey's fatal fall). He concludes no universal answer exists, offering one rule: the soloist must carefully weigh all these considerations beforehand.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 29 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Naar and Masala defend the 'Secret Underground Internet Seduction Community' by grounding it in Darwinian sexual selection (the peacock's tail, mate value, women prioritizing status and men prioritizing youth/beauty) and an Aristotelian ideal of happiness as excellence: they read the community's aim of becoming a well-rounded seducer as cultivating virtue and social/emotional 'mating intelligence' that yields eudaimonic fulfillment. Against the Kantian objection that seduction training uses women merely as means, they offer a consequentialist and 'deflationist' reply that deception and manipulation already pervade ordinary courtship (makeup, lying about age), so raising one's mate value is morally neutral, and they extend the point to women's active and passive seduction strategies (Cleopatra, groupies).
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 10 "Who is Who" — Titled 'Exterminate!', the chapter analyzes evil in Doctor Who through Augustine's privation theory and Kant's 'radical evil,' distinguishing irrational evil (Light in 'Ghost Light,' the Daleks) from rational 'lesser evil' calculations (the Rani, mad scientists). It reads the Daleks as Nazi-analogue Others bred for racial purity, invokes Arendt's banality of evil and capacity to think for oneself (Rose challenging the ninth Doctor over the lone Dalek and the Delta wave), and cites Kierkegaard on losing oneself when one does evil alone.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 12 "Who is Who" — This chapter tests the Doctor's ethics against consequentialism and Kantian/Nagelian deontology, arguing both fail because his alien longevity and time-travelling relation to consequences resist algorithmic moral judgment ('School Reunion,' 'Attack of the Cybermen'). It proposes instead de Beauvoir's 'ethics of ambiguity' rooted in Romanticism and Sartrean radical freedom and bad faith (the student anecdote; Turlough refusing the Enlightenment diamond), casting the Doctor as a Promethean figure who liberates companions into risky self-perfection.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 11 "9. The Handmaid’s Tale as Philosophy Autonomy and Reproductive Freedom" — Robison-Greene argues that Gilead's core wrong is denying women autonomy, reducing them from Kantian moral agents to moral patients — walking incubators. She uses Frankfurt's theory of personhood (second-order desires and volitions about what we care about) to show how Gilead dismantles a woman's will by restricting first-order options, language, and critical thinking, so Offred's Scrabble tiles and forbidden reading become acts of reclaimed autonomy. She situates the Sons of Jacob's 'feminine function' ideology in Plato's Republic classes, Aristotle's natural slaves and History of Animals, Aquinas's natural-law subordination of women, and Malebranche's brain-fiber claims, contrasting Beauvoir's complicity of women and framing forced reproduction as the deontology-versus-consequentialism clash over whether species survival could ever justify treating women as mere means.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 53 "50. The Cabin in the Woods as Philosophy Cinematic Reflections on Ethical Complexity, Human Nature, and Worthw" — Kowalski argues Whedon and Goddard's The Cabin in the Woods stages a clash between classical utilitarianism and an ethics of care, and cinematically favors the latter. The Facility, sacrificing five campers to placate the Ancient Ones and save humanity, embodies Mill's greatest-happiness reasoning, but its callous celebration while Dana suffers on the dock undercuts that view. When the Director tells Dana she must kill her only remaining friend Marty to save the world, Dana's refusal is defended via Noddings's care ethics and Aristotle's claim that obligations track close personal relationships (special obligations), with Aristotle's Poetics catharsis and Plato's Leontius grounding the film's theory of worthwhile horror: 'people are more important than humanity.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 56 "53. Tarantino as Philosopher Vengeance – Unfettered, Uncensored, but Not Unjustified" — Johnson treats Tarantino's post-2000 filmography as an argument that vengeance is morally permissible when proportionate and directed at the genuinely guilty: Beatrix in Kill Bill, Shosanna in Inglourious Basterds, and Django all get celebrated revenge, while The Hateful Eight is used to distinguish vengeance from retribution and legal versus 'frontier' justice via Nozick's and Bacon's definitions. He rebuts common and historical objections—reading Plato's Gorgias as endorsing due punishment, arguing Spinoza's monism and Hobbes's and Locke's social-contract views do not forbid proportional revenge, and citing Nietzsche and Beauvoir's Eye for an Eye (her refusal to pardon the collaborator Brasillach) to conclude cost-free, proportional revenge can be justified though mercy remains praiseworthy.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 81 "76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain" — Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.

### Emptiness (sunyata)

Emptiness, or sunyata, is the teaching that all things lack any fixed, independent essence and exist only in dependence on causes, conditions, and conceptual designation. It was developed most rigorously by the Indian philosopher Nagarjuna, founder of the Madhyamaka school, who used relentless dialectical arguments to show that positing self-existent entities leads to contradiction. Rather than a claim that nothing exists, emptiness holds that things are real precisely because they are dependently arisen and thus without inherent nature. For Nagarjuna this insight dissolves the grasping and metaphysical confusion that bind beings to suffering.

- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 21 "Analyzing Emptiness" — Paul Gass reads the Dead's hippie milieu (the Beats, the Acid Tests, Buddhist-monk lyricist Peter Monk) as a conduit for Buddhist doctrine, taking the 'Eyes of the World' chorus as an invitation to awaken to Buddha-nature. He explains the Four Noble Truths, karma, and the five aggregates to argue the self is an illusion, using the image of a flame passed between lighters at a Dead show to picture rebirth without a persisting soul. The chapter then presents Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka middle way — emptiness itself must not be clutched as an absolute truth — and reads the 'redeemer... wagon loaded with clay' verse of 'Eyes of the World' as the Mahayana bodhisattva liberating all beings, with emptiness finally discarded like the boat after crossing the river.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 26 "Sudden Enlightenment" — Luke Cuddy and Michael Bruce ask whether Beatrix Kiddo could reach enlightenment, reading Kill Bill's nonlinear plotting as a Buddhist interconnected web of causes: Pai Mei's Five Point Palm technique causes both the coffin escape and Bill's death, and Budd's degraded trailer life is karma catching up. Beatrix grasps the structure of suffering and its cause—she locates it in Bill and the squad and eliminates them—but mistakes that for ending suffering itself, and her declared lack of 'mercy, compassion, and forgiveness' blocks the compassion enlightenment requires, while Bill's 'natural born killer' story contradicts impermanence and no-self. The chapter closes on her bathroom-floor ecstasy as a candidate case of Zen sudden enlightenment, left to the reader to judge by how she would one day treat a vengeful Nikki.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 26 "Mr. Monk Murdered Trudy" — Green argues Monk is an unintentional Bodhisattva whose OCD enacts the Four Bodhisattva Vows: the compulsion to touch lampposts is the first vow's blind desires, his monastic minimalism the Dharma gate, and his crime-solving compassion for a disordered world the third vow, with the Dhammapada's teaching that the untamed mind produces suffering exemplified by Monk and by Harold Krenshaw's rival ordering. Like Vimalakirti feigning illness, or Shawn Spencer in Psych, and like the father in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable, Monk and his writers use skillful deception to awaken viewers to suffering and loving kindness. The title thesis is that Monk cannot solve Trudy's murder because he accepts responsibility for it: by Thich Nhat Hanh's Interbeing there is no absolute self and other, so solving the case requires the Zen 'kill the Buddha' eradication of the self, Monk's nirvana-as-extinction and the end of the series.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 8 "2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma" — Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 34 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Bernard Wills takes the reference to The Cloud of Unknowing in 'The Window' as the key to Cohen's lifelong fascination with apophatic, negative mysticism - God sought beyond every image in a 'naked intent of love,' as in the medieval Cloud, Dionysius, Maimonides, and Kabbalah - against the kataphatic way of affirmation. He reads Recent Songs as an album of exile and the play of union and separation ('Un Canadien Errant,' 'Ballad of the Absent Mare'), where the incarnate Word is 'stuttered' and 'frozen,' a passion without resurrection. Cohen's later Zen turn is thus prefigured: the emptiness of sunyata and the Neo-Platonic descent from and return to the One are positive nothingness - self-overcoming in the service of compassion rather than the black-romantic nihilism of self-annihilation.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 36 "22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy" — Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 17 "8. Ode to Joi" — Steve Bein first tests Joi against Mary Anne Warren's five functionalist personhood criteria — consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness — and finds she passes, which makes Luv's stomping of the emanator a murder. The Buddha's no-self doctrine then denies that anyone, Joi included, is an enduring person: we are bundles of fleeting psychophysical processes, 'like tears in rain', which threatens to let Luv plead that the Luv who killed Joi no longer exists. Nagarjuna's two truths resolve the courtroom problem: ultimately there are no persons, but conventionally 'Luv killed Joi' is perfectly true, and the karma ripples through the whole network.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — De Cruz and De Smedt argue that ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang's training is slow and non-linear, he needs dedicated teachers, and saving the world is a team effort in which Katara leads and Sokka plans. The show's central theme is oneness, voiced by Guru Pathik's 'illusion of separation' ('The Guru') and Huu's banyan-grove tree ('The Swamp'), which the editors trace to Daoist, Huayan Buddhist (Fazang's golden lion), and Indigenous traditions of interdependence. They frame the volume's engagement with genocide, imperialism, ecological destruction, and Ba Sing Se's authoritarian denial as proof that philosophy is needed for human flourishing.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan Muir argues Lost's narrative world, unlike Jane Eyre's, requires its own metaphysics, and that this metaphysics is an order of balanced binary oppositions: Jacob and the Man in Black as twins diverged at birth, the cave scale's light and dark stones that Locke knocks out of balance in 'The Substitute,' science/faith, with characters like Jack converting from one pole into its opposite. The proper model is the yin-yang in motion - the Tao as a balanced ontological flow in which interdependent opposites wax and wane - so that treating the poles as independent is the delusion that threatens the island's order. The finale, where both Jacob and the Man in Black cease to exist and the castaways are freed, enacts the Mahayana Buddhist Middle Way: enlightenment as letting go of rigid oppositions that interdependence double-negates.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 21 "Genius All the Time The Beats, Spontaneous Presence, and Primordial Ground" — Marc Olmsted reads Beat spontaneity through Tantric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, arguing that 'first thought, best thought' and Kerouac's 'Mind is shapely, art is shapely' rest on the view that enlightenment/awareness is already present and need only be recognized. He maps Ginsberg's poetics onto the Tantric terms Ground, Path, and Fruition, tying shamatha-vipashyana practice and the doctrine of anatta (no-self) to the poet catching the first pre-conceptual thought. Ginsberg's Blake visions, his study under Trungpa and Gelek Rinpoche, and Burroughs's cut-up 'homemade yankee tantra' are offered as evidence that Beat composition enacts a Buddhist recognition of primordial, empty, self-existing awareness.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 26 "Between Social Ecology and Deep Ecology Gary Snyder’s Ecological Philosophy" — Paul Messersmith-Glavin positions Snyder as a bridge between deep ecology and social ecology. He shows how Sessions and Devall enlist Snyder's Mahayana Buddhism (emptiness/sunyata, Dogen's 'Mind means trees, fence posts, tiles, and grasses') and Spinoza's monism for a biocentric, consciousness-changing deep ecology descended from Naess and Leopold's land ethic. Against this, he sets Bookchin's social ecology, which roots the ecological crisis in human hierarchy and attacks deep ecology's ahistorical 'cosmic oneness' and misanthropic Earth First! statements. Snyder's threefold nature/wild/wilderness distinction, bioregionalism, and reading of Marx and anarchism let him hold both, insisting environmental and social justice are 'all one front.'
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan S. Muir argues that Lost deliberately withholds its metanarrative so viewers must construct its metaphysics, which he identifies as an order of balanced binary oppositions. Drawing on the spinning Taoist yin-yang, he reads the interdependent, mutually converting poles—Jack from man of science to man of faith, Sawyer from con man to protector—and the light/dark scales in Widmore's painting and the cave (Locke throwing out the white rock) as figures for a Tao whose balance sustains existence. Invoking Derrida's traces and Mahayana Buddhism's Middle Way and emptiness, he reads Jacob and the Man in Black as twins whose oppositions must be annihilated, so that only when both cease to exist in 'The End' are the castaways set free.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 84 "79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine" — Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.

### Socratic Method (elenchus)

The Socratic method, or elenchus, is a form of cooperative inquiry in which a claim is tested through a disciplined series of questions rather than asserted or refuted directly. Socrates would draw out a person's definition of some notion such as justice or courage, then expose contradictions among the beliefs they held alongside it, leading them to abandon or refine the original view. Its aim is less to win an argument than to clear away false confidence and move both parties closer to a defensible understanding. The method treats knowledge as something arrived at through examination, not received ready-made.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 9 "Unknown" — Irwin parallels Neo's mission with Socrates' divine commission from the Oracle at Delphi to 'wake up' Athens: both are driven by a single question ('What is the Matrix?' versus 'What is the good life?'), both are charged by the authorities, and both sting a complacent public. He explains the Socratic method through the Euthyphro exchange on holiness, where a follow-up question ('Is the holy holy because the gods approve it, or do they approve it because it is holy?') exposes Euthyphro's ignorance, and introduces Socrates' mantra 'I know nothing' as the humility that launches his quest just as Neo's lack of self-knowledge launches his.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 10 "Unknown" — Irwin compares the film's kitchen-table Oracle with the Pythia at Delphi: both utter cryptic prophecies that seekers misread, from Croesus's doomed war to Morpheus's certainty that Neo is the One, and both make self-knowledge the real key to interpretation. He reads the 'Temet Nosce' sign and the cookie scene through the Delphic maxims 'Know thyself' and 'Nothing in excess', arguing Neo fulfills the prophecy only when he comes to know and believe in himself, and closes by linking Socrates' gadfly mission and 'the unexamined life is not worth living' to Fight Club, Boys Don't Cry, and Memento.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 19 "Kant, Aristotle, and the Cheater" — Answering Cal Ripken's Socratic question 'What is cheating?' (raised by Sammy Sosa's corked bat and Gaylord Perry's spitball), Randolph Feezell stages a dialogue between Abbey's Kantian absolutism, Trev's traditionalism, and Ron's win-at-all-costs realism. Kant's categorical imperative grounds the absolutist: intending to break a rule to gain an edge is making yourself an arbitrary exception to rules that bind all players equally. Aristotle's virtue ethics then lets the traditionalist say that some strategic rule-breaking belongs to a sport's 'prescriptive atmosphere' (stealing signs, the balk pickoff, catching framing), since honesty and courage are means between excess and defect guided by judgment rather than exceptionless rules, while corking a bat stays cheating because it defies the tradition and hides from umpires.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 35 "Last Pitch" — Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 27 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Takes Digory's dying remark 'It's all in Plato' as the key to the Chronicles. It compares the Professor's guided questioning of Peter and Susan about Lucy's wardrobe testimony to the Socratic method, though noting he supplies evidential maxims rather than eliciting a virtue-definition as Socrates does with Cephalus on justice. It maps Underland in The Silver Chair onto the Allegory of the Cave (Rilian bound in his silver chair like the chained prisoners, the Green Witch's enchantment that denies any world beyond), observing that the Witch 'plays Aristotle' by ridiculing Aslan as an invented perfect Form, while Puddleglum's 'stand by the play-world' speech echoes Socrates's reply to Glaucon that the ideal pattern is none the worse for being unrealizable. Finally it reads the 'real Narnia' of The Last Battle ('world within world, Narnia within Narnia') as Christian Platonism, with the nested heavens even raising Plato's Third Man problem.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 9 "From Rhyme to Reason This Shit Ain’t Easy" — The editors' introduction argues that hip hop and philosophy are both street-born examinations of life in pursuit of wisdom: Socrates's elenchus is likened to MC lyrical battles and call-and-response (his interrogations compared to Rakim's technique, his execution for corrupting the youth to the fate of a controversial rapper), while Plato's philosopher-king parallels Kurtis Blow and Run-D.M.C. claiming thrones. After a Bronx hip-hop history sketch (Kool Herc, BDP's "The Bridge is Over"), they frame the volume around hip hop's suppressed fifth element of knowledge and preview its pairings: Aquinas and Rakim on God, Plato and Lauryn Hill on love, Sartre and Lil' Kim's gaze, Kant and Ice Cube on punishment, Hegel and Nas, Hobbes and Dead Prez, Mill and Chappelle on epithets. Record companies don't own hip hop and universities don't own philosophy, they conclude - both belong to whoever understands, loves, and respects them.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 87 "Chapter 13 - Political Bullshit and the Stoic Story of Self" — Evans concludes that the antidote to political bullshit is a discursive culture trained in Socratic skills of self-examination — citizens taught to recognize how their own views may be imperfect and how to refine them — together with the analytic-philosophical style his Oxford tutor called 'a very good bullshit detector'. Experts may lead debates by their greater factual knowledge and critical acumen, but the debates must stay democratically inclusive rather than become an elite monopoly. Citing G.A. Cohen, he warns that too much fashionable philosophy disparages truth and so itself produces bullshit, and that using the ubiquity of bullshit to justify the cynicism thesis's crippling inertia would be potentially catastrophic.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — Introduces Part I by casting South Park, The Daily Show, and The Colbert Report as modern Socratic gadflies. It previews Young's comparison of the show's 'corruption of the youth' controversies to Socrates' trial, Arp's use of Johnnie Cochran's Chewbacca Defense to teach logic and fallacies, and Johnson's use of Colbert's 'wikiality' and 'truthiness' to attack relativism and the myth that everyone has a right to their opinion.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 12 "Springsteen’s Revolution" — Anderson and Anderson open with the Che Guevara t-shirt problem and Marcuse's one-dimensional man: the system assimilates protest, so internal critique (Springsteen on the cover of Rolling Stone, its Chevrolet calendar, the Eagles sold at Wal-Mart, Adorno's verdict on co-opted popular music) is a sop to Cerberus. Against this they set Springsteen's own account of his music as 'a very long conversation with my audience' — a transactional public service — and argue he survives the co-optation charge as a 'Socratic revolutionary' who, like Socrates refusing to leave Athens, works from within: listening without obeying ('I liked the old Bruce better'), refusing to ride the Born to Run wave, turning to Guthrie and Seeger, and drawing no hard conclusions, only opening spaces of reflection ('Born in the U.S.A.', 'Radio Nowhere', 'Long Walk Home'). Revolution is just another form of work — practice, sweat, and the personal job of 'growin' up.'
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 26 "The Final Word That’s Right, I Said Preliminary Thoughts" — Patton starts from wildly disputed Springsteen interpretations — Reagan's 1984 campaign use of 'Born in the U.S.A.,' Flint protesters playing 'My Hometown' as civic pride, Kerry's 'No Surrender' — and asks whether any reading is better than another. He frames the issue as Socratic dialectic versus Gorgias-style rhetoric, passes through Augustine's polysemy (multiple intended levels of meaning, as in 'I'm on fire') to Nietzsche's claim that the text disappears beneath its interpretation, extended by Foucault (truth as an instrument of power) and Derridean deconstruction. His conclusion: authorial intent cannot settle meaning, but some readings ('Born in the U.S.A.' as pro-Reagan anthem) are non-starters, otherwise it is rhetoric all the way down and the sophists win.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 28 "Springsteen’s Martyrdom" — The Bells parallel Socrates' forcible 'abduction' to the house of the arms merchant Cephalus in Republic Book I with Springsteen's 1984 political abduction, when Reagan and Mondale both pretended he had endorsed them and George Will invited him to be laureate of 'joyous overconsumption.' They read the Republic's luxurious city — its Ring of Gyges parasites, censorship of poets, and wars born of appetite — as an elenchus run against the control (epoche) of the healthy working city of Book II, so readers who take the 'ideal' city at face value err exactly like fans who hear patriotism in 'Born in the U.S.A.' Songs like 'Youngstown,' 'The Angel' and 'Galveston Bay' likewise critique overconsumption, imperialism and the censorship of artists, and both artist-critics risk the martyrdom Socrates suffered for speaking truth to the powerful.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 14 "Democratization of Media—Philosophy for All!" — Parker recounts training for the Seoul Marathon on a treadmill with philosophy podcasts (Philosophy Talk, Philosophy Bites, LibriVox) to argue the iPod works as a 'next-generation book' that can democratize philosophy -- yet, like the book, it cannot supply the two-way dialogue that Socrates practiced in the agora and that Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum, and Epicurus's Garden were built to sustain. He distinguishes studying philosophy -- compiling, say, Kant's claim that one cannot act except in ways one could will all others to act -- from doing it, and argues that credentials and canon cannot displace each person's inescapable role as 'the arbiters of our own thoughts.' The Nazis' misconstrual of Nietzsche is his example of interpretation without critical guardianship, and he concludes that the academy's stronghold on teaching philosophy is loosening even if wikis and virtual forums never fully replace professional expertise.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 15 "After Forgetting" — Sturgis argues that iPods plus the collaborative Web 2.0 will end education's age of memorization: the school 'cheaters' storing test answers in lyrics files are early adopters of a world where, as Plato's Meno already allowed, knowledge can be retrieved rather than remembered, and a remote server is no more crash-prone than a brain ('the server could crash, but so could I'). His own podcasted environmental-ethics course shows Socratic, question-driven lecturing and radio's 'theater of the mind' reaching distance learners, while MIT OpenCourseWare and Berkeley webcasts (a trucker listening to Hubert Dreyfus) globalize elite content. Following Dewey on reflection and artistry, he predicts a post-factual pedagogy of assessing sources -- he catches Wikipedia misreading an iPod '90 percent market share' claim -- collaborative creation, and candid acceptance that we are already integrated with technological devices.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 30 "19 - The Rhodesian Stranger" — A comic Socratic dialogue, a pastiche of Plato's Phaedrus, in which a time-lost 'Rhodesian Stranger' wanders in mid-conversation to defend reading against Socrates' retelling of the Thamus-and-Thoth myth — writing as inert painting that gives 'the semblance of truth', summed up in the Stranger's quoting his 'fellow Rhodish' philosopher Schopenhauer: thoughts on paper are footprints in the sand, the path seen but not what was seen along the way. Socrates' elenchus (the ship ticket versus the journey, walking beside a friend and turning back to check on him rather than posting signposts) drives the Stranger into inventing a myth in which gods replace abused speech with pea-pods whose planted seeds become pod-casts gathered by pod-catchers — podcasting imagined as friends dialoguing together toward the true and the good. Socrates closes skeptically, doubting that disconnected pod-communication escapes trivia and universal broadcast, but concedes 'surely beauty is as faithful a guide towards the good as is truth.'
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 7 "Setting Up the Game" — Editor Luke Cuddy's introduction: he argues videogames, and the Zelda franchise in particular, deserve philosophical attention, then frames the book's spirit with Plato's Meno. Just as Socrates' questioning leads the slave boy from thinking he knows to actually knowing that a double-sized square has area sixteen, the gamer's struggle through dungeons is rewarded with the item-room fanfare (the ladder, the silver arrow) as an 'AHA!' feeling of insight. The chapter lists the franchise's games and the book's guiding questions, stressing that the gamer guides Link rather than passively watching.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 20 "Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We" — Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 43 "Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation" — Argues Doctor Who is philosophy's ally by way of Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching, which produces justified true belief, and rhetoric, which wins by persuasion: the Master is the master rhetorician whose hypnotic manipulation manufactures unreliable beliefs, while the Doctor is the Socratic teacher who gives information and lets companions decide. Socrates's descriptions of philosophy (the good life, sense of wonder, love of real knowledge) are matched to the show's career as an educational program that teaches viewers to reflect on how they reason, how they treat 'others' like Daleks and Silurians, and to revise their views, that is, to live the examined life.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 10 "A Toolbox for Your Holmes" — Sami Paavola and Lauri Jaervilehto reconstruct the textbook on detection Holmes never wrote: following Jaakko Hintikka's interrogative (Socratic) model, where the right question cracks the case, as with the dog that did nothing in the night-time in 'Silver Blaze', and Peirce's triad of deduction, induction and abduction, the backward reasoning from effects to causes exemplified by the Watson-just-from-Afghanistan chain in A Study in Scarlet. They add Peirce's categories of Firstness, Secondness and Thirdness to show Holmes succeeds because he fuses imagination and reverie with fieldwork, experiment and exact inference. The chapter closes with a twelve-point practical toolbox distilled from the canon.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 25 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Carl Ehrett and Sarah Worth ask whether D&D is really a game (imagining Bill and Ted challenging Death to a campaign) and model the search for a definition of 'game' on Socrates dismantling Euthyphro's attempted definitions of piety, only for Wittgenstein's family resemblance to dissolve the project. On that view D&D still counts as a game despite lacking winning and losing, because its rule-governedness survives 'rule 0' license to bend rules whenever bending them crafts a better story. To explain why players who know the world is not real are nonetheless engrossed, they present Radford's paradox of fiction and adopt Walton's make-believe theory: the miniature on the table is a prop prescribing the imagining of an owlbear, so genuine quasi-emotions respond to truths in the fiction, making D&D an unusually gripping interactive story.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 19 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Timothy Sexton traces Jeopardy!'s format to the fallout from the 1950s quiz show scandals, when Charles Van Doren's rigged run on Twenty-One destroyed the elitist model of expert knowledge and television pivoted to anti-elitist game shows like The Price Is Right. He reads that pivot as parallel to the Cold-War abandonment of Dewey's progressive education for a utilitarian, worker-training curriculum, as documented by Diane Ravitch and Olaf Hoerschelmann. Jeopardy! endures as the 'Gnostic' compromise between quiz show and game show: it keeps elitist knowledge but demands that it be displayed in the Socratic ritual of answering in the form of a question, which lets a trivia show rise above the dumbed-down Millionaire era.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 23 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Rick Mayock stops a fictional Jeopardy! clock to apply Plato's divided line: most contestants, like the cave prisoners rewarded for predicting shadow sequences, trade in doxa - conjecture (eikasia) and belief (pistis) - while the Meno's slave boy shows how Socratic questioning ties true opinions down into knowledge. Winning requires only dianoia, hypothetical reasoning from hypotheses and definitions, never noesis, the dialectic that ascends to the eternal Forms; the Phaedo's example of perfect 'equality' shows why the 'Aha!' of recognition is re-cognition by an immortal soul already acquainted with the Forms. Watson, lacking such a soul, can clear a buzz threshold but never have an Aha! moment - it is Daedalus's statue, lifelike but sure to run away from the truth unless tied down.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 26 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Daniel Wanless reads Jeopardy! through the Meno: contestants can formulate the right question only because the answer is already given, just as Socrates answers Meno's paradox by claiming that all inquiry is recollection of truths the immortal soul already holds - latent knowledge that explains how Ken Jennings buzzes in before he consciously knows the response. A priori logical ability (the slave boy's doubled square, the law of non-contradiction applied to which of three cities is southernmost) guides the search for answers, while Final Jeopardy!'s blind wagering embodies Kierkegaard's 'life is only understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards.' Socrates would bet it all, Wanless concludes, because the unexamined life is not worth living: his whole life was preparation for the ultimate Final Jeopardy!, lived in the form of a question.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 22 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Fisher argues The Wire makes homosexuality a source of excellence: Omar and Kima blend masculine and feminine traits in something like Butler's gender-performative terms, build Aristotelian friendships of virtue (Kima and Cheryl pushing each other's careers), and can make the sacrifices - solitude, giving up family - that excellence in the drug war demands, while the homophobia of the streets and the precinct forces them to keep proving themselves. Omar's crossword comfort with 'them myths' frames him as a contemporary Socrates: a mentor-lover of boys, accused of amorality by Levy much as Socrates was charged with corrupting Athens's youth, answering with a Socratic reversal ('I got the shotgun, you got the briefcase'), and dying for his code in the city he would not leave. The chapter reads the show's refusal of coming-out storylines - Rawls's silent gay-bar cameo, Snoop's never-confirmed sexuality - as its most radical statement about sexuality in America.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 31 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — John Huss asks whether Andy Serkis deserved an Oscar nomination for playing Caesar through performance capture, and argues that 'What is acting?' is a Socratic-style definitional question (like stumping Euthyphro on piety) of the sort Wittgenstein diagnosed as a language confusion, since the definition of movie acting is in flux. Using the seeing-as debate, Kuhnian theory-ladenness of observation versus Fodor's Muller-Lyer point that belief does not dictate sight, he explains why animators and fans see such different things in the identical raw footage. He concludes, with James Franco, that acting is an emergent ensemble property of actors reacting to one another on a shared stage, which performance capture enables rather than threatens, and a coda notes PETA's hope that CG performers will end the use of animal actors.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 9 "Psych and Philosophy" — Michaud argues that Shawn's whole psychic career runs on fallacies of relevance - the red herring of claiming to be psychic to dodge arrest, plus ad hominem mockery that deflects Lassiter's fraud accusations - so the show's comedy turns on bad logic being used to lead people to true conclusions. Socrates supplies the opposing voice: like the Sophists who argued any side for money, Shawn reasons for convenience and amusement, and his deception is an inconsistency of the kind Socrates refused in Plato's Crito, where he would not bribe his way out of a death sentence. An invented Platonic-style dialogue has Socrates question Shawn until he concedes that lying breeds more lying and harm - 'her name is Truth!' - before Shawn escapes the elenchus by spotting lipstick on Socrates's collar. The chapter leaves the verdict open: Shawn saves lives and raises the world's happiness, but his trickery also trains Santa Barbara to reason badly and trust con artists.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 30 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Cobb treats the show's storytellers as narrative pedagogues. Nucky's wharf-rat speech is story truth rather than happening truth - Plato's Republic question of true and false tales - and because it allows no dialogue or questioning it fails as full pedagogy; Chalky's story of his father's lynching ties past to present in the interrogation of the Klansman; Rothstein's billiard-ball anecdote for Frankie Yale is episodic memory shaped into identity and threat, a coerced but genuine reasoning exchange ('Do you know what the moral is of this tale, Mr. Yale?'). Measured against Socrates' question-posing inquiry in the Euthyphro, Kant's On Education, and Freire's dialogical 'critical co-investigators,' Nucky, Chalky, and Rothstein all emerge as reflective but deficient pedagogues at large.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 30 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Mills-Knutsen reads the Brain Spawn - floating brains whose pain at others' thoughts drives them to dumb life down and finally to hoard all knowledge in the Infosphere ('The Day the Earth Stood Stupid,' 'The Why of Fry') - as Futurama's funhouse mirror of the West's distrust of intellectuals, from Pandora and Eve to Frankenstein and comic-book evil geniuses. Fry, the delta-brainwave-lacking hero made stupid by doing 'the nasty in the pasty,' stabs the Big Brain with Bonfire of the Vanities and later banishes the Brains to another dimension, just as Athens executed Socrates. A close reading of Plato's Apology - Socrates's feigned ignorance exposing everyone else's, his demand of free meals in lieu of exile, and his prophecy of even more annoying successors - maps onto the Big Brain's snobbery and onto universities (Wernstrom's tenure scam in 'A Big Piece of Garbage,' Amy's doctorate in 'That Darn Katz!') as society's way of paying intellectuals to stay out of the way.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 7 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cam Cobb weighs Battle School against competing philosophies of education: Plato's Republic supplies vocational sorting by natural aptitude (complete with the myth of the metals as a 'noble lie'), while Socratic dialogue and Paulo Freire's problem-posing pedagogy demand the shared critical inquiry Ender never gets. He argues Graff's curriculum is almost purely vocational - military history, tactics, the Giant's Drink, battleroom drills - leaving no liberal paideia, and that the teachers' constant rule-changing leaves Ender feeling like 'someone's pawn,' exactly the banking-style teacher domination Freire warned against.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 51 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Roger Hunt reads Bill Hicks's stand-up as a Socratic comedy exposing Satan's three-point plan: suppress knowledge, breed ignorance, and profit from hypocrisy - from the Waffle House 'readah' scene to Bush-era Gulf War spin ('we looked at the receipts'), JFK-assassination distraction via American Gladiators, and pop stars and marketers who 'suck Satan's cock' (Rick Astley, corporate rock, advertising). Where the Genesis serpent offered knowledge, Hicks's Devil is the force that suppresses it, and Hicks paid a Socratic price - an early death for 'corrupting' his audience - for pointing this out.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 20 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Christopher Lauer argues Cohen's lyrics seduce through Socratic irony as Kierkegaard analyzes it in The Concept of Irony: ostentatious self-concealment that makes hearers aware of the gap between words and intentions, building 'personality' and promising intimacy. Songs like 'Closing Time,' 'Everybody Knows,' and 'Democracy' oscillate between cynical third-person verdicts and sudden second-person address, offering a hidden sincerity only to withdraw it - an erotic improvement on Plato's Socrates that dissolves its own ironic distance. 'Hallelujah' and 'Anthem' make the program explicit, treating brokenness as the space in which love develops, while 'Tower of Song' shows the bleak side: irony collapsing into pure cynicism, the singer speaking sweetly from the Tower long after all promises of genuine intimacy have been disavowed.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 19 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Roger Hunt answers 'what do philosophers do?' through Dennis's seduction methodology. Frank embodies empiricism, leaving the comfort of principle for the messiness of the world as Hume did when he found no impression of causation, space, or time; Mac embodies rationalism, reasoning with total confidence from a principle he cannot doubt, as Descartes did from the cogito; and the dialectic of Socrates and Plato, questioning beliefs in dialogue to see what survives scrutiny, describes philosophy as it is actually practiced. Boethius's Consolation - the imprisoned author consoled by dialogues with Lady Philosophy - supplies the frame of philosophy as an encounter with a woman one pursues, and each D.E.N.N.I.S. step maps onto the craft: Demonstrating value to the problem, Engaging physically in its awkward grind, Nurturing dependence through thesis panic, Neglect and Inspiring hope on the road to the defense, then Separating entirely - 'be a sociopath about it.'
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 21 "8. Should Jane Get to Be Bored" — Daniel Addison defends Louie's 'you don't get to be bored' admonishment of Jane in 'Country Drive' against Mathew Remski's charge that it transfers adult anxiety, pointing to Louis's Conan 'forever empty' monologue and reddit advice as proof that Louis insists on facing despair rather than fleeing it. The real aim, he argues, is Socratic: Louis wants Jane and the plane-complaining generation brought to aporia, the perplexity Plato's Socrates induces in the Meno's slave boy so that, no longer thinking he knows, he 'would be glad to find out.' Aristotle grounds the optimism - every human by nature desires to know, philosophy begins in wonder, and our deepest happiness lies in contemplating - so Louis's 'everything's amazing' tirade is a demand that we become philosophical rather than 'kinda satisfied' consumers. Boredom, on this reading, is failed wonder, and Louie is playing Socrates to his daughter.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 13 "4. Scoundrels, the Lot of Us" — Karavitis finds a Hegelian dialectic in the three-panel Dilbert strip (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) delivered through irony, then tests that irony against philosophy: Socrates' feigned-ignorance questioning that leaves interlocutors in aporia, Hegel's complaint that irony is vanity withdrawing from objective reality, and Kierkegaard's dissertation on the concept of irony plus Either/Or, where irony is the bridge from the aesthetic to the ethical life. The punchline is that after nearly three decades of Dilbert the white-collar workplace has not changed, so readers who feel superior to their bosses and co-workers have taken the vain, narcissistic, aesthetic reading Hegel warned against, making the joke a scoundrelly way of avoiding responsibility. A Leo Strauss aside casts Adams as an esoteric writer whose irony preserves him from the powerful.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 29 "17. Sweeping Up God’s Debris" — Robison-Greene reads God's Debris as a Socratic dialogue on speed: the Avatar, like Socrates after the Delphic oracle, guts the Postman's confidence so he can unlearn, and the whole book functions as a Cartesian skeptical hypothesis in the dream-and-evil-demon lineage, here that we are the dust of a self-destructed God and perception is illusion, with gravity re-described as probability. Her counterattack is that the cosmology commits category mistakes, since probability cannot cause dust to reappear any more than Joe can consist of tallness, and that God made of probability is incoherent even for an omnipotent being.
