The five levels of awareness collapse too: level-four skeptics are just people who trust reliable methods, and the Avatar's claim that the mind is an illusion generator is self-defeating, since his own omniscience presupposes objective truth.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 15 "6. No Wisdom to Offer You" — Distinguishes public intellectuals like Chomsky, who deliver their own conclusions, from public philosophers who get audiences thinking for themselves, and argues Schumer is the latter. Her memoir claim that she has 'no wisdom to offer' is set beside the Socratic ignorance of Plato's Apology, where wisdom is worth nothing. Sketches like 'Football Town Nights', whose coach condemns rape only to praise violent domination, and 'The Trial of Bill Cosby' withhold conclusions and force viewers to work out for themselves the links between football and rape culture, or between un-conflicted entertainment and justice.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 18 "7. Rick and Morty as Socratic Television" — The chapter argues Harmon and Roiland write the show as Socratic dialogue: in 'Mortynight Run' Morty's confident moral position (saving Fart from Krombopulos Michael is right) is dismantled until Morty himself pulls the trigger, leaving him in aporia; in 'Auto Erotic Assimilation' Summer's faith in freedom is razed by Unity's happy paternalist hive and the nipple-shaped race war it unleashes; and 'Look Who's Purging Now' refuses to choose between liberalism and conservatism when the post-purge town instantly re-founds the Festival. Like Socrates in Plato's Meno, the show's goal is not to teach lessons but to reduce viewers to confusion, because doing philosophy begins there.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 32 "19. The Citadel of Ricks Is Untruth" — The chapter reads Rick C-137's war on the Citadel through Kierkegaard's claim that the crowd is untruth: the Council of Ricks is the leveling public, envying and punishing the passionate individual ('You're a rogue Rick, irrational, passionate'), as Rick J-22's breakdown over Simple Rick's wafers in 'The Ricklantis Mixup' dramatizes, while our Rick stays himself by refusing consensus. From Philosophical Fragments, via Socrates's maieutic midwifery, it draws Kierkegaard's ethics of selfhood: one person can only be the occasion for another's self-knowledge and must then push them away to become individuals. That is exactly Rick's advice to Beth in 'The ABCs of Beth', to leave Jerry, saddle her universe, and become herself, since only Beth can make Beth.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 13 "4. The Gently Socratic Inquiry of Fred Rogers" — Ben Lukey and Steve Bein, veterans of p4c Hawai'i, argue Rogers ran a 'gently Socratic' community of inquiry on television: unlike Socrates the public gadfly who made asses of interlocutors, Rogers created intellectual safety, treating Daniel Striped Tiger's 'What does assassination mean?' (after MLK's murder) and the Officer Clemmons kiddie-pool scene as philosophy with children. Using Dr. Tom Jackson's Good Thinker's Toolkit to show children are philosophers, they defend 'little p philosophy' as activity over 'Big P Philosophy' as content, casting Rogers and Socrates as midwives rather than lecturers.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 43 "30. Socratic Superheroism" — Stages a dialogue between Socrates and Nebula to build a four-part scorecard of 'Socratic Heroism' — question all assumptions, intellectual humility (Socrates before the Delphic oracle: 'I am very conscious that I am not wise at all'), improve society without ever doing injustice, and courage unto death (the gadfly of the Apology) — then scores Thanos 0 for 4: 'I am incapable of error' and 'reality can be whatever I want' are the very opposites of humility and of objective, heavenly truth. It nominates Doctor Strange as the MCU's Socratic hero, whose humbling at Kamar-Taj, willingness to hand over the Time Stone against the obvious choice, and trust in the one winning future among 14,000,605 pass the tests.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 14 "“Consider Your Verdict!”" — Splits Wonderland's nonsense into the tolerable kind (strange but lawful regularities, like mushroom side-effects and walking the opposite way to reach the Red Queen, which Alice masters by experiment) and the intolerable kind (the creatures' eristic logic). Using Hume's fork of relations of ideas versus matters of fact, George Dunn and Brian McDonald argue Alice rightly concludes the pig-baby is merely an out-of-the-way matter of fact, while the White Queen's 'jam every other day: to-day isn't any other day' and the King's beheading of the bodiless Cheshire Cat repeat the Sophists' tricks from Plato's Euthydemus, which Socrates deflates from the standpoint of common sense and the examined life. The Knave's trial ('sentence first, verdict afterwards') lands on cable-news pundits who, like the show trials of Stalin, argue from predetermined conclusions.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 24 "A Nonsense Too Far" — Places Carroll's nonsense in a Greco-Roman tradition of philosophically useful absurdity: Socrates exposing Euthyphro's definitions of piety as nonsense, Plato's tongue-in-cheek Republic calculation that the tyrant's life is 729 times worse, and Diogenes ridiculing slavery even while sold on the auction block. Charles Taliaferro and Elizabeth Olson argue the jokes land only because Alice stays sane, curious, polite, and self-controlled, the stable foil who keeps the death threats and cruelty of Wonderland and the Looking-Glass on the amusing side of the ledger, and that nonsense goes 'too far' in Kafka's The Trial, where losing the sane, good center turns absurdity into meaninglessness.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 14 "Hoist by his Own Petard" — Powell reads Norman Osborn's Dark Reign as a living lesson from Plato's Gorgias and Alcibiades: Osborn's media-staged killing of the Skrull Queen and his hollow rebranding of S.H.I.E.L.D. into H.A.M.M.E.R. are the sophistic 'knack' of persuasion substituting for the genuine craft of statecraft, just as Polus's ideal Sophist imagines power without self-control. Like Alcibiades, Osborn lacks the Socratic self-knowledge that comes only through critical self-reflection with honest friends, and instead surrounds himself with flatterers and villains while his own Goblin persona—mirrored in the Sentry's Void—grows stronger. Loki's goading of the unsanctioned Siege of Asgard completes the cautionary tale: the sophist who created fake institutions is destroyed by them, hoist by his own petard.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 16 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Barad maps fifth-century Athens onto contemporary America to cast Stewart as a Socratic reformer confronting modern sophists, advertisers, pundits and media figures who make weaker arguments appear stronger without caring about truth, exemplified by Ed Helms admitting network stories are pre-written from 'conventional wisdom' and Ann Coulter's conformity-peddling. She details the shared method: flattering the 'expert', feigned ignorance, and layer-by-layer questioning that traps targets like Rumsfeld ('It may not seem like much, but for this administration it's a huge policy shift') in contradiction, with Socratic irony doing the work of Stewart's awestruck deadpan and mute astonished reactions to Bush clips. Against Bill O'Reilly's 'stoned slacker' charge she cites the Annenberg finding that the show's young audience is better informed, and weighs Ken Tucker's 'monkey' question through the Crossfire 'I'm not going to be your monkey' exchange, concluding that, like Socrates facing trial and execution, Stewart uses irony as means and truth as end.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 20 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Blessing and Marren mine Stewart's two interviews with Harry Frankfurt to work out the lie/bullshit distinction: liars like Edwards, Weiner and Clinton know and care about the truth they distort, while bullshitters, from Travelodge PR stunts to subprime lenders, are indifferent to truth in service of selling, which is why Frankfurt calls bullshit the more corrosive force. They take up Stewart's Socratic questioning of whether political spin is a subset of bullshit, and answer that spinners, unlike bullshitters, must know the truth in order to color it, making spin closer to lying in attitude, tolerated because Spin Alley agrees not to call bullshit on it. Documenting the PR-ization of media (the Cardiff University study behind Flat Earth News, the Wall Street Journal press-release finding), they close with Frankfurt's On Truth sequel, that a society cannot survive without truth, with ridicule of the kind The Daily Show practices as the best defense.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 10 "The Sorcerer Socratic" — Timm argues Strange follows Socrates' path from arrogance to Socratic heroism: the hand injury forces intellectual humility (the Oracle-at-Delphi moment), the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor and astral-form lesson ('to show you just how much you don't know') enact the Socratic method of questioning the supposedly wise, and the astral projection is literally the examined life — Socrates' unexamined life not worth living. Strange's commitment to protecting humanity from interdimensional evil parallels the gadfly who risks death to improve Athens, his refusal to do injustice even under pressure echoes the Crito, and his repeated willingness to die for others (facing Dormammu, holding the Shambler back) completes the Socratic Hero profile.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 25 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Ehrett and Worth ask whether D&D is really a game and why we invest so much in it. Against the Socratic model (the Euthyphro dialogue's search for a common thread defining piety, here applied to 'game'), they deploy Wittgenstein's family-resemblance account from the Philosophical Investigations, concluding D&D lacks clear winning and losing but is rule-governed, with the twist that rule-breaking is legitimate exactly when it serves the game's primary purpose of group storytelling. They then take up the paradox of fiction: since players know the world is not real, Radford's puzzle arises, and Kendall Walton's make-believe theory of props and fictional truths supplies their answer, making D&D an especially gripping fiction because players are participants rather than observers.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 7 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cam Cobb pits Socratic critical inquiry and Plato's Republic-style vocational streaming (classes sorted by the 'myth of the metals,' sold through a noble lie) against the Battle School curriculum, which is almost purely vocational and lacks the music, poetry, and liberal paideia that harmonize the soul. Testing Socrates' dialogic method, Dewey's aptitude-tracking education, and Freire's problem-posing alternative against the battleroom, the Giant's Drink, and Graff's secretly rewritten game rules, Cobb concludes Ender's schooling mixes conflicting pedagogies and ends in the teacher domination Freire feared, crystallized in Ender's lament 'I've spent my life as someone's pawn.'
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 7 "Setting Up the Game" — Editor Luke Cuddy's introduction argues that videogames, and Zelda in particular, deserve philosophy because the gamer actively guides Link instead of passively watching, which raises questions about Link's will, Hyrule's space and time, the Triforce, timeline theories, and death. It surveys the franchise from the 1986 NES original through Phantom Hourglass and the fandom culture around it. Its central move is reading Plato's Meno — Socrates questioning the slave boy until the boy truly knows the doubled square — as the model of the 'AHA!' feeling, which it parallels to Link triumphantly hoisting a dungeon item like the ladder while the four rising notes play.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 12 "And Now, Deep Thoughts…" — Reynolds places comedy on a spectrum from philosophy to satire to smart-assery and argues SNL mostly sits at the silly end: Gumby, Mr. Robinson, Hermione's cleavage, and Hobbit Office are parody with an absurd twist but no constructive target, unlike genuine satire such as Mr. Bill. He develops the comparison through Aristophanes' Clouds, whose caricature of Socrates at the Thinkery helped send him to his death, and through the 'Playboy Philosophy' sketch with Belushi as Socrates. Socrates himself emerges as a satirist: the oracle of Delphi, his claim to know only that he knows nothing, and his elenchus that unmasks the supposedly wise are read as comedy in the service of seriousness, before the chapter concedes SNL's absurdism is philosophical mainly in mocking an absurd world.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 33 "31_LaRocca_Chapter_030.html" — Hoffman reads Sarah Polley's Stories We Tell and Joshua Oppenheimer's The Act of Killing through Kierkegaard's account of indirect communication and 'deceiving into the truth.' Like the Socratic maieutic teacher who removes his authority and lets pupils reach their own conclusions, both directors withhold voice-of-God assertion and instead present multiple, conflicting, sometimes ethically monstrous storytellers, indulging their delusions to expose them. Polley stages fake Super-8 home movies and rival accounts of her mother and paternity so that truth becomes subjective appropriation rather than objective fact; Oppenheimer lets Indonesian genocide perpetrators reenact their killings as Hollywood fantasies until Anwar Congo is 'deceived' into his own broken self-awareness, indicting the regime that still celebrates him.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 43 "Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation" — Courtland Lewis's closing essay argues Doctor Who and philosophy are complementary enterprises devoted to teaching rather than mere persuasion. Using Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching and rhetoric, he casts the Master as the master rhetorician who produces unreliable beliefs (even via hypnosis), while the Doctor is a Socratic teacher committed to truth who gives people information and lets them decide. He contends the show, begun as educational, challenges viewers to reflect on their own reasoning, on how they treat others (Daleks, Cybermen, strangers), and to revise beliefs in light of evidence, so that watching it is living philosophically engaged.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 23 "13. Chuckrates v. The Saulphists" — Staged as a mock disciplinary-board trial, the chapter casts Chuck McGill as Socrates and Jimmy as a Sophist to replay Plato's dialectic-versus-rhetoric quarrel. Chuck prosecutes Jimmy as a mere rhetorician who 'makes the weaker argument defeat the stronger,' quoting the Gorgias, Apology, and Republic, while Jimmy counters that Socrates was himself a self-righteous show-off and that the legal system runs on Sophistic persuasion (juries, opening statements) as much as on truth. The Board's verdict finds Chuck blind to his own rhetoric and Jimmy a quintessential but empathetic Sophist, using the McGill brothers to argue that law fuses dialectic and rhetoric just as ancient Athens did.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 9 "The Talking Cure for Our Culture" — Young argues that South Park, like Socrates in Plato's Apology, is accused of corrupting youth and impiety but is really a philosophical gadfly. Kyle and Stan reach moral conclusions (e.g., refusing to kill Stan's grandfather) through Socratic questioning and dialogue, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty mirrors Arendt's banality of evil in Eichmann. Young reads the show's vulgarity through Freud, arguing its crude jokes release repressed drives so we can examine them, making the show a Socratic 'talking cure' for a mindless culture.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 16 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Judith Barad argues Stewart plays reformer in America as Socrates did in Athens, both confronting sophists—now advertisers, spin doctors, and media pundits like Coulter and O'Reilly—who teach persuasion detached from truth. She maps the Daily Show correspondents' interview technique (flatter the 'expert,' expose a contradiction) directly onto the Socratic method, and reads Stewart's ironic self-deprecation, feigned confusion, and one-on-one listening as Socratic irony deployed, like Socrates', as a means to truth rather than mere entertainment, culminating in the Crossfire confrontation with Carlson and Begala.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 34 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Decker asks whether 'Stephen Colbert' the persona is an 'existential ironist,' tracing irony from Socrates's Delphic-oracle-inspired questioning through Schlegel, Hegel (irony as freedom but an abdication of responsibility), and Kierkegaard (the ironist detached from and not taking community practices seriously). He reads Colbert's centerless self-redescription and Super PAC stunt via Rorty's 'ironist' and 'final vocabulary' (built from Nietzschean self-creation and Deweyan plasticity through language), then argues that truthiness is a dangerous subjectivism—and that Colbert, unlike a pure Rortian ironist, drops the mask to side with the powerless.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 10 "Oh, the Places You’ll Go! The Examined, Happy Life" — Benjamin Rider reads Oh, the Places You'll Go! through Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living. He argues the Sneetches' star-obsession, Yertle's tower, Gertrude McFuzz's feathers, and the Once-ler's 'biggering' are the false, unexamined beliefs about wealth and status that Socrates said wreck the soul, while Bartholomew Cubbins and Horton model the wise, courageous endurance Socrates seeks but fails to define with the generals Laches and Nicias in Plato's Laches. The 'Waiting Place' becomes the life of someone who never questions what really makes him happy, and Seuss's call to use 'the brains in your head' echoes Socrates' insistence in the Crito and Phaedo on living by rational reflection.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 13 "Socratic Seuss Intellectual Integrity and Truth-Orientation" — Matthew Pierlott casts Seuss as a Socratic gadfly for intellectual integrity, built on Frankfurt's distinction between the liar (who respects truth) and the bullshitter (who is indifferent to it). Sam-I-Am's reluctant friend in Green Eggs and Ham is 'bullshitting' to be left alone; the boasting rabbit and bear of 'The Big Brag' are humbled by a worm who plays Socrates as in Plato's Euthyphro; Horton Hatches the Egg and Mulberry Street show self-delusion (believing what we wish were true); and 'What Was I Scared Of?' shows fear distorting the interpretation of evidence, all mapped against Pierlott's five aspects of intellectual integrity.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 27 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Gilmore reads Persuasion as itself a rumination on persuasion, arguing the word means different things in different contexts. He uses Plato's Gorgias to split persuasion into Persuasion I (mere conviction without knowledge, based on appearance and social prudence, which led Anne to break with Wentworth) and Persuasion II (persuasion with knowledge that changes one's whole schema of value). He grounds this in Wittgenstein's later view that meaning is use within a language game and a form of life, so 'persuasion,' 'constancy,' and 'only Anne' shift sense across the novel. Reading the plot via Cavell's 'comedy of remarriage,' he argues Anne and Wentworth's separation yields the self-knowledge that legitimates their reunion.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "Chapter 5 Twain’s Last Laugh" — Kristina Gehrman argues that reading Huck as a moral hero who overcomes racism is Twain's ironic trap. Using Arne Naess's idea of identification, Aristotle on habituation of character, and Iris Murdoch's 'just and loving attention,' she gives a developmentally attuned reading of Huck as a traumatized, morally immature, still-racist child whose regard for Jim never generalizes ('I knowed he was white inside'). Twain lures his white readers into identifying with Huck's supposed triumph, then exposes their own stunted moral growth about race; Jim is the only mature adult yet is barred from identification by the novel's racist caricature. The novel's greatness is Socratic and gadfly-like rather than triumphant.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Chapter 11 Socratic Irony in Twain’s Skeptical Religious Jeremiads" — Jacquette demands a precise definition of Twain's much-invoked irony, adopting Vlastos's/Quintilian's formula that irony says the contrary of what is meant while letting the real meaning be recovered. He classifies Twain's irony as local vs. global and comic vs. sober (tragic/historical): 'Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc' is globally ironic (falsely presented as de Conte's eyewitness manuscript), while the relic-mocking passages of 'The Innocents Abroad' (St. Luke's Madonna, kegs of true-cross nails, three skulls of John the Baptist) are local comic irony. Jacquette concludes Twain's irony is distinctively Socratic: like Socrates interpreting the Delphic oracle, Twain makes a moral and epistemic virtue of ridiculing experts who claim to know what no one can know about God, sin, and the afterlife.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 18 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Parker defends the coffeehouse as an accessible venue for real philosophy through Christopher Phillips's Socrates Café movement (and Marc Sautet's cafés-philos), arguing that Socratizing — sustained questioning that offers objections and alternatives, not mere talk — makes everyone a potential 'Socrates.' Answering the charge that amateur café philosophy is mere sophistry, he turns to Plato's Sophist to note the sophist is the one who takes payment and has an agenda, so it is salaried professors, not unpaid Phillips, who resemble sophists. Framing thoughtlessness (via Nietzsche's 'oblivion' and David Foster Wallace's cruise-ship essay) as philosophy's true adversary, he endorses a softened Socratic/Nozickian maxim that the unexamined life is simply not lived as fully.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 25 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Johnson argues that the Santa Claus lie is immoral and should be abandoned, giving three reasons: it is deceptive lying (Kant's absolute prohibition is too strong, but the lie lacks life-saving justification and functions as a Platonic 'noble lie' no more noble than a cult leader's); Santa robs parents of credit and warps children's moral development and trust, illustrated by anguished 'finding out' stories and Virginia O'Hanlon's letter; and it damages credulity, invoking Clifford's 'Ethics of Belief' against belief on insufficient evidence while James's 'Will to Believe' cannot rescue Santa since evidence against him is overwhelming. He recommends revealing the truth early, even via a Socratic-Method questioning game.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 31 "GARDENING" — Cotton reads the grower image in Plato's Phaedrus—the wise gardener who sows seed in proper soil for a slow harvest rather than the frivolous 'gardens of Adonis'—as Plato's model of philosophical education as natural growth. The educator plants logoi (discourse) in a 'proper soul,' where it must be cultivated by the learner's own reflection and eventually reproduces itself in others, against Thrasymachus's vessel model of pouring knowledge in. She connects this to the Republic's cave, the Apology's gadfly, and the Symposium/Theaetetus images of pregnancy and midwifery, then argues Plato's own aporetic, contradiction-laden dialogues and the corpus as a whole act as the wise grower, teaching readers to become 'gardeners of their own souls.'
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 19 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 17 "NOTES" — Matthews argues that certain children's books are 'subversive' in a Socratic sense: they problematize concepts adults assume they command, challenging adult epistemic authority the way Socrates exposed the pretended knowledge of Athens' elite. Morris the Moose raises Aristotelian questions of natural kinds and essence-versus-accident; Leese Webster probes the concept of art; The Shrinking of Treehorn destabilizes 'normal' child development; Frog and Toad's 'The Garden' dramatizes the post hoc, ergo propter hoc fallacy about causation. In the Ozma of Oz Tik-Tok discussion, nine-year-old Paul reconstructs an argument that only brains think, which Matthews aligns with Searle's claim in The Mystery of Consciousness that consciousness is caused by specific neurobiological processes; he explicitly distinguishes his subversive stories from those promoting Pyrrhonian skepticism or Protagorean relativism.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 9 "The Talking Cure for Our Culture" — William Young argues that South Park stands in the Socratic-Platonic tradition and that its critics repeat the charges (impiety, corrupting youth) that condemned Socrates in the Apology. Kyle and Stan's dialogues over euthanizing Stan's grandpa model Socratic questioning and thinking from others' perspectives, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty illustrates Arendt's banality of evil (Eichmann). Young adds a Freudian reading in which the show's vulgarity works like joke-telling to release repressed drives, so the crude cartoon actually serves the examined life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 73 "69. Larry David as Philosopher Interrogating Convention" — Carroll treats Curb Your Enthusiasm as a Kantian/Marxian 'critique'—an inquiry into the conditions of possibility—of everyday norms of civility, built on incongruity humor and Mary Douglas's theory of jokes as 'anti-rites.' Through episodes like the handicapped-stutterer, the new-house tour Larry refuses, the phone-call cutoff time, Ben Stiller's no-gifts party, and the buried five-wood, David shows that manners are non-necessary and arbitrary yet held in place only by intense (uncurbed) emotional 'enthusiasm,' epitomized by Susie Greene's operatic rage. Carroll answers the analytic skeptic by casting David's method as Socratic/maieutic (like Plato's Meno): the argument is completed in the reflective viewer's mind.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 83 "78. The Witness as Philosophy How Knowledge Is Constructed" — Cuddy asks what epistemology Blow built into The Witness's frustrating puzzles and its windmill videos (Burke, Feynman, Moriarty, Spira, Gangaji). He rejects the sophistic/Protagorean 'knowledge depends on the observer' reading (most puzzles have objective, inductive-and-deductive solutions, e.g. the yellow-glass bunker) and the strict scientific realism of the Burke video defended by Putnam's no-miracles argument. Using Plato's cave and the aporia of Socrates' Meno (the puzzle's 'ah-ha' epiphanies), and Kuhn's incommensurable paradigm shifts (the game's 'hard left turns' forcing players to overhaul their understanding), he concludes the game argues that true knowledge is attainable, individually and collectively, though reached by a nonlinear, paradigm-shifting route rather than pure realism or relativism.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 9 "1. Engaging Life Like the Doctor" — The chapter casts the Doctor as a 'flâneur' who teaches an engaged, critical-thinking way of life, illustrated through episodes like 'Blink,' 'Heaven Sent,' and 'Kerblam!' where the Doctor (and viewer) solve mysteries through trial and error. It uses Hume and William James to argue the mind actively constructs reality into a narrative, and pairs the Doctor with Socrates as a truth-seeking 'midwife' teacher who withholds answers so companions can learn by living rather than being told. The Doctor's rejection of Time Lord non-interference models the Socratic examined life of engaging the world to know oneself and others.

### Virtue Ethics (arete)

Virtue ethics, in the tradition stemming from Aristotle, locates the moral life in the cultivation of good character rather than in obedience to rules or the calculation of consequences. Its central notion is arete, or excellence, a stable disposition to feel and act well that is developed through habit and practice over time. On this view the key ethical question is what kind of person one should become, and virtues such as courage, temperance, and justice are the traits that enable a human being to live and function well. Aristotle sets out this approach in the Nicomachean Ethics, tying virtue to the fulfillment of our nature as rational, social beings.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 10 "George and Virtue—Like Oil and Water" — Daniel Barwick runs George through Aristotle's function argument and finds him wanting: a paradigm of 'the many' who thinks happiness is fortune and momentary victories over others (free parking, perfect airport pickups) rather than activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. His 'do the opposite' epiphany in 'The Opposite' embraces the more extreme vice rather than steering toward the rationally chosen mean, and his self-hatred, laziness, and pleasure-seeking fail all three of Aristotle's tips for hitting the mean. Since George will never practice virtuous action until it becomes habit, Barwick concludes George is doomed to his miserable existence - which is, conveniently for us, why he is funny.
- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 24 "Elaine, Kramer, and Newman Not Wise" — Aeon Skoble argues Seinfeld explicates Aristotelian virtue ethics against utilitarian and Kantian rivals: Jerry's 'I don't want to be an orgy guy' and George's fear of becoming 'one of those guys' ask what sort of person to be, not which rule to follow. George's 'do the opposite' in 'The Opposite' is an update of the Delphic oracle - only he who recognizes his own idiocy (Socratic ignorance) can act well, with Jerry deducing the logic and serving as his phronemos, alongside Superman. Elaine's rule-worship and Jujyfruits utilitarianism backfire, Kramer lacks the social dialectic virtue needs, and the ironic appeals to Newman as arbiter expose the paradox that choosing a role model wisely already requires the wisdom one lacks.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 22 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Aeon Skoble uses Tolkien's characters to defend Aristotelian virtue ethics against Kantian and utilitarian rivals. Sam's loyalty is a virtue because critically directed at a worthy friend while Wormtongue's loyalty to Saruman is not; Sméagol's instant murder of Déagol reveals prior vice that let the Ring corrupt him quickly, whereas Bilbo resists it for sixty years; Aragorn's temperance and teachableness contrast Boromir's resentment and pride. Working through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean (courage between cowardice and rashness), practical wisdom, and the phronemos as role model, he argues that rule-following cannot capture moral perception (do we owe truth to Black Riders?) and that utilitarianism absurdly requires Galadriel's foresight.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 19 "Kant, Aristotle, and the Cheater" — Answering Cal Ripken's Socratic question 'What is cheating?' (raised by Sammy Sosa's corked bat and Gaylord Perry's spitball), Randolph Feezell stages a dialogue between Abbey's Kantian absolutism, Trev's traditionalism, and Ron's win-at-all-costs realism. Kant's categorical imperative grounds the absolutist: intending to break a rule to gain an edge is making yourself an arbitrary exception to rules that bind all players equally. Aristotle's virtue ethics then lets the traditionalist say that some strategic rule-breaking belongs to a sport's 'prescriptive atmosphere' (stealing signs, the balk pickoff, catching framing), since honesty and courage are means between excess and defect guided by judgment rather than exceptionless rules, while corking a bat stays cheating because it defies the tradition and hides from umpires.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 11 "Why Not to Buy the Porsche" — Skoble uses Manhattan's confrontation scene — Isaac telling Yale 'you're too easy on yourself... you'd rather buy the Porsche' over the hominid skeleton — to build an account of integrity as fidelity to correct moral principles, requiring an integrated character in which reason and desire agree. He distinguishes integrity from mere consistency (the 'consistent Nazi') and from stubbornness, and models it on Plato's just person who 'harmonizes the three parts of himself'. Aristotle's account of habituation defends Isaac's slippery slope: Yale's repeated lies for expediency are forming the kind of character who would inform on friends, so integrity is an objective yardstick of a well-lived life, as Isaac's amends to Tracy at the end confirms.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 18 "“Just What They Say It for I Never Knew”" — South argues Allen's signature old recordings from the American songbook are a philosophical device grounded in Aristotle: the Rhetoric's view that emotions carry cognitive orientations that reshape judgment, and the Politics' claim that music forms character, explain why songs comment on the plots they score. He reads Hannah and Her Sisters through 'You Made Me Love You', 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered', and 'I'm in Love Again' — scoring Elliot's inconstancy, Mickey's 'You don't deserve Cole Porter' judgment of Holly, and her growth into someone whose new musical taste signals ethical maturity — and Everyone Says I Love You as a darker cycle where fantasy and finitude ('It's Later Than You Think') drive the compulsion to love again. The happy ending is precisely why Allen called the film a 'cop out': its music says love fades and is out of our control, while the plot pretends otherwise.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 43 "NOTES" — Argues Snape's redemption is gradual virtue-building rather than instant transformation, since vice and virtue are habits built up over time and his resentments persist even as his actions serve the good. His doe Patronus, matching Lily's, manifests Aristotle's beloved as a second self, his remorse, an emotion he shares with Harry but Voldemort cannot feel, begins to knit his damaged soul whole, and Harry's forgiveness, naming his son Albus Severus for 'the bravest man I ever knew', completes the arc love began.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 31 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Jonathan Sanford distinguishes necessity of the end, of compulsion, and of nature to argue Christ's passion was both necessary and free: justice requires reparation for the harmony Adam and Eve broke, God cannot simply waive it without making a mockery of sin, yet no compulsion operates on Christ — unlike the blind inner drives Nietzsche's will to power or Schopenhauer's will would represent. Using Aristotle, he argues Christ's fully virtuous character (practical wisdom plus courage and temperance become a 'second nature') makes disobedience nearly unimaginable, and his divinity makes it impossible, so his choice 'could not have been different' precisely because it was perfectly free; the Gethsemane agony shows not division in the God-man but the difficulty of holding his human and divine wills in unity.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 81 "Superheroes and the Ring of Gyges" — The chapter's heart: Glaucon's Ring of Gyges and 'harsh view' of human nature — justice as the weak's compact against the strong, a lineage running from Hobbes to Nietzsche — are powerfully denied by superheroes and by Frodo, who resist the power of the ring. Socrates' tripartite soul and justice-as-psychic-harmony are read as preparation for the Republic's real answer, the ascent to the eternal Form of the Good, which the chapter extends through Aristotle's teleology and virtue ethics: super-powered people, denied any standard social role, must wrestle with what their potential is for — from Kingdom Come's retired Superman and Spider-Man 2's Peter Parker to Astro City's Samaritan, with Uncle Ben's 'With great power comes great responsibility' as the upshot.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 99 "Reasons to Be Moral" — Extracts two candidate answers from Spider-Man — Reason One, that immorality rebounds on you (Uncle Ben's death), tested and weakened by the Ms. Poore poverty-theft case, and Spider-Man's agonized "Because it is right" to the Green Goblin, the Kant-and-Bradley motive of duty — and finds both insufficient to show morality is rational. It then tests Plato's answer that only the moral have harmony of soul (reason governing appetite and spirit) against Flash Thompson and self-forgiving sinners, and Aristotle's "virtue is its own reward" against the thought experiment of virtuous Arachnid-Girl rotting in prison while the fraudulent Norm Osborne flourishes.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 131 "Switching Identities" — Maps Superman and Batman onto Plato and Aristotle — the otherworldly philosopher of the heavenly Good versus the this-worldly master of logic and applicable science — then argues that Bruce Wayne's years of intentional self-transformation may have swapped the mask, making Batman the core identity and Bruce the disguise. With Mark Waid, he sees Superman inwardly embracing his alien otherness as the path of authenticity, both cases yielding a fused "heterosis" of identities; Aristotle, Pascal and William James back the closing lesson that who we are is a matter of what we repeatedly do, so every mask may eventually become the face.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 21 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Bill Davis argues that Narnia works as a classical moral-education environment: against Experiment House's science-worship, Narnia supplies the three ingredients Aristotle and Aquinas require, namely instruction, virtuous exemplars to imitate (Reepicheep's courage, Puddleglum's temperance), and habituation through repeated right action, which together transform Peter's indecision, Edmund's treachery, Lucy's envy, and Jill's timidity. What finally lasts beyond Narnia, he contends, is a transforming encounter with Aslan: Eustace's dragon skin torn off by the Lion, Jill's drink at the stream where 'there is no other stream,' and Digory's tearful confession. He closes by arguing today's self-esteem-based character education cannot replicate this, since it pursues virtue from love of self rather than love of the good.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 13 "Poker and Philosophy" — Young reads David Sklansky's fundamental theorem of poker — play as if you could see all the cards — through Aristotle and Husserl. Aristotle's phronesis and virtue-as-habituation explain how excellent players come to perceive the particulars (pot odds, opponent tendencies, the best possible hand) and stay unharmed even when losing with the best play, while Husserl's Cartesian Meditations, translated hand-by-hand into poker terms, supply analogical appresentation for knowing the other minds seated across the table. Chris Moneymaker's 2003 'Bluff of the Century' all-in with nothing against Sammy Farha shows how bluffing randomizes play and lets you shape the truth you seek, until a slow-played quad aces ends the night in Socratic humility about the limits of knowledge.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 26 "U2 and Philosophy" — Werther answers Tollefsen with Aristotle's Politics: musical images of character effect real 'change[s] of soul', so a three-premise argument concludes that repeated exposure to U2's images of fine character and good action can habituate delight in virtue - King's courage in 'Pride (In the Name of Love)' (whatever the botched time of day, and as proved when Adam Clayton stepped between Bono and an FBI-confirmed death threat), the indignation and shame at global poverty in 'Crumbs from Your Table', and the compassion of 'Miracle Drug' for the locked-in writer Christopher Nolan. 'Exit' purges the band's demons and 'Until the End of the World' offers purification through holy fear, matching the medical and religious readings of Aristotelian catharsis. C.S. Lewis's Abolition of Man closes the case: without the aid of trained emotions the intellect is powerless, so a culture raised on U2's feelings may be better prepared to act well than one raised on syllogisms alone.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 14 "“Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place" — Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics: the survivors' mall orgy curdles into boredom ('What have we done to ourselves?'), illustrating pleonexia, the graspingness for more than one's share of the goods of fortune that Aristotle roots in an unlimited desire for mere living - which may even explain why Romero's dead return, grasping from beyond the grave for more un-death. Aristotle's dismissal of the life of enjoyment as fit for cattle, his account of eudaimonia as the life in which our rational capacities flourish, and his defense of acquisition bounded by the good life explain why unlimited consumption zombifies the living, and why Peter and Fran must finally leave the mall empty-handed.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 18 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Taliaferro and Le Gall rebut Paul Johnson's 1958 charge that Doctor No combines 'the sadism of a schoolboy bully', adolescent sex longings, and suburban snobbery. They show Bond kills for justice rather than spite (his reluctant assignment against von Hammerstein in 'For Your Eyes Only'), that Colonel Sun repudiates de Sadean torture before dying, and that the disturbing 'semi-rape' passage of The Spy Who Loved Me reflects Vivienne Michel's voice, not Bond's conduct. They read Bond's eros as an ironic use of the medieval courtly-love and Mariology tradition in which sex redeems 'lost women' like Pussy Galore, defend his dress and manners through the ancient heroic tradition (Theseus's fatal neglect of the white sails, Leonidas combing his beard at Thermopylae), and conclude Bond is a chivalric, comic hero - a 'delightful impossibility' in Aristotle's Poetics' sense who embodies Socratic soldierly virtue and Platonic optimism.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 27 "Lessons Learned" — McAleer maps The Office onto Aristotle's ethics: David Brent is the buffoon who is 'the slave of his sense of humor,' Gareth the literalist boor who cannot take a joke, and Tim the ready wit whose irony responds to the situation — together illustrating that a virtue is a qualitative mean of acting and feeling appropriately, fixed by practical wisdom rather than rules. That humor cannot be codified mirrors the uncodifiability of Aristotelian ethics, and wit's very status as a virtue shows Aristotle's morality is broader than modern duty-and-outcome ethics: it aims at the flourishing (eudaimonia) of the whole person.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 29 "Questioning Everything The Birds" — The Deavels argue that Hitchcock's suspense is fundamentally epistemological. In the social world, heroines in love - Constance in Spellbound, Lina in Suspicion, Rose in The Wrong Man - must weigh mounting evidence of their beloveds' guilt against the Aristotelian premise that character is consistent because virtue and vice are habits: Constance rightly bets that J.B.'s gentleness with her proves he is no murderer, Lina reasonably concludes Johnnie may poison her, and Rose survives only by inventing a persecutory 'they'. With The Birds the question widens to nature itself: Mrs. Bundy's ornithology assumes past bird behavior predicts future behavior, and the film's terror is Hume's worry that causal order may be an unfounded projection, leaving Mitch to stake his family's escape on the humble observed pattern that attacks come in waves.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 26 "“Just Like Mary Shelley, Just Like Frankenstein”" — Chuck Ward uses 'Mama Tried' (the meek family's rebel son doing life without parole) and the mysterious birthmark in 'Mississippi Half-Step Uptown Toodleloo' to ask whether character is fixed from birth, setting the songs' fatalism against Aristotle's account of character as habituated choice and Plato's claim that traits tend to be inherited. He surveys behavioral genetics, twin studies, The Bell Curve, and the supposed 'criminality gene' before arguing that genetic determinism is a mistaken reductionism: like the groovy atmosphere of a Dead show, which shapes the very individuals who produce it, complex systems admit top-down causation, so genes never act alone. The chapter's payoff is that the songs' studied ambiguity — mama tried, yet 'that leaves no one but me to blame' — shows art expressing, rather than resolving, the tension between free will and determinism.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 23 "“Unchained” The Inspired Anger of a Religious Man" — Dan Haggerty uses Aristotle's account of anger as a virtuous mean—felt at the right people, time, and degree—to show that songs like 'San Quentin,' 'The Man in Black,' and 'Oney' express justified anger at real injustices done to prisoners and workingmen, contra pop psychology's blanket rejection of anger. He then coins 'inspired anger' (drawing on Plato's Ion: the artist possessed and blown away by emotion): a painful, hopeless desire for a justice or restoration that can never be, exemplified by Cash's 'Hurt' video and its regret over irrecoverable time—mourning rather than self-pity or depression. The chapter closes with 'Unchained' as a prayer showing how a Christian like Cash can live with this futile desire rather than argue it away.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 27 "Redemption" — Stephen Bilynskyj tests John Hick's soul-making theodicy—that God allows suffering because virtues like courage, temperance, and compassion need pain to form—against Cash's life and songs. Using Aristotle on habituation by pleasure and pain (Cash's first amphetamine euphoria and the ostrich-attack painkillers as missed occasions for temperance) and Aquinas on innate aptitude and divinely infused virtue, he argues virtue can form without suffering (by genes or miracle), so soul-making alone cannot justify evil, as Cash himself implies about his mother's grief after Jack's death. Cash instead locates redemption in Christ's suffering ('Redemption,' 'Why Me, Lord?'), while the intervention by his son John Carter shows pain still occasioning real growth in temperance.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 22 "Learning from Our Mistakes" — Tamplin defends democracy through the Baltar election: Roslin's attempted theft failed, the voters' bad choice produced the New Caprica occupation, and this is exactly what Plato and Aristotle predicted of democracy as the deviant rule of the many, contrasted with Aristotle's polity aimed at the common advantage and a virtue 'every city' must care for. A thought experiment — an infallible computer advising citizens on every choice — shows that following it would abolish democracy, whose value lies not in results but in Aristotle's freedom, 'living as one wants.' Only by being allowed to frak things up can citizens learn from their mistakes, the road Apollo points to in his 'Crossroads' trial speech about collective shame, which is why Baltar's acquittal is a good sign.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 9 "Dorothy Growing Up in the Land of Oz" — McCall and Auxier use Aristotle's virtue ethics to unpack the Wizard's claim to be 'a good man but a bad wizard' and to argue that no external token—the diploma, heart watch, or medal—can confer virtue, which is cultivated only through practice and experience. Each companion lacks something specific: the Scarecrow the intellectual virtues and phronesis, the Tin Man the feelings and stable states of character that regulate emotion, the Lion the sophrosyne that balances thinking and feeling into courage as the mean between recklessness and cowardice. Aristotle's three grades of friendship (utility, pleasure, virtue) frame the companions' bond with Dorothy, and MacIntyre's account of virtues internal to practices explains why the Wizard's public recognition still matters. Dorothy herself begins as the child Aristotle says cannot yet be virtuous—fleeing Miss Gulch in Kansas—but by defending Toto against the Lion and leading the quest she grows into a responsible moral agent, which is what her delayed homecoming requires.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 19 "Roll Credits" — Dunn contrasts Baum's book, where evil is wonderfully 'small'—Dorothy melts the Witch in a fit of righteous anger at a stolen Silver Shoe, and personal plus social virtues (kindness repaid by the field-mice Queen) reliably conquer it—with the 1939 film, which smuggles back the 'heartaches and nightmares' Baum banished and resolves the Witch only by an accidental stroke of luck. He sorts Oz's harms into moral evils (the Witch's enslavements, the Wizard's frauds) and natural evils (the cyclone, the Deadly Poppy Field), cites Hume's catalogue of the world's ills, and observes that Baum needs neither Kant's postulate of God and a future life to join virtue with happiness nor John Hick's 'vale of soul-making' theodicy—Oz simply delivers the reward. Dorothy's abundant virtue at age five rebukes Aristotle (children, he says, cannot be virtuous or happy) and instead embodies Rousseau's Emile, natural goodness uncorrupted by civilization, while Chesterton's Doctrine of Conditional Joy and Tolkien's insistence on serious, non-technological magic frame the Old-World Christian outlook that Baum's demystified American fairy tale—and the movie's ending—quietly betray.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 16 "This Is Really Happening (So Do Something)" — Milsky argues that Radiohead practice what environmental virtue ethics preaches, organizing the chapter around Aristotle's akrasia (Nicomachean Ethics VII): Sting, who champions rainforests while advertising Jaguar and topping the 'dirtiest band' carbon table, acts against his own better judgment, whereas Radiohead — confronted with an audit showing their 2003 and 2006 tours emitted roughly 11,368 tons of CO2, mostly from fans driving — changed their actual practice (venues near public transit, car-pool lots, sea freight instead of air, LED lighting and auxilary power units). He reads the King Canute imagery of The Eraser and lines from 'The Clock' and 'And It Rained All Night' as environmental narrative in the tradition of Thoreau's Walden and Leopold's Sand County Almanac, obligating listeners to act or risk akrasia themselves, and presents the band's Friends of the Earth 'Big Ask' commitment as linking environmental virtue to human flourishing. 'Idioteque'''s 'this is really happening' becomes the wake-up call to the akratic fan driving to Lollapalooza with a bottled water.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 24 "“Livin’ and Dyin’ in Three-Quarter Time”" — Randall Auxier uses Buffett's catalog to think about fortune and fate, reading Buffett's bold career moves (walking out on Nashville for the beach, later annexing it via 'It's Five o'Clock Somewhere') through Machiavelli's advice to marry Fortuna and master her tricks with virtù. Against Aristotle's demanding answer that only aretē, moral excellence, defends happiness against bad luck, he takes Vico's middle path: natural causes, moral causes, and the occasions of fortune are gathered under providence, so Buffett's seaplane crash ('God, Buddha, St. Christopher, my guardian angel... luck, and the United States Navy water-survival training') shows any fate can be turned to good ends for others. Sorting Buffett's songs into places, times, meetings, sentiments, and thoughts — the key sentiment being the wistful — the chapter lands on contentment as gratitude: being 'livin' and dyin' in three-quarter time.'
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 17 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Eyestone argues Transformers are genuinely alive with souls by applying Aristotle's De Anima: self-motion, perception, and intellect fit Ratchet (who tells Buster 'I'm a machine, and I hear you!'), and even the troublesome nutritive faculty is secured, since Energon ingestion, agelessness, and building each other suit naturally immortal, semimortal beings whose reproduction resembles Primus's creation. He extends arete to machines - Megatron has the excellence of a military leader but not of a person, while Optimus's chosen, trained goodness (Grimlock's 'Autobot training,' the Aerialbots' decision in 'War Dawn') makes him virtuous - and answers his title question 'why not?', since Aristotle's mortal soul gives Transformers no worse a shot at heaven than we have.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 29 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Plauche grounds Optimus Prime's line 'Freedom is the right of all sentient beings' in 'Aristotelian liberalism': since Energon, like our food, is scarce and requires labor and creativity, any volitional artificial life needs a moral code whose standard is flourishing (following Foot's natural goodness), cultivating intellectual and moral virtues from prudence, independence, and honesty to benevolence and courage. Ricardo and Mises's law of association - illustrated by Ratchet and a human mechanic both profiting from specialization despite Ratchet's absolute superiority - plus the ruinous cost of war give even superior aliens reason to respect our rights to life, liberty, and property rather than enslave or exterminate us, as Megatron would.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 10 "Explaining Moral Doubt" — Steven Gimbel reads the Formidable Opponent segment - red-tie Colbert debating blue-tie Colbert - as a glimpse of authentic moral deliberation that the flip-flop-phobic punditry satirized by the show (and Jon Stewart's Crossfire rant) has abandoned. Moral doubt is good because perspectives are partial and the Enlightenment 'marketplace of ideas' of Locke and Mill tests beliefs only through challenge. It has a source: 'morally right' bundles five dimensions - the actor's character shaped by habit (Aristotle's virtue ethics), the act itself judged by Kant's categorical imperative, the pleasure-versus-pain consequences tallied Bentham-style, the rights of the person affected from Locke and Hobbes's social contract, and the special care obligations of close relationships (Noddings and Ruddick) - and hard cases like abortion and flag burning are exactly where these dimensions pull apart. So emulate the dueling Colberts: fear not the flip-flop, since deciding which value trumps which requires open-minded conversation with oneself.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 12 "Sin, Play, and the “Synagogues of Satan”" — Rachael Sotos argues the Report performs Platonic play: like the divine puppet of Plato's Laws with its competing cords, Colbert reveals what moves us (fear, hope, the ThreatDown bears, the 'golden cord' of the good) and so teaches freedom through play. Colbert's pompous self-authority - claiming to be 'the canon and measure' of virtue in I Am America - parodies Aristotle's serious man (spoudaios, megalopsychos) and the sophists Protagoras and Prodicus with their Orpheus voices, proving Heraclitus right that 'time is a child at play' and Aristotle wrong that play is mere medicinal rest. Tracking the war on fun from Chrysostom through Aquinas's eutrapelia (there is sin in a lack of play) to Erasmus's Praise of Folly and the Puritans' ban on theaters as 'Synagogues of Satan,' she reads Colbert's playing-at-sin - the man-seed eugenics bit, the 'black friend' boasts, the Ellen DeGeneres Paradox on Wikiality - as Erasmian folly that heals America's Puritan hangover in the culture wars.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 9 "12" — Four 'Phase Three' essays on world conquest. Terjesen asks whether Doctor Doom's magnanimity (Aristotle's great-souledness, contra the unity-of-virtues thesis Aquinas held and Philippa Foot qualified) makes him less villainous than The Authority, whose purely consequentialist paternalism - like Doom's Emperor Doom or Ozymandias's plot - usurps a free choice no mere power can justify. Barringer reads Marvel's Civil War through Hobbes: the Stamford explosion and unrestrained superpowers recreate the state of nature, the Registration Act is the surrender of freedom to a sovereign, and Stark, Richards, and Pym repeat Hobbes's flawed faith in 'scientific' deductive politics, sealed by the clone-Thor killing of Goliath. Hillerbrand and Sandburg pit Rorschach's Kantian deontology (no compromise, not even to save the world) against Ozymandias's utilitarian murder of three million New Yorkers in Watchmen, arguing via Laplace's Demon that even Dr. Manhattan - nihilist or Schopenhauerian recluse - cannot verify the outcome, so watchmen can be trusted only by knowing their limits. Ostrander's fictional NSC interview has Amanda Waller's Suicide Squad defended with Benthamite utility, the rejection of natural rights as 'nonsense on stilts,' and the Augustinian just-war criteria of just cause, right intent, and proportionality, while the interviewer exposes how conveniently those limits bend.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 19 "This Is Our World" — Miguel Sicart reads the 'Gnome Tea Party' — dozens of nearly nude gnome warriors parading in Ironforge to protest Warrior-class nerfs until Blizzard banned their accounts — as non-violent protest in the tradition of Thoreau and Gandhi. Against Blizzard's models of players-as-consumers and players-as-troublemakers, which he traces to Huizinga's Homo Ludens, he argues that players are Homo poieticus: creative beings who make the values they play by and act on them. Using the 'Flourishing Ethics' framework built from Aristotle's virtue ethics and Wiener's information ethics, he concludes that WoW's architectures of control and account-banning are an unethical design that damages players' capacity to flourish — Azeroth is our world too.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 12 "You Don’t Have to Be Like Him to Like Him" — Levitt reads Monk through Aristotle's virtue ethics: a man of character whose police virtues survive Trudy's murder but whose phobias produce akrasia — in the pilot he knows he must descend the germ-filled sewer to save Sharona and freezes anyway, doing the right thing only at agonizing cost. Virtue as habit and the golden mean (friendliness as the mean between obsequiousness and standoffishness) frame his slow progress toward acting rightly without thinking, which is also why Stottlemeyer cannot recommend his reinstatement — he doubts the illness, not the man. Aristotle's three friendships sort Monk's relationships: utility (the department, employer Sharona), pleasure, and virtue — Natalie, who after watching Monk save Julie's fish over the priceless moon rock saw her late husband's goodness in him. Ethos, pathos, logos and catharsis then explain viewer identification: watching Monk move from akrasia toward balance (Dr. Kroger's 'N. Hope' note that turns out to mean New Hope) lets audiences identify with, and be ennobled by, a character we would never want to be.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 21 "Redemption and Hope for the Future" — Peters applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of courage — the mean between confidence and fear, shown only in facing an honorable death in war for a noble motive — to Colin MacLeod's two-thousand-year hunt for Marcus Octavius, the Immortal Roman who killed his wife Moya, in Highlander: The Search for Vengeance. Because MacLeod fights from pain and rage, 'like wild beasts,' and secretly seeks death as refuge from grief ('to seek death as a refuge from poverty, or love... is not the act of a brave man'), Aristotle would judge him a coward despite his fearlessness — Amergan the spirit guide diagnoses him the same way. Redemption comes only when Dahlia and the villagers threatened by Marcus's new Rome give him a noble cause and hopefulness: he becomes their general, fights with discipline instead of rage, and turns Marcus's own quickening to destroying the virus, illustrating the chapter's closing thought that for an Immortal dying is easy and living courageously is hard.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 19 "Forgiveness and the Fenway Faithful" — Rory Kraft uses Aristotle's virtue ethics to explain why Red Sox Nation forgave Tim Wakefield (whose mistake Aaron Boone turned into the 2003 ALCS-ending homer) and Ted Williams, but scapegoated Bill Buckner for 'the error' and eventually cast off Manny Ramirez. Because Aristotle judges a complete life, one swallow does not make a summer, Buckner's .991 fielding percentage and 2,715 hits should contextualize his lapse, yet some acts are bad without degrees like Aristotle's adultery, theft and murder, and a World Series-deciding error crossed that line. Kraft distinguishes Aristotle's categories, Wakefield's mistake (ignorance of Boone's changed plan) versus Buckner's misadventure (contrary to reasonable expectation) versus Manny's voluntary injustices, concluding that learning when to forgive players who are family taught the Nation what forgiveness itself means, sealed by Buckner's 2008 standing ovation.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 33 "Tie Goes to the Runner" — St. Martin runs the Fenway 'pink hat' controversy through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the virtuous fan is the mean between the deficient bandwagoner who waves at NESN cameras mid-pitch and the excessive diehard who memorizes Dice-K's ERA to belittle others. Terry Francona's courage in sending Dave Roberts in the 2004 ALCS (versus a reckless Ortiz steal attempt) illustrates virtue as the mean between cowardice and foolhardiness, and Aristotle's contrast between the love of honor and the love of contemplation shows both pink hatters and stats-obsessed diehards err by making fandom about themselves. She concludes that accepting fans in any color hat is the truly virtuous mean.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 14 "“Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place" — Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead's survivors, who loot the mall, gorge, grow bored, and degenerate into glitzy despair beside the zombies clawing to get back in, through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics. Peter's 'They're us' is glossed by pleonexia, the grasping disposition to want more, which Aristotle roots in being serious about mere living rather than living well, and the quartet's hedonistic 'sweet life' is the life of enjoyment Aristotle dismisses as fit for cattle because it atrophies the rational capacities that make us human. Romero is no Puritan scold: material goods remain instrumentally useful and the mall a sanctuary, but like Aristotle he shows a life of unlimited acquisition is a kind of living death, which is why Peter and Fran must leave empty-handed.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 19 "Cold Clammy Consistency" — Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents because they meet Aristotle's test of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgment that 'evildoers... taste better') and retain free will, since their blood-lust is a craving not a compulsion and Louis's rat diet in Interview with the Vampire, like Angel's in Buffy, proves an alternative exists. TASTE, full potential, and spiritual peace all fail to justify human blood, because killing a person brings more unnecessary suffering than killing a rat, the same suffering-based principle that condemns factory farming. The 'cold clammy consistency' punchline: since humans need not eat meat, condemning vampire blood-drinkers while dining on chicken, pork, and beef is hypocrisy, because we are vampiric too and only our choice of which life to ingest separates the monstrous from the virtuous.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 13 "Extra Time" — Kent argues soccer is Aristotle's favorite sport because everything in both is organized around the goal: the four causes explain shinguards (plastic, curved shape, Mitre's workers, protection) and the game itself, with the final cause—scoring—defining a thing's identity and goodness, so two differently made balls are both soccerballs if kicked toward a net. Soccer best fulfills sport's three purposes (physical and moral discipline, theatrical imitation with catharsis, recreation): its ninety minutes of uninterrupted continuity force hundreds of renewed acts of self-mastery in Aristotle's sense of courage and the right amount, its single referee with limited powers embodies Aristotle's preferred limited monarchy, and Argentina's sportsmanlike throw-in returning the ball after Cameroon kicks it out for an injured player exemplifies equity—making a rightful exception to the letter of the law. Own goals, where a defender's error harms his own side, supply the hamartia of Aristotelian tragedy, giving fans a healthy catharsis of pity and fear.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 29 "The Final Whistle" — Andrew Lambert defends the rationality of being a football fan by updating Aristotle: living well in a liberal consumer democracy demands an accessible source of beauty, catharsis, belonging, public discourse, and altruism, and fandom trains exactly these sensibilities — from his childhood prayers for Everton to the 1914 Christmas Truce match and supporters' trusts that own clubs like Exeter City. The mature 'fan of football' takes an ironic view of the 'loyal fan's' tribal passions, gaining the practical wisdom that keeps rivalry (the Liverpool–Everton derby, the 1969 'Football War') from curdling into violence. Fandom thus answers critics who dismiss it as consumerist escapism or bad faith.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 7 "Free Your Mind, and Your Roundhouse Will Follow" — Young argues that dojo courtesy is not the fantasy that good manners win fights (Napoleon and the Karate Kid's Johnny lost on skill, not rudeness) but the framing of a craft within a way of life. He maps Aristotle's techne/ethos distinction onto the Japanese jutsu/do pairing to show founders like Kano, Funakoshi and Ueshiba treated fighting as one part of a whole ethical character, reads his seiza apology to an injured yellow belt through Confucian ren, li, yi and shu, and traces Shinto purity into the sincerity (kime) of committed sparring. His black-belt humiliation by seniors becomes Zen's 'courtesy of brutal': ego-deflating violence that trains no-mindedness (muga, Takuan Soho's fudoshin).
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 17 "The Way of the Place" — Beattie uses Henri Lefebvre's account of the production of space to read the dojo as a 'differential space' practitioners actively create against abstract, conformist space. He shows how bow-ins, founder portraits, Japanese counting, mats, dogi and belt hierarchies mark ownership, bind the school to a lineage, separate 'dojo' from 'street', and shape bodies and safety (with Kendo's door-side seating and MMA's display of physique as hierarchy written into space). Play matters too: Aristotle's point that virtues are built by habit explains how playing at combat in a safe place breeds real courage, and the whole exercise teaches a moving balance between inside and outside.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 25 "Jousting for Virtue" — Farrell argues that the medieval code of chivalry is a living case study for Aristotle's virtue ethics: Lancelot, 'mekest in hall and sternest to his foe', embodies the paradox C.S. Lewis names as meek and fierce 'to the nth', which Farrell reads as Aristotle's courage, the golden mean between cowardice and rashness, exercised 'to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive'. The joust, meanwhile, was a proving ground where knightly virtues became second nature through habituated practice, since as Aristotle says 'it is no easy task to be good'. Western martial arts, he concludes, are 'moral kung fu': a fencing match with one's own standards of virtue.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 26 "Boxing, a School for Virtues" — Marino answers colleagues who call college boxing 'teaching violence' with an Aristotelian defense: courage is the mean between fearlessness and excessive fear, and the ring is one of the few workshops where fear is actually practiced. He cites Wacquant's boxing gym as 'a school of morality' in Durkheim's sense, Rotella's 'education at the fights', and boxers like Maja Cavlovic and George Foreman on how training takes over when fear hits, to argue boxing forges emotional self-command. His challenge to his own students: 'How can you be consistently honest or just if you don't have the mettle to take a hit?'
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 11 "In All Fucking Seriousness" — Arp asks why well-placed 'fucks' in Onion headlines like 'Guy In Philosophy Class Needs To Shut The Fuck Up' are funny, and answers with the golden mean traced to Aristotle and Confucius, who both prized self-control and being a good role model to children: swearing is virtuous when it hits the mean between the vice of too much (gangsta rap's every-other-word profanity, the cemetery gardener's rant, Glengarry Glen Ross) and the vice of too little. He sorts Onion stories into vice tables—'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer' illustrates the vice of cowardice, with courage as the hitting-the-mark mean—and concludes that a well-placed fuck is both funny and virtuous precisely because so many people treat the word as taboo.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 22 "World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent" — Dan Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant, uses Onion medical stories — 'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer,' the 'Vehicular Manslaughter Doctor,' animal hoarder Tricia McCory's 'I'm A Diseased And Deformed Animal Lover,' and the Terry Schiavo American Voices — to survey how end-of-life decisions actually get made. He runs each dilemma through Mill's consequentialism, Kant's deontology, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (with Monty Python's Philosopher's Song as running gag), then through Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of medical ethics, showing that McCory's kindness to dying animals fails autonomy and nonmaleficence because kindness can be cruel. The chapter closes by restoring 'euthanasia' to its Greek meaning of 'good death,' arguing that accepting the 100 percent death rate means planning ahead with living wills and honest bad-news delivery rather than dying tube-filled in an ICU.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Smith reads the Doctor–Rose tragedy through Kantian deontology: shaped by Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's virtue ethics into a good will, both must still choose duty over inclination, so in 'Parting of the Ways' and the Battle of Canary Wharf in 'Doomsday' they each act from the categorical imperative — sacrificing their love to save humanity — because love, as Kant warns, impels partiality. Even in 'Journey's End' the Doctor sends Rose to Pete's World with the meta-crisis Doctor for the greater good, ending alone under Kant's starry heavens and the moral law within.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 25 "Why the Doctor Is So Special" — Applying Singer's animal-liberation concept of speciesism — judging moral worth by capacity to feel pain rather than by intelligence or likeness — the authors argue the Daleks are 'super-speciesist' and that Lumic's emotional inhibitors make the Cybermen the same failure, unable to share a universe with unlike beings. Since emotions are judgments that can be educated into fitting responses (Nussbaum, Aristotle), and since Daleks infused with Rose's or Diagoras's DNA collapse into empathetic beings, the chapter concludes that emotion and empathy are why the Daleks will never win and why the Doctor, marked by his companions, is special among Time Lords.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 34 "I Am the Bad Wolf" — Answers Davros's charge that the Doctor fashions companions into weapons by examining his character through virtue ethics: his unifying virtue is Heideggerian 'authentic concern', always offering aggressors like the Nestene or the Sycorax a choice so they become genuinely responsible, as in the fly-swatting thought experiment. Companions instead act from compassion, which lacks impartiality and produces the 'Bad Wolf Syndrome' (Rose's Dalek genocide, Martha's Osterhagen Key, Jack's warp star). Since for Aristotle a friend is 'another himself', the companions' actions are in a sense the Doctor's own yet founded on a distorted disposition, which is why he runs from his past.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 16 "The Spice of Meaning" — Mines Dune for an account of the meaningful life by contrasting the Harkonnens, who amass power for its own sake and grind Yueh's very identity to dust, with the Fremen, whose rigid rituals give meaning but suffocate anyone who lives entirely inside them—with Duke Leto's abolition of the beggars' water-towel custom as the failure case in between. Following Aristotle's method of starting from 'the views of the wise,' the chapter argues virtue is an open-ended, formulaless skill: rising above inherited identities while repairing the social bonds they sustain, as Paul and Jessica do by breaking selected Fremen rules and leaving the sietch stronger. The worm-rider, feet shifting on sand above a creature that can never be fully controlled, is the closing image of a struggle that never finally resolves.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 17 "Alone into the Desert" — Audits Duniverse lives by Socrates's standard—the condition of the soul over wealth and power, with justice, courage, temperance, and wisdom—finding Baron Harkonnen utterly wanting, 'Leto the Just' compromised by forgery and concubinage, Paul unjust in his myth-making holy war (though Plato's Republic would smile on ruling myths), and the Fremen admirable in temperance and courage but fatally sure of themselves where Socrates prized knowing that you do not know. Aristotle's function argument and golden mean follow: Paul's first worm-ride is courage between rashness and cowardice, but Paul's and Leto II's extreme, humanity-saving selflessness has no excess to moderate and so breaks the doctrine of the mean. The author concludes Socrates is too harsh and Aristotle closer, yet even he fails: sometimes the best life requires extreme virtue and even injustice, as with the two Atreides emperors.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 18 "Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love" — Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing).
