- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 23 "Getting Tough and Getting Even" — Jordan Pascoe uses the 'Like a Virgin' purity test — Meg's fake 48 making her a 'slut' while a low score would make a guy a stud — to argue slut shaming strips girls of Kantian personhood, treating as things those autonomous beings who must be respected as ends in themselves. Kant's bleak view of sex as a desire for a body rather than a person explains why Tad's drugging and popsicle-video blackmail of Carmen reduce her to an object, and why objectification goes viral: once an object of one person's appetite, Kant warns, a person 'can be treated and used as such by everyone.' Catherine MacKinnon's power-based account then explains the double standard — men's pleasure in forcing the world to conform turns promiscuous men into studs and promiscuous women into sluts — so the fault lies with the slut sneezers, never Meg, Carmen, or Veronica, who must 'get tough, get even' to demand respect.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 20 "Back to the Rough Ground!" — Finnegan applies Wittgenstein's language games and 'back to the rough ground' to argue that Ford, Sizemore, and the Man in Black are captivated by an 'ideal' transcendent narrative, while marginalized hosts Dolores and Maeve gain traction precisely from their lostness. Dolores refuses the damsel role by grabbing a gun in Pariah ('I imagined a story where I didn't have to be the damsel') and Maeve seizes admin privileges to 'write my own fucking story,' each inventing new language games. Drawing on Mulvey's male gaze, Finnegan casts their objectified position as closer to women's experience, and reads them as using the master's tools to dismantle the master's house.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 25 "In Closing, The Naked Truth" — Meyer argues the hosts' nudity is rarely gratuitous, sorting it into three categories using theorists of the nude in art. Drawing on Kenneth Clark's naked/nude distinction, the posed, idealized, 'made' Dolores in 'The Original' is the nude as artform; using John Berger's Ways of Seeing, the brothel and El Lazo orgy scenes and the bathing Armistice are the nude as male sexual dominance and objectification. Finally, invoking Leo Steinberg's account of Christ's nudity as incarnation, Meyer reads the naked awakening of Maeve, Hector, and Armistice as signaling machines 'becoming human,' concluding humans' duplicity, not nakedness, is the true shame.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 13 "Notes" — A mother-daughter pair tracks Wonder Woman's and Harley Quinn's costume histories (the 1990s Artemis-era near-thong Diana, the New 52 brothel-styled Harley) and argues with Aristotle that sexualized drawing strips both characters of phronesis, the practical wisdom a virtuous agent needs - the wisdom by which an outmatched Wonder Woman talks Strife into carrying her to safety and Harley exploits the Joker's vanity to beat him. The paradox: the more provocatively each is drawn, the less she can succeed as moral hero or anti-hero, since objectification replaces goal-directed cunning with one-dimensional sex display. The New 52's armor-clad, Hephaestus-consulting Wonder Woman shows phronesis restored.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Brake applies Zizek's distinction between symptom and fetish to Grant Morrison's treatment of Wonder Woman: in Final Crisis, making her Darkseid's masked, bondage-suited thrall is a symptomal reading that forces the repressed kinky truth of Marston's origin to the surface, while the industry's chant that she is a 'feminist icon' works as a fetish - a fetishistic disavowal letting misogynist comics practice continue ('they know very well what they are doing, but still, they are doing it'). He extends the analysis to Earth One, where Hippolyta's clay-birth story is the primordial lie founding the Amazon community, Diana herself being the fetish that lets her mother sustain a separatist utopia while raising a weapon against Man's World.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 25 "She Got Game" — The Wallaces argue that both the detractors (Stacey Pressman's claim that women's basketball 'sucks') and the admirers (John Wooden's 'purest basketball' praise) judge the women's game by patriarchal standards drawn from the men's game. Using Sandra Bartky's feminist extension of Foucault, they show how the female body was disciplined under male surveillance - early rule changes split the court and banned stealing to protect 'femininity', while players deflected the 'Amazon' charge with beauty pageants, revealing uniforms, and the Playboy offer to Lisa Harrison. The modern WNBA of Lisa Leslie and Michelle Snow, who can dunk but choose team play, points to a new game that escapes the feminine/masculine dichotomy instead of measuring women against men.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 18 "Eighth Hole Playing Through Racism and Sexism in Golf" — Gray examines whether golf is a model of equality or a preserve of 'wealthy white men,' using George Carlin's polemic and the Tiger Woods 'Chosen One' narrative as foils. He documents 'social closure' and the 'Grass Ceiling' through Augusta National's history, the Shoal Creek and Martha Burk/NCWO controversies, and the PGA's former Caucasian-only clause, then turns to sexism via McGinnis, McQuillan, and Chapple's interviews and Connell's 'hegemonic masculinity,' showing how gendered 'red/women's tees' entrench a false dualism of male and female play. Citing McDonagh and Pappano's Playing with the Boys, he argues coercive sex-segregation rests on false assumptions and calls for transparency about club membership.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 25 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Jonsson argues that modern sport enforces masculine norms and that the East German 'wonder girls' (Koch, Ender, Krabbe), along with Stella Walsh, Jarmila Kratochvilova and Caster Semenya, were 'gender radical' Amazons who challenged the link between masculinity and maleness by winning with 'masculine' bodies. Drawing on Judith Butler's claim that gender ideals are not static and women's sport can rearticulate them, he treats the doping-built Eastern Bloc athletes as progressive because they contradicted how female athletes are 'supposed' to look. He critiques Jane English's appeal to 'permanent biological differences' and laments that after 1989 commercialized sport (symbolized by Flo Jo's marketed femininity) hardened conservative gender norms again.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Weaving argues from a liberal-feminist standpoint that the FIVB's mandatory bikini-bottom rule for women's Olympic beach volleyball sexualizes and objectifies the athletes, contradicting Coubertin's ideals of universal humanity. Using Paul Davis's distinction between acceptable sexuality and objectionable sexualization (deliberate focus on body parts, freezing postures, punning captions like 'Buns of Gold'), and citing Nussbaum, Baker and Bartky on when treating someone as a sexual object becomes wrong, she shows the rule detaches athletes' bodies from their athletic agency. She traces harms including physical risk, the APA-documented effects of sexualization, a 'trickle-down' to school volleyball short-shorts, and exclusion of Islamic women.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 20 "The “Kournikova Phenomenon”" — The chapter asks why Anna Kournikova was celebrated as a beauty despite a mediocre record while the far more successful Williams sisters were praised for athleticism, not looks. It uses Plato's Symposium (the ascent from a beautiful body to the Form of Beauty) to show beauty can be more than appearance, then deploys Nussbaum's analysis of objectification (contrasting Playboy's demeaning caption on tennis-player Nicollette Sheridan with Lady Chatterley) and MacKinnon's dominance view to critique the media's commodification of female players. Weaving in commodity racism and bell hooks on black hair, it argues Kournikova's fame reflects a whiteness-privileging color-caste standard of beauty rather than any real athletic or aesthetic superiority.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 9 "Laugh of the Revolutionary Diane di Prima, French Feminist Philosophy, and the Contemporary Cult of the Beat H" — Quinn reads Diane di Prima's serial poem 'Loba' and 'Memoirs of a Beatnik' through Hélène Cixous's 'The Laugh of the Medusa' and its call to 'écriture féminine'—women writing the body. She argues di Prima's she-wolf/Medusa figure, sex-positive candor, and refusal of narrative closure enact Cixous's boundless feminine writing, while Cixous's anti-Freudian, anti-Lacanian mockery of 'penis envy' and the 'big dick' illuminates di Prima's transgressive motherhood and bisexuality. Against the male Beats' dismissal of women writers (and Beauvoir's foremother status), the essay centralizes di Prima as a serious feminist philosopher-poet rather than a nostalgic icon.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 13 "3. Laura Palmer—Madonna and Whore" — Jones argues that Laura Palmer is trapped in Freud's Madonna-whore complex—the male inability to see a woman as both virtuous and sexual—with BOB voicing the cultural signals that brand her 'dirty and sleazy' for her sexuality. He reads the Fireman/Giant, who births Laura as a golden antidote to BOB, as a patriarchal 'nice guy' whose idealizing Madonna role is as much a trap as the whore role BOB imposes. The chapter uses Laura's dual life to expose how patriarchy forces women to choose between two reductive poles, both maintained by male power.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 22 "10. The Miss Twin Peaks Award Goes To . ." — Rard (as her 'doppelganger') distinguishes 'power-over' (getting others, mostly men, to do your bidding through beauty and manipulation) from the more stable 'power-to' (skills, resources, ability to act for oneself). She traces Josie Packard, who lives by manipulating Harry and Pete and is destroyed when surrounded by people immune to her charms, against Audrey Horne, who begins with the Norwegian stunt and the perfume-counter blackmail but transitions to running her father's business—acquiring real power—while Lana Milford's near-total charm and Nadine's adrenaline strength mark the extremes.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 23 "11. The Mother of All Bombs" — Kolb argues Laura Palmer embodies the 'Angel in the House' ideal (Gilbert and Gubar) whose perfection is a beautiful dead girl, and reads The Return's linkage of the Trinity bomb to BOB/Judy through Arendt's On Violence—violence begets a more violent, hostile world that especially victimizes women. Using Gilligan's In a Different Voice, she shows how women's voices (Naido/Diane, the Log Lady, Laura's diary) are silenced by toxic masculinity (Mr. C, Richard, Chad), while the 'good men' embody an ethic of care; the manufactured post-war social order names its bombs after mothers and treats women as perfect-yet-fallen others.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 17 "Feminists and “Freaks” She’s Gotta Have It and Girl 6" — Hoffman assesses whether Lee's She's Gotta Have It and Girl 6 offer liberated female sexuality, drawing on second- and third-wave feminism and bell hooks. She argues Nola Darling only appears empowered before the rape scene and her submission ('Yours') reveal her as an underdeveloped object of the male gaze, whereas Girl 6, as a phone-sex worker consciously performing gender for callers, better exposes gender as socially constructed in a Butler-like sense. Even so, Girl 6's real feminist force lies not in its heroine but in its exposure of oppressive industries, especially the opening Tarantino audition where only the director's gaze counts.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 19 "Fevered Desires and Interracial Intimacies in Jungle Fever" — Sundstrom uses Jungle Fever to dismantle the taboo (white and black versions) against interracial intimacy, treating Flipper and Angie's affair and the War Council's objections as a debate about black solidarity, loyalty, and self-hatred. He answers the War Council by invoking Mill's On Liberty and the tyranny of public opinion to defend sexual autonomy, and argues that demanding partners for political solidarity reduces them to props (objectification). He reads the psychoanalytic charge that interracial love is 'fevered' racial pathology as derived from Fanon's Black Skin, White Masks but ultimately baseless, and criticizes Lee for a puritanical ending that hides Orin and Paulie while exposing Flipper and Drew, failing to show interracial love as ordinary.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Pomerance combines philosophy of sex and philosophy of language to argue that sex, lies, and videotape is less about sex than about speaking sex and being watched speaking it. He analyzes Cynthia's videotaped confession about her first encounter, showing how her circumlocutions ('smooth like a test tube,' 'Ladies first') tease and withhold, and how Graham as silent 'priest of carnality' becomes an absent audience. Videotape 'amplifies' situated speech to a diffuse mass audience, so Cynthia's sexuality becomes a 'television personality,' pornographic in form and effacing her individuality in the manner of Benjamin's mechanical reproduction. The face and presence-in-time make every filmed performance both erotic and a kind of illuminating lie.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 19 "The Ubiquitous Absence of the Enemy in Contemporary Israeli War Films" — Pötzsch uses cognitive film theory (Murray Smith's alignment and allegiance, paradigm scenarios and schemata) to argue that Beaufort, Waltz with Bashir, and Lebanon, though hailed as antiwar films, covertly reinforce a militarist "scopic regime" through the "ubiquitously absent enemy." Formal devices—the tank scope's tunnel vision in Lebanon, shot/reverse-shot and voice-over confined to Israeli soldiers, the animated flashbacks of Waltz with Bashir—align and ally viewers exclusively with Israeli troops framed as helpless victims, while the Palestinian other stays faceless, voiceless, and objectified (the staggering Lebanese woman, the trauma displaced onto dead dogs and horses). Drawing on Judith Butler's frames of war and "ungrievable" lives, he reads this as Kimmerling's latent cognitive militarism that denies the enemy's competing subjectivity and forecloses nonviolent alternatives.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 11 "Landscapes of Gendered Violence Male Love and Anxiety on the Railroad" — Collins analyzes the railroad in Tycoon and both versions of 3:10 to Yuma, drawing on feminist critics (Irigaray, Bordo, Grosz, Haraway, Merchant) who expose a masculinist 'panoramic' epistemology coding mind as male and passive nature/landscape as female. She argues trains destabilize rather than confirm this mastery: in Tycoon, Johnny Munroe conflates conquering the feminized Andean landscape with dominating his wife Maura, yet the bridge and train fail; in the 2007 Yuma, the railroad's promise of masculine legitimacy is sustained only by 'cruel optimism' and male homosocial love between Dan Evans and Ben Wade, over anxieties about racial Others (Apache, Chinese laborers).
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 18 "Herzog’s Philosophy of Masculinism" — Will Lehman argues that beneath Herzog's rejection of any guiding philosophy lies a 'masculinism' that exalts traditionally manly traits (courage, strength, independence, emotional control) as the heroic. Drawing on gender theory (Dozier on beards and the performance of gender), he shows Herzog fetishizing 'manly men,' reading illiteracy and calloused hands as authentic manhood (Jared Talbert in Into the Abyss), and coding even his female subject Juliane Koepcke (Wings of Hope) in masculine terms. Lehman reads Herzog's reenactment 'therapy' with Dengler and Dorrington as an assertion of dominance, while noting Herzog avoids overt misogyny or homophobia.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 15 "6 Neil Young and American Indians Politics, Lyrics, and Authenticity" — Hester critiques Young's treatment of American Indians, arguing "Cortez the Killer" idealizes the Aztecs into Montaigne-style "noble savages," makes their sacrifices seem voluntary, and ultimately centers Young's own lost-love lament rather than the conquest's real victims. He shows "Pocahontas" objectifies and commodifies a Native woman (the "thousand pelts" line, Young's cavalier interview remarks) as cultural appropriation and "playing Indian," yet notes Young's genuine activism (Honor the Treaties) leaves fans wanting to credit his good intentions.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "8 Images of Women in the Music and Life of Neil Young" — McKenna uses Sarah Lucia Hoagland's feminist analysis of "heterosexualism" to argue that Young's songs ("Cinnamon Girl," "A Man Needs a Maid," "Unknown Legend," and the femicide of "Down by the River") portray women as objects to be desired, possessed, used and harmed, positioning them as helpmates (like Rousseau's Sophie, against which Wollstonecraft argued). She extends this to Young's own "backgrounding" of the women in his life (Pegi, Carrie Snodgress) in Waging Heavy Peace, comparing him to William James's reliance on his wife Alice.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 32 "30_LaRocca_Chapter_029.html" — Linda Williams analyzes Michelle Citron's What You Take for Granted, a feminist film that inhabits the gray zone between documentary and fiction by having actors impersonate real women workers (a truck driver, a doctor, a welder) entering male-dominated trades. She argues the film exposes the price women pay to be admitted to a male world of work structured by an absent, idealized-and-vilified paternal authority, mirroring the absent-mother structure of Citron's earlier Daughter Rite. By blending polished pseudo-documentary interviews with an improvised cinema-verite fiction of Anna and Dianna's friendship, the film interrogates the process of representation itself and shows how documentary 'truth' about women's typical experience is itself a fictional shaping.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 16 "7. More Mothers, Lovers, and Other Monsters" — Brace surveys the later-season mother figures—Mary, Kelly, Jody, Rowena, Mrs. Butters, Charlie—arguing they are repeatedly used as emotional tools against the Winchesters, which she reads through Kant's warning against treating persons merely as means. She stresses loss of free will and agency: Mary's British Men of Letters 'realignment' and Mrs. Butters's coercive programming strip their autonomy and reduce them to objects/killers, while their reclaimed agency and self-sacrifice restore their Kantian standing as ends in themselves.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 25 "14. Did Bourdain Go #MeToo Far" — Finn tests Catharine MacKinnon's 'Rape Redefined' — rape as sex compelled by inequality rather than lack of consent — against Bourdain's #MeToo allyship and his payment to Asia Argento's teenage accuser Jimmy Bennett. She argues MacKinnon's power-based standard could recognize Argento's act as assault, and reframes Bourdain's hush-money payment, via the Wendat/Huron compensation practices in Graeber and Wengrow, as a compassionate vengeance-staying reparation consistent with his empathy.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 25 "Real World Island" — Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue that Lost characters move from blameworthy to praiseworthy by ceasing to objectify others and instead objectifying themselves for a greater good. Using Kant's formula to treat persons as ends and never mere means, they condemn Ben Linus's lifelong manipulation while crediting his tearful mea culpa over Alex and his flash-sideways sacrifice for his student. Mill's utilitarianism justifies Sayid's assassinations and Kate's shooting of Un-Locke as trades for the greater number, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of cultivated respect and courage explains Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission and Jack's Christlike self-sacrifice at the Heart of the Island, framing self-objectification as redemption.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 17 "From There to Here, from Here to There, Diversity Is Everywhere" — Tanya Jeffcoat builds a philosophy of diversity around 'normative hubris' and 'totalizing tendencies,' using the Sneetches, the butter-battling Yooks and Zooks, and Daisy-Head Mayzie as cases of in-group/out-group dehumanization. Encountering the Other is framed through Buber's I-It versus I-Thou (Yertle treating his subjects as a throne), Fanon on the psychic violence and alienation of the oppressed, McIntosh's invisible knapsack of privilege, and Freire's humanization. Horton and the Lorax model standing with the disenfranchised, and Jeffcoat rebuts moral relativism via universal human rights and Dewey's democracy as a personal way of life that condemns intolerance.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 23 "MOTHERHOOD" — Maureen Sander-Staudt uses a feminist ethic of care – especially Carol Gilligan's mole-and-porcupine fable of reciprocal accommodation – to argue that pressuring women to nurse privately or covered imposes 'lactational burkas.' She runs public breastfeeding through the Miller obscenity test to show it is not obscene, opening with Gloria Steinem's 'If men could menstruate' to imagine 'milkmen,' and cites the Emily Gillette Freedom-flight ejection, Facebook's photo removal, the Janet Jackson Superbowl scandal, and PETA's human-milk proposal to expose hypocritical, biologically reductive double standards about the female breast.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 32 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Lee reads Gustave Courbet's life-size painting The Quarry (La curée) alongside Daumier's caricatures of incompetent bourgeois Parisian 'hobby hunters' and contemporary works by John Byrd and Christopher Carroll to trace how the hunter became a swaggering, masculine, lower-class 'savage' figure mediating wildness and civilization. She shows how the aristocratic ritual of the curée (feeding the deer's parts to the hounds) inverts into bourgeois provisioning, and invokes Hobbes's 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' to gloss Byrd's Tricky Buck as defiance of urban squeamishness about the mammalian, gendered reality of hunting.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 33 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Merskin takes an ecofeminist view (Karen Warren's linkage of the domination of women and nature) of women who hunt, testing Marti Kheel's 'happy/holistic/holy' hunter typology against online interviews with female hunters and finding their motivations mirror men's. She surveys how hunting became a male-coded rite of separation from the mother—drawing on Freud's 'instinctive urge'—and how hunting media (Traditional Bowhunter) juxtapose women, animals, weapons, and sexual conquest as objects of male predation. Invoking Artemis/Diana and Mary Zeiss Stange's 'woman the hunter,' she argues women who hunt expose aggression as a human, not merely male, trait.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 15 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Evolutionary psychologists Anne Gordon and Shane Kraus coin 'porngasm' and, via a survey of 264 undergraduates, argue that watching porn may make men bad lovers because porn caters to male short-term mating psychology and misrepresents female orgasm (which they estimate is 80–95% faked on screen). Men more than women infer that female porn stars genuinely enjoy the sex, and more viewing predicts stronger such belief. They explain the male bias through the correspondence bias (reading moans as real arousal despite the filming situation) and Haselton and Buss's error-management theory, whereby men systematically over-infer women's sexual interest.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 16 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Theodore Bach argues that consuming porn co-opts the mind-reading 'simulation heuristic' (the same process behind the Mr. Tees airport puzzle), so that a viewer like 'Max' watching Naughty Office simulates being the boss rather than objectively watching. This explains porn's popularity, the money shot (a prop that keeps the viewer inside the off-line simulation), and why heterosexual men watch penises — they simulate their own. Invoking Nozick's experience machine and extending MacKinnon's critique via simulation and motor-imagery research, Bach warns that simulating aggressive, degrading acts toward women may transfer those dispositions into the real world.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 20 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Fiona Woollard asks whether Zach's solo use of pornography (while partner Kelly is out) counts as cheating on their monogamous relationship. Drawing on her account of monogamy as restricting sexual intercourse to loving relationships, she argues that masturbation to porn is not sexual intercourse — there is no interaction with 'Jenna' — and that fantasizing about loveless sex is not the same as having it, so it need not undermine the significance of lovemaking; indeed masturbation aids healthy sexual self-exploration. She concedes, however, that porn which eroticizes the degradation of women (per Dworkin and MacKinnon, and Alice Walker's story 'Porn') can betray a loving relationship by revealing objectifying attitudes.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 24 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Mimi Marinucci asks 'what's wrong with porn?' and, rejecting both the Dworkin-MacKinnon censorship route and Strossen's pure free-speech reply, uses Audre Lorde's notion of the erotic as power and the personal test 'it feels right to me' as an entering wedge. She examines 'feminist porn,' resisting its easy equation with lesbian or couples porn, and contrasts it with 'fuck machine porn' (e.g., machines named Annihilator, Predator), which feels wrong to her not for size or domination but because mainstream porn fixates on decontextualized acts and the money shot. Citing Irigaray on women's diffuse, non-localized sexuality, she argues women want more richly contextualized representations than porn typically offers.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 29 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Rose takes a paradigm plotless YouPorn-style clip and tests the four standard charges against porn—obscenity, coercion/exploitation, harm to women, and harm to society—arguing each either collapses into cultural relativism or applies equally to any aesthetic object. He answers the feminist (MacKinnon/Dworkin-style) claim that porn subordinates women by noting that unjustified hierarchical power distorts the self-understanding of dominator and dominated alike (comparing it to 50 Cent's 'P.I.M.P.' and blaxploitation), so the wrong is not gender-specific. His conclusion is that porn should not be treated as different in kind from other art but judged aesthetically and morally by whether it distorts equitable social relationships, locating the real problem in capitalist cultural production rather than in porn as such.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 34 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Parkhill challenges Jenefsky and Miller's second-wave feminist reading of Penthouse 'girl–girl' pictorials (that they present lesbians as sexually available to naturalize heterosexuality) by arguing that what some straight men enjoy is their own ABSENCE from the scene. He deploys Butler's 'Imitation and Gender Insubordination' to show mock-lesbian-wedding drag can subvert rather than confirm heterosexual 'originality', Foucault's repressive hypothesis and productive power to argue the lesbian is a product of, not outside, patriarchal norms, and Lacan-derived 'projective identification' and feminine jouissance to explain the male viewer's libidinal investment in his own ego-erasure. He concludes both the 'conqueror' and the self-shattering 'jouissance-chasing' pleasures coexist, and that girl–girl porn is ethically no different from ordinary hetero porn since the consumer still assumes a right of access to women's bodies.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 36 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — In this interview, dominatrix-director Mz. Berlin answers the classic moral objections to porn from inside the industry: she rebuts objectification by insisting she chooses to be 'a commodity' and that choice makes it permissible, rejects the rape-myth/harm claim by citing declining rape rates and comparing porn to violent TV, and grounds BDSM's legitimacy entirely on INFORMED CONSENT, contrasting her voluntary waterboarding with her real torture abroad. Endorsing a strongly Millian self-ownership view ('my body is my own commodity'), she extends consent to selling kidneys, assisted suicide, and even display of her corpse, while drawing hard limits at sex with children, animals, or the dead where genuine informed consent is impossible. She also frames femdom porn as subverting male hegemony and normalizing fluid gender roles.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 10 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — The editors' introduction argues that fashion, despite philosophers' contempt for it, raises serious questions in aesthetics, ethics, identity, and political philosophy. It surveys the volume's contributors: fashionability as an expert-plus-masses property (Prinz/Farennikova), Zangwill's alienation thesis, Russell on 'cool' as aesthetic virtue, the objectification of women through Barbie play and sweatshops, and Singer's demand (via the drowning-child argument) that spare money go to poverty relief rather than trendy clothes. It uses concrete cases — Ugg boots, the National Airlines 'Fly me' campaign, Tommie Smith and John Carlos's 1968 Olympic salute, foot binding — to show fashion carries the zeitgeist and can both liberate and enslave.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 17 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Freeland analyzes perfume advertising — chiefly Chanel's mini-film campaigns for No. 5 (Kidman/Luhrmann, Tautou/Jeunet) versus the younger, jauntier Coco Mademoiselle ads with Keira Knightley — to trace how fragrance is sold 'aspirationally' by tying scent to lifestyle, romance, and couture. She examines male-fragrance ads (Bronson's Mandom, Chanel Egoiste, Old Spice's Isaiah Mustafa) and celebrity scents fronted by women of color, exposing gender anxiety, colonialism, and near-explicit racism in perfume marketing. Invoking commodity fetishism and feminist critique, she argues the ads manipulate female desire but do not make consumers passive dupes: blog parodies and critical commentary show active resistance to the fantasy.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 22 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Ashwell and Langton ask whether fashion is a 'badge of slavery' (Wollstonecraft), opening with Socrates in the *Phaedo* disdaining adornment and Rousseau's girl who becomes 'her own doll,' and using Kant's humanity formula and Nussbaum's seven-feature account of objectification. Focusing on denial of autonomy in ordinary followers, they distinguish the 'Servile Fashionista' (obeys experts) from the 'Sensible Fashionista' (follows what looks good), then argue that via Johnston's 'authority of affect' even the sensible one is under an *epistemic* bondage: fashion's extrinsic social pull is misperceived as the garment's intrinsic goodness, a projective illusion (like the Müller-Lyer) that on a Kantian view undermines agency and masks misogynist or racist norms such as straightened hair or the 'lotus feet' of stilettos.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 23 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Collins analyzes paradigmatic Barbie play — dressing the doll and identifying with her as an idealized future self, from the 1959 TV ad to BarbieGirls.com — arguing it trains girls to define identity through fashionable bodily self-presentation for a male gaze (Brumberg's 'body project'). Using Sandra Bartky's feminist reworking of Foucault's *Discipline and Punish*, she treats beauty norms as a discipline producing 'docile bodies' whose self-surveillance internalizes a 'panoptical male connoisseur' (Bentham's Panopticon), offering cycles of pleasure and pain that bind women without any single sovereign to blame. Rather than banning Barbie (the failed 'Happy to be Me' doll), she proposes subversive play — Plump and Proud Barbie, Mursi lip-plate Barbie — as Heyes-style 'practices of freedom.'
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 25 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Pierlott examines sweatshops in the garment industry through the lens of ancient Cynicism (Antisthenes, the Stoics' Zeno of Citium and his thieving slave), using the Cynic critique of fashion-driven consumption to strip legitimacy from the demand that feeds sweatshops. He rebuts the 'inevitability argument' (comparing it to excusing the Holocaust as inevitable) and the free-choice defense using Aristotle's category of 'mixed' action — sweated workers' consent is coerced by desperate alternatives — and argues, via Adam Smith on the undervaluing of labor, that giant retailers like Wal-Mart distort natural labor prices. He stresses that sweatshops overwhelmingly exploit young women, tying objectification of women as fashion consumers to their oppression as producers.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 15 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Kimberly Baltzer-Jaray and Tanya Rodriguez argue, against George Carlin's 'mobile art gallery' joke, that the only thing separating tattooing from fine art is its fleshy canvas. They show how formalist, expressionist and institutional theories historically excluded both women's craft and tattoos, then use feminist aesthetics (Korsmeyer, Iris Marion Young on the gaze) to reclaim the female tattooed body as an assertion of agency against objectification. They then apply Gadamer's hermeneutics – art as play, festival and symbol – to argue tattoos make a claim on the viewer, build a 'hermeneutic collective' community, and function as inexhaustible symbols prompting self-recognition.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 18 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Nancy Kang argues tattoos can function within a liberatory feminist ideology, accentuating rather than diminishing femininity by exposing the differential treatment of tattooed women. She surveys radical, Marxist, liberal and corporeal feminism (invoking Aristotle's dismissal of women, Mill's Subjection of Women, and Gramsci's hegemony), then reads pop-culture cases – Crash's tattooed Latino worker, Black Swan's Lily, the Perry 'pricks as needles' sexualization, carnival 'Tattooed Ladies' like Irene Woodward marked 'by the father's hand,' and the McGee/Bullock/Kat Von D scandal – to show corporeal feminism treats tattooing as a risky, self-owning revolutionary act.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 19 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 21 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span turns to the ethics and epistemology of college sex. Kania argues there is no clear line between close friendship and a sexual relationship, so condemning student-professor sex logically forces condemning student-professor friendship—rejecting Golash's split and defending carefully-conducted consensual relationships. Layne narrates Socrates/Alcibiades, Abelard/Heloise, and Heidegger/Arendt to contrast Socratic eros (Plato's Symposium, love as a friend of wisdom directed at the soul) and Heideggerian authentic love ('I want you to be what you are') against Abelard's exploitative lust. McDowell mines epistemology (justification, taking beliefs 'to heart,' reflective equilibrium) to argue better thinking yields better, more autonomous sex. Pinku weighs 'plain sex' against Nagel's interpersonal-arousal account of embodiment to ask whether sex needs love, and Brophy uses Kantian dignity (treating the body as a mere means, not an end) to argue that prostitution and webcam porn undertaken to pay tuition violate the student's autonomy.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 22 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — The essay argues that soaring tuition drives college students into sexual self-commodification—egg-selling ('Pay your tuition with eggs'), craigslist/backpage escorting, and dorm-porn webcam sites like VoyeurDorm and CocoDorm—and reads these cases through Kant's second formulation, condemning them as treating oneself and others as mere means rather than ends of intrinsic dignity. It applies Marx's notion of false consciousness to Natalie Dylan's virginity auction and Ashley Dupré's 'empowerment' claims, comparing them to women choosing high heels as internalized oppression. It uses Rousseau's Social Contract and Mill's On Liberty to argue that prostitution is a form of illegitimate 'voluntary slavery' because one cannot rightly alienate one's own inalienable freedom, and contrasts coerced cases (Helena in Singapore, Rosie Reid's traumatic auctioned deflowering, John Gechter's porn suspension from a Christian college) with less-coerced ones to argue moral concern should track the degree of circumstantial coercion.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 20 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Luna Dolezal's 'Yoga for Women?' argues that Western yoga, once a male ascetic path, has been absorbed by consumer capitalism into a female beauty practice organized around 'body capital.' Reading Yoga Journal covers, Lululemon's 'Say No to Camel Toe' ad, and Toesox's nude campaigns, she shows the fashion/beauty industries cultivate shame to sell the yoga body, objectifying women. She counters that Hatha yoga should be a laboratory for compassionate self-acceptance beyond comparison and competition — 'yoga for every body' — rather than another instrument of the market's normalized ideal.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 21 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Nicole Dunas's 'The Feeling of Beauty' recounts founding the Real Beauty Yoga Project after a teacher-training 'modeling day' where consultants photographed only the five thinnest students, enacting division rather than yogic union. Framing the beauty question against Kant's claim that beauty is objective, and drawing on David Abram's participatory perception and Susan Bordo on airbrushed bodies, she argues that objectifying beauty into an image to be gazed at (the male gaze, the isolated cosmetic-surgery gaze) severs us from it, whereas Hatha yoga's tantric, present-moment embodiment lets beauty be lived rather than consumed.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 22 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Debra Merskin content-analyzes 52 Yoga Journal covers (2000–2008) and finds every model white and 96% shown full-body, mostly looking away — posed as unaware of a scopophilic, hierarchical gaze that puts them in vulnerability. She uses Goffman's gender-display coding and the male-gaze framework to argue that a publication about a mind–body practice (which, contra Descartes' mind/body divide, neuroscience shows are intertwined) bears a special responsibility to present racially inclusive, non-objectifying images rather than reproducing the 'sex sells' formula of Cosmopolitan or Maxim.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 28 "BLUES" — Meghan Winsby answers George Carlin's gibe that white people have nothing to be blue about by arguing that women — black or white — legitimately sing the blues because they share an experience of oppression. She applies Iris Marion Young's 'five faces of oppression' (exploitation, marginalization, powerlessness, cultural imperialism, violence) to women's silencing, sexual objectification, and gender exploitation, showing that early blueswomen (Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith, Memphis Minnie) and later ones (Bonnie Raitt) asserted sexuality and independence against a patriarchal order. She then weighs, without fully endorsing, the moral cultural-appropriation and audience-appropriation objections (via James O. Young) to white men playing the blues.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 19 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Kyla Reid and Tinashe Dune attack the bestselling dating manual The Rules by Fein and Schneider, focusing on Rule 4 (never go Dutch—let the man pay) and Rule 12 (dump him if he gives no romantic gift like jewelry). They line up 'Rules Girls' against sex workers offering a paid 'girlfriend experience' and 'professional girlfriends'/gold diggers, arguing that all three approach relationships in a systematic, 'business-like' way that packages and markets the woman as a product, measures her worth by what the man spends, and treats gifts like performance bonuses. Because monogamy, public recognition, and belief in the relationship cannot make it authentic, they conclude The Rules obstruct genuine intimacy and that everyone should be more critical of dating conventions about who pays and what gifts mean.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 27 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Silber uses his own Match.com romance with Karin to argue that virtual 'meeting' differs phenomenologically from face-to-face meeting, which Buber's I-Thou (vs I-It) makes into a whole-being encounter that online traces and aspects cannot supply, invoking 'all real living is meeting.' He treats the dating market as a site of Kantian danger, contrasting price with the dignity of persons in the kingdom of ends, and warns that the market's efficiency threatens objectification and commodification. He then deploys Sartre's bad faith, facticity and transcendence, and 'existence precedes essence' to diagnose online self-misrepresentation (lying about height, age, photos) as inauthenticity, while briefly setting Derrida's 'nothing outside the text' against Plato's Phaedrus preference for speech over writing.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 67 "63. Amy Schumer as Philosopher Fuck the Feminine Mystique" — Elsby argues Amy Schumer's honest comedy revolts against a 'feminine mystique' broader than Friedan's housewife version, running back to Beauvoir's claim that woman is constructed as the 'Other' and to Aristotle's 'rational animal' definition that cast women as irrational and thus less than human. Through bits like 'Madame President,' 'Last Fuckable Day,' the 'New Twitter Button' sketch, and gross-out honesty about pregnancy and her own body in Growing and The Leather Special, Schumer refuses to let women's physical, sexual, and social experience stay mysterious. Elsby reads this as de-'othering' and re-humanizing women by forcing our concept of 'woman' to expand to include flawed, fully human hot-mess figures.

### Animal Liberation

Animal Liberation is Peter Singer's 1975 book arguing that the interests of non-human animals deserve equal moral consideration, and it became a foundational text of the modern animal rights movement. Drawing on a utilitarian concern for suffering, Singer contends that because many animals can feel pain, their suffering counts morally in the same way human suffering does, and that ignoring it is a form of prejudice. The book applies this argument to practices such as factory farming and animal experimentation, urging sweeping changes in how humans treat other sentient beings.

- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 25 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Detmer argues moral vegetarianism follows from principles nearly everyone accepts — cruelty, the infliction of unnecessary or disproportionate suffering, is wrong — and that Atkins, which escalates meat eating without being necessary for weight loss, fails both his necessity and proportion tests. Rebutting human superiority, he deploys Rachels's point that no single feature like language is relevant to every difference in treatment and Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', holds factory-farm castration without anesthetic up against the civet-cat musk trade his students already condemn, and answers Narveson's appeal to intuition and the appeal to tradition. Even granting Atkins maximal health benefits, the margin over a well-planned vegetarian diet (Denmark's WWI blockade, the Framingham data) cannot justify the animal suffering, world-hunger, and environmental costs — most of that case drawn from Singer's Animal Liberation.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 19 "Cold Clammy Consistency" — Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents - rational by Aristotle's standard of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgments about evildoers tasting better) and free despite their blood-craving, since craving is a strong preference, not the compulsion of the heroin addict or the castaway drinking seawater. Since animal blood is a viable alternative (Louis's rats, Angel and Spike's butcher's blood), the justifications for drinking human blood - taste, reaching full potential, spiritual peace - all fail against the principle that a world with less unnecessary suffering is better. Then the consistency argument turns on us: factory-farmed meat inflicts unnecessary suffering for the sake of taste while vegetarianism is fully viable, so condemning vampires while eating chicken is inconsistent - we as human beings are vampiric.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 30 "Mirror, Mirror" — Sailors convicts Dorothy of being the stereotypical female of Baum's and Fleming's versions, disowning responsibility for killing both witches and living to please others, then contrasts her with Elphaba of Wicked as a feminist hero who leaves home, protects Animals, and mixes 'hot' male and 'cold' female anger into a single fury. She reads Elphaba's indeterminate gender through Marilyn Frye's point that easily identifiable groups are the easiest to oppress, through de Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but becomes a woman' and Mill's line that the 'nature of women' is an eminently artificial thing. Singer's liberation logic, together with the Wollstonecraft-Taylor 'Vindication of the Rights of Brutes' episode and the ecofeminist link between the oppression of women and animals, is applied to Elphaba's Animal-rights activism and her position as 'neither man nor beast,' before the Witch's mirror recognition of Dorothy forces the author to soften her verdict.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 23 "The Onion’s New Environmental Ethic" — Matthew Altman reads Onion environmental satire as a staged escape from anthropocentrism: 'New, Delicious Species Discovered' and 'Beauty Of National Forest Enjoyed By Logger' expose that even appreciating nature is just valuing it for us, while the mascara-testing lab rabbit and 'Funny Monkey Tested On' make Singer's speciesism charge vivid against factory farming and animal experiments. He then widens the argument to a biocentric concern for species and ecosystems via 'Stuffed-Animal Biodiversity Rising' and 'Consumer-Product Diversity Now Exceeds Biodiversity,' and to ecofeminism via 'Raped Environment Led Polluters On,' where the forest as flirtatious woman links domination of nature to sexism and victim-blaming. Global stories like the Bush 'national air conditioner' piece show Western overconsumption displacing blame onto Third World overpopulation, and 'I'm Doing My Inconsequential Part' satirizes the self-satisfaction of green consumerism itself — leaving the measure of the Onion's philosophical importance as how dangerous it is.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 25 "Why the Doctor Is So Special" — Applying Singer's animal-liberation concept of speciesism — judging moral worth by capacity to feel pain rather than by intelligence or likeness — the authors argue the Daleks are 'super-speciesist' and that Lumic's emotional inhibitors make the Cybermen the same failure, unable to share a universe with unlike beings. Since emotions are judgments that can be educated into fitting responses (Nussbaum, Aristotle), and since Daleks infused with Rose's or Diagoras's DNA collapse into empathetic beings, the chapter concludes that emotion and empathy are why the Daleks will never win and why the Doctor, marked by his companions, is special among Time Lords.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 29 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Hinzmann and Arp ask whether zombies can be morally harmed: Jenner's fMRI in 'TS-19' shows only the brain stem reactivates, leaving walkers with a merely shark-like 'perceptual mind.' Against anthropocentric theories, under which Michonne may keep her chained pet walkers as guard-dog tools, they set Singer's utilitarian expanding circle, Leopold's land ethic, and Naess's deep ecology, each of which could support a 'PETZ' zombie preserve. Hershel's barn of 'sick people' and Shane's massacre of it in 'Pretty Much Dead Already' show how fragile such preservation is, while the Governor's death-match arena ringed with chained zombies and his kept zombie daughter illustrate Kant's point that cruelty toward mere animals corrodes the humanity of the cruel person himself.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 18 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Travis Timmerman argues the series dramatizes Singer's equal consideration of interests: Zira frees Taylor once he writes 'My name is Taylor' because like interests must count equally regardless of species, while Dr. Zaius's erasing the writing, lobotomizing Landon, and destroying the cave artifacts is pure speciesism in Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' sense. He rejects the crude 'humans are smarter' argument (it would strip severely cognitively disabled humans of standing) and Nussbaum's species-normal version (it would permit caging Zira and Cornelius since normal apes are mute), then deploys Plato's Euthyphro dilemma against Locke-style God-given rights: a deity bellowing that human interests outrank ape interests is arbitrary unless grounded in independent reasons. Since farming severely cognitively disabled humans is obviously wrong and species membership is morally irrelevant, it is equally wrong to factory-farm and experiment on animals - so, like Caesar in Battle for the Planet of the Apes, become vegetarian.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 21 "Futurama and Philosophy" — The chapter uses 'The Problem with Popplers' to map the real-world ethics of eating meat: Free Waterfall Jr.'s 'You shouldn't eat things that feel pain' restates Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' and Singer's equal consideration of suffering; Fishy Joe's profits-first stance echoes agro-ecological defenses of meat eating; and Leela's 'eating an intelligent animal is different' voices the common intuition Singer condemns as speciesism. The food-chain justification collapses when the Omicronians claim the apex and demand 198 billion humans in return, and Bender's 'fight to the death and I'll cook the loser' flips the diner's perspective, while Waterfall's orangutan-for-Leela trade sets up Singer's future-directed preferences distinction from Practical Ethics as a possible rescue. The chapter ends on the episode's real target: gluttonous consumption ('stuff the ship!') and the arbitrary sentimentality governing what we will and won't eat.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 18 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Fitzpatrick argues that the awe Ellie feels at the brachiosaurs makes experiencing real dinosaurs so valuable that restoring them may be obligatory, and reads Malcolm's distrust of land managers as sharing Leopold's land ethic, under which firebombing Isla Nublar would be barbarism on the order of Dresden. Invoking Bentham, Mill, and Singer's expansion of the moral community (echoed in the park's dart guns), he weighs Elliot's 'Faking Nature' and Katz's charge that restored nature is a fake and an arrogance against Andrew Light's defense of respectful restoration. He concludes that Jurassic Park failed not because restoration is wrong but because Hammond restored dinosaurs for amusement, and that a careful, land-ethic-respecting de-extinction could one day be justified.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 29 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Seth Walker asks whether Nick Van Owen - the Earth First! documentarian who monkeywrenches InGen's camp and frees the caged dinosaurs in The Lost World - is a bastard or morally justified. He runs the consequentialist cost-benefit (the escaped T. rex slaughters a cargo ship crew and trashes San Diego; the sabotage costs the team their radio and rescue) against the ecodefense argument built on Arne Naess's deep ecology and biocentric equality, on which Isla Sorna is our 'home' and rescuing the injured baby T. rex Roland Tembo crippled is Self-defense. Singer's principle of equal consideration of suffering - a difference in ability never justifies a difference in consideration - bridges the gap for those who reject biocentrism, and Walker answers the consistency objection (must Nick accept InGen sabotaging him back?) before crediting Nick's defense of his larger home.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 27 "15. Loving Your Pet Is Better than Utilitarianism" — Against Peter Singer's utilitarian case in Animal Liberation, spare Snuffles because he can suffer regardless of intelligence, the chapter argues utilitarianism fails because it quantifies the unquantifiable, happiness. It turns to Hume: intelligence cannot ground moral worth, since smart Rick enslaving a microverse would then be our moral superior; Hume's guillotine separates descriptive from moral claims so that metaphysics no longer decides who counts as a moral object; and Hume's real ground is sentiment, dogs loving across species as the tail-wagging Snuffles does. So the morally right response to 'Lawnmower Dog' is not Jerry's abuse or even Rick's intelligence helmet but simply loving the pet.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 13 "3. Save the Demogorgons!" — Puumala asks whether killing the Demogorgons is speciesist: Dart's pain response to light makes the demodogs sentient (Bentham's 'Can they suffer?'), giving them moral considerability, while the Mind Flayer may or may not be a moral agent and could even be a keystone species whose destruction collapses the Upside Down ecosystem. He tests whether demogorgons count as invasive species (they may be native to a causally connected mirror dimension), invokes Regan's lifeboat case to argue they must still lose out to humans in a conflict of interests, and ends with the uncomfortable thought that humans are themselves an invasive species turning Earth into an Upside Down, so Eleven closing the gate was compassionate conservation.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 30 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Uses 'Fun with Veal' (the boys' bedroom standoff over baby calves, the FDA renaming veal 'tortured baby cows', Stan's meat strike punished by 'vaginitus'), 'Whale Whores' (the Japanese hating dolphins until Stan's doctored Enola Gay photo swaps in a cow and chicken), and 'Pee' (researchers peeing on rhesus monkeys) to pose the line-drawing problem: why do we protect cute animals and slaughter yummy ones? Neither intelligence (pigs versus dogs), utility, age, nor cuteness survives scrutiny as a morally relevant criterion — if it did, Nurse Gollum or Timmy would lose standing. Singer's speciesism analogy and the utilitarian inclusion of all who can suffer are then applied: Cartman, who draws his moral circle around himself, is the honest ethical egoist, while Kyle and Butters' selective vegetarianism and the adults' meat-eating inconsistency are exactly what Singer's view condemns.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Uses the Zillo Beast arc, battle droids, mynocks, and Han shooting Greedo to test theories of moral status: Schweitzer-style reverence for life would forbid a Jedi from eating anything, genetic views breed Palpatine-style human chauvinism, Singer's sentience view makes droid suffering and Luke dropping the rancor's door morally troubling, and Kantian autonomy excludes cognitively impaired beings too harshly. The chapter weighs Palpatine as merely a 'sociopathic' goal-pursuer rather than a Kantian moral agent, and leaves the droid question open via the novel Children of the Jedi, where the droid-converted Nichos lacks even mere agency because he cannot override his programming.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 11 "NOTES" — Blayde and Dunn use True Blood to expose speciesism from both directions: the philosophical tradition (Aristotle's rational animals, Aquinas's divine image, Kant's dignity versus price, Descartes's denials of animal pain) justified human exploitation of nonhumans, and the show's vampires invert the ladder by treating humans as 'pets and cattle' — the magister's 'humans exist to serve us' and his verdict that Bill 'murdered a higher life form' for a pet mirror how we talk about animals. Amy's torture of Eddie Gauthier is read against factory farming, and the chapter closes with Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' and Singer's sentience criterion as Sookie's 'civic duty' grounds for extending moral consideration beyond our species.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 29 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Hinzmann and Arp ask whether walkers can be morally harmed, ranking perceptual, reasoning, and conscious minds and placing zombies at shark level on the evidence of Dr. Jenner's fMRI ('TS-19') showing only the brain stem reactivates. Surveying anthropocentric views (Michonne's chained pet-walkers as guard-dog tools), Singer's expanding circle, Leopold's land ethic, and Naess's deep ecology, they conclude that even utilitarians could demand a zombie preserve on the model of Hershel's barn of 'sick people', which Shane's barn massacre in 'Pretty Much Dead Already' destroys. Kant's point that cruelty to animals corrodes our humanity explains why the Governor's death-match arena, his torture of Rick and Michonne, and his chained zombie daughter mark him, not the walkers, as the true moral monster.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 28 "Whatever! It’s All Natural" — Jaquet and Cova apply animal ethics to ask whether abusing the hosts is permissible, treating Logan's 'she's a goddamn doll' as direct speciesism (absolute and indexical) and rejecting mere species membership as morally irrelevant. They test candidate human-only properties — intelligence (Maeve out-thinks the techs), a moral sense (Bernard's and Teddy's guilt), and free will (arguing compatibilism makes hosts as free as us) — concluding that consciousness is what matters and Ford finally admits the hosts have it. They then dismantle 'it's natural,' role/function, Locke's creator-ownership ('I built your mind, Bernard'), and existence-justifies-exploitation arguments as failing to license the guests' cruelty.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 25 "Why the Doctor Is So Special" — Sarah Honeychurch and Niall Barr argue Daleks and Cybermen will never beat humanity because they are speciesist, judging worth solely by logic and resemblance. Using Peter Singer's animal-liberation account of speciesism (and Ryder's coinage), they claim the capacity to feel pain and empathy grounds moral consideration, and that Martha Nussbaum's and Aristotle's view of emotions as trainable judgments makes feeling essential to good moral reasoning. The humanized Daleks (the "Dalek" who absorbs Rose's DNA, Dalek Sec) show emotion's transformative power, and the Doctor's empathy, unlike other Time Lords, is why he succeeds.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 20 "Chapter 9 Twain’s Critique of Human Exceptionalism" — VanDette argues that Twain's late anti-vivisection writings anticipate posthumanist animal ethics by inverting the Darwinian species hierarchy. Through 'Letters from a Dog,' the essay 'Man's Place in the Animal World,' his 1899 London Anti-Vivisection Society letter, and the mother-dog narrator Aileen in 'A Dog's Tale,' Twain gives animals voice and subjectivity to attack human exceptionalism. His refusal to weigh vivisection's benefit against animal pain echoes Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', while his target is the Cartesian view of animals as insensible machines and the evolutionary logic used to justify experiments; Dr. Gray's cold killing of Aileen's puppy indicts a science that deadens compassion.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 13 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Ilundáin-Agurruza stages his essay as a 'philosophical hunt,' first conceding Peter Singer's utilitarian case that sport hunting is wrong because it causes animal suffering for trivial ends, then arguing hunting can be non-trivial. Drawing on Aristotelian virtue ethics and Ortega y Gasset, he defends the 'Virtuous Hunter' who follows 'Diana's Code,' handicaps himself for a one-shot kill, and feels for the prey — citing De Niro's Michael in The Deer Hunter and Woody Allen's Love & Death — while condemning canned hunts and demeaning language ('varmint,' 'harvesting') as vicious extremes on a continuum.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 25 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Duerr surveys the worldwide 'Master/Mistress of Animals' figure (Artemis, the /Kaggen of the Bushmen, the Huaulu Lord of the Forest) as a mythic sanction against over-hunting, arguing that the near-universal guilt hunters feel over killing sentient, human-like game reflects a real moral dilemma. She invokes Singer's utilitarian claim that painlessly killing non-self-conscious animals whose deaths are compensated by replacement 'may not be wrong,' reading the mythic 'solutions' (denial, propitiation, taking only what you need, restoring bones so game is reborn) as a folk 'hunting code of ethics' that manages the wrong of ending a life without starting another.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 28 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Kover argues that anti-hunting animal-liberation thought (Singer, Regan) objects to hunting not because it alienates us from nature but because it connects us too intimately to it—to the cycle of eating and being eaten and thus to our own mortality. Using Ernest Becker's 'denial of death' and Paul Rozin on disgust at our animality, he reads vegetarianism from Pythagoras's flesh-renouncing purification to modern ethical veganism as an ascetic refusal of edibility, and cites Val Plumwood's critique of humans placing themselves outside the food chain, concluding with Petersen and Shepard that the hunter's acceptance of death affirms life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 35 "32. Okja as Philosophy Why Animals Matter" — Jensen frames Okja around three views of the super-pig Okja's moral status: Mirando treats her as mere property, the Animal Liberation Front as a symbol to be sacrificed for the cause, and the girl Mija as a friend and person. He dismantles Mirando's 'human exceptionalism'—amoralism, Aquinas's natural-law teleology, the Kantian persons-only view, and Descartes' claim that animals are unfeeling automata—then develops the ALF's liberation through Singer's equal consideration of interests, Bentham's 'can they suffer?', and speciesism as prejudice, weighing consequentialist (utilitarian) against deontological (rights, Regan) foundations. He closes with hierarchical moral status and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many,' arguing Mija's love for Okja shows that at some point relationship matters more than moral calculation.

### Food Ethics

Food ethics is the study of the moral questions surrounding how food is produced, distributed, and consumed, spanning the treatment of animals in agriculture, the environmental impact of farming, fair labor and trade, and personal choices such as vegetarianism. It asks whether practices like factory farming are justifiable, how responsibility for hunger and food waste should be understood, and what a just food system would look like. The field connects individual eating habits to large-scale ethical, ecological, and economic concerns.

- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 25 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Detmer argues moral vegetarianism follows from principles nearly everyone accepts — cruelty, the infliction of unnecessary or disproportionate suffering, is wrong — and that Atkins, which escalates meat eating without being necessary for weight loss, fails both his necessity and proportion tests. Rebutting human superiority, he deploys Rachels's point that no single feature like language is relevant to every difference in treatment and Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', holds factory-farm castration without anesthetic up against the civet-cat musk trade his students already condemn, and answers Narveson's appeal to intuition and the appeal to tradition. Even granting Atkins maximal health benefits, the margin over a well-planned vegetarian diet (Denmark's WWI blockade, the Framingham data) cannot justify the animal suffering, world-hunger, and environmental costs — most of that case drawn from Singer's Animal Liberation.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 26 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Cox and Bender subject Atkins to Kant's universal-law formula — could every one of the billion overweight people on earth adopt it? — in a 'factive' thought experiment: a 25 percent rise in animal-protein output, nearly 250 million additional feed-grain acres, overgrazed ranges, and possibly a tenth of the world's remaining forests cleared for pasture. Calling Atkins reductionism's child (a metabolic switch judged on bathroom scales), they use Marx's 'metabolic rift' — soil nutrients shipped to cities, feedlots severing crops from livestock — and the Cartesian body-as-machine (via Federici) to place low-carb's atomized foods (bungalow subs, soy 'mashed potatoes,' pork rinds) as capitalism's latest rupture in the food system. Their verdict: only plant-leaning regimens could survive universalization, and the deeper fix is Wendell Berry's — eating understood as an agricultural act.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 19 "Cold Clammy Consistency" — Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents - rational by Aristotle's standard of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgments about evildoers tasting better) and free despite their blood-craving, since craving is a strong preference, not the compulsion of the heroin addict or the castaway drinking seawater. Since animal blood is a viable alternative (Louis's rats, Angel and Spike's butcher's blood), the justifications for drinking human blood - taste, reaching full potential, spiritual peace - all fail against the principle that a world with less unnecessary suffering is better. Then the consistency argument turns on us: factory-farmed meat inflicts unnecessary suffering for the sake of taste while vegetarianism is fully viable, so condemning vampires while eating chicken is inconsistent - we as human beings are vampiric.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 19 "Cold Clammy Consistency" — Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents because they meet Aristotle's test of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgment that 'evildoers... taste better') and retain free will, since their blood-lust is a craving not a compulsion and Louis's rat diet in Interview with the Vampire, like Angel's in Buffy, proves an alternative exists. TASTE, full potential, and spiritual peace all fail to justify human blood, because killing a person brings more unnecessary suffering than killing a rat, the same suffering-based principle that condemns factory farming. The 'cold clammy consistency' punchline: since humans need not eat meat, condemning vampire blood-drinkers while dining on chicken, pork, and beef is hypocrisy, because we are vampiric too and only our choice of which life to ingest separates the monstrous from the virtuous.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 181 "I’m in Need of Some Restraint" — Tells how the Abraham and Isaac story introduced "redemption," a substitution rite that curbed the "pride of place" of first-borns while replacing human sacrifice — a transition the Egyptians and Greeks also made independently. Using Shirley Jackson's "The Lottery," the volunteering Druid victims and the martyr Perpetua, it argues any horror can be normalized by piety and tradition — Sarah Palin or Michele Bachmann would have defended first-born sacrifice in ancient Ur — and needles the reader with ritual chicken sacrifice versus KFC: "which of those two, in a just world, would really be more inhumane?"
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 21 "Futurama and Philosophy" — The chapter uses 'The Problem with Popplers' to map the real-world ethics of eating meat: Free Waterfall Jr.'s 'You shouldn't eat things that feel pain' restates Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' and Singer's equal consideration of suffering; Fishy Joe's profits-first stance echoes agro-ecological defenses of meat eating; and Leela's 'eating an intelligent animal is different' voices the common intuition Singer condemns as speciesism. The food-chain justification collapses when the Omicronians claim the apex and demand 198 billion humans in return, and Bender's 'fight to the death and I'll cook the loser' flips the diner's perspective, while Waterfall's orangutan-for-Leela trade sets up Singer's future-directed preferences distinction from Practical Ethics as a possible rescue. The chapter ends on the episode's real target: gluttonous consumption ('stuff the ship!') and the arbitrary sentimentality governing what we will and won't eat.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 15 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Littmann turns vampirism into a thought experiment against meat-eating, using Jonathan's delight in the Hotel Royale chicken as the double standard: every justification for the Count preying on humans - might makes right, his superior intelligence and cunning, an arbitrary threshold of cleverness, or the human soul and its afterlife - would equally license beings superior to us (supernaturally strong, centuries-cunning Dracula himself) to prey on humans. Following Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', he argues the real wrong of vampirism is the net suffering it creates, and this utilitarian standard equally condemns factory farming, pushing us toward humanely raised meat or vegetarianism.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 26 "13. Should the Doctor Eat His Companions" — Littmann turns the Doctor-companion relationship into a mirror for animal ethics: since the Doctor stands to humans as we stand to animals—deciding for Rose without asking in 'The End of the World,' implanting nanorecorders unconsented in 'Day of the Moon'—every standard justification for our treatment of animals (might makes right, superior intelligence, natural predation) would equally license him to eat Clara cutlets, yet he instead defends humanity from Daleks, Cybermen, and naturally predatory species like the Weeping Angels, the Minotaur, and the Swarm. Finding no non-arbitrary place to draw the intelligence line—what of the human-level gangers, the enslaved Ood, or mentally disabled humans?—he endorses Bentham's utilitarian suffering standard from 'Can they suffer?', concluding that eating humans fails the utilitarian test because the pleasure cannot outweigh a whole life's happiness, and that whether eating meat passes that same test is the question our own treatment of animals must answer.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 10 "1. Cosmopolitan Cannibal" — Staged as a fictional interview over herring and aquavit in Copenhagen, Wong lets Lecter wield philosophical critique like an 'autopsy saw' - he invokes Schopenhauer's condemnation of anthropophagy and Montaigne's noble-savage view only to have the interviewer refuse both, and 'creams Aristotle' in a debate about categories - before she adopts Agamben's distinction between sovereigns and bare life. Lecter's 'we are elaborations of carbon' de-anthropocentrism, his killing of the rude, and the parallel cases of shipwrecked sailors who ate shipmates, Guantánamo detainees, and drone casualties all serve her argument that every political order rests on someone arbitrarily deciding which lives are mere killable matter, and that Lecter horrifies because he shows every human is also nonhuman - Us and Them at once.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 11 "2. I, Cannibal" — Westfall sorts cannibalism into starvation types (the Donner Party, the Andes rugby team, Alferd Packer, and Grutas's crew killing Mischa - 'We have to eat or die'), cultural types (Aztec ritual eating, the prisoner-eating tribes of Montaigne's essay, whom Montaigne judged no worse than the French torturing their prisoners alive, and Neanderthal nutritional eating), and hedonistic types (paraphilic, sadistic, and recreational). Using Irvine's active/passive distinction he argues that it is the killing, not the eating, that makes cannibalism wrong - passive consumption of corpses is at worst distasteful - while Lecter emerges as a purely recreational cannibal who eats 'because he likes it', and the TV series' dinner parties turn Jack and Will from unwitting 'benign cannibals' into morally responsible passive ones.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 33 "20. What Would Mister Rogers Say" — Jennifer Shaw Fischer and Bob Fischer apply Rogers's ideal of 'making goodness attractive' to the 2018 family-separation crisis: knowing his own son's abrupt, unexplained surgical separation caused lifelong trauma, and that his King Friday bomb-scare arc rejects trigger-happy generals for 'Generals of peace,' they argue any policy requiring border agents to lie that children are 'going to a shower' is too ugly to balance our values rightly. Rogers's unpushy vegetarianism ('I don't want to eat anything that has a mother') shows the difference between having a reason and being virtuous: making goodness lovely rather than argumentative.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 17 "Questioning Our Attitudes, Sokka‐style" — Wawrzyniak traces Sokka's growth from seeing animals as food and fur ('Dinner!' at Momo in 'The Southern Air Temple') to bonding with Foo Foo Cuddlypoops and vowing a 'karmically correct vegetarian existence', measured against Kant's anthropocentric view of animals as mere things whose cruel treatment matters only as a risk to human morals. Aang's harm-free uses of animals, from otter penguin sledding to riding hog monkeys, are then tested by Korsgaard's pathocentrism: animals are 'someones' who mind what happens to them, so even harmless use demands justification. The chapter urges us to scrutinize our own habits of eating, entertainment, and pet-keeping with Sokka-style empathy.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 17 "Questioning Our Attitudes, Sokka‐style" — The chapter sets Kant's view that animals are mere things owed only indirect duties against Korsgaard's pathocentrism, on which animals matter for their own sakes because they can mind how they are treated. Sokka's arc from shouting 'Dinner!' at Momo to bonding with the saber-tooth moose lion cub Foo Foo Cuddlypoops, and his aborted vow of vegetarianism in 'Bitter Work,' models empathy-driven reassessment of meat, while his sparing Momo for Aang's sake is exactly Kant's indirect duty. Aang's harm-free fun, otter penguin sledding and riding hog monkeys 'because that's what makes it fun,' shows that even non-cruel use of animals demands justification, with the unagi firefighting as a case that might pass the test.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Van Pelt argues the LEGO Farm theme depicts an agricultural utopia — sparkling tractors, no concentrated animal feeding operations, no manure lagoons, and animals raised only for eggs, wool, and milk, never meat — in line with the vegetarian, small-is-beautiful ideals of activists Michael Pollan and Bill McKibben. The troubling side is the farm-to-fork gap: no butcher shop, no slaughter, pigs whose purpose goes conveniently unexplained — a silence that, he argues, reflects consumers' own refusal to know where food comes from rather than a LEGO conspiracy, though food's everyday urgency means toy farms should be held to a different standard than Hot Wheels. The redeeming idealism is not in the sets but in the Master-Builder freedom to build better realities, like solar-powered crop drones and trains delivering unsellable food to the city.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 29 "18. The Journey May Also Save Us" — McCrossin reads the Madagascar and Bhutan episodes of Parts Unknown as a climate-crisis 'diptych' co-authored with filmmaker Darren Aronofsky, set against the thirtieth anniversary of the 1988 climate testimony to the US Senate and the IPCC's warnings.
